title: Erdős problem #3
open: If a set $A$ of natural numbers has divergent reciprocal sum, must $A$ contain arithmetic progressions of every length? Formally, does $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}=\infty$ imply that $A$ contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions?
status: The problem is essentially equivalent to obtaining good bounds on $r_k(N)$, the size of the largest subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no non-trivial $k$-term arithmetic progression; a bound like $r_k(N) \ll_k \frac{N}{(\log N)(\log\log N)^2}$ would suffice. Even the case $k=3$ is non-trivial, but was proved by Bloom and Sisask [BlSi20], and much better bounds for $r_3(N)$ were subsequently proved by Kelley and Meka [KeMe23]. Green and Tao [GrTa17] proved $r_4(N)\ll N/(\log N)^{c}$ for some small constant $c>0$. Gowers [Go01] proved $r_k(N) \ll \frac{N}{(\log\log N)^{c_k}}$ where $c_k>0$ depends on $k$. The current best bounds for general $k$ are due to Leng, Sah, and Sawhney [LSS24], who show $r_k(N) \ll \frac{N}{\exp((\log\log N)^{c_k})}$ for some constant $c_k>0$ depending on $k$. Erdős [Er83c] thought this conjecture was the 'only way to approach' the conjecture that there are arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions of prime numbers, now a theorem of Green and Tao [GrTa08] (see [219]). In [Er81] Erdős makes the stronger conjecture that $r_k(N) \ll_C \frac{N}{(\log N)^C}$ for every $C>0$ (now known for $k=3$ due to Kelley and Meka [KeMe23]). Key works: erdosproblems.com/3; Erdős references: [Er74b] [Er75b] [Er77c] [Er80,p.92] [Er80c] [Er81] [Er82e] [Er83].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ with $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}=\infty$ contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions; equivalently, a bound such as $r_k(N) \ll_k \frac{N}{(\log N)(\log\log N)^2}$ would suffice. The conjecture carries a $5000 prize (Erdős).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it is a natural density analogue of the primes-in-AP phenomenon and sits at the heart of additive combinatorics.
aliases: Erdős #3; number theory / additive combinatorics / arithmetic progressions

title: Erdős problem #5
open: For an arbitrary constant $C \geq 0$, must there exist an infinite sequence of indices $n_i$ along which the normalized prime gap satisfies $\lim_{i\to\infty} \frac{p_{n_i+1}-p_{n_i}}{\log n_i} = C$? Equivalently, is the set $S$ of limit points of $(p_{n+1}-p_n)/\log n$ the entire extended half-line $[0,\infty]$?
status: Let $S$ be the set of limit points of $(p_{n+1}-p_n)/\log n$; the problem asks whether $S=[0,\infty]$. It remains unproven, though much is known. Westzynthius [We31] showed $\infty\in S$ via large prime gaps, and Goldston, Pintz, and Yildirim [GPY09] showed $0\in S$ via small prime gaps. Erdős [Er55] and Ricci [Ri56] independently proved $S$ has positive Lebesgue measure; Hildebrand and Maier [HiMa88] showed $S$ contains arbitrarily large finite numbers. Pintz [Pi16] proved $[0,c]\subset S$ for some small constant $c>0$; Banks, Freiberg, and Maynard [BFM16] showed at least $12.5\%$ of $[0,\infty)$ lies in $S$; and Merikoski [Me20] improved this to at least $1/3$ of $[0,\infty)$ and showed $S$ has bounded gaps. In [Er65b], [Er85c], and [Er97c], Erdős asks whether $S$ is everywhere dense; Weisenberg notes that since $S$ is closed, this is equivalent to asking whether $S=[0,\infty]$. See also [234].
solved_when: A proof that $S = [0,\infty]$; that is, for every $C \geq 0$ (and including $C=\infty$) there are infinitely many $n$ for which the normalized gap $(p_{n+1}-p_n)/\log n$ approaches $C$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (problem #5), tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it would give a complete picture of how prime gaps behave relative to their expected scale $\log n$.

title: Erdős problem #7
open: Does there exist a covering system of the integers in which all moduli are distinct and odd? Equivalently, can the integers be covered by congruence classes whose distinct moduli are all odd?
status: Asked by Erdős and Selfridge (sometimes also with Schinzel), who also asked whether a covering system can have all moduli odd and squarefree — this stronger question was answered negatively by Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba [BBMST22]. Hough and Nielsen [HoNi19] proved that at least one modulus must be divisible by either $2$ or $3$; Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba [BBMST22] gave a simpler proof and also showed that if an odd covering system exists, the least common multiple of its moduli must be divisible by $9$ or $15$. Selfridge (as reported in [Sc67]) showed such a covering system would exist if there were a covering system with moduli $n_1,\ldots,n_k$ such that no $n_i$ divides any other $n_j$, but the latter has been shown not to exist (see [586]). Filaseta, Ford, and Konyagin [FFK00] report Erdős's and Selfridge's opposing prize offers: Erdős, convinced an odd covering exists, offered \$25 for a proof of nonexistence; Selfridge, convinced no odd covering exists, offered \$300 for the first explicit example, with no award promised for a non-constructive proof of existence.
solved_when: An explicit (or existence) construction of a distinct covering system with all moduli odd is exhibited, or a proof that no such covering system exists. Historical stakes: Erdős offered \$25 for a proof of nonexistence; Selfridge offered \$300 for the first explicit example (with no award promised for a non-constructive proof of existence, per [FFK00]).

title: Erdős problem #10
open: Is there some fixed $k$ such that every sufficiently large integer is the sum of a prime and at most $k$ powers of 2? In other words, do primes together with a bounded number of powers of 2 form an additive basis for the large integers?
status: Erdős described this as 'probably unattackable'. In [ErGr80] Erdős and Graham suggest that no such $k$ exists, although in [Er80] Erdős conjectured with 'trepidation' that such a $k$ does exist. Gallagher [Ga75] has shown that for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists $k(\epsilon)$ such that the set of integers which are the sum of a prime and at most $k(\epsilon)$ many powers of 2 has lower density at least $1-\epsilon$. Granville and Soundararajan [GrSo98] have conjectured that at most $3$ powers of 2 suffice for all odd integers, and hence at most $4$ powers of 2 suffice for all even integers. The restriction to odd integers is important here: Bogdan Grechuk has observed that $1117175146$ is not the sum of a prime and at most $3$ powers of 2, and pointed out that parity considerations, coupled with the fact that there are many integers not the sum of a prime and $2$ powers of 2 (see [9]), suggest that there exist infinitely many even integers which are not the sum of a prime and at most $3$ powers of 2. See also [9], [11], and [16].
solved_when: A specific integer $k$ is shown to exist such that every sufficiently large integer is the sum of a prime and at most $k$ powers of 2 (or it is proved that no such $k$ exists).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a long-standing question about whether primes plus boundedly many powers of 2 form an additive basis.
aliases: Erdős #10; number theory / additive basis / primes

title: Erdős problem #11
open: Is every sufficiently large odd integer $n$ expressible as the sum of a squarefree number and a power of $2$?
status: Odlyzko has verified the claim up to $10^7$, and Hercher [He24b] has verified it for all odd integers up to $2^{50}\approx 1.12\times 10^{15}$. Granville and Soundararajan [GrSo98] proved a close connection to Wieferich primes (those $p$ with $2^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod{p^2}$): if every odd integer is the sum of a squarefree number and a power of $2$, then a positive proportion of primes are non-Wieferich. Erdős often posed the problem under the weaker assumption that $n$ is not divisible by $4$; he thought the two-powers-of-2 variant might be easy, and could prove the statement (with a single power of two) for almost all $n$. The problem appears as A19 in Guy's collection [Gu04]; see also [9], [10], and [16].
solved_when: A proof that all sufficiently large odd integers $n$ (or, under Erdős's weaker formulation, all sufficiently large $n$ not divisible by $4$) are the sum of a squarefree number and a power of $2$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and Granville and Soundararajan showed it is deeply tied to the distribution of Wieferich primes — for instance, a positive answer would imply a positive proportion of primes are non-Wieferich.

title: Erdős problem #12
open: For an infinite set $A$ of positive integers containing no three distinct elements $a,b,c$ with $a \mid (b+c)$ and $b,c>a$, how dense can $A$ be, and how sparse must it be? Specifically: does such an $A$ exist with $\liminf |A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|/N^{1/2}>0$; is there an absolute constant $c>0$ forcing $|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|<N^{1-c}$ for infinitely many $N$; and must $\sum_{n\in A} 1/n$ converge?
status: Erdős and Sárközy [ErSa70] proved $A$ must have density $0$ and that this is essentially best possible: for any $f(x)\to\infty$ there is such an $A$ with $|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|>N/f(N)$ for infinitely many $N$ (their example uses integers in $(y_i,\frac{3}{2}y_i)$ congruent to $1$ modulo $(2y_{i-1})!$ for a fast-growing sequence $y_i$). The squares of primes $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$ give such an $A$ with $\liminf |A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|N^{-1/2}\log N>0$, and Elsholtz and Planitzer [ElPl17] constructed one with $|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|\gg N^{1/2}/((\log N)^{1/2}(\log\log N)^2(\log\log\log N)^2)$. For pairwise coprime $A$, Schoen [Sc01] proved $|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|\ll N^{2/3}$ for infinitely many $N$, improved by Baier [Ba04] to $\ll N^{2/3}/\log N$. DeepMind has provided a construction showing the answer to the second question is no, and hence the answer to the first is yes.
solved_when: All three questions are settled: whether some such $A$ has $\liminf |A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|/N^{1/2}>0$; whether some absolute $c>0$ exists such that $|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|<N^{1-c}$ for infinitely many $N$; and whether $\sum_{n\in A} 1/n<\infty$ for every such $A$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/12; it probes the exact density boundary between the known zero-density obstruction and the near-$N^{1/2}$ constructions.

title: Erdős problem #14
open: Must every set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ leave many integers without a unique representation as a sum of two elements of $A$? Formally, if $B$ is the set of integers representable in exactly one way as such a sum, is it true that for all $\epsilon>0$ and large $N$, $|\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus B| \gg_\epsilon N^{1/2-\epsilon}$ — or could this complement even be $o(N^{1/2})$?
status: The problem was apparently originally considered by Erdős and Nathanson, though Erdős later attributed it to Erdős, Sárközy, and Szemerédi without giving a reference; there he claims a construction of an $A$ with $|\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus B| \ll_\epsilon N^{1/2+\epsilon}$ for all $\epsilon>0$ and large $N$, while for all $\epsilon>0$ there are infinitely many $N$ with $|\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus B| \gg_\epsilon N^{1/3-\epsilon}$. Erdős and Freud studied the finite analogue in [ErFr91], proving there exists $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that the number of integers not representable in exactly one way as a sum of two elements of $A$ is $<2^{3/2}N^{1/2}$, and suggested the constant $2^{3/2}$ may be best possible.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that for every $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ and every $\epsilon>0$, the count of integers in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ not uniquely representable is $\gg_\epsilon N^{1/2-\epsilon}$ for all large $N$; alternatively, a construction showing it can be $o(N^{1/2})$. A matching answer to the finite analogue with the conjecturally best constant $2^{3/2}$ would also resolve the corresponding question.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; resolving it would settle a basic extremal question about unique representation in sumsets, a natural companion to Sidon-type problems in additive combinatorics, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.
aliases: Erdős #14; number theory / sidon sets / additive combinatorics

title: Erdős problem #15
open: Does the alternating series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n \frac{n}{p_n}$ converge, where $p_n$ denotes the $n$-th prime?
status: Erdős suggested that a computer could be used to explore this and saw no other method of attack. Tao [Ta23] has proved that the series does converge assuming a strong form of the Hardy-Littlewood prime tuples conjecture. In [Er98] Erdős further conjectures that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n \frac{1}{n(p_{n+1}-p_n)}$ converges and $\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n \frac{1}{p_{n+1}-p_n}$ diverges. Weisenberg notes that the existence of infinitely many bounded gaps between primes (as proved by Zhang [Zh14]) implies the latter series does not converge. Weisenberg also has an argument showing that, assuming the Hardy-Littlewood prime $k$-tuples conjecture, that series is unbounded in at least one direction (positive or negative). Erdős further conjectured that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n \frac{1}{n(p_{n+1}-p_n)(\log\log n)^c}$ converges for every $c>0$, and reports that he and Nathanson can prove this series converges absolutely for $c>2$ (and can show, conditional on 'hopeless' conjectures about the primes, that this sum does not converge absolutely for $c=2$). solved_when: A proof or disproof of the convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n \frac{n}{p_n}$ is given.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and its resolution would illuminate how cancellation in alternating prime sums interacts with the irregularity of the primes.

title: Erdős problem #17
open: Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that every even number $n \le p-3$ can be written as a difference of two primes $q_1 - q_2$ with $q_1, q_2 \le p$? Formally, are there infinitely many such primes, given that the first prime failing the property is $97$?
status: The first prime without the property is $97$; the primes with it (called cluster primes) form OEIS sequence A038133. Blecksmith, Erdős, and Selfridge [BES99] proved their count is $\ll_A x/(\log x)^A$ for every $A>0$, and Elsholtz [El03] improved this to $\ll x\exp(-c(\log\log x)^2)$ for every $c<1/8$. The problem is discussed as C1 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A proof that infinitely many primes $p$ have the property that every even $n \le p-3$ is a difference of two primes $q_1 - q_2 \le p$; equivalently, a proof that the counting function of these primes tends to infinity.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it probes how densely the differences of primes below $p$ must cover all even numbers up to $p-3$.

title: Erdős problem #18
open: Are there infinitely many practical numbers $m$ — numbers for which every integer $1\leq n<m$ is a sum of distinct divisors of $m$ — for which some uniformly bounded number $h(m)$ of divisors always suffices, with $h(m)<(\log\log m)^{O(1)}$? In particular, is $h(n!)<n^{o(1)}$, or perhaps even $h(n!)<(\log n)^{O(1)}$?
status: Almost all numbers are not practical. Erdős originally showed $h(n!)<n$, and Vose [Vo85] proved the existence of infinitely many practical $m$ with $h(m)\ll(\log m)^{1/2}$. The practical numbers form OEIS sequence A005153. A reward of \$250 is offered in [Er81h] for a proof or disproof of whether $h(n)<(\log\log n)^{O(1)}$ for infinitely many practical $n$. See also [304] and [825].
solved_when: A proof or disproof is given of whether $h(n)<(\log\log n)^{O(1)}$ for infinitely many practical $n$; more sharply, a bound $h(n!)<n^{o(1)}$ or $h(n!)<(\log n)^{O(1)}$ settles the factorial cases.
why: A solution would resolve one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying his $250 reward and full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #23
open: Can every triangle-free graph on $5n$ vertices be made bipartite by deleting at most $n^2$ edges? Equivalently, is $n^2$ the maximum number of edges one must remove from such a graph to destroy all odd cycles?
status: The blow-up of $C_5$ shows that the bound $n^2$ would be best possible. The best known bound is due to Balogh, Clemen, and Lidicky [BCL21], who proved that deleting at most $1.064n^2$ edges suffices. In [Er92b] Erdős asks, more generally, whether a graph on $(2k+1)n$ vertices in which every odd cycle has size $\geq 2k+1$ can be made bipartite by deleting at most $n^2$ edges. The problem is #58 in Extremal Graph Theory in the graphs problem collection. Key works: erdosproblems.com/23; Erdős references: [Er71] [Er90] [Er93,p.343] [Er97b] [Er97f] [Er92b].
solved_when: A proof that every triangle-free graph on $5n$ vertices can be made bipartite by deleting at most $n^2$ edges, matching the $C_5$ blow-up lower bound.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would settle a natural extremal question about how far triangle-free graphs are from bipartite.

title: Erdős problem #25
open: Given any increasing sequence of moduli $1\leq n_1<n_2<\cdots$, each with a chosen residue class $a_i \pmod{n_i}$, consider the set $A$ of integers that "escape" every sieve layer — integers $n$ such that for each $i$, either $n<n_i$ or $n\not\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$. Must the logarithmic density of $A$ exist?
status: This number-theoretic problem is a special case of [486]; it is catalogued at erdosproblems.com/25, with references including [Er95].
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given that for every choice of increasing moduli $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ and residue classes $a_i \pmod{n_i}$, the set $A = \{n : n<n_i \text{ or } n\not\equiv a_i \pmod{n_i} \text{ for all } i\}$ has a well-defined logarithmic density.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carried with full history and context at erdosproblems.com, so settling it closes a tracked item from his problem collection.

title: Erdős problem #28
open: If a set of natural numbers is an asymptotic additive basis — its pairwise sums cover all but finitely many integers — must the number of representations of some integers grow without bound? Formally, must $\limsup\, 1_A \ast 1_A(n) = \infty$?
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Turán. They also suggest the stronger conjecture that $\limsup\, 1_A \ast 1_A(n)/\log n > 0$. Another stronger conjecture would be that the hypothesis $|A \cap [1,N]| \gg N^{1/2}$ for all large $N$ suffices. See also [40], and [1145] for a stronger generalisation. This is discussed in problem C9 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $A+A$ containing all but finitely many integers satisfies $\limsup\, 1_A \ast 1_A(n) = \infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with a $500 Erdős prize), asking whether an asymptotic basis must necessarily have representation counts that are unbounded.

title: Erdős problem #30
open: Let $h(N)$ be the maximum size of a Sidon set in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Is it true that for every $\epsilon>0$ we have $h(N) = N^{1/2}+O_\epsilon(N^\epsilon)$ — that is, is the true size of the largest Sidon set within a sub-polynomial error of $N^{1/2}$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Turán; Erdős speculated it may even be true that $h(N)=N^{1/2}+O(1)$, though he remarked this is perhaps too optimistic. Erdős and Turán [ErTu41] proved an upper bound of $N^{1/2}+O(N^{1/4})$, with an alternative proof by Lindström [Li69]; both proofs in fact give $h(N) \leq N^{1/2}+N^{1/4}+1$. Balogh, Füredi, and Roy [BFR21] improved the error term to $0.998N^{1/4}$, further optimised by O'Bryant [OB22]. The current record is $h(N)\leq N^{1/2}+0.98183N^{1/4}+O(1)$, due to Carter, Hunter, and O'Bryant [CHO25]. Singer [Si38] was the first to show $h(N)\geq (1-o(1))N^{1/2}$ for all $N$. For a detailed survey see [OB04]; see also [241] and [840]. This problem is Problem 31 on Green's open problems list and is discussed as problem C9 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $h(N) = N^{1/2}+O_\epsilon(N^\epsilon)$ for every $\epsilon>0$.
why: A positive answer would pin down the maximal size of Sidon sets essentially exactly, resolving one of Erdős's personally posed problems (carrying his $1000 prize) and settling a basic question in additive combinatorics about how dense a set with all pairwise sums distinct can be.
aliases: Erdős #30; number theory / sidon sets / additive combinatorics

title: Erdős problem #32
open: Does there exist a set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$, an additive complement to the primes, of size $\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert = o((\log N)^2)$ such that every large integer can be written as $p+a$ for some prime $p$ and $a\in A$? More sharply: can $O(\log N)$ be achieved, and must any such $A$ satisfy $\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{\log N} > 1$?
status: Erdős [Er54] proved such an $A$ exists with $\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\ll (\log N)^2$, improving Lorentz [Lo54]'s $\ll (\log N)^3$. Wolke [Wo96] achieved $\ll (\log N)^{1+o(1)}$ for almost all integers; Kolountzakis [Ko96] improved this to $\ll (\log N)(\log\log N)$, and Ruzsa [Ru98c] to $\ll \omega(N)\log N$ for any $\omega\to\infty$. The third question is answered affirmatively: Ruzsa [Ru98c] showed $\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{\log N}\geq e^\gamma\approx 1.781$. This is problem E1 in Guy's collection [Gu04], where Erdős's \$50 prize for the $O(\log N)$ question is noted.
solved_when: A set $A$ is constructed such that every large integer is $p+a$ with $p$ prime and $a\in A$, and $\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \ll \log N$; alternatively, the third question is settled by determining the exact value of $\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{\log N}$.

title: Erdős problem #33
open: Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be such that every large integer can be written as $n^2+a$ for some $a\in A$ and $n\geq 0$. What is the smallest possible value of $\limsup \frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{N^{1/2}}$, and is $\liminf \frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{N^{1/2}}>1$?
status: Such a set $A$ is called an additive complement of the set of squares. Erdős observed that there exist $A$ for which the $\limsup$ is finite and $>1$. Moser [Mo65] proved that, for any such $A$, $\liminf \frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{N^{1/2}}>1.06$. The best-known lower bound is $\liminf \frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{N^{1/2}}\geq\frac{4}{\pi}\approx 1.273$, proved by Cilleruelo [Ci93], Habsieger [Ha95], and Balasubramanian and Ramana [BaRa01]. The problem of minimising the $\limsup$ appears to have been much less studied: van Doorn has a construction of such an $A$ in which, for all $N$, $\frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{N^{1/2}}<2\phi^{5/2}\approx 6.66$, where $\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ is the golden ratio.
solved_when: The exact minimal value of $\limsup \frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{N^{1/2}}$ over all such $A$ is determined, and the question of whether $\liminf \frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{N^{1/2}}>1$ is settled (with the sharp constant identified).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; determining the optimal density of an additive complement to the squares resolves a classical question in additive number theory.

title: Erdős problem #39
open: Does there exist an infinite Sidon set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ whose counting function satisfies $\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg_\epsilon N^{1/2-\epsilon}$ for every $\epsilon>0$? In other words, can an infinite Sidon set attain essentially the maximal conceivable density $N^{1/2}$ up to an $N^\epsilon$ loss?
status: The trivial greedy construction achieves $\gg N^{1/3}$. The first improvement was by Ajtai, Komlós, and Szemerédi [AKS81b], who found an infinite Sidon set with growth rate $\gg (N\log N)^{1/3}$. The current best bound, $\gg N^{\sqrt{2}-1+o(1)}$, is due to Ruzsa [Ru98]. Erdős [Er73] offered \$25 for any construction achieving $N^c$ for some $c>1/3$, and later ([Er77c] and [Er80]) offered \$100 for a construction achieving $\omega(N)N^{1/3}$ for some $\omega(N)\to\infty$. On the negative side, Erdős proved that for every infinite Sidon set $A$, $\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}=0$. Erdős and Rényi constructed, for any $\epsilon>0$, a set $A$ with $\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg_\epsilon N^{1/2-\epsilon}$ for all large $N$ and $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\ll_\epsilon 1$ for all $n$; this is discussed in problem C9 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: An explicit (or existence-proof) construction of an infinite Sidon set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ is given with $\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg_\epsilon N^{1/2-\epsilon}$ for all $\epsilon>0$. Progress prizes were attached to weaker quantitative targets: \$25 for any construction achieving $N^c$ for some $c>1/3$, and \$100 for one achieving $\omega(N)N^{1/3}$ for some $\omega(N)\to\infty$; the record lists a prize of \$500 (Erdős).
why: It asks whether the trivial counting obstruction of $\sqrt{N}$ for Sidon sets is the only obstruction to density for infinite Sidon sets; a positive answer would essentially close the gap between what is constructible and what is combinatorially possible.
aliases: Erdős #39; number theory / sidon sets / additive combinatorics

title: Erdős problem #40
open: For which functions $g(N)\to\infty$ does any set of positive integers with density at least $\gg N^{1/2}/g(N)$ in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ necessarily have unbounded representation function, i.e. $\limsup\, 1_A \ast 1_A(n) = \infty$? Formally: for what $g$ does $\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg N^{1/2}/g(N)$ imply that $\limsup$ of the convolution is infinite?
status: The problem is a stronger form of the Erdős–Turán conjecture [28], since establishing it for any function $g(N)\to\infty$ would imply a positive solution to [28]. It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carries a $500 prize offered by Erdős, and is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/40 (Erdős references [Er95], [Er97c]).
solved_when: A function $g(N)\to\infty$ is identified for which every set $A$ satisfying $\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg N^{1/2}/g(N)$ has $\limsup\, 1_A\ast 1_A(n)=\infty$; equivalently, a characterization of all such $g$ is given.
why: This is a strengthening of the Erdős–Turán conjecture [28]: a positive answer for any single $g(N)\to\infty$ would resolve that conjecture, one of the central open problems on additive bases.

title: Erdős problem #41
open: Can an infinite set of natural numbers whose triple sums are all distinct (up to trivial coincidences) be so dense that its counting function stays above a constant times $N^{1/3}$ infinitely often? Formally, must such a set $A$ satisfy $\liminf |A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|/N^{1/3}=0$?
status: Erdős proved the analogous statement for pairwise sums: if $a+b$ are all distinct aside from trivial coincidences, then $\liminf |A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|/N^{1/2}=0$. The general problem, discussed as C11 in Guy's collection [Gu04], asks whether for all $h\geq 2$, $\liminf |A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|/N^{1/h}=0$ whenever sums of $h$ terms of $A$ are distinct; Guy records Erdős's \$500 prize for it. It was proved for $h=4$ by Nash [Na89] and for all even $h$ by Chen [Ch96b]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/41; Erdős references: [Er77c] [Er80,p.99] [Er81] [Er85c] [Er91] [Er95] [Er97c] [Va99,1.23].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every infinite $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with all triple sums $a+b+c$ distinct aside from trivial coincidences, $\liminf |A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|/N^{1/3}=0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a $500 prize he offered for the general version, and is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it is a basic density question for Sidon-type sets in additive combinatorics.
aliases: Erdős #41; number theory / sidon sets / additive combinatorics

title: Erdős problem #44
open: Can every Sidon set inside $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be extended, by adding elements above $N$, into a Sidon set that is essentially as large as possible? Formally: given $N\geq 1$, a Sidon set $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$, and any $\epsilon>0$, do there exist $M$ and $B\subset \{N+1,\ldots,M\}$ (possibly depending on $N,A,\epsilon$) such that $A\cup B\subset \{1,\ldots,M\}$ is a Sidon set of size at least $(1-\epsilon)M^{1/2}$?
status: See also [329] and [707]; indeed a positive solution to [707] implies a positive solution to this problem, which in turn implies a positive solution to [329]. The problem is discussed as problem C9 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every $N\geq 1$, every Sidon set $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$, and every $\epsilon>0$, there are $M$ and $B\subset \{N+1,\ldots,M\}$ such that $A\cup B$ is a Sidon set of size at least $(1-\epsilon)M^{1/2}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it sits in a chain of implications among problems on Sidon sets.
aliases: Erdős #44; number theory / sidon sets / additive combinatorics

title: Erdős problem #50
open: Schoenberg proved that for every $c\in [0,1]$ the density of $\{n\in \mathbb{N} : \phi(n)<cn\}$ exists; call it $f(c)$. Does there exist any point $x$ at which $f'(x)$ exists and is positive?
status: Erdős [Er95] could prove that the distribution function is purely singular.
solved_when: It is shown that no $x$ exists with $f'(x)$ existing and positive (or, if the conjecture fails, an explicit such $x$ is produced).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a $250 prize from Erdős himself, and its full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #51
open: Is there an infinite set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$, contained in the image of Euler's totient function $\phi$, such that if $n_a$ is the smallest integer with $\phi(n_a)=a$, then the ratio $n_a/a\to\infty$ as $a\to\infty$ through elements of $A$? In other words, can totient preimages be arbitrarily far, relative to their value, from the smallest integer mapping to them?
status: Carmichael asked whether there is an integer $t$ for which $\phi(n)=t$ has exactly one solution. Erdős proved that if such a $t$ exists, then there must be infinitely many such $t$; see also [694]. The problem is discussed in problems B36 and B39 of Guy's collection [Gu04], and full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/51. Key works: Erdős references [Er95] [Er98] [Gu04].
solved_when: An infinite set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ is exhibited such that every $a\in A$ lies in the image of $\phi$, and for the smallest $n$ with $\phi(n)=a$ the ratio $n_a/a\to\infty$ as $a\to\infty$; or a proof that no such set exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would clarify how the multiplicative structure of $\phi$ spreads its preimages.

title: Erdős problem #52
open: Let $A$ be a finite set of integers. Is it true that for every $\epsilon>0$,\[\max( \lvert A+A\rvert,\lvert AA\rvert)\gg_\epsilon \lvert A\rvert^{2-\epsilon}?\] That is, must every finite integer set $A$ have either a sumset or a product set of size nearly quadratic in $|A|$?
status: Erdős and Szemerédi [ErSz83] proved a lower bound of $|A|^{1+c}$ for some constant $c>0$, as well as an upper bound of $|A|^2 \exp(-c \log|A|/\log\log|A|)$ for some constant $c>0$. The lower bound has been improved a number of times; the current record is $\max(|A+A|, |AA|) \gg |A|^{\frac{1962}{1469}-o(1)}$ due to Cushman [Cu25] (note $1962/1469 = 1.3356\cdots$). A complete history of sum-product bounds can be found at this webpage. Erdős and Szemerédi also posed a similar question for finite sets of real or complex numbers; the best lower bound for reals is Cushman's same bound, though the original conjecture is false for sets of reals. For complex numbers, the best bound is $\max(|A+A|, |AA|) \gg |A|^{\frac{4}{3}+c}$ for some absolute constant $c>0$, due to Basit and Lund [BaLu19]. The question can be asked in any setting where addition and multiplication are defined, once trivial obstructions such as zero are avoided.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given that for every finite set $A$ of integers and every $\epsilon>0$, $\max(|A+A|, |AA|) \gg_\epsilon |A|^{2-\epsilon}$; equivalently, the lower-bound exponent is pushed from the current $1962/1469 - o(1) = 1.3356\cdots$ up to $2-\epsilon$ for every $\epsilon>0$.
why: This is the sum-product problem, one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with a $250 prize), and it drives the central principle that no set of integers can be simultaneously highly additive and highly multiplicative — a cornerstone of additive combinatorics.

title: Erdős problem #60
open: Must every graph on $n$ vertices with more than $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_4)$ edges contain $\gg n^{1/2}$ copies of $C_4$?
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Simonovits, who could not even prove that at least $2$ copies of $C_4$ are guaranteed. The behaviour of $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_4)$ is the subject of [765]. He, Ma, and Yang [HeMaYa21] have proved this conjecture when $n=q^2+q+1$ for some even integer $q$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that such graphs necessarily contain $\gg n^{1/2}$ copies of $C_4$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #61
open: For any graph $H$ is there some $c=c(H)>0$ such that every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices that does not contain $H$ as an induced subgraph contains either a complete graph or independent set on $\geq n^c$ vertices?
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Hajnal [ErHa89], who proved that a complete graph or independent set must exist on $\geq \exp(c_H\sqrt{\log n})$ vertices for some constant $c_H>0$. This was improved by Bucić, Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour [BNSS23] to $\geq \exp(c_H\sqrt{\log n\log\log n})$. The conjecture has been proved for $H$ with $\leq 4$ vertices by Erdős and Hajnal [ErHa89]; for the 'bull' graph on $5$ vertices (a $P_4$ with a new vertex adjacent to the two middle vertices) by Chudnovsky and Safra [ChSa08]; for $C_5$ by Chudnovsky, Scott, Seymour, and Spirkl [CSSS23]; and for $P_5$ by Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour [NSS26]. Alon, Pach, and Solymosi [APS01] proved that the family of $H$ for which the conjecture holds is closed under vertex substitution; together with the three results above this means the conjecture is now known for all $H$ on $5$ vertices. Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour [NSS24] proved that if $H$ is a path then all $H$-free graphs on $n$ vertices contain either a complete graph or independent set on $\geq 2^{(\log n)^{1-o(1)}}$ vertices. A detailed account of this problem, including the proof of some special cases, is given in the erdosproblems.com entry.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that for every fixed graph $H$ there exists a constant $c(H)>0$ such that every $H$-induced-free graph on $n$ vertices contains a clique or independent set on at least $n^{c(H)}$ vertices.
why: This is the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture, one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it would establish that forbidding any single induced subgraph forces much larger homogeneous sets than Ramsey's theorem guarantees.

title: Erdős problem #62
open: If two graphs each have chromatic number $\aleph_1$, must they share a common subgraph of chromatic number $4$ — or even $\aleph_0$?
status: Erdős also asked [Er87] about finding a common subgraph $H$ (with chromatic number either $4$ or $\aleph_0$) in any finite collection of graphs with chromatic number $\aleph_1$. Every graph with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ contains all sufficiently large odd cycles (which have chromatic number $3$), see [594]; this was proved by Erdős, Hajnal, and Shelah [EHS74]. Erdős wrote [Er87] that 'probably' every graph with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ contains as subgraphs all graphs with chromatic number $4$ with sufficiently large girth.
solved_when: It is shown that any two graphs of chromatic number $\aleph_1$ contain a common subgraph with chromatic number $4$ (or, at minimum, $\aleph_0$); the analogous finite-collection version posed in [Er87] likewise counts.
why: A solution would resolve one of Erdős's personally posed problems and clarify how strongly high chromatic number forces common highly chromatic structure across graphs, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #64
open: Does every finite graph with minimum degree at least 3 contain a cycle of length $2^k$ for some $k\geq 2$?
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Gyárfás, who believed the answer must be negative, and in fact for every $r$ there must be a graph of minimum degree at least $r$ without a cycle of length $2^k$ for any $k\geq 2$. This was solved in the affirmative if the minimum degree is larger than some absolute constant by Liu and Montgomery [LiMo20] (therefore disproving the above stronger conjecture of Erdős and Gyárfás). Liu and Montgomery prove a much stronger result: if the average degree of $G$ is sufficiently large then there is some large integer $\ell$ such that for every even integer $m\in [(\log \ell)^8,\ell]$, $G$ contains a cycle of length $m$. An infinite tree with minimum degree $3$ shows that the answer is trivially false for infinite graphs. The conjecture has been confirmed for various families of graphs; see the comment by Alfaiz for a list. This problem is #69 in Extremal Graph Theory in the graphs problem collection. Key works: erdosproblems.com/64; Erdős references: [Er93,p.343] [Er94b] [Er95,p.174] [Er96] [Er97b] [Er97c].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the statement for finite graphs with minimum degree at least 3; equivalently, a finite graph of minimum degree at least 3 with no cycle whose length is a power of two with exponent $k\geq 2$, or a proof that no such graph exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a $1000 prize, and is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles the last case of the Erdős–Gyárfás power-of-two cycle question at the minimum threshold of minimum degree 3.

title: Erdős problem #65
open: Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices and $kn$ edges, and let $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ be the lengths of its cycles. Is the reciprocal sum $\sum 1/a_i$ minimized when $G$ is a complete bipartite graph?
status: A problem of Erdős and Hajnal. Gyárfás, Komlós, and Szemerédi [GKS84] proved that $\sum 1/a_i \gg \log k$, leaving only the second question. Liu and Montgomery [LiMo20] proved the asymptotically sharp lower bound $\geq (\tfrac{1}{2}-o(1))\log k$. Montgomery's survey of this problem mentions forthcoming work of himself, Milojević, Pokrovskiy, and Sudakov showing that for sufficiently large $k$, $\sum 1/a_i$ is maximized when $G$ is a complete bipartite graph. This problem is #65 in Extremal Graph Theory in the graphs problem collection; see also [57].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the extremal claim: among all graphs on $n$ vertices with $kn$ edges, the quantity $\sum 1/a_i$ is minimized by the complete bipartite graph.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with Hajnal), tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle the remaining half of a classical extremal question about how cycle lengths distribute in dense graphs.

title: Erdős problem #66
open: Is there a subset $A$ of the natural numbers such that the convolution $1_A \ast 1_A(n)$, normalized by $\log n$, tends to a limit that exists and is nonzero?
status: A suitably constructed random set has this property if an exceptional set of density zero may be ignored; the challenge is obtaining it with no exceptional set. Erdős believed the answer should be no, and in [Er80,p.98] he explicitly asked whether such a set exists with limit $1$, not believing such a sequence existed. Erdős and Sárközy proved that $\lvert 1_A\ast 1_A(n)-\log n\rvert/\sqrt{\log n}\to 0$ is impossible. Erdős suggested it may even be true that the $\liminf$ and $\limsup$ of $1_A\ast 1_A(n)/\log n$ are always separated by some absolute constant. Horváth [Ho07] proved that $\lvert 1_A\ast 1_A(n)-\log n\rvert\leq(1-\epsilon)\sqrt{\log n}$ cannot hold for all large $n$.
solved_when: A set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is exhibited for which $\lim_{n\to\infty} 1_A\ast 1_A(n)/\log n$ exists and is nonzero (in particular, Erdős asked in [Er80,p.98] for such a set where the limit is $1$), or a proof is given that no such set exists.

title: Erdős problem #68
open: Is the sum $\sum_{n\geq 2}\frac{1}{n!-1}$ irrational? More precisely, must this fast-converging series of unit fractions over shifted factorials fail to be a ratio of integers?
status: The decimal expansion is A331373 in the OEIS. Weisenberg has observed that this sum can also be written as $\sum_{k\geq 1}\sum_{n\geq 2}\frac{1}{(n!)^k}$. Erdős [Er88c] notes that $\sum \frac{1}{n!+t}$ should be transcendental for every integer $t$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\sum_{n\geq 2}\frac{1}{n!-1}$ is irrational; the natural quantitative targets are irrationality of $\sum \frac{1}{n!+t}$ for fixed integer $t$, and transcendence in line with Erdős's expectation.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/68; a resolution would settle a long-standing question about the arithmetic nature of a simply defined factorial series.

title: Erdős problem #70
open: Let $\mathfrak{c}$ be the ordinal of the real numbers, $\beta$ be any countable ordinal, and $2\leq n<\omega$. Is it true that $\mathfrak{c}\to (\beta, n)_2^3$?
status: Erdős and Rado proved that $\mathfrak{c}\to (\omega+n,4)_2^3$ for any $2\leq n<\omega$. Key references: erdosproblems.com/70; Erdős references: [Er87] [Va99,7.83].
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that $\mathfrak{c}\to (\beta, n)_2^3$ holds for every countable ordinal $\beta$ and every $2\leq n<\omega$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.
aliases: Erdős #70; graph theory / ramsey theory / set theory

title: Erdős problem #75
open: Does there exist a graph on $\aleph_1$ vertices with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ in which every large subgraph on $n$ vertices contains an independent set of size greater than $n^{1-\epsilon}$ for every $\epsilon>0$? Can one strengthen this to an independent set of size $\gg n$?
status: Conjectured by Erdős, Hajnal, and Szemerédi [EHS82]. In [Er95] Erdős asks this without the condition that the graph also have $\aleph_1$ vertices, but this is an oversight, since already in [EHS82] they provide such a construction. In [Er95d] Erdős offers \$1000 for a complete solution to all problems of this type (for example including also [74]), and a 'generous reward for any significant partial results'. See also [750].
solved_when: A graph of chromatic number $\aleph_1$ on $\aleph_1$ vertices is constructed such that for all $\epsilon>0$, every sufficiently large $n$-vertex subgraph contains an independent set of size $>n^{1-\epsilon}$; alternatively, the stronger variant is settled by such a graph whose $n$-vertex subgraphs contain independent sets of size $\gg n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, offered with a \$1000 reward for a complete solution to all problems of this type, and tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #77
open: Does the exponential growth rate of the diagonal Ramsey numbers settle down? Formally, determine the value of $\lim_{k\to\infty} R(k)^{1/k}$, where $R(k)$ is the least $n$ such that every 2-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$.
status: Erdős offered \$100 for just a proof of the existence of this constant, without determining its value, and \$1000 for a proof that the limit does not exist — though he called that 'really a joke as [it] certainly exists' (in [Er88] he raises this prize to \$10000). Erdős proved $\sqrt{2}\leq\liminf_{k\to\infty}R(k)^{1/k}\leq\limsup_{k\to\infty}R(k)^{1/k}\leq 4$. The upper bound was improved to $4-\tfrac{1}{128}$ by Campos, Griffiths, Morris, and Sahasrabudhe [CGMS23], and then to $3.7992\cdots$ by Gupta, Ndiaye, Norin, and Wei [GNNW24]. A shorter and simpler proof of an upper bound of strength $4-c$ for some constant $c>0$, with a generalisation to more than two colours, was given by Balister, Bollobás, Campos, Griffiths, Hurley, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba [BBCGHMST24]. In [Er93] Erdős writes 'I have no idea what the value of $\lim R(k)^{1/k}$ should be, perhaps it is $2$ but we have no real evidence for this.'
solved_when: The limit $\lim_{k\to\infty}R(k)^{1/k}$ is shown to exist and its value is determined. (Erdős offered \$100 for a proof of existence alone, without determining its value.)
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it is #3 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection, and the limit is closely related to lower-bound questions for $R(k)$ (see [1029]).

title: Erdős problem #78
open: Is there an explicit construction of graphs whose largest clique and largest independent set are exponentially small compared to the Ramsey bound? Formally, give a constructive proof that $R(k) > C^k$ for some constant $C>1$, where $R(k)$ is the minimal $n$ such that every $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$.
status: Erdős gave a simple probabilistic proof that $R(k) \gg k2^{k/2}$. In [Er69b] Erdős asks for even a construction whose largest clique or independent set has size $o(n^{1/2})$, which is now known. Cohen [Co15] (see the introduction for further history) constructed a graph on $n$ vertices which does not contain any clique or independent set of size $\geq 2^{(\log\log n)^{C}}$ for some constant $C>0$. Li [Li23b] has recently improved this to $\geq (\log n)^{C}$ for some constant $C>0$. This problem is #4 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: A constructive (explicit) proof exhibits, for infinitely many $k$, graphs witnessing $R(k) > C^k$ for some constant $C>1$; equivalently, an explicit construction of a graph on $n$ vertices with no clique or independent set of size $\geq c\log n$ for some constant $c>0$.
why: It would supply the first explicit Ramsey graphs matching the exponential scale that random graphs achieve, resolving one of Erdős's personally posed problems (carrying a $100 prize) tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #80
open: How large a book must every triangle-covered graph contain? Formally, for $c>0$, estimate $f_c(n)$, the maximal $m$ such that every graph on $n$ vertices with at least $cn^2$ edges — each edge lying in at least one triangle — must contain a book of size $m$ (an edge shared by at least $m$ triangles). In particular, is $f_c(n)>n^{\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$, or at least $f_c(n)\gg \log n$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Rothschild. Alon and Trotter showed that, provided $c<1/4$, $f_c(n)\ll_c n^{1/2}$. Szemerédi observed that his regularity lemma implies $f_c(n)\to \infty$. Edwards (unpublished) and Khadzhiivanov and Nikiforov [KhNi79] independently proved that $f_c(n) \geq n/6$ when $c>1/4$ (see [905]). Fox and Loh [FoLo12] proved $f_c(n) \leq n^{O(1/\log\log n)}$ for all $c<1/4$, disproving the first conjecture of Erdős. The best known lower bounds come from Szemerédi's regularity lemma and remain very poor. See also [600] and the entry in the graphs problem collection. Key works: erdosproblems.com/80; Erdős references: [Er87].
solved_when: A proof that, for some $\epsilon>0$, $f_c(n)>n^{\epsilon}$ (or that $f_c(n)\gg \log n$); the weaker conjecture $f_c(n)>n^{\epsilon}$ is already disproved for $c<1/4$, so the natural target is a lower bound beating the very poor regularity-lemma bounds, e.g. $f_c(n)\gg \log n$, or matching upper bounds.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a long-standing question on the unavoidable book sizes in dense triangle-covered graphs.

title: Erdős problem #81
open: Can the edge set of every chordal graph on $n$ vertices be partitioned into at most $n^2/6+O(n)$ cliques? Equivalently, is $n^2/6+O(n)$ an asymptotically tight upper bound for the minimum number of cliques needed to cover the edges of any chordal graph?
status: The problem was asked by Erdős, Ordman, and Zalcstein [EOZ93], who proved an upper bound of $(1/4-\epsilon)n^2$ cliques for some very small $\epsilon>0$. The example of all edges between a complete graph on $n/3$ vertices and an empty graph on $2n/3$ vertices shows that $n^2/6+O(n)$ cliques are sometimes necessary. Every split graph is chordal, and Chen, Erdős, and Ordman [CEO94] showed that any split graph can be partitioned into $\frac{3}{16}n^2+O(n)$ cliques. See also [1017].
solved_when: A proof that every chordal graph on $n$ vertices admits an edge partition into $n^2/6+O(n)$ cliques, matching the known lower-bound construction.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle the asymptotically optimal clique-partition size for chordal graphs.

title: Erdős problem #84
open: How many different sets of cycle lengths can a graph on $n$ vertices realize? If $f(n)$ counts the possible cycle sets $A \subseteq \{3,\ldots,n\}$, is it true that $f(n) = o(2^n)$ and that $f(n)/2^{n/2} \to \infty$?
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Faudree, who showed $2^{n/2} < f(n) \leq 2^{n-2}$. The $f(n) = o(2^n)$ problem was solved by Verstraëte [Ve04], who proved $f(n) \ll 2^{n - n^{1/10}}$; this was improved by Nenadov [Ne25] to $f(n) \ll 2^{n - n^{1/2 - o(1)}}$. One can also ask about the existence and value of $\lim f(n)^{1/n}$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/84; Erdős references: [Er94b] [Er95] [Er96] [Er97d] [Ve04] [Ne25].
solved_when: It is proved that $f(n) = o(2^n)$ and that $f(n)/2^{n/2} \to \infty$. (One may additionally ask whether $\lim f(n)^{1/n}$ exists and determine its value.)
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with its full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it pins down the asymptotic counting of realizable cycle-length sets in graphs.

title: Erdős problem #85
open: Let $f(n)$ be the smallest integer such that every graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree at least $f(n)$ contains a $C_4$. Is $f$ eventually monotone — that is, does $f(n+1)\geq f(n)$ hold for all sufficiently large $n$?
status: The function $f(n)$ is a reformulation of the Ramsey number $R(C_4,K_{1,n})$: $R(C_4,K_{1,n})=\min\{ m : f(m)\leq m-n\}$ and $f(n)=\min\{ m : m\geq R(C_4, K_{1,n-m})\}$. The behaviour of this Ramsey number more generally is studied in [552]. A weaker version of the conjecture asks for some constant $c$ such that $f(m)>f(n)-c$ for all $m>n$; the question can also be asked for other graphs than $C_4$. The bounds in [552] imply in particular that $f(n)<\sqrt{n}+1$ and $f(n)=(1+o(1))\sqrt{n}$. It is easy to check that $f(4)=2$.
solved_when: It is proved that there exists $n_0$ such that $f(n+1)\geq f(n)$ for all $n\geq n_0$ (the record states no quantitative threshold on $n_0$).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/85; resolving it would settle a basic regularity question about extremal degree thresholds for $C_4$-freeness.

title: Erdős problem #86
open: Does every subgraph of the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph $Q_n$ (which has $2^n$ vertices and $n2^{n-1}$ edges) with at least $\left(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\right)n2^{n-1}$ edges necessarily contain a $C_4$? Equivalently, if $f(n)$ denotes the maximum number of edges in a $C_4$-free subgraph of $Q_n$, is $f(n)\leq \left(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\right)n2^{n-1}$?
status: Erdős [Er91] showed $f(n) \geq \left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{c}{n}\right)n2^{n-1}$ for some constant $c>0$. Brass, Harborth, and Nienborg [BHN95] improved this to $f(n) \geq \left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{c}{\sqrt{n}}\right)n2^{n-1}$ for some constant $c>0$. On the upper-bound side, Balogh, Hu, Lidicky, and Liu [BHLL14] proved $f(n)\leq 0.6068\, n2^{n-1}$, improved to $\leq 0.60318\, n2^{n-1}$ by Baber [Ba12b]. A similar question can be asked for other even cycles; see also [666] and the entry in the graphs problem collection (erdosproblems.com/86).
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the bound $f(n)\leq \left(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\right)n2^{n-1}$ for the maximum number of edges in a $C_4$-free subgraph of $Q_n$; Erdős offered $100 for settling it, and wrote it is 'perhaps not hopeless' to determine $f(n)$ exactly.

title: Erdős problem #87
open: Is every graph of chromatic number $k$ nearly as Ramsey-hard as the complete graph on $k$ vertices? Formally, for every $\epsilon>0$, is it true that for all sufficiently large $k$, $R(G)>(1-\epsilon)^k R(k)$ for every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)=k$; and more strongly, does there exist $c>0$ such that $R(G)>cR(k)$ for every such $G$ and all large $k$?
status: Erdős originally conjectured $R(G)\geq R(k)$, which is trivial for $k=3$ but fails already for $k=4$: Faudree and McKay [FaMc93] showed $R(W)=17$ for the pentagonal wheel $W$. Since $R(k)\leq 4^k$, the weaker question is trivial for $\epsilon\geq 3/4$. Yuval Wigderson observes that $R(G)\gg 2^{k/2}$ for any $G$ with chromatic number $k$ (via a random colouring), which asymptotically matches the best-known lower bounds for $R(k)$. The problem is #12 and #13 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: Proof (or disproof) that for every $\epsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $k$, every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)=k$ satisfies $R(G)>(1-\epsilon)^k R(k)$; or, for the stronger form, proof (or disproof) that some absolute constant $c>0$ gives $R(G)>cR(k)$ for all large $k$ and all such $G$.
why: A positive answer would show Ramsey hardness is governed essentially by chromatic number rather than completeness, a structural dichotomy central to understanding which graphs force large Ramsey numbers.

title: Erdős problem #89
open: Does every set of $n$ distinct points in the plane determine at least $n/\sqrt{\log n}$ distinct distances (up to a constant factor)? A stronger conjecture of Erdős asserts that the distances are plentiful not just in aggregate but on average from the points themselves: $\sum_{x\in A} d(x) \gg n^2/\sqrt{\log n}$, where $d(x)$ counts the distinct distances from $x$.
status: A $\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}$ integer grid shows the conjectured bound would be best possible. The problem was nearly solved by Guth and Katz [GuKa15], who proved there are always $\gg n/\log n$ distinct distances. A stronger form (see [604]) may be true: that a single point determines $\gg n/\sqrt{\log n}$ distinct distances, or even $\gg n$ points do, or even that this holds averaged over all points — in [Er75f] Erdős conjectured $\sum_{x\in A} d(x) \gg n^2/\sqrt{\log n}$ for any $n$-point set $A\subset\mathbb{R}^2$. See also [661], and [1083] for the generalisation to higher dimensions.
solved_when: A proof (up to constants) that every $n$-point set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determines $\gg n/\sqrt{\log n}$ distinct distances; a stronger solution establishes $\sum_{x\in A} d(x) \gg n^2/\sqrt{\log n}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a $500 prize and tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle the exact order of the minimum number of distinct distances determined by planar point sets.

title: Erdős problem #91
open: Among all $n$-point sets in the plane, are there at least two non-similar minimisers of the number of distinct distances — that is, two non-similar sets of the same size $n$, each achieving the minimum possible number of distinct distances? The conjecture, for $n$ sufficiently large, is that there are at least two (and probably many) such non-similar extremal sets.
status: For $n=3$ the equilateral triangle is the only such set. For $n=4$ the square or two equilateral triangles sharing an edge give two non-similar examples. For $n=5$ the regular pentagon is the unique such set (which has two distinct distances). Erdős mysteriously remarks in [Er90] this was proved by 'a colleague'. (In [Er87b] this is described as 'a colleague from Zagreb (unfortunately I do not have his letter)'.) A published proof of this fact is provided by Kovács [Ko24c]. In [Er87b] Erdős says that there are at least two non-similar examples for $6\leq n\leq 9$. The minimal possible number of distinct distances is the subject of [89].
solved_when: A proof that, for sufficiently large $n$, there exist at least two non-similar $n$-point subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$, each minimising the number of distinct distances among all $n$-point sets.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; resolving it would clarify the rigidity or multiplicity of extremal configurations in the distinct distances problem, and it is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #96
open: Can $n$ points in the plane forming a convex polygon determine only a linear number of unit-distance pairs? Formally, is the number of pairs at distance $1$ always $O(n)$?
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Moser. In [Er92e] Erdős credits the conjecture that the true upper bound is $2n$ to himself and Fishburn. Füredi [Fu90] proved an upper bound of $O(n\log n)$, with a short proof given by Brass and Pach [BrPa01]. The best known upper bound is $\leq n\log_2 n + 4n$, due to Aggarwal [Ag15]. Edelsbrunner and Hajnal [EdHa91] constructed $n$ such points with $2n-7$ unit-distance pairs, disproving an early stronger conjecture of Erdős and Moser that the true answer was $\frac{5}{3}n + O(1)$. A positive answer would follow from [97]; see also [90]. In [Er92e] Erdős makes the stronger conjecture that, if $g(x)$ counts the largest number of points equidistant from $x$ in $A$, then $\sum_{x\in A} g(x) < 4n$; the Edelsbrunner–Hajnal example shows $\sum_{x\in A} g(x) > 4n - O(1)$ is possible.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the number of unit-distance pairs among $n$ points in convex position is bounded by $Cn$ for an absolute constant $C$; the conjectured sharp bound is $2n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a positive answer would settle a long-standing question in combinatorial geometry about unit distances in convex position.

title: Erdős problem #97
open: Does every convex polygon have a vertex from which no other four vertices are all equidistant? More precisely, must there exist a vertex $v$ such that no distance from $v$ is shared by $4$ other vertices?
status: Erdős originally conjectured in [Er46b] that every convex polygon has a vertex with no other $3$ vertices equidistant from it, but Danzer constructed a convex polygon on 9 points where every vertex has three vertices equidistant from it (with the distance depending on the vertex); this construction is explained in [Er87b]. Fishburn and Reeds [FiRe92] found a convex polygon on 20 points where every vertex has three vertices equidistant from it at the same distance for all vertices. Whether the statement fails for $4$ is open, and Erdős asked whether some constant might make it hold. In [Er75f] Erdős claimed Danzer proved it false for every constant — for any $k$ a convex polygon where every vertex has $k$ equidistant vertices — but since this claim was not repeated in later papers, presumably Erdős was mistaken. The answer is no without convexity (noted by Boris Alexeev and Dustin Mixon): for any $d$ there are graphs with minimum degree $d$ that can be embedded in t
solved_when: An answer (positive or negative) to the question for $4$ equidistant vertices, or a proof/disproof that for every constant $k$ there exists a convex polygon in which every vertex has $k$ vertices equidistant from it.
why: A positive answer for $k+1$ vertices would, by induction, give an upper bound of $kn$ for Erdős problem [96], so this is a direct route to that problem; it is also one of Erdős's personally posed problems with a $100 prize.

title: Erdős problem #99
open: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points with minimum distance equal to 1, chosen to minimise the diameter of $A$. If $n$ is sufficiently large then must there be three points in $A$ which form an equilateral triangle of size 1?
status: Thue proved that the minimal such diameter is achieved (asymptotically) by the points in a triangular lattice intersected with a circle. In general Erdős believed such a set must have very large intersection with the triangular lattice (perhaps as many as $(1-o(1))n$). Erdős [Er94b] wrote 'I could not prove it but felt that it should not be hard. To my great surprise both B. H. Sendov and M. Simonovits doubted the truth of this conjecture.' In [Er94b] he offers \$100 for a counterexample but only \$50 for a proof. The stated problem is false for $n=4$, for example taking the points to be vertices of a square. The behaviour of such sets for small $n$ is explored by Bezdek and Fodor [BeFo99]. See also [103].
solved_when: A proof that every such minimising configuration with $n$ sufficiently large contains three points forming a unit equilateral triangle; alternatively, a counterexample for arbitrarily large $n$ resolves the problem in the negative (Erdős offered \$100 for a counterexample and \$50 for a proof in [Er94b]).

title: Erdős problem #100
open: If $n$ points in the plane have all pairwise distances at least $1$, and any two distinct distances differ by at least $1$, must the diameter of the set grow linearly in $n$? Formally, is the diameter necessarily $\gg n$?
status: It is perhaps even true that the diameter is $\geq n-1$ for sufficiently large $n$. Piepmeyer has an example of $9$ such points with diameter $<5$. Kanold proved the diameter is $\geq n^{3/4}$. The bounds on the distinct distance problem [89] proved by Guth and Katz [GuKa15] imply a lower bound of $\gg n/\log n$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the diameter of any such set is $\gg n$; the conjectured sharper bound of $\geq n-1$ for sufficiently large $n$ would also settle it.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it links separation conditions on points and distances to the classic distinct distances phenomenon.

title: Erdős problem #101
open: Must any set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no five collinear determine only $o(n^2)$ lines that contain exactly four points? Formally, is the maximum number of 4-point lines in such a configuration subquadratic in $n$?
status: Examples with $\sim n^2/6$ collinear triples and no four points on a line are given by Burr, Grünbaum, and Sloane [BGS74] and Füredi and Palásti [FuPa84]. Grünbaum [Gr76] constructed an example with $\gg n^{3/2}$ such lines, and Erdős speculated this may be the correct order of magnitude; this is false, as Solymosi and Stojaković [SoSt13] constructed a set with no five on a line and at least $n^{2-O(1/\sqrt{\log n})}$ lines containing exactly four points. See also [102] and [669]; a generalisation is asked in [588]. The problem is Problem 71 on Green's open problems list.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that, for every set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no five on a line, the number of lines containing four points is $o(n^2)$; a disproof requires a construction with $\Omega(n^2)$ such lines.
why: Resolving it settles one of Erdős's personally posed problems (carrying a $100 prize) on the interface of combinatorial incidence geometry and extremal point configurations, determining whether forbidding five collinear points genuinely forces rich lines to be rare.

title: Erdős problem #102
open: Suppose a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determines at least $cn^2$ lines each containing more than three points. Must some line contain very many of the points? Formally, define $h_c(n)$ as the largest integer guaranteed to appear on a single line under these conditions, and determine how $h_c(n)$ grows with $n$ — in particular, is it true that $h_c(n)\to\infty$ for every fixed $c>0$?
status: This is a problem of Erdős and Purdy. It is not even known whether $h_c(n)\geq 5$ (see [101]). It is easy to see that $h_c(n) \ll_c n^{1/2}$, and Erdős at one point [Er95] suggested that perhaps a similar lower bound $h_c(n)\gg_c n^{1/2}$ holds. Zach Hunter has pointed out that this is false, even replacing $>3$ points on each line with $>k$ points: consider the set of points in $\{1,\ldots,m\}^d$ where $n\approx m^d$. These intersect any line in $\ll_d n^{1/d}$ points, and have $\gg_d n^2$ many pairs of points each of which determine a line with at least $k$ points. This is a construction in $\mathbb{R}^d$, but a random projection into $\mathbb{R}^2$ preserves the relevant properties. This construction shows that $h_c(n) \ll n^{1/\log(1/c)}$.
solved_when: The function $h_c(n)$ is estimated, with the specific question of whether $h_c(n)\to\infty$ for each fixed $c>0$ resolved; even establishing $h_c(n)\geq 5$ would settle the first open threshold.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it probes a basic gap in our understanding of how rich families of rich lines force local concentration.

title: Erdős problem #103
open: Let $h(n)$ count the number of incongruent sets of $n$ points in the plane that minimize diameter under the constraint that all pairwise distances are at least $1$. Does $h(n)$ tend to infinity as $n$ grows?
status: It is not even known whether $h(n)\geq 2$ for all large $n$. See also [99]. Reference: [Er94b]; erdosproblems.com/103.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $h(n)\to \infty$; in particular, resolving whether $h(n)\geq 2$ for all large $n$ would already settle a basic case.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would clarify the multiplicity of optimal diameter-minimizing point configurations in the plane.

title: Erdős problem #104
open: Given $n$ points in the plane, must the number of distinct unit circles passing through at least three of them be $o(n^2)$? Erdős further asked, with a £100 reward, whether the true answer is $O(n^{3/2})$.
status: Erdős [Er81d] proved that $\gg n$ circles are possible and that there cannot be more than $O(n^2)$, by the simple observation that every pair of points determines at most $2$ unit circles, via double counting. Erdős claimed in several places that this gives $n(n-1)$ as an upper bound, but Harborth and Mengerson [HaMe86] noted it in fact delivers $\frac{n(n-1)}{3}$. Elekes [El84] gave a simple construction with $\gg n^{3/2}$ such circles, which may be the correct order of magnitude. In [Er75h] and [Er92e] Erdős also asked how many unit circles must exist when the points are in general position, offering £100 in [Er92e] for a proof or disproof that the answer is $O(n^{3/2})$. The maximal number of unit circles achieved by $n$ points is OEIS sequence A003829. See also [506] and [831].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the count of unit circles determined by $n$ points is $o(n^2)$; separately, the £100 question is resolved by proving or disproving the bound $O(n^{3/2})$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems with a cash prize attached; resolving it settles the correct order of magnitude of a basic incidence quantity in combinatorial geometry.

title: Erdős problem #107
open: How many points in the plane, with no three collinear, are needed to guarantee that some $n$ of them form the vertices of a convex $n$-gon? Formally, if $f(n)$ is the minimal such number, prove that $f(n)=2^{n-2}+1$.
status: The problem originated in 1931 when Klein observed that $f(4)=5$; Turán and Makai showed $f(5)=9$. Erdős and Szekeres proved $2^{n-2}+1\leq f(n)\leq \binom{2n-4}{n-2}+1$ ([ErSz60] and [ErSz35] respectively). Several improvements of the upper bound followed, but all of the form $4^{(1+o(1))n}$, until Suk [Su17] proved $f(n) \leq 2^{(1+o(1))n}$. The current best bound is due to Holmsen, Mojarrad, Pach, and Tardos [HMPT20], who prove $f(n) \leq 2^{n+O(\sqrt{n\log n})}$. In [Er97e] Erdős clarifies that the \$500 is for a proof, and only offers \$100 for a disproof; Graham [Gr04] offers \$1000 for a proof. The problem is #1 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection; see also [216], [651], and [838].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $f(n)=2^{n-2}+1$; a proof earns the Erdős prize of \$500 (with \$100 offered for a disproof), and Graham [Gr04] offers \$1000 for a proof.
why: This is the Erdős–Klein–Szekeres "Happy Ending" problem, one of Erdős's personally posed problems with a cash prize, and a central open question in combinatorial geometry; it determines the exact threshold at which convex structure is forced in planar point sets.

title: Erdős problem #108
open: For every $r\geq 4$ and $k\geq 2$, is there some finite $f(k,r)$ such that every graph of chromatic number at least $f(k,r)$ contains a subgraph of girth at least $r$ and chromatic number at least $k$?
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Hajnal. Rödl [Ro77] has proved the $r=4$ case (see [923]). The infinite version (whether every graph of infinite chromatic number contains a subgraph of infinite chromatic number whose girth is $>k$) is also open. In [Er79b] Erdős also asks whether $\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{f(k,r+1)}{f(k,r)}=\infty$. See also the entry in the graphs problem collection and [740] for the infinitary version.
solved_when: For every $r\geq 4$ and $k\geq 2$, a finite bound $f(k,r)$ is exhibited (or proved nonexistent) such that every graph of chromatic number at least $f(k,r)$ contains a subgraph of girth at least $r$ and chromatic number at least $k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would settle a foundational question about how chromatic number forces high-girth, highly chromatic subgraphs.
aliases: Erdős #108; graph theory / chromatic number / cycles

title: Erdős problem #111
open: If $G$ is a graph, let $h_G(n)$ be the least number such that any $n$-vertex subgraph of $G$ can be made bipartite by deleting at most $h_G(n)$ edges. What is the behaviour of $h_G(n)$, and in particular is it true that $h_G(n)/n\to\infty$ for every graph $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$?
status: A problem of Erdős, Hajnal, and Szemerédi [EHS82]. Every $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ must have $h_G(n)\gg n$, since $G$ must contain, for some $r$, $\aleph_1$ many vertex disjoint odd cycles of length $2r+1$. On the other hand, Erdős, Hajnal, and Szemerédi proved that there is a $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that $h_G(n)\ll n^{3/2}$. In [Er81] Erdős conjectured that this can be improved to $\ll n^{1+\epsilon}$ for every $\epsilon>0$. See also [74].
solved_when: The growth of $h_G(n)$ is determined (up to the conjectured order) for graphs of chromatic number $\aleph_1$ — specifically, when it is shown whether $h_G(n)\ll n^{1+\epsilon}$ for every $\epsilon>0$ for such $G$, or a counterexample is produced; the conjecture $h_G(n)/n\to\infty$ is proved or refuted.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would pin down how far uncountable chromatic number forces finite subgraphs away from being almost bipartite.
aliases: Erdős #111; graph theory / chromatic number / set theory

title: Erdős problem #112
open: Let $k=k(n,m)$ be the smallest integer such that every directed graph on $k$ vertices contains either an independent set of size $n$ or a transitive tournament of size $m$. Determine $k(n,m)$.
status: The problem originates with Erdős and Rado [ErRa67], who showed $k(n,m) \ll_m n^{m-1}$, more precisely $k(n,m) \leq \frac{2^{m-1}(n-1)^m+n-2}{2n-3}$. Larson and Mitchell [LaMi97] improved the dependence on $m$, establishing in particular $k(n,3)\leq n^{2}$. Zach Hunter observed that $R(n,m) \leq k(n,m)\leq R(n,m,m)$, which in particular proves the upper bound $k(n,m)\leq 3^{n+2m}$. In the graphs problem collection on the same site the problem replaces the transitive tournament with a directed path, and Zach Hunter and Raphael Steiner have a simple argument proving, for that alternative definition, that $k(n,m)=(n-1)(m-1)$.
solved_when: An exact formula, or tight asymptotics, for $k(n,m)$ is established for general $n$ and $m$.

title: Erdős problem #114
open: Among all monic polynomials $p(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z]$ of degree $n$, is the length of the lemniscate $\{z\in\mathbb{C}: |p(z)|=1\}$ maximised when $p(z)=z^n-1$?
status: The problem originates with Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], is listed as Problem 4.10 in [Ha74] (attributed to Erdős), and in [Va99] it is asked whether the length is at most $2n+O(1)$. Writing $f(n)$ for the maximal length: the curve for $p(z)=z^n-1$ has length $2n+O(1)$, so the conjecture implies $f(n)=2n+O(1)$. Dolzhenko [Do61] proved $f(n)\leq 4\pi n$, though few were aware of this work; Pommerenke [Po61] proved $f(n)\ll n^2$; Borwein [Bo95] proved $f(n)\ll n$ while unaware of Dolzhenko's earlier work, and reported the $250 prize. Eremenko and Hayman [ErHa99] proved the full conjecture for $n=2$ and $f(n)\leq 9.173n$ for all $n$. Danchenko [Da07] proved $f(n)\leq 2\pi n$. Fryntov and Nazarov [FrNa09] proved $z^n-1$ is a local maximiser and solved the problem asymptotically with $f(n)\leq 2n+O(n^{7/8})$. Tao [Ta25] proved that $p(z)=z^n-1$ is the unique (up to rotation and translation) maximiser for all sufficiently large $n$. Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58] also ask whether the length is at least $2$ (record truncated).
solved_when: It is proved that the maximum length $f(n)$ is achieved by $p(z)=z^n-1$ for every $n$; equivalently, $f(n)=2n+O(1)$ with equality attained by $z^n-1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a $250 prize, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/114.

title: Erdős problem #117
open: Let $h(n)$ be minimal such that any group $G$ with the property that any subset of $>n$ elements contains some $x\neq y$ such that $xy=yx$ can be covered by at most $h(n)$ many Abelian subgroups. Estimate $h(n)$ as well as possible.
status: group theory Pyber [Py87] has proved there exist constants $c_2>c_1>1$ such that $c_1^n<h(n)<c_2^n$. Erdős [Er97f] writes that the lower bound was already known to Isaacs.

title: Erdős problem #120
open: Given an infinite set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, must there exist a set $E\subset\mathbb{R}$ of positive measure that contains no set of the shape $aA+b$ for any $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ with $a\neq 0$?
status: The conjecture is true when $A$ is unbounded or dense in some interval, so it suffices to consider the case where $A=\{a_1>a_2>\cdots\}$ is a countable strictly monotone sequence converging to $0$. Steinhaus [St20] showed the statement is false whenever $A$ is a finite set. The conjecture is known in many special cases, but remains open even for $A=\{1,1/2,1/4,\ldots\}$, which is Problem 94 on Green's open problems list. For an overview of progress, see the survey by Svetic [Sv00]; more recent progress is surveyed by Jung, Lai, and Mooroogen [JLM24]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/120; Erdős references: [Er74b] [Er81b,p.29] [Er83d] [Er90] [Er97f] [Va99,2.46] [St20].
solved_when: For every infinite $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, a positive-measure set $E$ is exhibited (or its existence proved) avoiding all affine copies $aA+b$ with $a\neq 0$; or a counterexample — an infinite $A$ every copy of which meets every positive-measure set.
why: This is the Erdős similarity problem, one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with a $100 prize), carrying full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #122
open: For which number-theoretic functions $f$ does the following hold: whenever $F(n)$ satisfies $F(n)/f(n)\to 0$ for almost all $n$, there are infinitely many $x$ such that $\frac{\#\{n\in\mathbb{N}: n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}}{F(x)}\to\infty$? Informally, which functions perturb the integers so mildly that the shifted values $n+f(n)$ pile up far more densely than expected on infinitely many short intervals?
status: In [Er97] Erdős only considers number-theoretic functions growing 'slowly', i.e. slower than $(\log n)^{1-c}$ for some $c>0$. The question is considered by Erdős, Pomerance, and Sárközy [EPS97], who prove in particular that if $\omega(n)$ counts the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$, then for all large $x$ there are intervals $I,J\subset[1,x]$ of width $|I|\asymp\left(\frac{\log x}{\log\log x}\right)^{1/2}$ and $|J|\asymp(\log\log x)^{1/2}$ such that if $n\in I$ then $n+\omega(n)\in J$ (note the normal order of $\omega$ is $\log\log x$, hence $(\log\log n)^{1/2}/\omega(n)\to 0$ for almost all $n$). In [Er97] and [Er97e] Erdős reports that he, Pomerance, and Sárközy can prove the more general claim for $f=\tau(n)$, the divisor function, or $\omega(n)$, and states it 'probably fails' for $\phi(n)$ or $\sigma(n)$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/122; Erdős references: [Er97,p.155] [Er97e,p.533] [Er97].
solved_when: A characterization is given of the number-theoretic functions $f$ for which every $F$ with $F(n)/f(n)\to 0$ almost everywhere admits infinitely many $x$ with the displayed ratio tending to infinity.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would clarify how additive shifts by arithmetic functions such as $\omega(n)$ or $\tau(n)$ concentrate in short intervals.

title: Erdős problem #128
open: If every induced subgraph on at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ vertices of an $n$-vertex graph has more than $n^2/50$ edges, must the graph contain a triangle?
status: A problem of Erdős and Rousseau; the constant $50$ would be best possible, as witnessed by a blow-up of $C_5$ or the Petersen graph. Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp [EFRS94] proved it with $50$ replaced by $16$, and more generally that for any $0<\alpha<1$, if every set of $\geq \alpha n$ vertices contains $>\alpha^3n^2/2$ edges then $G$ contains a triangle. Krivelevich [Kr95] proved it with $n/2$ replaced by $3n/5$ (and $50$ replaced by $25$). Keevash and Sudakov [KeSu06] proved it under the additional assumption that $G$ has at most $n^2/12$ edges or at least $n^2/5$ edges. Norin and Yepremyan [NoYe15] proved it if $G$ has at least $(1/5-c)n^2$ edges for some constant $c>0$. Razborov [Ra22] proved it with $\frac{1}{50}$ replaced by $\frac{27}{1024}$. See also the entry in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: A proof (or a counterexample) resolving the question as stated: every induced subgraph on at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ vertices having more than $n^2/50$ edges forces a triangle, with the constant $50$ being best possible.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with a $250 prize), and a resolution would settle a natural extremal question about how local density forces a triangle.

title: Erdős problem #130
open: Let $A\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be an infinite set containing no three points on a line and no four points on a circle, and form the graph on $A$ joining two points exactly when their distance is an integer. How large can the chromatic number and clique number of this graph be — in particular, can the chromatic number be infinite?
