status: The question was asked by Andrásfai and Erdős. Erdős [Er97b] also asked whether such a graph could contain an infinite complete graph, but this is impossible by an earlier result of Anning and Erdős [AnEr45]. See also [213].
solved_when: Sharp bounds (or exact values) are determined for the possible chromatic numbers and clique numbers of these integer-distance graphs; in particular, it is decided whether the chromatic number can be infinite.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a solution would clarify how rich the combinatorial structure induced by integer distances can be even under strong general-position constraints.

title: Erdős problem #131
open: Let $F(N)$ be the largest size of a set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ in which no element divides the sum of any collection of distinct other elements of $A$. What is the correct order of growth of $F(N)$ — in particular, is it true that $F(N) > N^{1/2-o(1)}$?
status: The problem was studied by Erdős, Lev, Rauzy, Sándor, and Sárközy [ELRSS99], who call such a property 'non-dividing' and prove the explicit bound $F(N)<3N^{1/2}+1$. In [Er97b] Erdős credits Csaba with a construction proving $F(N) \gg N^{1/5}$; such a construction was also given in [ELRSS99], where it is linked to non-averaging sets (see [186]). Since every such set is non-averaging, the result of Pham and Zakharov [PhZa24] implies $F(N) \leq N^{1/4+o(1)}$, showing the answer to the original question is no, though the correct growth of $F(N)$ remains open. In [Er75b] Erdős writes that he originally thought $F(N) < (\log N)^{O(1)}$, but that Straus proved $F(N) > \exp((\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{\log 2}}+o(1))\sqrt{\log N})$. See also [13]. The problem is discussed as C16 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: The growth rate of $F(N)$ is determined up to $N^{o(1)}$ factors (or otherwise sharply); this would supersede the known bounds $F(N) \gg N^{1/5}$ from below and $F(N) \leq N^{1/4+o(1)}$ from above, answering whether $F(N) > N^{1/2-o(1)}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/131, and resolving it would settle the correct growth of 'non-dividing' sets, a natural question linking divisibility, non-averaging sets, and additive structure.

title: Erdős problem #132
open: Among any $n$ points in the plane, must there exist two distinct distances that each occur between at most $n$ pairs of points? More sharply, must the number of such "small-multiplicity" distances tend to infinity as $n\to\infty$?
status: Asked by Erdős and Pach. Hopf and Pannowitz [HoPa34] proved that the largest distance between points of $A$ can occur at most $n$ times, but it is unknown whether a second such distance must occur. It may be true that there are at least $n^{1-o(1)}$ many such distances. In [Er97e] Erdős offers \$100 for 'any nontrivial result'. Erdős [Er84c] believed that for $n\geq 5$ there must always exist at least two such distances; this is false for $n=4$, as witnessed by two equilateral triangles of the same side-length glued together. Erdős and Fishburn [ErFi95] proved this is true for $n=5$ and $n=6$. Clemen, Dumitrescu, and Liu [CDL25] proved that there are always at least two such distances if $A$ is in convex position (no point lies inside the convex hull of the others), and also if the set $A$ is 'not too convex', in a specific technical sense. See also [223], [756], and [957].
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved) that every set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determines at least two distances occurring at least once but between at most $n$ pairs; stronger progress would show the number of such distances tends to infinity as $n\to\infty$, possibly matching the conjectured lower bound of $n^{1-o(1)}$.
why: A resolution would settle one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with a \$100 prize attached), and even nontrivial partial results would advance our understanding of how often distances can repeat in planar point sets.

title: Erdős problem #137
open: Can the product of $k \geq 3$ consecutive positive integers ever be powerful, where $N$ is called powerful if every prime $p \mid N$ also satisfies $p^2 \mid N$? Equivalently, is $m(m+1)\cdots(m+k-1)$ never powerful for $k \geq 3$?
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Selfridge. There are infinitely many $n$ such that $n(n+1)$ is powerful (see [364]). Erdős and Selfridge [ErSe75] proved that the product of $k \geq 3$ consecutive positive integers can never be a perfect power. Erdős remarked that this "seems hopeless at present". In [Er82c] he further conjectures that, if $k$ is fixed and $n$ is sufficiently large, then, for all $m$, there must be at least $k$ distinct primes $p$ such that $p \mid m(m+1)\cdots(m+n)$ and yet $p^2$ does not divide the right-hand side. See also [364].
solved_when: A proof that for every $k \geq 3$ and every $m$, the product $m(m+1)\cdots(m+k-1)$ is not powerful; or a counterexample exhibiting such a product.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and sits in the same difficult territory as the Erdős–Selfridge theorem on perfect powers in products of consecutive integers.

title: Erdős problem #138
open: How fast does the van der Waerden number $W(k)$ — the least $N$ such that every $2$-colouring of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ contains a monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progression — actually grow with $k$? In particular, prove or disprove that $W(k)^{1/k}\to\infty$.
status: For prime $p$, Berlkamp [Be68] proved $W(p+1)\geq p2^p$. Gowers [Go01] proved $W(k) \leq 2^{2^{2^{2^{2^{k+9}}}}}$. The best general lower bound is $W(k)\gg 2^k$, due to Kozik and Shabanov [KoSh16]. In [Er81] Erdős further asks whether $W(k+1)/W(k)\to\infty$ or $W(k+1)-W(k)\to\infty$; DeepMind has proved $W(k+1)\geq W(k)+k$, answering the second question. In [Er80] Erdős asks whether $W(k)/2^k\to\infty$. The analogous question for $r\geq 3$ colours was resolved by Fox and Hunter [FoHu26], who proved $W_3(k)^{1/k}\geq C^{\log_* k}$ for some constant $C>1$.
solved_when: A proof or disproof of $W(k)^{1/k}\to\infty$ is given (a $500 prize problem posed by Erdős in [Er80,p.90]); related sub-goals include whether $W(k)/2^k\to\infty$ and whether $W(k+1)/W(k)\to\infty$.
why: It resolves one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with a \$500 prize attached, and would settle the true exponential order of the fundamental threshold for monochromatic arithmetic progressions in two colours.

title: Erdős problem #141
open: For a given $k\geq 3$, do there exist $k$ consecutive primes that form an arithmetic progression? More precisely, are there $k$ primes, consecutive in the sequence of all primes, whose values lie in arithmetic progression?
status: Green and Tao [GrTa08] proved that there must always exist some $k$ primes in arithmetic progression, but these need not be consecutive. Erdős called this conjecture 'completely hopeless at present'. The existence of such progressions for small $k$ has been verified for $k\leq 10$, see the Wikipedia page. It is open, even for $k=3$, whether there are infinitely many such progressions. See also [219]. This is discussed in problem A6 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: For some $k\geq 3$, a proof (or disproof) of the existence of $k$ consecutive primes in arithmetic progression; the case $k=3$ alone, especially whether infinitely many such progressions exist, would already resolve the central open question.
why: A solution would extend the Green–Tao theorem from arbitrary prime progressions to progressions genuinely consecutive among the primes, a substantial strengthening of our understanding of the fine distribution of primes.
aliases: Erdős #141; additive combinatorics / primes / arithmetic progressions

title: Erdős problem #143
open: Let $A\subset(1,\infty)$ be a countably infinite set such that $|kx-y|\ge 1$ for all distinct $x,y\in A$ and all integers $k\ge 1$. Must such a set be sparse — in particular, must $\sum_{x\in A}\frac{1}{x\log x}$ converge, or $\sum_{x\in A,\,x<n}\frac{1}{x}=o(\log n)$?
status: For sets of integers the condition forces $A$ to be a primitive set (no element divides another), for which Erdős [Er35] proved $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n\log n}$ converges, and Behrend [Be35] proved $\sum_{x<n,\,x\in A}\frac{1}{n}\ll \frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}$; Erdős, Sárkőzy, and Szemerédi [ESS67] improved the $O(\cdot)$ bound to $o(\cdot)$. In [Er73] and [Er77c] Erdős mentions an unpublished proof of Haight that $\lim \frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x}=0$ holds when the elements of $A$ are independent over $\mathbb{Q}$, and over the years he asked for various quantitative estimates such as $\liminf \frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x}=0$ or $\sum_{x<n,\,x\in A}\frac{1}{x}\ll \frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}$. In [Er97c] he offered \$500 for resolving the main questions; Koukoulopoulos, Lamzouri, and Lichtman [KLL25] partially resolved this by proving $\sum_{x<n,\,x\in A}\frac{1}{x}=o(\log n)$. See also [858].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every such $A$ satisfies $\sum_{x\in A}\frac{1}{x\log x}<\infty$, or at least $\sum_{x<n,\,x\in A}\frac{1}{x}=o(\log n)$, is given.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a $500 prize, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/143; it extends the classical theory of primitive sets to real settings.

title: Erdős problem #145
open: Let $s_1<s_2<\cdots$ be the sequence of squarefree numbers. Does the average $\frac{1}{x}\sum_{s_n\leq x}(s_{n+1}-s_n)^\alpha$ converge to a limit as $x\to\infty$, for every $\alpha \geq 0$?
status: Erdős [Er51] proved the limit exists for all $0\leq \alpha \leq 2$, and Hooley [Ho73] extended this to all $\alpha \leq 3$. Greaves, Harman, and Huxley showed (in Chapter 11 of [GHH97]) that this is true for $\alpha \leq 11/3$. Chan [Ch23c] has extended this to $\alpha \leq 3.75$. Granville [Gr98] proved that the statement for all $\alpha \geq 0$ follows from the ABC conjecture. See also [208].
solved_when: The limit $\lim_{x\to \infty}\frac{1}{x}\sum_{s_n\leq x}(s_{n+1}-s_n)^\alpha$ is proved to exist for every $\alpha \geq 0$ (or a counterexample is exhibited for some $\alpha$).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; a solution would settle the fine-scale distribution of gaps between squarefree numbers, and it is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #148
open: Let $F(k)$ be the number of ways to write $1$ as a sum of reciprocals of $k$ distinct increasing integers, $1 = \frac{1}{n_1} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n_k}$ with $1 \leq n_1 < \cdots < n_k$. How large is $F(k)$, and can we find good estimates for it?
status: The best known bounds are $2^{c^{k/\log k}} \leq F(k) \leq c_0^{(\frac{1}{5}+o(1))2^k}$, where $c > 0$ is an absolute constant and $c_0 = 1.26408\cdots$ is the 'Vardi constant'. The lower bound is due to Konyagin [Ko14] and the upper bound to Elsholtz and Planitzer [ElPl21].
solved_when: Sharp asymptotic (or near-sharp) bounds on $F(k)$ are obtained, substantially closing the gap between the current lower bound $2^{c^{k/\log k}}$ and upper bound $c_0^{(\frac{1}{5}+o(1))2^k}$, where $c > 0$ is an absolute constant and $c_0 = 1.26408\cdots$ is the Vardi constant.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and resolving it would settle a long-standing question on the density of Egyptian fraction representations of $1$; its full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/148.

title: Erdős problem #149
open: Is it true that every graph with maximum degree $\Delta$ admits a strong edge-coloring with at most $\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$ colors — that is, a partition of its edges into at most $\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$ induced matchings?
status: Asked by Erdős and Nešetřil in 1985 (see [FGST89]). The conjectured bound would be best possible, as witnessed by a blowup of $C_5$, although improvements may be possible for odd $\Delta$. It is easy to see that $\mathrm{sq}(G)\leq 5$ when $\Delta\leq 2$; in general, the trivial bound $\mathrm{sq}(G)\leq 2\Delta^2-2\Delta+1$ follows from the observation that the number of neighbours of any edge of $G$ is $\leq 2\Delta^2-2\Delta$. Molloy and Reed [MoRe97] improved this to $\mathrm{sq}(G)\leq 1.998\Delta^2$ for $\Delta$ sufficiently large; Bruhn and Joos [BrJo18] improved it to $1.93\Delta^2$; Bonamy, Perrett, and Postle [BPP22] to $1.835\Delta^2$; and the best bound currently available is $1.772\Delta^2$, proved by Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos, and Kang [HJK22]. Mahdian has proved an upper bound of $(2+o(1))\frac{\Delta^2}{\log \Delta}$ under the additional assumption that $G$ is $C_4$-free. Andersen [92] and Horák, He, and Trotter [HHT93] have independently shown that $\mathrm{sq}(G)\leq 1$
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\mathrm{sq}(G)\leq\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$ for every graph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta$; equivalently, that the chromatic number of the square of the line graph $L(G)^2$ is at most $\frac{5}{4}\Delta^2$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, posed with Nešetřil in 1985, and its full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/149; a proof would settle the conjectured optimal constant in the strong chromatic index, a central quantitative question in extremal graph coloring.

title: Erdős problem #151
open: Does every graph on $n$ vertices admit a clique transversal of size at most $n - H(n)$, where $\tau(G)$ is the minimal number of vertices hitting every maximal clique of size at least two and $H(n)$ is the largest integer such that every triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices has an independent set of that size?
status: It is easy to see that $\tau(G) \leq n-\sqrt{n}$, and if $G$ is triangle-free then trivially $\tau(G) \leq n-H(n)$. The problem is listed in [Er88,p.82] as a problem of Erdős and Gallai, who were unable to make progress even assuming $G$ is $K_4$-free; there Erdős remarked that the conjecture is 'perhaps completely wrongheaded'. It later appeared as Problem 1 in [EGT92]. The general behaviour of $\tau(G)$ is the subject of [610].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\tau(G) \leq n - H(n)$ holds for every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #153
open: Let $A$ be a finite Sidon set and $A+A=\{s_1<\cdots<s_t\}$. Is it true that\[\frac{1}{t}\sum_{1\leq i<t}(s_{i+1}-s_i)^2 \to \infty\]as $\lvert A\rvert\to \infty$?
status: The problem remains open; a similar problem can be asked for infinite Sidon sets.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given that the average of the squared gaps between consecutive elements of the sumset $A+A$ tends to infinity as $|A|\to\infty$ for finite Sidon sets $A$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a basic structural question about how spread out the sumset of a Sidon set must be.

title: Erdős problem #155
open: Must the largest Sidon subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ grow as slowly as possible, adding at most one element when the interval is extended by $k$ places? Formally, writing $F(N)$ for the size of the largest Sidon subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, is it true that $F(N+k)\leq F(N)+1$ for every fixed $k\geq 1$ and all sufficiently large $N$?
status: The problem is open at erdosproblems.com/155, which notes the inequality may even hold with $k\approx \epsilon N^{1/2}$; Erdős references: [Er92c] [Er94b].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for each fixed $k\geq 1$, the inequality $F(N+k)\leq F(N)+1$ holds for all sufficiently large $N$; the record also notes the stronger possibility $k\approx \epsilon N^{1/2}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (Erdős #155, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com), so a resolution settles a long-standing question in the theory of Sidon sets in additive combinatorics.

title: Erdős problem #156
open: Does there exist a maximal Sidon set $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ of size $O(N^{1/3})$? In other words, can the known polylogarithmic overhead in constructions of small maximal Sidon sets be removed?
status: This is a question of Erdős, Sárközy, and Sós [ESS94]. The greedy construction of a maximal Sidon set in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is easily shown to have size $\gg N^{1/3}$. Ruzsa [Ru98b] constructed a maximal Sidon set of size $\ll (N \log N)^{1/3}$. See also [340].
solved_when: A maximal Sidon subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is exhibited whose size is bounded by a constant times $N^{1/3}$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles whether the true order of the smallest maximal Sidon set is $N^{1/3}$.

title: Erdős problem #158
open: If an infinite set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ has at most $2$ solutions to $a+b=n$ with $a\leq b$ for every $n$, must its counting function be $o(N^{1/2})$ along a subsequence — that is, must $\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}=0$?
status: For the analogous question with the bound $2$ replaced by $1$, the set $A$ is a Sidon set, and Erdős proved the result in that case; the case of at most $2$ solutions remains open. See erdosproblems.com/158.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given showing that every infinite $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ with at most $2$ representations of each $n$ as $a+b$ (with $a\leq b$) satisfies $\liminf_{N\to\infty}\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\rvert/N^{1/2}=0$, or an explicit such set with positive $\liminf$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #159
open: Is there a positive constant $c$ such that the Ramsey number $R(C_4,K_n)$ grows slower than quadratically, that is, $R(C_4,K_n) \ll n^{2-c}$?
status: Erdős offered a \$100 prize in [Er78] for a proof or disproof. The current bounds are $\frac{n^{3/2}}{(\log n)^{3/2}}\ll R(C_4,K_n)\ll \frac{n^2}{(\log n)^{2}}$. The upper bound is due to Szemerédi (mentioned in [EFRS78]), and the lower bound is due to Spencer [Sp77]. The problem is #17 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: Constants $c>0$ and $C$ are exhibited with $R(C_4,K_n) \le C n^{2-c}$ for all large $n$, or the statement is disproved; either resolution earns the \$100 prize offered in [Er78].
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/159.

title: Erdős problem #160
open: How many colours are needed to colour the integers $1$ through $N$ so that every four-term arithmetic progression receives at least three distinct colours? Formally, if $h(N)$ is the smallest $k$ for which such a colouring exists, estimate the growth of $h(N)$ in $N$.
status: Investigated by Erdős and Freud. The problem has been discussed on MathOverflow, where LeechLattice shows $h(N) \ll N^{2/3}$. In the comments of that site, Hunter improves this to $h(N) \ll N^{\frac{\log 3}{\log 22}+o(1)}$ (note $\frac{\log 3}{\log 22}\approx 0.355$). The observation of Zach Hunter in that question, coupled with recent progress on the size of subsets without three-term arithmetic progressions (see [BlSi23], which improves slightly on the bounds due to Kelley and Meka [KeMe23]), implies $h(N) \gg \exp(c(\log N)^{1/9})$ for some $c>0$.
solved_when: The order of magnitude of $h(N)$ is determined up to constants in the exponent — equivalently, one has matching upper and lower bounds of the form $h(N) = N^{\alpha+o(1)}$ (or a proof that no such exponent exists), improving on the current bounds $h(N) \gg \exp(c(\log N)^{1/9})$ and $h(N) \ll N^{\log 3/\log 22 + o(1)}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (#160), tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it sits at the interface of colouring problems and arithmetic-progression-free sets; sharp bounds would illuminate how stringently arithmetic structure forces colour diversity.

title: Erdős problem #161
open: For a fixed $t$-uniform hypergraph Ramsey setting, how does the threshold function $F^{(t)}(n,\alpha)$ behave as the density parameter $\alpha$ grows from $0$ to $1/2$ — does it increase continuously, or only through jumps, and if through jumps, is there just one? Formally, for $2$-colourings of the complete $t$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices in which every sufficiently large vertex set contains at least an $\alpha$-proportion of its $t$-sets in each colour, does the minimal guaranteed set size jump only once?
status: For $\alpha=0$ this is the usual Ramsey function. A conjecture of Erdős, Hajnal, and Rado (see [562]) implies that $F^{(t)}(n,0)\asymp \log_{t-1} n$, and results of Erdős and Spencer imply $F^{(t)}(n,\alpha) \gg_\alpha (\log n)^{\frac{1}{t-1}}$ for all $\alpha>0$, with a similar upper bound holding for $\alpha$ close to $1/2$. Erdős said in [Er90b]: 'If I can hazard a guess completely unsupported by evidence, I am afraid that the jump occurs all in one step at $0$. It would be much more interesting if my conjecture would be wrong and perhaps there is some hope for this for $t>3$. I know nothing and offer \$500 to anybody who can clear up this mystery.' Conlon, Fox, and Sudakov [CFS11] proved that, for any fixed $\alpha>0$, $F^{(3)}(n,\alpha) \ll_\alpha \sqrt{\log n}$; coupled with the lower bound above, this implies that for $t=3$ there is only one jump, at $\alpha=0$. For all $\alpha>0$ it is known that $F^{(t)}(n,\alpha)\gg_t (\log n)^{c_\alpha}$. See [563] for more on the case $t=2$. This problem is #40 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: The structure of $F^{(t)}(n,\alpha)$ as $\alpha$ ranges over $(0,1/2)$ is determined: whether it has a single jump (conjecturally all at $\alpha=0$, i.e. $F^{(t)}(n,\alpha)$ comparable to $F^{(t)}(n,0)$ for all $\alpha>0$) or multiple jumps. Natural quantitative targets from the record: establish $F^{(t)}(n,\alpha) \ll_\alpha \sqrt{\log n}$ (or the analogous bound) for general $t$, and close the gap against the lower bound $F^{(t)}(n,\alpha)\gg_\alpha (\log n)^{1/(t-1)}$.
why: This determines whether positive-density Ramsey-type guarantees come for free once ordinary Ramsey homogeneity is achieved, and Erdős himself offered \$500 for resolving it, suggesting the possibility of genuinely new phenomena for $t>3$.
aliases: Erdős #161; combinatorics / hypergraphs / ramsey theory / discrepancy

title: Erdős problem #162
open: For every fixed $0\leq \alpha \leq 1/2$, is $F(n,\alpha)$ — the largest $k$ such that some 2-colouring of $K_n$ makes every induced subgraph on at least $k$ vertices contain more than $\alpha\binom{\lvert H\rvert}{2}$ edges of each colour — asymptotic to $c_\alpha \log n$ as $n\to\infty$?
status: It is easy to show with the probabilistic method that there exist constants $c_1(\alpha),c_2(\alpha)$ such that $c_1(\alpha)\log n < F(n,\alpha) < c_2(\alpha)\log n$, so the correct order of magnitude is known up to constant factors.
solved_when: For every fixed $0\leq \alpha \leq 1/2$, a proof that $F(n,\alpha)\sim c_\alpha \log n$ as $n\to\infty$ for some constant $c_\alpha$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; its resolution would pin down the exact asymptotics of a natural two-colour discrepancy parameter, and it is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #165
open: What is the asymptotic behavior of the Ramsey number $R(3,k)$? In other words, determine the leading constant $c$ such that $R(3,k) \sim c\,k^2/\log k$.
status: It is known that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that for large $k$, $(c+o(1))\frac{k^2}{\log k}\leq R(3,k) \leq (1+o(1))\frac{k^2}{\log k}$. The lower bound is due to Kim [Ki95]; the upper bound is due to Shearer [Sh83], improving an earlier bound of Ajtai, Komlós, and Szemerédi [AKS80]. The value of $c$ in the lower bound has seen a number of improvements: Kim's original proof gave $c\geq 1/162$; $c\geq 1/4$ was proved independently by Bohman and Keevash [BoKe21] and Pontiveros, Griffiths and Morris [PGM20], the latter of whom conjectured this to be the true order of magnitude. It was improved by Campos, Jenssen, Michelen, and Sahasrabudhe [CJMS25] to $c\geq 1/3$, and further by Hefty, Horn, King, and Pfender [HHKP25] to $c\geq 1/2$; both papers conjecture that $c=1/2$ is the correct asymptotic. See also [544], and [986] for the general case; see [1013] for a related function.
solved_when: An asymptotic formula for $R(3,k)$ is established; in particular, the constant $c$ in $(c+o(1))\,k^2/\log k \leq R(3,k) \leq (1+o(1))\,k^2/\log k$ is pinned down (conjecturally $c = 1/2$).

title: Erdős problem #168
open: Let $F(N)$ be the size of the largest subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ containing no triple of the form $\{n,2n,3n\}$. Is the limit $\lim_{N\to\infty} F(N)/N$ irrational?
status: The existence of the limit was proved by Graham, Spencer, and Witsenhausen [GSW77], who showed it equals $\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k\in K}\frac{1}{d_k}$, where $d_1<d_2<\cdots$ are the $3$-smooth numbers and $K$ is the set of $k$ for which $f(k)>f(k-1)$, where $f$ counts the largest subset of $\{d_1,\ldots,d_k\}$ avoiding $\{n,2n,3n\}$. Similar questions can be asked for the density or upper density of infinite sets without such configurations. The limit can be estimated by elementary arguments (see the comments). Eberhard has used the formula of [GSW77] to calculate the value of the limit as $0.800965\cdots$.
solved_when: The irrationality of the limit $\lim_{N\to\infty} F(N)/N$ is proved or disproved.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it resolves a long-standing question about the arithmetic structure of this extremal density.

title: Erdős problem #169
open: How large can the reciprocal sum of a set of positive integers be if the set contains no $k$-term arithmetic progression? Formally, letting $f(k)$ denote the supremum of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ over progression-free sets $A$, estimate $f(k)$ — in particular, is $\lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{f(k)}{\log W(k)}=\infty$, where $W(k)$ is the van der Waerden number?
status: Berlekamp [Be68] proved $f(k) \geq \frac{\log 2}{2}k$, and Gerver [Ge77] improved this to $f(k) \geq (1-o(1))k\log k$. It is trivial that $\frac{f(k)}{\log W(k)}\geq \frac{1}{2}$, but improving the right-hand side to any constant $>1/2$ is open. Gerver also proved (see the comments for an alternative argument of Tao) that [3] is equivalent to $f(k)$ being finite for all $k$. For small $k$: the current record is $f(3)\geq 3.00849$, due to Wróblewski [Wr84], and Walker [Wa25] proved $f(4)\geq 4.43975$. Walker [Wa25] showed that it suffices to consider Kempner sets — sets of integers whose base $b$ digits lie in some fixed $S\subset\{0,\ldots,b-1\}$ — since for any $k\geq 3$ and $\epsilon>0$ there is a progression-free Kempner set $A$ with $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\geq f(k)-\epsilon$. In [Er80] Erdős asks whether for every $\epsilon>0$ and $k\geq 3$, any set of integers without a $k$-term arithmetic progression whose minimum is sufficiently large in terms of $\epsilon$ and $k$ satisfies $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}<\epsilon$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/169; Erdős references: [Er77c] [Er80,p.92] [Be68] [Ge77].
solved_when: The question of estimating $f(k)$ is resolved; in particular, the limit $\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{f(k)}{\log W(k)}$ is shown to be infinite (or determined otherwise), and the known lower bound $f(k)/\log W(k)\geq \frac{1}{2}$ is improved to some constant $>1/2$.
why: A solution would pin down the exact scale at which density constraints forbid arithmetic progressions in reciprocal-sum terms, sharpening the connection between progression-free sets and van der Waerden numbers; it is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #170
open: How small can a "sparse ruler" be — a set $A\subset\{0,1,\ldots,N\}$ whose difference set $A-A$ covers all of $\{0,1,\ldots,N\}$? Determine the value of $\lim_{N\to\infty} F(N)/N^{1/2}$, where $F(N)$ is the smallest possible size of such an $A$.
status: This is the Sparse Ruler problem in additive combinatorics. Rédei asked whether the limit exists, which was proved by Erdős and Gál [ErGa48]. Bounds on the limit were improved by Leech [Le56]. The limit is known to lie in the interval $[1.56,\sqrt{3}]$: the lower bound is due to Leech [Le56], the upper bound to Wichmann [Wi63]. Computational evidence by Pegg [Pe20] suggests the upper bound is the truth. A similar question can be asked without the restriction $A\subset\{0,1,\ldots,N\}$.
solved_when: The limit $\lim_{N\to\infty} F(N)/N^{1/2}$ is determined exactly (its existence is already known).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve a classical question in additive combinatorics on the optimal density of difference bases.

title: Erdős problem #172
open: Is it true that in any finite colouring of the natural numbers there exist arbitrarily large finite sets $A$ such that all sums and products of distinct elements of $A$ are the same colour?
status: First asked by Hindman. Hindman [Hi80] proved the statement is false for an infinite $A$ when 7 colours are allowed. In [Er77c] Erdős asks about an infinite $A$ with just 2 colours (see [1198]). Moreira [Mo17] proved that in any finite colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ there exist $x,y$ such that $\{x,x+y,xy\}$ are all the same colour. Alweiss [Al23] proved the finite-set statement in question for $\mathbb{Q}\backslash\{0\}$, and Bowen and Sabok [BoSa22] had earlier proved the first non-trivial case $\lvert A\rvert=2$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every finite colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ admits arbitrarily large finite $A$ with all sums and products of distinct elements monochromatic.

title: Erdős problem #173
open: Must every 2-colouring of the plane contain a monochromatic congruent copy of every triangle, with at most one exception? That is, is it true that in any 2-colouring of $\mathbb{R}^2$, all but at most one triangle $T$ appear monochromatically somewhere in the colouring?
status: The "at most one" allowance is necessary: the colouring by alternating strips shows that for some colourings a single equilateral triangle must be excluded. Shader [Sh76] proved the statement holds when restricted to a single right-angled triangle. References: erdosproblems.com/173; Erdős references: [Er75f,p.108] [Er83c] [Sh76].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that in every 2-colouring of $\mathbb{R}^2$, every triangle except possibly one admits a monochromatic congruent copy — including whether exactly one exception can occur.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles a natural Euclidean Ramsey question about which finite configurations are unavoidable under 2-colouring.

title: Erdős problem #174
open: Which finite configurations of points in Euclidean space are unavoidable in every finite colouring of a sufficiently high-dimensional space? Formally, characterise the Ramsey sets $A\subset\mathbb{R}^n$: those such that for every $k\geq 1$ there is a dimension $d=d(A,k)$ in which any $k$-colouring of $\mathbb{R}^d$ contains a monochromatic copy of $A$.
status: Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus [EGMRSS73] proved that every Ramsey set is spherical, lying on the surface of some sphere. Graham has conjectured that every spherical set is Ramsey, while Leader, Russell, and Walters [LRW12] conjectured instead that a set is Ramsey if and only if it is subtransitive, i.e. embeddable in some higher-dimensional set on which rotations act transitively. Sets known to be Ramsey include the vertices of $k$-dimensional rectangles [EGMRSS73], non-degenerate simplices [FrRo90], trapezoids [Kr92], and regular polygons/polyhedra [Kr91].
solved_when: A complete characterisation of the Ramsey sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is given — equivalently, a proof of Graham's conjecture that every spherical set is Ramsey, or of the Leader–Russell–Walters conjecture that a set is Ramsey if and only if it is subtransitive (or a refutation separating these classes).
why: The problem sits at the heart of Euclidean Ramsey theory, where the basic dichotomy between spherical and non-spherical sets is understood but no candidate characterisation has been settled; a resolution would settle the fundamental question of which geometric configurations are chromatically unavoidable.

title: Erdős problem #176
open: Let $N(k,\ell)$ be the least $N$ such that every two-colouring $f:\{1,\ldots,N\}\to\{-1,1\}$ contains a $k$-term arithmetic progression $P$ with $\left\lvert \sum_{n\in P}f(n)\right\rvert\geq \ell$. How fast does $N(k,\ell)$ grow? In particular, is it true that for every $c>0$ there exists $C>1$ with $N(k,ck)\leq C^k$, and do even the special cases $N(k,2)\leq C^k$ and $N(k,\sqrt{k})\leq C^k$ admit exponential upper bounds?
status: When $\ell=k$ this is the van der Waerden number $W(k)$ (see [138]). Spencer [Sp73] proved that if $k=2^tm$ with $m$ odd then $N(k,1)=2^t(k-1)+1$. Erdős and Graham write that 'no decent bound' is known even for $N(k,2)$. Erdős [Er63d] proved that for every $c>0$, $N(k,ck)>(1+\alpha_c)^k$, where $\alpha_c\to 0$ as $c\to 0$ and $\alpha_c\to \sqrt{2}-1$ as $c\to 1$. Hunter, in the comment section, observes that the local lemma implies $N(k,ck)\gg \frac{2^k}{k^{O(1)}\sum_{i>\frac{1+c}{2}k}\binom{k}{i}}$, so that as $c\to 1$ we have $N(k,ck)\geq (2-o(1))^k$ for all large $k$, where the $o(1)$ term $\to 0$ as $c\to 1$.
solved_when: A proof that for any $c>0$ there is $C>1$ with $N(k,ck)\leq C^k$; or, for the weaker cases, good (ideally exponential $C^k$) upper bounds for $N(k,2)$ and $N(k,\sqrt{k})$.
aliases: Erdős #176; additive combinatorics / arithmetic progressions / discrepancy

title: Erdős problem #181
open: Is the Ramsey number of the $n$-dimensional hypercube at most a constant multiple of its vertex count? Formally, prove that $R(Q_n) \ll 2^n$, where $Q_n$ has $2^n$ vertices and $n2^{n-1}$ edges.
status: Conjectured by Burr and Erdős, although in [Er93] Erdős says the behaviour of $R(Q_n)$ was considered by himself and Sós, who could not decide whether $R(Q_n)/2^n\to \infty$ or not. The trivial bound is $R(Q_n)\leq R(K_{2^n})\leq C^{2^n}$ for some constant $C>1$. This was improved a number of times; the current best bound, due to Tikhomirov [Ti22], is $R(Q_n)\ll 2^{(2-c)n}$ for some small constant $c>0$ (in fact $c\approx 0.03656$ is permissible). This problem is #20 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection. Key works: erdosproblems.com/181; Erdős references: [Er93,p.346] [Er93] [Ti22].
solved_when: A proof that $R(Q_n) \leq C\cdot 2^n$ for some absolute constant $C$ and all $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and resolving it would settle whether the hypercube's Ramsey number is linear in its number of vertices — a basic open question in graph Ramsey theory with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #184
open: Can every graph on $n$ vertices be decomposed into at most $O(n)$ edge-disjoint cycles and edges? Formally, is there a constant $C$ such that every $n$-vertex graph's edge set partitions into at most $Cn$ pieces, each a cycle or a single edge?
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Gallai, who proved that $O(n\log n)$ many cycles and edges suffice (Section 5 of [EGP66]). The graph $K_{3,n-3}$ shows that at least $(1+c)n$ many are required for some constant $c>0$. In [Er71], Erdős suggests that only $n-1$ many cycles and edges are required if they need not be edge-disjoint. The best bound is due to Bucić and Montgomery [BM22], who prove that $O(n\log^* n)$ cycles and edges suffice, where $\log^*$ is the iterated logarithm. Conlon, Fox, and Sudakov [CFS14] proved that $O_\epsilon(n)$ cycles and edges suffice if $G$ has minimum degree at least $\epsilon n$, for any $\epsilon>0$. See also [583] for the analogous problem of decomposing into paths, and [1017] for decomposing into complete graphs.
solved_when: A proof that some absolute constant $C$ makes $Cn$ cycles and edges suffice for every $n$-vertex graph (or a construction showing more than linear is needed).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; settling it resolves a decades-old question on the linear structure of cycle decompositions.

title: Erdős problem #187
open: What is the best possible function $f(d)$ guaranteeing that, in any 2-colouring of the integers, some colour class contains an arithmetic progression of common difference $d$ and length $f(d)$, for infinitely many $d$?
status: Originally asked by Cohen. Erdős observed that the colouring according to whether $\{\sqrt{2}n\}<1/2$ or not implies $f(d)\ll d$ (using the fact that $\|\sqrt{2}q\|\gg 1/q$ for all $q$, where $\|x\|$ is the distance to the nearest integer). In [Er80] he states that Petruska and Szemerédi proved $f(d)\ll d^{1/2}$, and he expected $f(d)\leq d^{o(1)}$. Beck [Be80] improved this via the probabilistic method, constructing a colouring showing $f(d)\leq (1+o(1))\log_2 d$. Van der Waerden's theorem implies $f(d)\to\infty$ is necessary. Key works: erdosproblems.com/187; Erdős references: [Er73] [Er80,p.93] [Er80].
solved_when: The optimal asymptotic behaviour of $f(d)$ is determined — in particular, whether Erdős's expectation $f(d)\leq d^{o(1)}$ holds, and how this compares against the known colouring upper bounds $f(d)\leq (1+o(1))\log_2 d$ and the necessary divergence $f(d)\to\infty$ from van der Waerden's theorem.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a sharp answer would resolve a long-standing question in Ramsey theory on arithmetic progressions.
aliases: Erdős #187; additive combinatorics / ramsey theory / arithmetic progressions

title: Erdős problem #188
open: What is the smallest $k$ such that the plane admits a red/blue colouring with no two red points at unit distance apart and no $k$-term blue arithmetic progression whose common difference is $1$?
status: Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus [EGMRSS75] proved $k\geq 5$, and Tsaturian [Ts17] improved this to $k\geq 6$. Erdős and Graham claimed $k\leq 10000000$ ('more or less') but gave no proof. Their original question asked for any blue $k$-term arithmetic progression (not necessarily with common difference $1$), but Alon observed no such $k$ exists: in any red/blue colouring of the integer points on a line, either two red points are distance $1$ apart, or the blue set together with its shift by $1$ covers all integers, so van der Waerden's theorem yields arbitrarily long blue arithmetic progressions. From context, Erdős and Graham most likely intended the blue progression to have common difference $1$, though they did not state this restriction in their papers.
solved_when: The exact value of $k$ is determined; in particular, whether some finite $k$ (Erdős and Graham suggested $k\leq 10000000$, 'more or less', without proof) suffices.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #195
open: What is the largest $k$ such that every permutation of $\mathbb{Z}$ must contain a monotone $k$-term arithmetic progression $x_1<\cdots<x_k$?
status: Geneson [Ge19] proved that $k\leq 5$, and Adenwalla [Ad22] improved this to $k\leq 4$. See also problems [194] and [196].
solved_when: The exact value of this largest $k$ is determined.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and its full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/195.

title: Erdős problem #196
open: Must every permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ contain a monotone 4-term arithmetic progression? That is, given a permutation $x$ of $\mathbb{N}$, must there exist indices satisfying either $i<j<k<l$ or $i>j>k>l$ such that $x_i,x_j,x_k,x_l$ form an arithmetic progression?
status: Davis, Entringer, Graham, and Simmons [DEGS77] have shown that every permutation must contain a monotone 3-term arithmetic progression, while a permutation need not contain a 5-term arithmetic progression. See also [194] and [195].
solved_when: A proof that every permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ contains a monotone 4-term arithmetic progression as defined above, or an explicit permutation of $\mathbb{N}$ avoiding all monotone 4-term arithmetic progressions.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it completes the picture of which monotone arithmetic progressions are unavoidable in permutations.

title: Erdős problem #197
open: Can the natural numbers be split into two sets such that each set admits a permutation avoiding monotone 3-term arithmetic progressions? If three sets are allowed, such a partition is known to exist.
status: Open. It is known that if three sets are allowed, such a partition is possible; the case of two sets remains unresolved.
solved_when: A partition of $\mathbb{N}$ into two sets is exhibited, each of which can be permuted so as to contain no monotone 3-term arithmetic progression.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and a resolution would close a long-standing entry in his problem list, which is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com (see erdosproblems.com/197).

title: Erdős problem #200
open: Does the longest arithmetic progression consisting entirely of primes in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ have length $o(\log N)$? In other words, is the upper bound of about $\log N$ on such progressions far from tight?
status: It follows from the prime number theorem that such a progression has length $\leq(1+o(1))\log N$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the maximal length of an arithmetic progression of primes in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is $o(\log N)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would settle a long-standing question about how long prime arithmetic progressions can be.

title: Erdős problem #201
open: How large a progression-free subset must every set of $N$ integers contain? Formally, if $G_k(N)$ is the largest integer such that any set of $N$ integers has a subset of size at least $G_k(N)$ with no $k$-term arithmetic progression, determine the size of $G_k(N)$ and how it relates to $R_k(N)$, the size of the largest subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ without a $k$-term arithmetic progression — in particular, is it true that $\lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{R_3(N)}{G_3(N)}=1$?
status: First asked and investigated by Riddell [Ri69]. It is trivial that $G_k(N)\leq R_k(N)$, and it is possible that $G_k(N) < R_k(N)$: for example $G_3(5)=3$ while $R_3(5)=4$, and $G_3(14)\leq 7$ while $R_3(14)=8$. Komlós, Sulyok, and Szemerédi [KSS75] have shown that $R_k(N) \ll_k G_k(N)$.
solved_when: The asymptotic size of $G_k(N)$ is determined, and the relationship to $R_k(N)$ is resolved — in particular, the limit $\lim_{N\to\infty} R_3(N)/G_3(N)$ is shown to equal $1$ (or some other value).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would clarify whether arbitrary integer sets can be forced to contain nearly progression-free subsets as large as those found in the initial interval.

title: Erdős problem #203
open: Does there exist an integer $m\geq 1$ with $(m,6)=1$ such that none of the numbers $2^k3^\ell m+1$ are prime, for any $k,\ell\geq 0$?
status: Positive odd integers $m$ such that none of $2^km+1$ are prime are called Sierpinski numbers — see [1113] for more details. Erdős and Graham also ask more generally about $p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_r^{k_r}m+1$ for distinct primes $p_i$, or $q_1\cdots q_rm+1$ where the $q_i$ are primes congruent to $1\pmod{4}$. (Dogmachine has noted in the comments this latter question has the trivial answer $m=1$ — perhaps some condition such as $m$ even is meant.)
solved_when: An explicit integer $m\geq 1$ coprime to 6 is produced (or its nonexistence proved) such that $2^k3^\ell m+1$ is composite for all $k,\ell\geq 0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it probes the limits of Sierpiński-type phenomena when two prime powers are allowed in the multiplier.

title: Erdős problem #208
open: How small are the gaps between consecutive squarefree numbers? In other words, if $s_1<s_2<\cdots$ is the increasing sequence of squarefree numbers, is it true that, for any $\epsilon>0$ and large $n$, $s_{n+1}-s_n \ll_\epsilon s_n^{\epsilon}$, and even that $s_{n+1}-s_n \leq (1+o(1))\frac{\pi^2}{6}\frac{\log s_n}{\log\log s_n}$?
status: Erdős [Er51] showed that there are infinitely many $n$ with $s_{n+1}-s_n > (1+o(1))\frac{\pi^2}{6}\frac{\log s_n}{\log\log s_n}$, so this bound would be best possible. In [Er79] Erdős says perhaps $s_{n+1}-s_n \ll \log s_n$, but he is 'very doubtful'. Filaseta and Trifonov [FiTr92] proved an upper bound of $s_n^{1/5+o(1)}$, and Pandey [Pa24] improved the exponent to $1/5-c$ for some constant $c>0$. Granville [Gr98] showed that $s_{n+1}-s_n\ll_\epsilon s_n^\epsilon$ for all $\epsilon>0$ follows from the ABC conjecture. See also [489] and [145]; a more general form of this problem is given in [1101].
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved) that $s_{n+1}-s_n \ll_\epsilon s_n^{\epsilon}$ for every $\epsilon>0$ and all large $n$, and in particular whether the sharp bound $s_{n+1}-s_n \leq (1+o(1))\frac{\pi^2}{6}\frac{\log s_n}{\log\log s_n}$ holds.
why: A positive answer would settle one of Erdős's personally posed problems on the distribution of squarefree numbers, giving essentially optimal control on their gaps; the problem is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/208.

title: Erdős problem #212
open: Is there a dense subset of the plane in which every pairwise distance is rational? Equivalently, does there exist a dense set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ such that the distance between any two points of $S$ is a rational number?
status: The conjecture is attributed to Ulam, while Erdős believed no such set exists. Terence Tao, in a blogpost, showed that no such set exists assuming the Bombieri–Lang conjecture; Shaffaf [Sh18] independently obtained the same conclusion. In fact, Shaffaf and Tao proved that any such rational distance set must be contained in a finite union of real algebraic curves. Solymosi and de Zeeuw [SdZ10] then proved unconditionally that a rational distance set contained in a real algebraic curve must be finite, unless the curve contains a line or a circle. Ascher, Braune, and Turchet [ABT20] observed that, combined, these facts imply that a rational distance set in general position must be finite, conditional on the Bombieri–Lang conjecture. In [Er87b] Erdős mentions that Besicovitch conjectured that the limit points of a rational distance set cannot contain arbitrarily large convex sets.
solved_when: A dense subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ with all pairwise distances rational is exhibited, or it is proved that no such set exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would settle a long-standing question at the intersection of combinatorial geometry and Diophantine geometry.

title: Erdős problem #213
open: For some $n\geq 4$, do there exist $n$ points in the plane, with no three on a line and no four on a circle, such that all pairwise distances between them are integers?
status: Anning and Erdős [AnEr45] proved that no infinite such set exists. Harborth constructed such a set for $n=5$, and the best construction to date, due to Kreisel and Kurz [KK08], has $n=7$. Ascher, Braune, and Turchet [ABT20] showed, conditional on the Bombieri–Lang conjecture, that there is a uniform upper bound on the size of such a set. Greenfeld, Iliopoulou, and Peluse [GIP24] proved unconditionally that any such set must be very sparse: if $S\subseteq [-N,N]^2$ has no three on a line, no four on a circle, and all pairwise distances integers, then $|S| \ll (\log N)^{O(1)}$. See also [130].
solved_when: Such a set is exhibited for any $n\geq 4$ (or the nonexistence of any such set is proved).

title: Erdős problem #217
open: For which $n$ does there exist a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, with no three on a line and no four on a circle, that determines exactly $n-1$ distinct distances, arranged so that (in some ordering of the distances) the $i$th distance occurs exactly $i$ times?
status: An example with $n=4$ is an isosceles triangle with the point in the centre. Erdős originally believed this was impossible for $n\geq 5$, but Pomerance constructed a set with $n=5$ (see [Er83c] for a description). Palásti [Pa87] constructed such a set with $n=7$. According to [Pa89], when Erdős saw this he asked whether there exists such a set of $5$ points with no equilateral triangles; Palásti [Pa89] constructed a set of $n=6$ points satisfying these restrictions, with no equilateral triangles. Palásti [Pa89b] has constructed a set with $n=8$. Erdős believed this is impossible for all sufficiently large $n$. This would follow from $h(n)\geq n$ for sufficiently large $n$, where $h(n)$ is as in [98].
solved_when: The set of such $n$ is characterized — either a construction is given for infinitely many (or all sufficiently large) $n$, or it is proved that no such configuration exists for all sufficiently large $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and a resolution would settle his belief that such configurations are impossible for all sufficiently large $n$.

title: Erdős problem #218
open: When one prime gap is compared with the next, are increases and decreases equally common — and do equal consecutive gaps occur infinitely often? Formally, writing $d_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$, the set of $n$ with $d_{n+1}\geq d_n$ should have density $1/2$ (and likewise for $d_{n+1}\leq d_n$), and there should be infinitely many $n$ with $d_{n+1}=d_n$.
status: In [Er85c] Erdős also conjectures that $d_n=d_{n+1}=\cdots=d_{n+k}$ is solvable for every $k$, which is equivalent to $k$ consecutive primes in arithmetic progression (see [141]). Banks [Ba23] has given a heuristic argument, assuming a quantitative form of the prime tuples conjecture, that the first statement is true, and in fact that for any $c\geq 0$ and $\epsilon>0$ the number of $n$ such that $p_n\leq x$ and $d_{n+1}\geq cd_n$ is $\frac{\pi(x)}{c+1}+O\left(\frac{x}{(\log x)^{3/2+\epsilon}}\right)$.
solved_when: It is proved that both $\{n: d_{n+1}\geq d_n\}$ and $\{n: d_{n+1}\leq d_n\}$ have natural density $1/2$, and that $d_{n+1}=d_n$ for infinitely many $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and settling it would resolve the basic statistical question of whether consecutive prime gaps behave symmetrically under comparison with their neighbors — a natural refinement of results showing that prime gaps infinitely often increase and infinitely often decrease.

title: Erdős problem #222
open: Let $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ be the sequence of integers representable as a sum of two squares. How large can the consecutive differences $n_{k+1}-n_k$ be, and how small must they be bounded — that is, find good upper and lower bounds for these gaps?
status: Erdős [Er51] proved that, for infinitely many $k$, $n_{k+1}-n_k \gg \frac{\log n_k}{\sqrt{\log\log n_k}}$. Richards [Ri82] improved this to $\limsup_{k\to\infty} \frac{n_{k+1}-n_k}{\log n_k} \geq 1/4$. This constant has since been improved, most recently to $0.868\cdots$ by Dietmann, Elsholtz, Kalmynin, Konyagin, and Maynard [DEKKM22]. The best known upper bound is due to Bambah and Chowla [BaCh47], who proved $n_{k+1}-n_k \ll n_k^{1/4}$. The differences are listed at A256435 on the OEIS.
solved_when: Sharp upper and lower bounds for $n_{k+1}-n_k$ are established; at minimum, an improvement over the current bounds, namely the lower bound $\limsup_{k\to\infty} (n_{k+1}-n_k)/\log n_k \geq 0.868\cdots$ and the upper bound $n_{k+1}-n_k \ll n_k^{1/4}$.

title: Erdős problem #233
open: How large can the squares of consecutive prime gaps get on average? Formally, prove that $\sum_{1\leq n\leq N} d_n^2 \ll N(\log N)^2$, where $d_n = p_{n+1}-p_n$ and $p_n$ is the $n$th prime.
status: Cramér [Cr36] proved an upper bound of $O(N(\log N)^4)$ conditional on the Riemann hypothesis. Selberg [Se43] improved this slightly (still assuming the Riemann hypothesis) to $\sum_{1\leq n\leq N} d_n^2/n \ll (\log N)^4$. The prime number theorem immediately implies the matching lower bound $\sum_{1\leq n\leq N} d_n^2 \gg N(\log N)^2$, so the conjectured bound is best possible. The problem is discussed as A8 in Guy's collection [Gu04], the values of the sum are listed at A074741 in the OEIS, and it is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/233.
solved_when: A proof (unconditionally) that $\sum_{1\leq n\leq N} d_n^2 \ll N(\log N)^2$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; a solution would in particular yield $d_n \ll n^{1/2}\log n$ for all $n$, unconditionally — a bound currently known only under the Riemann Hypothesis.

title: Erdős problem #234
open: Does the density $f(c)$ of integers $n$ for which $\frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{\log n} < c$ exist for every $c \geq 0$, and if so, is it a continuous function of $c$?
status: Open. See also [5]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/234; Erdős references: [Er55c] [Er61].
solved_when: The density $f(c)$ is proven to exist for every $c \geq 0$ and to be continuous as a function of $c$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would settle a classical question on the distribution of normalized prime gaps.

title: Erdős problem #236
open: Let $f(n)$ count the number of representations of $n$ as $p+2^k$ with $p$ prime and $k\geq 0$. Is it true that $f(n)=o(\log n)$?
status: Erdős [Er50] proved that there are infinitely many $n$ such that $f(n)\gg \log\log n$. Erdős could not even prove that there do not exist infinitely many integers $n$ such that for all $1< 2^k<n$ the number $n-2^k$ is prime — see [1142]. The sequence of values of $f(n)$ is A109925 on the OEIS. See also [237]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/236; Erdős references: [Er55c] [Er61] [Er77c] [Er50].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $f(n)=o(\log n)$ as $n\to\infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a basic question about how often shifted powers of two can hit primes.

title: Erdős problem #238
open: Are there arbitrarily long strings of well-spaced consecutive primes? Given constants $c_1,c_2>0$, is it true that for all sufficiently large $x$ one can find more than $c_1\log x$ consecutive primes $\leq x$ such that the difference between any two of them exceeds $c_2$?
status: Erdős [Er49c] proved the statement is true for any $c_2>0$ provided $c_1>0$ is sufficiently small (depending on $c_2$); the case of general $c_1$ remains open. Key works: erdosproblems.com/238; Erdős references: [Er55c,p.7] [Er49c].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, for any $c_1,c_2>0$, the stated configuration exists for all sufficiently large $x$: more than $c_1\log x$ consecutive primes $\leq x$ with pairwise differences $>c_2$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a classical question on the distribution and spacing of consecutive primes.

title: Erdős problem #241
open: How large can a set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be if all its three-term sums $a+b+c$ are distinct apart from the trivial coincidences? Is the maximum size $f(N)$ asymptotic to $N^{1/3}$?
status: The problem was originally asked to Erdős by Bose. Bose and Chowla [BoCh62] gave a construction proving $(1+o(1))N^{1/3}\leq f(N)$. The best known upper bound is due to Green [Gr01]: $f(N)\leq ((7/2)^{1/3}+o(1))N^{1/3}$, where $(7/2)^{1/3}\approx 1.519$. The general Bose–Chowla conjecture — that $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with all $r$-fold sums distinct (aside from trivial coincidences) satisfies $|A|\sim N^{1/r}$ — is known only for $r=2$ (see [30]). The problem is discussed as C11 in Guy's collection [Gu04], and its full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/241 (Erdős references: [Er61] [Er69] [Er70b] [Er70c] [Er73] [Er77c] [Er80,p.99] [Gr01]).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $f(N)\sim N^{1/3}$; equivalently, an upper bound improving Green's constant $(7/2)^{1/3}\approx 1.519$ down to $1+o(1)$, matching the Bose–Chowla lower bound $(1+o(1))N^{1/3}$.
why: Resolving it would settle one of Erdős's personally posed problems (carrying a $100 prize), and is the $r=3$ case of the Bose–Chowla conjecture that sets with distinct $r$-fold sums have size $\sim N^{1/r}$, known only for $r=2$.

title: Erdős problem #242
open: Can every rational number of the form $4/n$ with $n>2$ be written as the sum of three distinct unit fractions? That is, do there always exist distinct integers $1\leq x<y<z$ such that $\frac{4}{n} = \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}$?
status: The Erdős-Straus conjecture. Perhaps the first place it appears in the literature is in a paper of Obláth [Ob50] (submitted in 1948), which describes it as a conjecture of Erdős. A representation of $4/n$ as the sum of at most four distinct unit fractions follows trivially from a greedy algorithm. Schinzel conjectured (see [Si56]) the generalisation that, for any fixed $a$, if $n$ is sufficiently large in terms of $a$ then there exist distinct integers $1\leq x<y<z$ such that $\frac{a}{n} = \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}$; when $a=5$ this conjecture is due to Sierpiński [Si56]. For more background and results on this generalisation see Pomerance and Weingartner [PoWe25]. It suffices to prove the conjecture when $n$ is prime, and it has been verified for all $n\leq 10^{18}$ [MiDu25]. Obláth [Ob50] noted it is true if $n+1$ is divisible by a prime $\equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, which implies almost all $n$ have the required decomposition. Arguing via parametric solutions, Mordell [Mo69] proved it for all $n$ except those congruent to one of $\{1,121,169,289,361,529\}$ modulo $840$, and Terzi [Te71] extended this.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every $n>2$ there exist distinct integers $1\leq x<y<z$ with $\frac{4}{n} = \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}$; it suffices to establish this when $n$ is prime.
why: This is the Erdős–Straus conjecture, one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve a foundational question on unit-fraction decompositions and the Schinzel-type generalizations built on it.

title: Erdős problem #243
open: Must a rapidly growing integer sequence whose reciprocal sum is rational and whose ratios satisfy $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n/a_{n-1}^2 = 1$ eventually follow Sylvester's recurrence? Formally, if $1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots$, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}^2}=1$, and $\sum\frac{1}{a_n}\in\mathbb{Q}$, must $a_n = a_{n-1}^2-a_{n-1}+1$ hold for all sufficiently large $n\geq 1$?
status: Erdős and Straus [ErSt64] proved that if $\lim a_n/a_{n-1}^2=1$ and $\sum 1/a_n$ is rational while $a_n$ does not satisfy the recurrence, then $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{[a_1,\ldots,a_n]}{a_{n+1}}\left(\frac{a_n^2}{a_{n+1}}-1\right)>0$. A sequence satisfying $a_n = a_{n-1}^2-a_{n-1}+1$ is known as Sylveter's sequence. Duverney [Du01] proved a weaker version: if $\sum_{n\geq 0}\left(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n^2}-1\right)$ converges, then $\sum 1/a_n$ is rational if and only if $a_n = a_{n-1}^2-a_{n-1}+1$ for all large $n$.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given showing that under the hypotheses $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n/a_{n-1}^2 = 1$ and $\sum 1/a_n \in \mathbb{Q}$, the recurrence $a_n = a_{n-1}^2 - a_{n-1} + 1$ holds for all sufficiently large $n$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would clarify when rationality of such reciprocal sums forces exact Sylvester-type growth.

title: Erdős problem #244
open: For a fixed real $C>1$, must the integers representable as $p+\lfloor C^k\rfloor$ — a prime plus a power-like sequence term — make up a set of positive density? Erdős conjectured yes.
status: The problem was originally asked to Erdős by Kalmár, and Erdős believed the answer is yes. Romanoff [Ro34] proved the answer is yes when $C$ is an integer. Ding [Di25] proved it for almost all $C>1$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every $C>1$ the set $\{p+\lfloor C^k\rfloor : p \text{ prime}, k\ge 0\}$ has positive density; equivalently, extending Romanoff's theorem from integer $C$ to arbitrary real $C>1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (#244), originally raised by Kalmár, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a classical question on primes plus lacunary sequences.

title: Erdős problem #247
open: If $1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots$ is a sequence of integers with $\limsup \frac{a_n}{n}=\infty$, must the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^{a_n}}$ be transcendental?
status: Erdős [Er75c] proved the answer is yes under the stronger condition that $\limsup n_k/k^t=\infty$ for all $t\geq 1$. Erdős [Er88c] remarks that 'many of these problems seem hopeless at present, but perhaps one can prove that if $a_n>cn^2$ then $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^{a_n}}$ is not the root of any quadratic polynomial'. The problem has been formalised in Lean as part of the Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures project. Key works: erdosproblems.com/247; Erdős references: [Er88c,p.106] [Er75c] [Er88c].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every strictly increasing integer sequence with $\limsup \frac{a_n}{n}=\infty$ yields a transcendental value of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^{a_n}}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and sits at the interface of Diophantine approximation and transcendence theory for lacunary binary expansions.

title: Erdős problem #249
open: Is the sum $\sum_n \frac{\phi(n)}{2^n}$, where $\phi$ is the Euler totient function, an irrational number?
status: The decimal expansion of this sum is recorded as sequence A256936 in the OEIS. The problem is referenced in Erdős's works [Er88c, p. 102] and tracked at erdosproblems.com/249.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the irrationality of $\sum_n \frac{\phi(n)}{2^n}$ is established.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a concrete entry in that famous problem collection.

title: Erdős problem #251
open: Is the sum $\sum \frac{p_n}{2^n}$ irrational, where $p_n$ denotes the $n$th prime?
status: Erdős [Er58b] proved that $\sum \frac{p_n^k}{n!}$ is irrational for every $k\geq 1$. In [Er88c] he further conjectures that $\sum \frac{p_n^k}{2^n}$ is irrational for every $k$, and that if $g_n\geq 2$ and $g_n=o(p_n)$ then $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{p_n}{g_1\cdots g_n}$ is irrational. (The example $g_n=p_n+1$ shows that some condition on the growth of the $g_n$ is necessary here.) The decimal expansion of this sum is A098990 on the OEIS.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the irrationality of $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{p_n}{2^n}$.

title: Erdős problem #252
open: For a fixed integer $k\geq 1$, is the series $\sum \frac{\sigma_k(n)}{n!}$, where $\sigma_k(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d^k$, irrational? The question is whether the sum of the generalized divisor function weighted by reciprocal factorials always fails to be rational.
status: Irrationality is known for $1\leq k\leq 4$. The cases $k=1,2$ are reasonably straightforward, as observed by Erdős [Er52]. The case $k=3$ was proved independently by Schlage-Puchta [ScPu06] and Friedlander, Luca, and Stoiciu [FLC07]. The case $k=4$ was proved by Pratt [Pr22]. The sum is known to be irrational for all $k\geq 1$ conditional on either Schinzel's conjecture (Schlage-Puchta [ScPu06]) or Dickson's conjecture (Friedlander, Luca, and Stoiciu [FLC07]). The problem is discussed as problem B14 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: The series is proven irrational for every integer $k\geq 1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and its history and progress are tracked at erdosproblems.com/252.

title: Erdős problem #254
open: Suppose $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ satisfies $\lvert A\cap [1,2x]\rvert -\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert \to \infty$ as $x\to\infty$ and $\sum_{n\in A}\{\theta n\}=\infty$ for every $\theta\in (0,1)$, where $\{x\}$ denotes the distance of $x$ from the nearest integer. Must every sufficiently large integer be expressible as a sum of distinct elements of $A$?
status: Cassels [Ca60] proved the analogous conclusion under stronger hypotheses: $\lim \frac{\lvert A\cap[1,2x]\rvert-\lvert A\cap[1,x]\rvert}{\log\log x}=\infty$ and $\sum_{n\in A}\{\theta n\}^2=\infty$ for every $\theta\in(0,1)$.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the statement that every set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ satisfying the two hypotheses above has the property that all sufficiently large integers are sums of distinct elements of $A$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a natural question on when sparse sequences are complete under additive-combinatorial density and equidistribution conditions.

title: Erdős problem #256
open: Given integers $1\leq a_1\leq\cdots\leq a_n$, how large must $\max_{|z|=1}\left|\prod_i(1-z^{a_i})\right|$ be? If $f(n)$ denotes the maximal such guaranteed value over all choices of the $a_i$, determine the growth of $f(n)$ — in particular, does $\log f(n)\gg n^c$ hold for some constant $c>0$?
status: Erdős and Szekeres [ErSz59] proved $\lim f(n)^{1/n}=1$ and $f(n)>\sqrt{2n}$. Erdős proved probabilistically that $\log f(n)\ll n^{1-c}$ for some constant $c>0$. Atkinson [At61] showed $\log f(n)\ll n^{1/2}\log n$, improved by Odlyzko [Od82] to $\log f(n)\ll n^{1/3}(\log n)^{4/3}$. For the variant $f^*(n)$ with strictly increasing $a_1<\cdots<a_n$, Bourgain and Chang [BoCh18] proved $\log f^*(n)\ll (n\log n)^{1/2}\log\log n$. Atkinson [At61] noted the connection to the Chowla cosine problem [510]: if for any set of $n$ integers $A$ there exists $\theta$ with $\sum_{n\in A}\cos(n\theta)<-M_n$, then $\log f^*(n)\ll M_n\log n$. The specific question asked is answered negatively: Belov and Konyagin [BeKo96] proved $\log f(n)\ll(\log n)^4$.
solved_when: The order of $\log f(n)$ is determined up to constant factors; the specific question is resolved by proving or disproving that $\log f(n)\gg n^c$ for some constant $c>0$ (this particular assertion is now known to be false, per Belov–Konyagin).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems with a fully tracked history, and it is tied to the Chowla cosine problem, so progress here feeds directly into that classical question.

title: Erdős problem #257
open: Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set. Is $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-1}$ always irrational?
status: If $A=\mathbb{N}$ the series equals $\sum_{n}\frac{\tau(n)}{2^n}$, where $\tau(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n$, which Erdős [Er48] proved is irrational. In general, if $f_A(n)$ counts the number of divisors of $n$ which are elements of $A$, then $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-1}=\sum_n \frac{f_A(n)}{2^n}$. The case when $A$ is the set of primes is [69]. This case (and when $A$ is the set of prime powers) was settled in the affirmative by Tao and Teräväinen [TaTe25]. Erdős [Er68d] proved this sum is irrational whenever $(a,b)=1$ for all $a\neq b\in A$ and $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}<\infty$, and thought that the condition $(a,b)=1$ could be dropped by complicating his proof. There is nothing special about $2$ here, and this sum is likely irrational with $2$ replaced by any integer $t\geq 2$. In [Er88c] Erdős goes further and speculates that $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-t_n}$ is irrational for every infinite set $A$ and bounded sequence $t_n$ (presumably of integers, and presumably excluding the case when $t_n=0$ for all $n$). This was disproved by Kovač and Tao [KoTa24], and in the comments Kovač has sketched a proof that there exists some choice of $t_n$ with $1\leq t_n$ (as given in the record).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given for every infinite $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ that $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{2^n-1}$ is irrational; the natural extension asks the same with $2$ replaced by any integer $t\geq 2$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles a basic question about the arithmetic nature of Lambert-type series.

title: Erdős problem #260
open: If $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ is an increasing integer sequence with $a_n/n\to\infty$, must the sum $\sum_n a_n/2^{a_n}$ be irrational?
status: Erdős [Er81l] proved the sum is irrational under the stronger assumptions $a_{n+1}-a_n\to\infty$ or $a_n \gg n\sqrt{\log n\log\log n}$. Erdős and Graham speculate that $\limsup a_{n+1}-a_n=\infty$ is not sufficient, but know of no example. In [Va99] the question is asked with $a_n/n\to\infty$ replaced by $a_{n+1}-a_n\to\infty$, which as above was proved by Erdős in [Er81l].
solved_when: A proof that $\sum_n a_n/2^{a_n}$ is irrational for every increasing sequence with $a_n/n\to\infty$ (or a counterexample sequence satisfying that growth condition for which the sum is rational).
why: Resolving it would settle one of Erdős's personally posed problems, completing the picture of how much growth of $(a_n)$ beyond linear forces irrationality of such binary sums.

title: Erdős problem #261
open: Are there infinitely many $n$ for which $\frac{n}{2^n}$ can be written as a finite sum of distinct terms $\frac{a_k}{2^{a_k}}$ with $t\geq 2$ and distinct integers $a_1,\ldots,a_t\geq 1$ — and is this in fact true for every $n$? Separately, is there a rational $x$ such that the equation $x = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{a_k}{2^{a_k}}$ has at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ solutions?
status: The problem sits in number theory and is related to [260]. In [Er88c] Erdős notes that Cusick had a simple proof that infinitely many such $n$ do exist, though Erdős does not record the argument; a later paper by Borwein and Loring [BoLo90] supplies the proof that for every positive integer $m$, taking $n=2^{m+1}-m-2$ gives $\frac{n}{2^n}=\sum_{n<k\leq n+m}\frac{k}{2^k}$. Tengely, Ulas, and Zygadlo [TUZ20] verified that all $n\leq 10000$ have the required property. In [Er88c] Erdős weakened the second question to asking merely for a rational $x$ with two solutions.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that infinitely many such $n$ exist — already known, so the criterion is sharpened to: a determination of whether all $n$ have the property, and a proof (or disproof) of the existence of a rational $x$ with at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ solutions to the infinite sum equation.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it completes a question he returned to across multiple papers.

title: Erdős problem #263
open: Is there a sequence $a_n$ so robustly "irrationality-producing" that any sequence $b_n$ asymptotic to it still yields an irrational sum $\sum 1/b_n$ — and does $a_n = 2^{2^n}$ have this property? More generally, must any increasing sequence with this property grow faster than exponentially, i.e. must $a_n^{1/n}\to\infty$?
status: This is one possible definition of an "irrationality sequence" (see also [262] and [264]). A folklore result states that $\sum 1/a_n$ is irrational whenever $\lim a_n^{1/2^n} = \infty$. Kovač and Tao [KoTa24] proved that any strictly increasing sequence with $\sum 1/a_n$ convergent and $\lim a_{n+1}/a_n^2 = 0$ is not such an irrationality sequence; on the other hand, if $\liminf \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n^{2+\epsilon}} > 0$ for some $\epsilon > 0$, the folklore result implies it is one. The problem was originally stated without the assumption that the sequence be increasing, and DeepMind gave a counterexample without that assumption (see the comments). Koizumi [Ko25c] proved that $a_n = \lfloor \alpha^{2^n} \rfloor$ is an irrationality sequence of this type for all but countably many $\alpha > 1$.
solved_when: It is determined whether $a_n = 2^{2^n}$ has the stated property, or whether every increasing sequence $(a_n)$ with the property — that every $b_n$ with $b_n/a_n \to 1$ gives an irrational $\sum 1/b_n$ — satisfies $a_n^{1/n}\to\infty$ (or a counterexample is produced).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a basic question about how fast a sequence must grow to force irrationality of all its asymptotic copies.

title: Erdős problem #264
open: Do the sequences $a_n=2^n$ and $a_n=n!$ have the property that for every bounded sequence of nonzero integers $b_n$ (with $a_n+b_n\neq 0$), the sum $\sum \frac{1}{a_n+b_n}$ is irrational? Equivalently, are they irrationality sequences in the sense of Erdős?
status: This is a possible definition of an 'irrationality sequence' (see also [262] and [263]). One example is $a_n=2^{2^n}$. In [ErGr80] they also ask whether such a sequence can have polynomial growth, but Erdős later retracted this in [Er88c], claiming 'It is not hard to show that it cannot increase slower than exponentially'. Kovač and Tao [KoTa24] have proved that $2^n$ is not such an irrationality sequence. More generally, they prove that any strictly increasing sequence of positive integers such that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ converges and $\liminf (a_n^2 \sum_{k>n} \frac{1}{a_k^2}) > 0$ is not such an irrationality sequence; in particular, any strictly increasing sequence with $\limsup a_{n+1}/a_n < \infty$ is not. On the other hand, they prove that for any function $F$ with $\lim F(n+1)/F(n)=\infty$ there exists such an irrationality sequence with $a_n \sim F(n)$.
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved) that $a_n=2^n$, and separately that $a_n=n!$, is an irrationality sequence in the above sense.
why: A solution would sharpen the boundary, currently drawn by Kovač and Tao, between growth rates that permit and forbid such sequences, resolving one of Erdős's personally posed problems tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #265
open: How fast can an increasing sequence of integers $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ grow if both $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ and $\sum \frac{1}{a_n-1}$ are rational? In particular, what is the precise doubly exponential growth exponent that such a sequence can achieve — can one have $\limsup a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$?
status: Cantor observed that $a_n = \binom{n}{2}$ is such a sequence. Replacing $-1$ by a different constant admits higher degree polynomials: for $\sum_{n\geq 2}\frac{1}{a_n}$ and $\sum_{n\geq 2}\frac{1}{a_n-12}$, the sequence $a_n = n^3 + 6n^2 + 5n$ makes both series rational. Erdős believed $a_n^{1/n} \to \infty$ is possible but $a_n^{1/2^n} \to 1$ is necessary. This has been almost completely solved by Kovač and Tao [KoTa24], who prove that such a sequence can grow doubly exponentially: there exists such a sequence with $a_n^{1/\beta^n} \to \infty$ for some $\beta > 1$. It remains open whether one can achieve $\limsup a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$. A folklore result states that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ is irrational whenever $\lim a_n^{1/2^n} = \infty$, so such a sequence cannot grow faster than doubly exponentially — the remaining question is the precise exponent possible.
solved_when: A construction is given of such a sequence with $\limsup a_n^{1/2^n} > 1$; more broadly, determining the optimal exponent of doubly exponential growth possible for sequences with both series rational.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would settle the exact growth boundary between the known doubly-exponential constructions and the folklore irrationality barrier.

title: Erdős problem #267
open: If $(n_k)$ is a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers whose growth is at least geometric, meaning $n_{k+1}/n_k \geq c$ for some fixed $c>1$, must the subseries $\sum_k 1/F_{n_k}$ of reciprocal Fibonacci numbers be irrational?
status: It may be sufficient to have $n_k/k\to\infty$. Good [Go74] and Bicknell and Hoggatt [BiHo76] have shown that $\sum 1/F_{2^n}$ is irrational — in fact, it equals $(7-\sqrt{5})/2$. Badea [Ba87] proved that $\sum 1/F_{2^n+1}$ is irrational. The full sum $\sum 1/F_n$ was proved irrational by André-Jeannin [An89]. The main problem has been proved for $c\geq 2$ by Badea [Ba93]; it remains open for $1<c<2$.
solved_when: A proof that $\sum_k 1/F_{n_k}$ is irrational for every increasing sequence with $n_{k+1}/n_k \geq c>1$, or a counterexample; in particular, the case $1<c<2$ is resolved.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would clarify how sparseness of a subsequence of Fibonacci indices alone forces irrationality of the corresponding reciprocal sum.

title: Erdős problem #269
open: Let $P$ be a finite set of primes with $|P|\geq 2$, and let $\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ be the set of natural numbers all of whose prime divisors lie in $P$. Is the sum $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{[a_1,\ldots,a_n]}$, where $[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ denotes the lowest common multiple of $a_1,\ldots,a_n$, irrational?
status: If $P$ is infinite the sum is always irrational; Erdős says this is a "simple exercise" in [Er88c,p.106]. The problem was posed by Erdős in a letter to the editor written January 1st 1973, published in issue 12 of the Fibonacci Quarterly, 1974, p. 335, where he states he can prove the sum is irrational if duplicate summands are removed. The problem is tracked at erdosproblems.com/269, with Erdős references [Er88c,p.106] [Er88c].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the sum is irrational for every finite set $P$ of at least two primes.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and a resolution would settle the finite-prime case of a natural irrationality question whose infinite counterpart is already understood.

title: Erdős problem #271
open: Start with two nonnegative integers, $0$ and $n$, and greedily extend the sequence: each new term is the least positive integer that keeps the whole sequence free of three-term arithmetic progressions. Can the resulting Stanley sequence $A(n)$ be explicitly determined, and how fast do its terms $a_k$ grow as a function of $k$?
status: It is easy to see that $A(1)$ is the set of integers with no 2 in their base 3 expansion. Odlyzko and Stanley [OdSt78] found similar characterizations for $A(3^k)$ and $A(2\cdot 3^k)$ for any $k\geq 0$, and conjectured in general that such a sequence always eventually satisfies either $a_k\asymp k^{\log_2 3}$ or $a_k \asymp k^2/\log k$. No sequence is known to satisfy the second growth rate, but Lindhurst [Li90] gives data suggesting that $A(4)$ does (it is OEIS A005487). Moy [Mo11] proved that for all such sequences and all $\epsilon>0$, $a_k\leq (\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon)k^2$ for all sufficiently large $k$; van Doorn and Sothanaphan noted (in the comment section) that Moy's proof can be upgraded to a fully explicit $a_k\leq \frac{(k-1)(k+2)}{2}+n$ for all $k\geq 0$. Such sequences — beginning with an initial segment and continued greedily to avoid three-term arithmetic progressions — are known as Stanley sequences.
