solved_when: An explicit characterization of the sequence $A(n)$ is given (or, failing that, a determination of its asymptotic growth), in particular resolving whether the growth is always eventually either $a_k\asymp k^{\log_2 3}$ or $a_k \asymp k^2/\log k$, and whether $A(4)$ realizes the second growth rate.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it sits at the basic question of how greedy avoidance of three-term arithmetic progressions shapes a sequence.

title: Erdős problem #272
open: Given an integer $N\geq 1$, how many subsets $A_1,\ldots,A_t$ of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ can one have if every pairwise intersection $A_i\cap A_j$ ($i\neq j$) must be a non-empty arithmetic progression? In other words, determine or closely estimate the maximal such $t$ as a function of $N$.
status: Simonovits and Sós [SiSo81] have shown that $t\ll N^2$. Erdős and Graham asked whether the maximal $t$ is achieved when we take the $A_i$ to be all arithmetic progressions in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ containing some fixed element, 'presumably the integer $\lfloor N/2\rfloor$'. This was disproved by Simonovits and Sós [SiSo81], who observed that taking all sets containing at most $3$ elements, containing some fixed element, produces $\binom{N}{2}+1$ many such sets, which is asymptotically greater than the number of arithmetic progressions containing a fixed element, which is $\sim \frac{\pi^2}{24}N^2$. If we drop the non-empty requirement then Graham, Simonovits, and Sós [GSS80] have shown that $t\leq \binom{N}{3}+\binom{N}{2}+\binom{N}{1}+1$, and this is best possible. Szabo [Sz99] proved that the maximal such $t$ is equal to $\frac{N^2}{2}+O(N^{5/3}(\log N)^3)$, resolving the asymptotic question. On the other hand, Szabo showed that the conjecture of Simonovits and Sós that $\binom{n}{2}+1$ is best possible is false, giving a construction which yields $t \geq \binom{N}{2}+\lfloor\frac{N-1}{4}\rfloor+1$. Szabo conjectures that the asymptotic $t=\binom{N}{2}+O(N)$ holds.
solved_when: The maximal $t$ is determined, in accordance with Szabo's conjecture that $t=\binom{N}{2}+O(N)$ holds.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving the exact asymptotic of the maximal family size would settle a long-standing extremal question about sets whose pairwise intersections are arithmetic progressions.

title: Erdős problem #273
open: Is there a covering system of the integers in which every modulus is of the form $p-1$ for some prime $p\geq 5$? In other words, can congruences with moduli drawn entirely from these shifted primes cover every integer?
status: Selfridge has found an example using divisors of $360$ if $p=3$ is allowed.
solved_when: An explicit covering system is exhibited whose moduli all equal $p-1$ for primes $p\geq 5$, or a proof is given that no such covering system exists.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked publicly at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #274
open: Can a group be partitioned into more than one coset of pairwise different sizes — that is, can every element of $G$ lie in exactly one of several cosets whose subgroups have distinct indices in $G$?
status: The question originates with Herzog and Schönheim, who conjectured more generally that if $G$ is any (not necessarily finite) group and $a_1G_1,\ldots,a_kG_k$ are finitely many cosets of subgroups of $G$ with distinct indices $[G:G_i]$, then the $a_iG_i$ cannot form a partition of $G$. Sun [Su04] proved the conjecture when all the $G_i$ are subnormal in $G$; in particular, for abelian $G$ (the special case asked about in [Er77c] and [ErGr80]) the answer to the original question is no. Margolis and Schnabel [MaSc19] proved the conjecture for all groups $G$ of size $<1440$.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the Herzog–Schönheim conjecture: no finite collection of cosets $a_1G_1,\ldots,a_kG_k$ of subgroups of a (not necessarily finite) group $G$ with distinct indices $[G:G_i]$ can form a partition of $G$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would settle a long-standing question at the intersection of group theory and covering systems.

title: Erdős problem #276
open: Is there an infinite Lucas sequence $a_0,a_1,\ldots$ with $a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n$ for $n\geq 0$ in which every term is composite, yet no single integer shares a common factor with all terms of the sequence — that is, can a composite Lucas sequence exist without an underlying covering system of congruences making it composite?
status: Whether such a composite Lucas sequence even exists was open for a while, but using covering systems Graham [Gr64] showed that $a_0 = 1786772701928802632268715130455793$ and $a_1 = 1059683225053915111058165141686995$ generate such a sequence. The problem asks whether one can have a composite Lucas sequence without an underlying system of covering congruences responsible. It has been 'conjecturally solved' by Ismailescu and Son [IsSo14], who provide an explicit infinite Lucas sequence in which all terms are composite and believe that no covering system is responsible; see the comment by van Doorn for more details. See also [1113] for another problem asking whether covering systems are always responsible.
solved_when: An explicit infinite Lucas sequence is exhibited in which every term is composite and it is proved that no system of covering congruences is responsible for the compositeness.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolves whether covering systems are the only mechanism that can force an entire Lucas sequence to be composite.

title: Erdős problem #278
open: Given a finite set of positive integers $A=\{n_1<\cdots<n_r\}$, how densely can a system of residue classes $a_i \pmod{n_i}$ cover the integers, and does the thinnest covering always arise when all the $a_i$ are chosen equal?
status: Simpson [Si86] observed that the density of integers covered is at least $\sum_i \frac{1}{n_i}-\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{[n_i,n_j]}+\sum_{i<j<k}\frac{1}{[n_i,n_j,n_k]}-\cdots$ (where $[\cdots]$ denotes the least common multiple), and that this bound is achieved when all the $a_i$ are equal, settling the second question.
solved_when: The minimum density of the covered integers is determined as a function of the moduli $n_1,\dots,n_r$ (with the conjectured/observed answer being the alternating lcm sum), together with a proof or disproof that equality of all $a_i$ is always extremal.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution closes a named entry in that catalogue of covering-system questions.

title: Erdős problem #279
open: For a fixed integer $k\geq 3$, can one choose a residue class $a_p \pmod{p}$ for every prime $p$ so that every sufficiently large integer $n$ is congruent to $a_p$ modulo some prime $p$ with quotient at least $k$, i.e. $n = a_p + tp$ for some prime $p$ and integer $t \geq k$?
status: Even the case $k=3$ seems difficult. It is speculated that the statement may remain true with the primes replaced by any set $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that $|A\cap [1,N]| \gg N/\log N$ and $\sum_{\substack{n\in A\\ n\leq N}}\frac{1}{n} - \log\log N \to \infty$ as $N\to\infty$. In a weakened almost-all form the answer is known: for any $k\geq 2$, any set $A$ with $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}=\infty$ represents almost all integers in this fashion.
solved_when: A construction of congruence classes $a_p \pmod{p}$ for the primes is given, for some $k \geq 3$, such that all sufficiently large integers admit a representation $n = a_p + tp$ with $p$ prime and $t \geq k$; the case $k = 3$ alone would already resolve the problem.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked publicly, so a resolution would close a long-standing entry in that catalogue of open questions.
aliases: Erdős #279; number theory / covering systems / primes

title: Erdős problem #282
open: Does the greedy algorithm for Egyptian fractions always terminate when the denominators are restricted to the odd numbers and the target rational $x\in(0,1)$ has odd denominator? Formally, choosing at each step the minimal eligible $n\in A$ with $n\geq 1/x$ and iterating on $x-\frac{1}{n}$: characterize the pairs $(x,A)$ for which this process terminates.
status: In 1202 Fibonacci observed that the process terminates for any $x$ when $A=\mathbb{N}$. The case where $A$ is the odd numbers is due to Stein and remains open. Graham [Gr64b] showed that $\frac{m}{n}$ is the sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators $\equiv a\pmod{d}$ if and only if $\left(\frac{n}{(n,(a,d))},\frac{d}{(a,d)}\right)=1$, but it is unknown whether the greedy algorithm always terminates in such cases. Graham [Gr64c] also showed that $x$ is the sum of distinct unit fractions with square denominators if and only if $x\in [0,\pi^2/6-1)\cup [1,\pi^2/6)$; Erdős and Graham believe the greedy algorithm does not always terminate here — perhaps it fails almost always. See also [206].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the process terminates for every rational $x$ with odd denominator when $A$ is the odd numbers, together with a characterization of the pairs $(x,A)$ for which termination holds — including, per the record's motivating cases, denominators in a residue class $\equiv a\pmod{d}$ and square denominators.

title: Erdős problem #287
open: For any representation of $1$ as a sum of reciprocals of $k\geq 2$ distinct integers $1<n_1<\cdots<n_k$, must some gap between consecutive denominators be at least $3$? Formally, is $\max(n_{i+1}-n_i)\geq 3$ forced by $1=\frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}$?
status: The example $1=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{6}$ shows that $3$ would be best possible. The lower bound of $\geq 2$ is equivalent to saying that $1$ is not the sum of reciprocals of consecutive integers, proved by Erdős [Er32]. The conjecture would follow for all but at most finitely many exceptions if it were known that, for all large $N$, there exists a prime $p\in[N,2N]$ such that $\frac{p+1}{2}$ is also prime. Key works: erdosproblems.com/287; Erdős references: [Va99,1.15] [Er32].
solved_when: A proof that every such representation satisfies $\max(n_{i+1}-n_i)\geq 3$, or a counterexample representation with all gaps at most $2$. The bound $3$ is best possible, as shown by $1=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{6}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/287; settling it would resolve a natural structural question about unit-fraction representations of $1$.

title: Erdős problem #288
open: Are there only finitely many pairs of intervals $I_1, I_2$ of positive integers for which the sum of reciprocals over the two intervals, $\sum_{n_1\in I_1}\frac{1}{n_1}+\sum_{n_2\in I_2}\frac{1}{n_2}$, is a whole number?
status: A simple example shows such representations exist, e.g. $\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{20}=1$. The problem is still open even in the restricted case $\lvert I_2\rvert=1$. It is perhaps true with two intervals replaced by any $k$ intervals.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that only finitely many such pairs of intervals exist; in particular, the case where the second interval has length 1 remains to be settled. Natural extensions: the answer for two intervals replaced by any $k$ intervals.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems on unit fractions, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #289
open: For all sufficiently large $k$, can the number $1$ be written as a sum of reciprocals of integers taken from $k$ finite intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_k\subset\mathbb{N}$ that are distinct, pairwise non-overlapping and non-adjacent, each of length at least $2$, i.e. $1=\sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{n\in I_i}\frac{1}{n}$?
status: Erdős and Graham posed this in [ErGr80] without the stipulation that the intervals be distinct, non-overlapping, or adjacent, but Kovac in the comments has provided a simple argument showing that it is easily possible without this restriction, and likely [ErGr80] just forgot to mention this natural restriction. As an example representing $2$ rather than $1$, Hickerson and Montgomery, in the solution to AMS Monthly problem E2689 proposed by Hahn, found $2=\sum_{i=1}^5 \sum_{n\in I_i}\frac{1}{n}$ where $I_1=[2,7]$, $I_2=[9,10]$, $I_3=[17,18]$, $I_4=[34,35]$, and $I_5=[84,85]$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that such intervals exist for all sufficiently large $k$, with each $\lvert I_i\rvert\geq 2$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution settles a natural open question on representing integers as sums of unit fractions over structured interval families.

title: Erdős problem #291
open: Let $L_n=\mathrm{lcm}(1,\ldots,n)$ and write the harmonic sum $\sum_{1\le k\le n} 1/k = a_n/L_n$ in lowest terms. Does the numerator $a_n$ share a common factor with $L_n$ for infinitely many $n$, and is it also coprime to $L_n$ for infinitely many $n$?
status: Steinerberger observed that the second question is trivially yes: any $n$ beginning with a $2$ in base $3$ has $3\mid (a_n,L_n)$; more generally, if the leading digit of $n$ in base $p$ is $p-1$, then $p\mid (a_n,L_n)$. There is a necessary and sufficient condition: a prime $p\le n$ divides $(a_n,L_n)$ if and only if $p$ divides the numerator of $1+\cdots+1/k$, where $k$ is the leading digit of $n$ in base $p$; this follows from writing $a_n = L_n/1+\cdots+L_n/n$, which is congruent to $1+\cdots+1/k$ modulo $p$ (the claim about $p-1$ follows from Wolstenholme's theorem). This yields a heuristic prediction (see a preprint of Shiu [Sh16]) of $\asymp x/\log x$ for the number of $n\in[1,x]$ with $(a_n,L_n)=1$ — so infinitely many such $n$, but of density zero; the heuristic is difficult to turn into a proof. Wu and Yan [WuYa22] have proved, conditional on $1/\log p$ being linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ for any finite collection of primes $p$ (itself a conse
solved_when: It is proved that both $(a_n,L_n)=1$ and $(a_n,L_n)>1$ hold for infinitely many $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #293
open: For each $k$, consider the set of denominators $n_1<\cdots<n_k$ appearing in Egyptian fraction representations $1=\frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}$, and let $v(k)$ be the smallest positive integer that never occurs as any $n_i$ in such a representation. How fast does $v(k)$ grow as a function of $k$?
status: Results of Bleicher and Erdős [BlEr75] imply $v(k) \gg k!$. It may be that $v(k)$ grows doubly exponentially in $\sqrt{k}$ or even $k$. An elementary inductive argument shows $n_k\leq ku_k$ where $u_1=1$ and $u_{i+1}=u_i(u_i+1)$, and hence $v(k) \leq kc_0^{2^k}$, where $c_0=\lim_n u_n^{1/2^n}=1.26408\cdots$ is the 'Vardi constant' (small improvements on this are possible as in [148]). van Doorn and Tang [vDTa25b] have proved $v(k)\geq e^{ck^2}$ for some constant $c>0$, and noted a close connection to [304]. In particular, if $N(b)\ll \log\log b$ as in [304], then it is likely the methods of [vDTa25b] prove $v(k)\geq e^{e^{ck}}$ for some $c>0$.
solved_when: Sharp asymptotic bounds on $v(k)$ are established — in particular, closing the gap between the lower bound $v(k)\geq e^{ck^2}$ and the upper bound $v(k)\leq kc_0^{2^k}$, or proving/disproving that $v(k)$ grows doubly exponentially in $\sqrt{k}$ or $k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; determining the growth rate of $v(k)$ resolves a basic question about the structure of unit fraction representations of 1.

title: Erdős problem #295
open: For each $N$, let $k(N)$ be the fewest unit fractions needed to write $1$ as a sum of reciprocals of distinct integers all at least $N$. Is it true that $\lim_{N\to\infty}\, k(N)-(e-1)N=\infty$?
status: Erdős and Straus [ErSt71b] have proved the existence of some constant $c>0$ such that $-c < k(N)-(e-1)N \ll \frac{N}{\log N}$.
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved) that $k(N)-(e-1)N\to\infty$ as $N\to\infty$, in the sense that for every $M$ there exists $N_0$ such that $k(N)-(e-1)N>M$ for all $N\geq N_0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems on Egyptian fractions, and its full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a basic question about how many large-denominator unit fractions are needed to represent $1$.

title: Erdős problem #301
open: How large can a subset $A$ of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be if it contains no distinct $a,b_1,\ldots,b_k\in A$ satisfying $\frac{1}{a}=\frac{1}{b_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{b_k}$? Is it true that $f(N)=(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))N$, where $f(N)$ denotes the size of the largest such set?
status: The example $A=(N/2,N]\cap\mathbb{N}$ shows $f(N)\geq N/2$. Wouter van Doorn has given an elementary argument proving $f(N)\leq(25/28+o(1))N$: consider the sets $S_a=\{2a,3a,4a,6a,12a\}\cap[1,N]$ as $a$ ranges over all integers of the form $8^b9^cd$ with $(d,6)=1$; all such $S_a$ are disjoint, and if $A$ has no solutions to the given equation, then $A$ must omit at least two elements of $S_a$ when $a\leq N/12$ and at least one element of $S_a$ when $N/12<a\leq N/6$, which an elementary calculation turns into the bound. Stijn Cambie and Wouter van Doorn have noted that if solutions with non-distinct $b_i$ are allowed, the maximal set has size at most $N/2$, this being the classical threshold for the existence of distinct $a,b\in A$ with $a\mid b$. See also [302] and [327].
solved_when: An asymptotic estimate of $f(N)$ is obtained; in particular, a proof (or refutation) that $f(N)=(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))N$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling the conjectured asymptotic would complete the basic picture of how dense a set of integers can be while avoiding all representations of a unit fraction as a sum of distinct unit fractions from the set.

title: Erdős problem #302
open: How large can a subset $A$ of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be if it contains no three distinct elements $a,b,c$ satisfying $\frac{1}{a}=\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}$? In particular, is the answer $f(N)=(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))N$?
status: The colouring version of this is [303], which was solved by Brown and Rödl [BrRo91]. Taking $A$ to be all odd integers in $[1,N]$, or all integers in $[N/2,N]$, shows $f(N)\geq (1/2+o(1))N$. Wouter van Doorn has proved (see this note) that $f(N)\leq (9/10+o(1))N$. Stijn Cambie has observed that $f(N)\geq (5/8+o(1))N$, taking $A$ to be all odd integers $\leq N/4$ together with all integers in $[N/2,N]$. Stijn Cambie has also observed that, if $b=c$ is allowed, then a solution must exist once $|A|\geq (\tfrac{2}{3}+o(1))N$, since then some $n,2n\in A$. See also [301] and [327].
solved_when: The function $f(N)$ is determined asymptotically, in particular confirming (or refuting) whether $f(N)=(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))N$.

title: Erdős problem #304
open: How many unit fractions are needed, in the worst case, to write a given fraction $a/b$ with $1 \le a < b$ as an Egyptian fraction? Formally, with $N(a,b)$ the minimal $k$ such that $a/b = 1/n_1 + \cdots + 1/n_k$ for integers $1 < n_1 < \cdots < n_k$, estimate $N(b) = \max_{1 \le a < b} N(a,b)$ — in particular, is it true that $N(b) \ll \log\log b$?
status: Erdős [Er50c] proved that $\log\log b \ll N(b) \ll \frac{\log b}{\log\log b}$. Vose [Vo85] improved the upper bound to $N(b) \ll \sqrt{\log b}$. For fixed $b$, the average of $N(a,b)$ is also of interest, and it is known that $\frac{1}{b}\sum_{1 \le a < b} N(a,b) \gg \log\log b$. The problem is related to [18] and closely connected to [293] (particularly via $N(b-1,b)$), a connection elucidated by van Doorn and Tang [vDTa25b]. It has been formalised in Lean as part of the Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures project.
solved_when: An estimate of $N(b)$ resolving the order of magnitude is obtained; the headline conjecture is settled affirmatively by a proof that $N(b) \ll \log\log b$, which would match Erdős's lower bound $\log\log b \ll N(b)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would pin down the worst-case complexity of Egyptian fraction representations of rational numbers.

title: Erdős problem #306
open: Given a positive rational $a/b$ in lowest terms with $b$ squarefree, can it always be written as a finite sum of reciprocals of integers, each of which is the product of two distinct primes? That is, do there exist integers $1<n_1<\cdots<n_k$, each a product of two distinct primes, with $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}$?
status: For $n_i$ the product of three distinct primes, the analogous statement is true when $b=1$, as proved by Butler, Erdős and Graham [BEG15] (this paper is perhaps Erdős' last paper, appearing 19 years after his death). For products of two distinct primes, several examples of such decompositions are known for $a/b=1$: the first was given by Barbeau [Ba77], and the shortest known examples have $47$ terms, discovered by Watanabe [Wa20] (see the introduction of [Wa20] for further history).
solved_when: A proof that every $a/b\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}$ with $b$ squarefree admits such a decomposition, or a counterexample exhibiting a rational with squarefree denominator that admits none.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a natural question in the Egyptian-fraction representation of rationals with restricted denominators.

title: Erdős problem #307
open: Do there exist two finite sets of primes $P$ and $Q$ such that the product of their reciprocal sums equals 1, that is, $1=\left(\sum_{p\in P}\frac{1}{p}\right)\left(\sum_{q\in Q}\frac{1}{q}\right)$?
status: The question was asked by Barbeau [Ba76]. If the requirement that all elements be prime is weakened to pairwise coprimality within each set, Cambie has found several examples, such as $1=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}\right)$ and $1=\left(1+\frac{1}{41}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}\right)$, though no examples are known for this weakened coprime version if one insists that $1\not\in P\cup Q$. For sets of primes it is easy to see that $P$ and $Q$ must be disjoint and that $\sum_{p\in P\cup Q}\frac{1}{p}\geq 2$, whence $|P\cup Q|\geq 60$.
solved_when: Explicit finite sets of primes $P,Q$ satisfying the identity are produced, or the impossibility of such sets is proved.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would settle a natural question about representing 1 via reciprocal sums of primes.

title: Erdős problem #311
open: How close can a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ come to having reciprocal sum exactly $1$? Formally, letting $\delta(N)$ be the minimal non-zero value of $\lvert 1-\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\rvert$ over all subsets $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$, is it true that $\delta(N)=e^{-(c+o(1))N}$ for some constant $c\in(0,1)$?
status: It is trivial that $\delta(N)\geq \frac{1}{[1,\ldots,N]}=e^{-(1+o(1))N}$, where $[1,\ldots,N]$ is the least common multiple of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. The formulation in [ErGr80] has the additional condition that $A$ contain no $S$ such that $\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}=1$, but Kovac in the comments has shown that the simpler formulation above is equivalent. Tang has shown that $\delta(N) \leq \exp\left(-c\frac{N}{(\log N\log\log N)^3}\right)$ for some constant $c>0$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\delta(N)=e^{-(c+o(1))N}$ for some constant $c\in(0,1)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would determine the true exponential scale at which unit-fraction subset sums can approximate $1$.

title: Erdős problem #312
open: Can one always carve a unit-fraction "sub-sum" nearly equal to 1 out of a multiset whose reciprocal sum is large? Formally, does there exist $c>0$ such that, for any $K>1$, whenever $A$ is a sufficiently large finite multiset of positive integers with $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}>K$ there exists some $S\subseteq A$ with $1-e^{-cK} < \sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}\leq 1$?
status: Erdős and Graham knew the statement with $e^{-cK}$ replaced by $c/K^2$.
solved_when: Such a constant $c>0$ is exhibited and proved, i.e. the bound $e^{-cK}$ is achieved in place of the known $c/K^2$ error term.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; a solution would resolve a long-standing question on how tightly unit-fraction subsums can approximate 1, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #313
open: Are there infinitely many ways to write $1-\frac{1}{m}$, with $m \geq 2$ an integer, as a sum of reciprocals of distinct primes $\frac{1}{p_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{p_k}$ with $p_1<\cdots<p_k$?
status: Two small examples are known: $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}=1-\frac{1}{6}$ and $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}=1-\frac{1}{42}$. It is clear that we must have $m=p_1\cdots p_k$, so in particular there is at most one solution for each $m$. The integers $m$ for which such a solution exists are known as primary pseudoperfect numbers, and $8$ are known, listed in A054377 at the OEIS.
solved_when: A proof that infinitely many such representations exist, or a proof that only finitely many exist; no quantitative target is stated in the record.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a long-standing question about unit fractions and primes.

title: Erdős problem #317
open: Can a signed sum of the first $n$ reciprocal integers, with each coefficient $\delta_k\in\{-1,0,1\}$, be made nonzero but exponentially small — specifically, is there a constant $c>0$ such that for every $n\geq 1$ one can choose coefficients with $0<\left|\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\delta_k}{k}\right|<\frac{c}{2^n}$? A complementary question asks whether, for sufficiently large $n$, every nonzero such sum satisfies $\left|\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\delta_k}{k}\right|>\frac{1}{[1,\ldots,n]}$ for any choice of $\delta_k\in\{-1,0,1\}$.
status: The non-strict version of the second claim is obvious; the problem is strict inequality, which fails for small $n$ — for example, $\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}=-\frac{1}{12}$. For the first question, arguments of Kovac and van Doorn (in the comment section of erdosproblems.com/317) prove a weak version with an upper bound of $2^{-n\frac{(\log\log\log n)^{1+o(1)}}{\log n}}$, and van Doorn gives a heuristic suggesting this may be the true order of magnitude.
solved_when: Either a constant $c>0$ is exhibited such that for every $n\geq 1$ there exist $\delta_k\in\{-1,0,1\}$ with $0<\left|\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\delta_k}{k}\right|<\frac{c}{2^n}$, or it is shown that for sufficiently large $n$ every nonzero sum $\left|\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\delta_k}{k}\right|$ (with $\delta_k\in\{-1,0,1\}$) exceeds $\frac{1}{[1,\ldots,n]}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it probes how finely sums of unit fractions with restricted coefficients can be made to cancel.

title: Erdős problem #319
open: How large can a set $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be if its reciprocal sums can be perfectly balanced — that is, there is a signing $\delta:A\to\{-1,1\}$ with $\sum_{n\in A}\delta_n/n=0$ — while no proper non-empty subset of $A$ admits such a signed zero-sum? In other words, what is the maximal size of such a "minimal" signed zero-sum set of unit fractions?
status: Adenwalla observed that a lower bound of $|A|\geq (1-\tfrac{1}{e}+o(1))N$ follows from the main result of Croot [Cr01], which states that there exists some set of integers $B\subset [(\tfrac{1}{e}-o(1))N,N]$ such that $\sum_{b\in B} 1/b = 1$. Since $\sum_{m\in[c_1N,c_2N]} 1/m$ is asymptotic to $\log(c_2/c_1)$, we must have $|B|\geq (1-\tfrac{1}{e}+o(1))N$. Then taking $A=B\cup\{1\}$ with $\delta(n)=-1$ for all $n\in B$ and $\delta(1)=1$ gives the construction. The problem has been formalised in Lean as part of the Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures project.
solved_when: The maximum size of such an $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is determined, up to exact value or asymptotically, as a function of $N$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would resolve a question in the unit-fraction arithmetic of Erdős's problem collection.

title: Erdős problem #322
open: Let $k\geq 3$ and let $A$ be the set of $k$th powers. How fast can the number $1_A^{(k)}(n)$ of representations of $n$ as a sum of $k$ many $k$th powers grow? In particular, do there exist some $c>0$ and infinitely many $n$ with $1_A^{(k)}(n) > n^c$?
status: Connected to Waring's problem. Hypothesis $K$ of Hardy and Littlewood asserted $1_A^{(k)}(n)\leq n^{o(1)}$, but Mahler [Ma36] disproved it for $k=3$ by constructing infinitely many $n$ with $1_A^{(3)}(n)\gg n^{1/12}$ ($A$ the cubes). Erdős believed Hypothesis $K$ fails for all $k\geq 4$, but this is unknown. The weaker Hypothesis $K^*$ of Hardy and Littlewood states that for all $N$ and $\epsilon>0$, $\sum_{n\leq N}1_A^{(k)}(n)^2 \ll_\epsilon N^{1+\epsilon}$; Erdős and Graham remarked: 'This is probably true but no doubt very deep. However, it would suffice for most applications.' Independently Erdős [Er36] and Chowla proved that for all $k\geq 3$ there are infinitely many $n$ with $1_A^{(k)}(n) \gg n^{c/\log\log n}$ for some $c>0$ depending on $k$. In [Er65b] Erdős claims an unpublished proof that if $B$ is the set of $k$th powers of any set of positive density, then $\limsup 1_B^{(k)}(n)=\infty$; this is discussed in problem D4 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. The problem is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/322.
solved_when: For a given $k\geq 3$, one exhibits a constant $c>0$ and infinitely many $n$ such that $1_A^{(k)}(n) > n^c$ (or proves no such $c$ exists).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, connected to Waring's problem and to the Hardy–Littlewood Hypothesis $K$; a resolution determines the true order of the representation function for sums of like powers.

title: Erdős problem #323
open: For $1\leq m\leq k$, let $f_{k,m}(x)$ count the integers up to $x$ expressible as a sum of $m$ nonnegative $k$th powers. Is $f_{k,k}(x) \gg_\epsilon x^{1-\epsilon}$ for every $\epsilon>0$, and, when $m<k$, is $f_{k,m}(x) \gg x^{m/k}$ for all sufficiently large $x$?
status: The case $k=2$ was resolved by Landau, who showed $f_{2,2}(x) \sim \frac{cx}{\sqrt{\log x}}$ for some constant $c>0$. For $k>2$ it is not known if $f_{k,k}(x)=o(x)$. The problem is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/323.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the two stated lower bounds: $f_{k,k}(x) \gg_\epsilon x^{1-\epsilon}$ for all $\epsilon>0$, and $f_{k,m}(x) \gg x^{m/k}$ for sufficiently large $x$ whenever $m<k$.
why: A solution would have significant applications to Waring's problem; Erdős and Graham described the problem as 'unattackable by the methods at our disposal'.

title: Erdős problem #324
open: Does there exist a polynomial with integer coefficients whose values form a Sidon set — that is, a polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ such that all sums $f(a)+f(b)$ with $a<b$ nonnegative integers are distinct?
status: The problem asks that $\{f(n): n\geq 1\}$ be a Sidon set. Probably $f(x)=x^5$ should work, and the Lander, Parkin, and Selfridge conjecture would imply that $f(x)=x^n$ has this property for all $n\geq 5$. Ruzsa [Ru01b] proved there exists $c\in[0,1]$ and $n_0\geq 1$ such that $\{n^5+\lfloor cn^4\rfloor : n\geq n_0\}$ is a Sidon set. It is easy to check that a quadratic $f$ cannot have this property; Dubickas and Novikas [DuNo21] showed that a cubic $f$ cannot; and it is a classical fact that $x^4$ cannot. These matters are discussed in problems C9, D1, and F30 of Guy's collection [Gu04], and the problem is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/324.
solved_when: An explicit $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is exhibited (or proven to exist) for which all sums $f(a)+f(b)$, $a<b$ nonnegative integers, are distinct; the conjectured instance $f(x)=x^5$ would suffice.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, which he and Graham described as "very annoying"; resolving it would settle a natural, long-standing question about polynomial Sidon sets.
aliases: Erdős #324; number theory / powers / sidon sets

title: Erdős problem #325
open: Must the set of integers up to $x$ representable as a sum of three nonnegative $k$th powers, with $k\geq 3$, have size at least on the order of $x^{3/k}$ — the counting function $f_{k,3}(x)$ satisfying $f_{k,3}(x) \gg x^{3/k}$? Or failing that, does at least $f_{k,3}(x) \gg_\epsilon x^{3/k-\epsilon}$ hold?
status: Mahler and Erdős [ErMa38] proved that $f_{k,2}(x) \gg x^{2/k}$. For $k=3$ the best known is due to Wooley [Wo15], $f_{3,3}(x) \gg x^{0.917\cdots}$. This problem has been formalised in Lean as part of the Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures project.
solved_when: A proof that $f_{k,3}(x) \gg x^{3/k}$, or the weaker $f_{k,3}(x) \gg_\epsilon x^{3/k-\epsilon}$, holds for $k\geq 3$; a disproof would also resolve the question.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a solution would settle a natural question about the density of sums of three powers.

title: Erdős problem #326
open: Does there exist a minimal additive basis of order 2 for the natural numbers whose counting function grows like a nonzero constant multiple of $k^2$? Formally, is there a set $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\subset \mathbb{N}$ such that every sufficiently large integer is a sum of two elements of $A$, no proper subset of $A$ has this property, and $\lim_{k\to\infty} a_k/k^2 = c$ for some $c\neq 0$?
status: Erdős originally asked this for any basis (not necessarily minimal); such a basis was constructed by Cassels [Ca57]. Erdős and Graham conjectured a negative answer to the minimal version.
solved_when: Such a minimal basis $A$ of order $2$ is exhibited with $\lim_{k\to\infty} a_k/k^2 = c$ for some $c \neq 0$, or it is proved that no minimal basis of order $2$ can satisfy this limit for any $c \neq 0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (Erdős #326), tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would clarify the growth constraints that minimality imposes on additive bases of order 2.

title: Erdős problem #327
open: Can a subset $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ in which $a+b\nmid ab$ for all distinct $a,b\in A$ be substantially larger than the odd numbers? Formally, must $|A|=o(N)$, and what changes if the condition is strengthened to $a+b\nmid 2ab$ for distinct $a,b\in A$?
status: Wouter van Doorn has given an elementary argument showing that any $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $|A|\geq (25/28+o(1))N$ must contain distinct $a,b$ with $a+b\mid ab$ (see the discussion in [301]); see also [302].
solved_when: One determines whether such sets must satisfy $|A|=o(N)$ (for either the $a+b\nmid ab$ or $a+b\nmid 2ab$ condition), with an asymptotic bound on the maximal size of $A$.
why: Since $\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}$ is a unit fraction exactly when $a+b\mid ab$, the problem probes how dense a set can be while avoiding unit-fraction sums, one of Erdős's personally posed problems tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #329
open: Suppose $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a Sidon set. How large can $\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}|}{N^{1/2}}$ be?
status: Erdős proved that $1/2$ is possible and Krückeberg [Kr61] proved $1/\sqrt{2}$ is possible. Erdős and Turán [ErTu41] proved the limsup is always $\leq 1$. In [Er80] Erdős writes that he and Krückeberg conjecture that $1$ is possible; this would follow if any finite Sidon set were a subset of a perfect difference set (see [44] and [707]). The analogous question for $B_2[g]$ sequences (where the number of solutions to $n=a_1+a_2$ with $a_1\leq a_2$ is at most $g$ for all $n$, so $B_2[1]$ is a Sidon set) is also open in general: Kolountzakis [Ko96] constructed a $B_2[2]$ sequence with limsup $1$, and for larger $g$ constructions were given by Cilleruelo and Trujillo [CiTr01].
solved_when: The limsup constant is determined exactly: either a Sidon set is constructed achieving $\limsup = 1$ (as Erdős and Krückeberg conjectured), or it is proved that the limsup is always $< 1$.

title: Erdős problem #332
open: Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and let $D(A)$ be the set of numbers that occur infinitely often as a difference $a_1-a_2$ with $a_1,a_2\in A$. Which conditions on $A$ are sufficient to guarantee that $D(A)$ has bounded gaps?
status: In number theory, Prikry, Tijdeman, Stewart, and others (see the survey articles [St78] and [Ti79]) have shown that a sufficient condition is that $A$ has positive density. Related variants remain open: one can ask what conditions on $A$ suffice for $D(A)$ to have positive density, for $\sum_{d\in D(A)}\frac{1}{d}=\infty$, or even just for $D(A)\neq\emptyset$.
solved_when: A characterization (or a verifiable sufficient condition) of those $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ for which $D(A)$ has bounded gaps is given.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a solution would clarify how much structure a set must have for its recurring differences to be syndetic.

title: Erdős problem #334
open: What is the smallest function $f(n)$ such that every integer $n$ can be written as a sum $n=a+b$ where both $a$ and $b$ are $f(n)$-smooth, i.e., neither is divisible by any prime $p>f(n)$?
status: Erdős originally asked whether even $f(n)\leq n^{1/3}$ holds; this is known, and the best bound is due to Balog [Ba89], who proved $f(n) \ll_\epsilon n^{\frac{4}{9\sqrt{e}}+\epsilon}$ for all $\epsilon>0$ (note $\frac{4}{9\sqrt{e}}=0.2695\ldots$). It is likely that $f(n)\leq n^{o(1)}$. See also Problem 59 on Green's open problems list. Key works: erdosproblems.com/334; Erdős references: [Er76e,p.272] [Er82d,p.55] [Ba89].
solved_when: The optimal order of $f(n)$ is determined; conjecturally this means showing $f(n)\leq n^{o(1)}$.

title: Erdős problem #335
open: Which pairs of positive-density sets of natural numbers have a sumset whose density is exactly the sum of the individual densities? Formally, characterize all $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with $d(A), d(B) > 0$ such that $d(A+B) = d(A) + d(B)$.
status: One known way for equality to hold is via rotations: there exists $\theta > 0$ such that $A = \{ n > 0 : \{n\theta\} \in X_A\}$ and $B = \{ n > 0 : \{n\theta\} \in X_B\}$, where $\{x\}$ denotes fractional part and $X_A, X_B \subseteq \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ satisfy $\mu(X_A + X_B) = \mu(X_A) + \mu(X_B)$. The question of whether all possible $A$ and $B$ arise similarly (using other groups) has been partially resolved by Ackelsburg and Richter [AcRi26] under the additional assumption that one of the sets meets every residue class in $\mathbb{N}$: roughly speaking, if $d(A) > 0$ and $d(A+B) = d(A) + d(B) < 1$ and $B$ meets every residue class, then either both $A$ and $B$ arise from a rotation on the product of the circle group with a finite cyclic group, or $A$ lies in a single residue class modulo some $h$ and $B$ 'looks like' the union of all but one residue class modulo $h$. A full characterization without the residue-class assumption seems hopeless; for example, taking $A = B$ to be a random subset of the even integers with density $1/4$ gives $d(A+A) = 1/2$. See erdosproblems.com/335.
solved_when: A complete structural characterization is given of all pairs $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of positive density satisfying $d(A+B) = d(A) + d(B)$, with no additional hypotheses (such as one set meeting every residue class).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would settle when sumsets behave additively with respect to natural density, a basic question in additive combinatorics.

title: Erdős problem #336
open: For $r\geq 2$, let $h(r)$ be the largest finite $k$ for which some basis $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of order $r$ (every large integer is a sum of at most $r$ elements of $A$) has exact order $k$ (every large integer is a sum of exactly $k$ elements of $A$). Does $\lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}$ exist, and what is its value?
status: A simple example where order and exact order differ is $A=\cup_{k\geq 0}(2^{2k},2^{2k+1}]$, which has order $2$ but exact order $3$. Erdős and Graham [ErGr80b] showed that a basis $A$ has an exact order if and only if the successive differences $a_2-a_1,a_3-a_2,a_4-a_3,\ldots$ are coprime, and proved $\frac{1}{4}\leq \lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}\leq \frac{5}{4}$. The best known bounds for the limit are $\frac{1}{3}\leq \lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}\leq \frac{1}{2}$, the lower bound originally due to Grekos [Gr88] and the upper bound to Nash [Na93]. Improved bounds in the lower-order terms were given by Plagne [Pl04]. Erdős and Graham [ErGr80b] showed $h(2)=4$; Nash [Na93] showed $h(3)=7$; the value of $h(4)$ is unknown, though it is known [Pl04] that $10\leq h(4)\leq 11$.
solved_when: The limit $\lim_r \frac{h(r)}{r^2}$ is determined (its existence and value are established); settling small cases such as $h(4)$, currently known only to satisfy $10\leq h(4)\leq 11$, would be natural progress.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; determining the limit resolves the asymptotic gap between the order and the exact order of additive bases.

title: Erdős problem #338
open: When does a basis have a restricted order — that is, when is every sufficiently large integer representable as a sum of at most $t$ distinct elements of $A$? Which conditions are necessary and sufficient for such a $t$ to exist, and can the restricted order be bounded in terms of the (ordinary) order of the basis?
status: Bateman observed that for $h\geq 3$ the set $A=\{1\}\cup \{x>0 : h\mid x\}$ is a basis of order $h$ with no restricted order. Kelly [Ke57] showed any basis of order $2$ has restricted order at most $4$ and conjectured it is always at most $3$, which he proved under the additional assumption of positive lower density; the conjecture was disproved by Hennecart [He05], who constructed a basis of order $2$ with restricted order $4$. The squares have order $4$ and restricted order $5$ (see [Pa33]), and the triangular numbers have order $3$ and restricted order $3$ (see [Sc54]). It remains open whether $A\backslash F$ being a basis for all finite $F$ forces $A$ to have a restricted order, and what happens if they are all bases of the same order. Hegyvári, Hennecart, and Plagne [HHP07] showed that for all $k\geq2$ there exists a basis of order $k$ with restricted order at least $2^{k-2}+k-1$.
solved_when: Necessary and sufficient conditions are given for a basis to admit a restricted order, together with an answer to whether it can be bounded in terms of the order of the basis (and when it equals the order).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would clarify how distinctness constraints affect additive bases, a basic structural question in additive number theory.

title: Erdős problem #340
open: Let $A=\{1,2,4,8,13,21,31,45,66,81,97,\ldots\}$ be the greedy Sidon sequence: we begin with $1$ and iteratively include the next smallest integer that preserves the Sidon property (i.e. there are no non-trivial solutions to $a+b=c+d$). What is the order of growth of $A$? Is it true that \[\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg N^{1/2-\epsilon}\] for all $\epsilon>0$ and large $N$?
status: This sequence is sometimes called the Mian-Chowla sequence. It is trivial that the sequence grows at least like $\gg N^{1/3}$. Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] also asked about the difference set $A-A$: whether it has positive density, and whether it contains $22$. It does contain $22$, since $a_{15}-a_{14}=204-182=22$. The smallest integer not known to be in $A-A$ is $33$ (see A080200). It may be true that all or almost all integers lie in $A-A$. The sequence is OEIS A005282. See also [156].
solved_when: The order of growth of the greedy Sidon sequence is determined; in particular, it is settled whether $\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg N^{1/2-\epsilon}$ holds for all $\epsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $N$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution settles a long-standing question about the basic structure of the greedy Sidon construction.
aliases: Erdős #340; number theory / additive combinatorics / sidon sets

title: Erdős problem #341
open: Given a finite set of positive integers $A=\{a_1<\cdots<a_k\}$, extend it to an infinite sequence by repeatedly taking $a_{n+1}$ ($n\geq k$) to be the least integer exceeding $a_n$ that is not a sum $a_i+a_j$ with $i,j\leq n$. Must the sequence of successive differences $a_{m+1}-a_m$ eventually become periodic?
status: This is an old problem of Dickson in number theory. Computationally, even a starting set as small as $\{1,4,9,16,25\}$ requires thousands of terms before periodicity occurs. The problem is discussed as Problem 7 on Green's open problems list and tracked at erdosproblems.com/341.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, for every finite starting set $A$, the difference sequence $a_{m+1}-a_m$ of the resulting greedy "non-sum" sequence is eventually periodic.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and its resolution would settle an old question of Dickson about the behavior of these greedy sequences.

title: Erdős problem #342
open: What can be said about the Ulam sequence defined by $a_1=1$, $a_2=2$, and $a_{n+1}$ ($n\geq 2$) the least integer greater than $a_n$ expressible uniquely as $a_i+a_j$ with $i<j\leq n$? In particular, do infinitely many pairs $a, a+2$ occur, do the differences eventually become periodic, and is the sequence's density $0$?
status: The sequence begins $1,2,3,4,6,8,11,13,16,18,26,28,\ldots$ and appears as OEIS A002858. It is discussed as Problem 7 of Green's open problems list, and is problem C4 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A characterization of the sequence's structure that resolves its basic behavior — for instance, determining whether infinitely many consecutive-odd pairs $a, a+2$ occur, whether the sequence of differences is eventually periodic, and whether the asymptotic density is $0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (a problem originally of Ulam), with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; even the most basic structural properties of the sequence remain unknown.

title: Erdős problem #345
open: For a complete sequence $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$, let $T(A)$ be the threshold of completeness — the least $m$ such that every $n\geq m$ lies in $P(A)=\{\sum_{n\in B}n : B\subseteq A \textrm{ finite}\}$. Are there infinitely many $k$ for which $T(n^k)>T(n^{k+1})$, i.e. infinitely many drops in the threshold sequence of the powers?
status: Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] remark that very little is known about $T(A)$ in general. It is known that $T(n)=1$, $T(n^2)=128$, $T(n^3)=12758$, $T(n^4)=5134240$, and $T(n^5)=67898771$. Erdős and Graham remark that a good candidate for the $k$ in the question are $k=2^t$ for large $t$, perhaps even $t=3$, because of the highly restricted values of $n^{2^t}$ modulo $2^{t+1}$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that there are infinitely many $k$ with $T(n^k)>T(n^{k+1})$.

title: Erdős problem #348
open: For which pairs $0\leq m<n$ does there exist a complete sequence $A=\{a_1\leq a_2\leq\cdots\}$ of integers that stays complete after removing any $m$ elements, yet fails to be complete after removing any $n$ elements?
status: The Fibonacci sequence $1,1,2,3,5,\ldots$ shows that $m=1$ and $n=2$ is possible, and the powers of $2$ show that $m=0$ and $n=1$ is possible; the case $m=2$, $n=3$ is not known. van Doorn has shown that no such sequence exists for $2\leq m<n$ under the strong notion of completeness requiring $\{\sum_{n\in B} n : \text{finite } B\subset A\}=\mathbb{N}$; Erdős and Graham most likely meant the weaker notion allowing finitely many exceptions.
solved_when: The set of attainable pairs $(m,n)$ is characterized — in particular, the case $m=2$, $n=3$ is decided.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #349
open: For which values of $t,\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ is the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ complete — meaning every sufficiently large integer can be written as a sum of distinct terms of the form $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$?
status: Even in the range $t\in(0,1)$ and $\alpha\in(1,2)$ the behaviour is surprisingly complex. Graham [Gr64e] has shown that for any $k$ there exists some $t_k\in(0,1)$ such that the set of $\alpha$ for which the sequence is complete consists of at least $k$ disjoint line segments. It seems likely that the sequence is complete for all $t>0$ and all $1<\alpha<\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$, but proving this seems very difficult, since we do not even know whether $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ is odd or even infinitely often.
solved_when: A characterization of all pairs $(t,\alpha)$ with $t,\alpha\in(0,\infty)$ for which $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is complete; a natural milestone is proving completeness for all $t>0$ and all $1<\alpha<\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolves a basic question about when Beatty-type exponential sequences form additive bases.

title: Erdős problem #352
open: Is there an absolute constant $c>0$ such that every measurable subset of the plane of measure at least $c$ contains the vertices of a triangle of area 1?
status: Erdős (unpublished, in geometry) proved the statement is true if $A$ has infinite measure, or if $A$ is an unbounded set of positive measure, stating in [Er78d] and [Er83d] that it "follows easily from the Lebesgue density theorem." In [Er78d] and [Er83d] he speculated that perhaps $C=4\pi/\sqrt{27}\approx 2.418$ works, which would be best possible, as witnessed by a circle of radius $<2\cdot 3^{-3/4}$. Further evidence comes from Freiling and Mauldin [Ma02], who proved that if $A$ has outer measure $>4\pi/\sqrt{27}$ then $A$ contains the vertices of a triangle with area $>1$; this also establishes the same threshold for the original problem under the assumption that $A$ is a compact convex set. Mauldin discusses the problem in [Ma13], noting that it suffices to prove the conjecture under the assumption that $A$ is the union of the interiors of $n<\infty$ compact convex sets, and Freiling and Mauldin (see [Ma13]) have proved the conjecture for $1\leq n\leq 3$.
solved_when: A specific constant $c>0$ is exhibited (Erdős conjectured the optimal value $C=4\pi/\sqrt{27}\approx 2.418$) and proved to guarantee a unit-area triangle in every measurable set of measure at least that value.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would settle a natural extremal question about which large planar sets must contain a prescribed configuration.

title: Erdős problem #354
open: Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ with $\alpha/\beta$ irrational. Must the multiset $\{\lfloor \alpha\rfloor,\lfloor 2\alpha\rfloor,\lfloor 4\alpha\rfloor,\ldots\}\cup\{\lfloor \beta\rfloor,\lfloor 2\beta\rfloor,\lfloor 4\beta\rfloor,\ldots\}$ be complete — that is, does every sufficiently large natural number $n$ admit a representation $n=\sum_{s\in S}\lfloor 2^s\alpha\rfloor+\sum_{t\in T}\lfloor 2^t\beta\rfloor$ for finite $S,T\subset\mathbb{N}$? Does the answer persist if $2$ is replaced by some $\gamma\in(1,2)$?
status: The question was first mentioned by Graham [Gr71]. Hegyvári [He89] proved completeness holds when $\alpha=m/2^n$ is a dyadic rational and $\beta$ is not, and also proved non-completeness when $\alpha\geq 2$ and $\beta=2^k\alpha$ for some $k\geq 0$. He later [He91] proved that for any fixed $\alpha>0$, the set of $\beta$ for which completeness holds has measure either $0$ or infinite measure, and in [He94] proved that the set of $(\alpha,\beta)$ for which the corresponding set of sums does not contain an infinite arithmetic progression has cardinality continuum. Jiang and Ma [JiMa24] and Fang and He [FaHe25] proved non-completeness when $1<\alpha<2$ and $\beta=2^k\alpha$ for sufficiently large $k$. Hegyvári conjectures that the assumption $\alpha/\beta$ irrational can be weakened to $\alpha/\beta\neq 2^k$ with at least one of $\alpha,\beta$ not dyadic. In the comments van Doorn proves completeness when $\alpha<2<\beta<3$, and proves that if either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ is not a dyadic rational, the corresponding sequence with ceiling functions replacing the floor functions is complete.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given that for all positive reals $\alpha,\beta$ with $\alpha/\beta$ irrational, every sufficiently large natural number $n$ can be written as $n=\sum_{s\in S}\lfloor 2^s\alpha\rfloor+\sum_{t\in T}\lfloor 2^t\beta\rfloor$ for finite $S,T\subset\mathbb{N}$, together with an answer to the variant where $2$ is replaced by $\gamma\in(1,2)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle the completeness of doubled floor sequences, a natural borderline case in the theory of complete sequences.

title: Erdős problem #357
open: Let $1\leq a_1<\cdots<a_k\leq n$ be integers such that all consecutive block sums $\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i$ are distinct, and let $f(n)$ be the maximal such $k$. Does $f(n)$ grow sublinearly — that is, is $f(n)=o(n)$?
status: Asked by Erdős and Harzheim. In [Er77c] Erdős asks about an infinite such set of integers, and whether such a set must have density $0$. He notes that a simple averaging process implies $a_k \gg k\log k$ for infinitely many $k$, and so the lower density is $0$. He also asks whether $\sum\frac{1}{a_k}$ must converge. Weisenberg in the comments observes that any set which satisfies [874] also has this property, which implies $f(n)\geq (2+o(1))n^{1/2}$. If $g(n)$ is the maximal $k$ such that there are $1\leq a_1,\ldots,a_k\leq n$ with all consecutive sums distinct (i.e. dropping the monotonicity assumption in the definition of $f$), then Hegyvári [He86] proved $\left(\frac{1}{3}+o(1)\right)n\leq g(n)\leq \left(\frac{2}{3}+o(1)\right)n$. The upper bound of Coppersmith and Phillips in [867] implies $g(n)\leq\left(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{512}+o(1)\right)n$. A similar question can be asked replacing strict monotonicity with weak monotonicity (allowing $a_i=a_j$). Erdős and Harzheim also ask what is the least $m$ which is not a sum of the given form, and whether it can be much larger than $n$; they can show that $\sum_{x<a_i<x^2}\frac{1}{a_i}\ll 1$.
solved_when: The growth rate of $f(n)$ is determined, and in particular the question of whether $f(n)=o(n)$ is resolved.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles the density behaviour of sets whose consecutive block sums are all distinct.

title: Erdős problem #359
open: Start from $a_1=n$ and define $a_{i+1}$ to be the least integer that is not a sum of consecutive earlier terms of the increasing sequence $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ — how dense is the resulting sequence? In particular, when $n=1$, is it true that $a_k/k\to\infty$ while $a_k/k^{1+c}\to 0$ for every $c>0$?
status: A problem of MacMahon, studied by Andrews [An75]. When $n=1$ the sequence begins $1,2,4,5,8,10,14,15,\ldots$, and is A002048 in the OEIS. Andrews conjectures $a_k\sim \frac{k\log k}{\log\log k}$. Porubsky [Po77] proved that, for any $\epsilon>0$, there are infinitely many $k$ such that $a_k < (\log k)^\epsilon \frac{k\log k}{\log\log k}$, and also that if $A(x)$ counts the number of $a_i\leq x$ then $\limsup \frac{A(x)}{\pi(x)}\geq \frac{1}{\log 2}$, where $\pi(x)$ counts the number of primes $\leq x$. See also [839].
solved_when: A determination of the density of the sequence; in the case $n=1$, a proof that $a_k/k\to\infty$ and $a_k/k^{1+c}\to 0$ for any $c>0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, so resolving it settles a longstanding item in the Erdős problem canon.

title: Erdős problem #361
open: How large can a subset $A$ of $\{1,\ldots,\lfloor cn\rfloor\}$ be, for $c>0$ and large $n$, while $n$ still cannot be written as a sum of distinct elements of $A$? Does the answer depend on $n$ in an irregular way?
status: The problem is listed as open among the Erdős problems in number theory, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/361.
solved_when: The maximum size of such a set $A$ is determined as a function of $c$ and $n$, and it is settled whether this quantity behaves irregularly as $n$ varies.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/361; a solution resolves a long-standing entry in that catalogue.

title: Erdős problem #364
open: Are there triples of consecutive positive integers that are all powerful, where a number is powerful if every prime dividing it does so with exponent at least two? Equivalently, do there exist $n$ such that $n-1$, $n$, and $n+1$ are all powerful?
status: Erdős originally asked Mahler whether there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive powerful numbers, but Mahler immediately observed that the answer is yes from the infinitely many solutions to the Pell equation $x^2=8y^2+1$. The conjecture was also made by Mollin and Walsh [MoWa86]. Erdős [Er76d] believed the answer to this question is no, and in fact that if $n_k$ is the $k$th powerful number then $n_{k+2}-n_k > n_k^c$ for some constant $c>0$. The abc conjecture implies there are only finitely many such triples. It is trivial that there are no quadruples of consecutive powerful numbers since one must be $2 \pmod{4}$. Chan [Ch25] has shown there are no triples $n-1,n,n+1$ of powerful numbers with $n$ a cube and $n-1,n+1$ both of the shape $p^3x^2$ for some prime $p$ and integer $x$. She [Sh25] has proved there are no triples with $n$ a cube and both $n-1,n+1$ of the shape $p^2x^3$ with $p$ a prime. By OEIS A076445 there are no such $n$ for $n<7.38\times 10^{28}$. See also [137], [365], and [938].
solved_when: A proof that no such triple exists, or an explicit example of one; alternatively, a proof or disproof of Erdős's stronger claim that if $n_k$ is the $k$th powerful number then $n_{k+2}-n_k > n_k^c$ for some constant $c>0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a natural question about the gaps between powerful numbers and their local distribution.

title: Erdős problem #365
open: Must every pair of consecutive powerful numbers arise from a Pell equation — that is, must one of the two numbers be a square? And how sparse are such pairs: is the count of $n \leq x$ with both $n$ and $n+1$ powerful bounded by $(\log x)^{O(1)}$?
status: Erdős originally asked Mahler whether there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive powerful numbers, but Mahler immediately observed that the answer is yes from the infinitely many solutions to the Pell equation $x^2=2^3y^2+1$. The list of $n$ such that $n$ and $n+1$ are both powerful is A060355 in the OEIS. The answer to the first question is no: Golomb [Go70] observed that both $12167=23^3$ and $12168=2^33^213^2$ are powerful. Walker [Wa76] proved that the equation $7^3x^2=3^3y^2+1$ has infinitely many solutions, giving infinitely many counterexamples. See also [364]. This is discussed in problem B16 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/365; Erdős references: [Er76d,p.31].
solved_when: The question is settled by a proof or disproof that the number of $n \leq x$ such that $n$ and $n+1$ are both powerful is bounded by $(\log x)^{O(1)}$ (the sub-question of whether all such pairs come from Pell equations, i.e. whether one of $n$, $n+1$ must be a square, having already been resolved negatively).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would clarify how sparse consecutive powerful numbers can be beyond the Pell-generated families.

title: Erdős problem #366
open: Do there exist any integers $n$ that are $2$-full while $n+1$ is $3$-full — that is, every prime dividing $n$ divides it at least to the second power, and every prime dividing $n+1$ divides it at least to the third power?
status: Erdős originally asked Mahler whether there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive powerful numbers, but Mahler immediately observed that the answer is yes from the infinitely many solutions to the Pell equation $x^2=8y^2+1$; note that $8$ is 3-full and $9$ is 2-full. Erdős and Graham asked if this is the only pair of such consecutive integers. Stephan has observed that $12167=23^3$ and $12168=2^33^213^2$ (a pair already known to Golomb [Go70]) is another example, but (by OEIS A060355) there are no other examples for $n<10^{22}$. In [Er76d] Erdős asks the weaker question of whether there are any consecutive pairs of $3$-full integers (which is also discussed in problem B16 of Guy's collection [Gu04]). Turturean notes that the ABC conjecture implies there are only finitely many such $n$.
solved_when: Either an example of a $2$-full $n$ with $n+1$ being $3$-full is exhibited, or it is proved that no such $n$ exists (or that only finitely many exist, e.g. unconditionally establishing what the ABC conjecture predicts).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles the exact structure of consecutive powerful numbers beyond the known Pell-family examples.

title: Erdős problem #367
open: For a block of $k$ consecutive integers, is the product of their $2$-full parts always nearly quadratic in size? Formally, writing $B_2(n)=n/n'$ where $n'$ is the product of all primes dividing $n$ exactly once, is it true that for every fixed $k\geq 1$, $\prod_{n\leq m<n+k}B_2(m)\ll n^{2+o(1)}$, or perhaps even $\ll_k n^2$?
status: van Doorn notes in the comments that for $k\leq 2$ one trivially has $\prod_{n\leq m<n+k}B_2(m)\ll n^2$, but this fails for all $k\geq 3$: in fact $\prod_{n\leq m<n+3}B_2(m)\gg n^2\log n$ infinitely often. The question is equivalent (up to constants) to [935]. It would also be interesting to bound the analogous product with $B_r$ for $r\geq 3$, where $B_r(n)$ is the $r$-full part of $n$ (the product of prime powers $p^a\mid n$ with $p^{a+1}\nmid n$ and $a\geq r$): is it true that for every fixed $r,k\geq 2$ and $\epsilon>0$, $\limsup \frac{\prod_{n\leq m<n+k}B_r(m)}{n^{1+\epsilon}}\to\infty$?
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every fixed $k\geq 1$ one has $\prod_{n\leq m<n+k}B_2(m)\ll n^{2+o(1)}$; the stronger target is the bound $\ll_k n^2$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would settle the behavior of powerful parts over short intervals.

title: Erdős problem #368
open: How large is the largest prime factor of $n(n+1)$? More precisely, if $F(n)$ denotes this prime factor, does $F(n)\gg (\log n)^2$ hold for all $n$?
status: Pólya [Po18] proved that $F(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to\infty$. Mahler [Ma35] showed that $F(n)\gg \log\log n$. Schinzel [Sc67b] observed that for infinitely many $n$ we have $F(n)\leq n^{O(1/\log\log\log n)}$. The truth is probably $F(n)\gg (\log n)^2$ for all $n$. Erdős [Er76d] conjectured that, for every $\epsilon>0$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $F(n) <(\log n)^{2+\epsilon}$. Pasten [Pa24b] has proved that $F(n) \gg \frac{(\log\log n)^2}{\log\log\log n}$. The largest prime factors of $n(n+1)$ are listed as A074399 in the OEIS.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the conjectured truth that $F(n)\gg (\log n)^2$ for all $n$; in particular, Erdős [Er76d] conjectured that for every $\epsilon>0$ there are infinitely many $n$ with $F(n) <(\log n)^{2+\epsilon}$, which together would pin the order of $F(n)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve the true order of the largest prime factor of a product of consecutive integers, a basic multiplicative question.

title: Erdős problem #371
open: Does the set of integers $n$ for which the largest prime factor of $n$ is smaller than the largest prime factor of $n+1$ have natural density $1/2$? Formally, writing $P(n)$ for the largest prime factor of $n$, show that $\{n : P(n) < P(n+1)\}$ has density $1/2$.
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Pomerance [ErPo78], who proved that this set and its complement both have positive upper density. The best unconditional lower bound is due to Lü and Wang [LuWa25], who prove $\#\{n < x : P(n) < P(n+1)\} > (0.2017 - o(1))x$, and the same lower bound for the complement. In [Er79e] Erdős also asks whether, for every $\alpha$, the density of the set of $n$ where $P(n+1) > P(n)n^\alpha$ exists. Teräväinen [Te18] proved that the logarithmic density of the set of $n$ with $P(n) < P(n+1)$ is $1/2$, and more generally, for any $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$, that the logarithmic density of the set of $n$ for which $P(n+1) > P(n)n^\alpha$ exists and equals $\int_{[0,1]^2} 1_{y \geq x+\alpha} u(x)u(y)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y$, where $u(x) = x^{-1}\rho(x^{-1}-1)$ and $\rho$ is the Dickman function. Tao and Teräväinen [TaTe19] proved that the asymptotic density is $1/2$ at 'almost all scales'. Wang [Wa21] proved that the same value holds for the asymptotic density (and in particular gave an affirmative answer to the original question) conditional on the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture for friable integers.
solved_when: The natural density $\#\{n < x : P(n) < P(n+1)\}/x$ is proved to exist and equal $1/2$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would resolve a long-standing question about the symmetry of largest prime factors of consecutive integers.

title: Erdős problem #373
open: Are there only finitely many ways to write a factorial as a product of smaller factorials, excluding the trivial cases? Formally, does $n! = a_1!a_2!\cdots a_k!$ with $n-1 > a_1 \geq a_2 \geq \cdots \geq a_k \geq 2$ have only finitely many solutions?
status: The finiteness would follow if $P(n(n+1))/\log n \to \infty$, where $P(m)$ denotes the largest prime factor of $m$ (see Problem [368]). Erdős [Er76d] proved it would also follow from showing that $P(n(n-1)) > 4\log n$. The condition $a_1 < n-1$ rules out the trivial solutions when $n = a_2!\cdots a_k!$. Surányi was the first to conjecture that the only non-trivial solution to $a!b! = n!$ is $6!7! = 10!$. More generally, Hickerson (as reported in [Er76d]) conjectured that the only non-trivial solutions are the four listed above. Luca [Lu07b] showed there are only finitely many solutions, conditional on the ABC conjecture, and proved unconditionally that the number of $n \leq x$ admitting a non-trivial solution is at most $\exp(f(x)\log x/\log\log x)$ for any function $f(x)$ tending to infinity. The problem is discussed in problem B23 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. For $k=2$, Erdős [Er93] proved that if $n! = a_1!a_2!$ with $n-1 > a_1 \geq a_2$, then $a_1 \geq n - 5\log\log n$, and says it 'would be nice' to prove $a_1 \geq n - o(\log\log n)$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the above equation has only finitely many non-trivial solutions; the conjectured complete list is $9!=2!3!3!7!$, $10!=6!7!$, $10!=3!5!7!$, and $16!=14!5!2!$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would settle a long-standing question about how multiplicative factorials can be.

title: Erdős problem #374
open: For any $m\in \mathbb{N}$, let $F(m)$ be the minimal $k\geq 2$ (if it exists) such that there are $a_1<\cdots <a_k=m$ with $a_1!\cdots a_k!$ a square. Let $D_k=\{ m : F(m)=k\}$. What is the order of growth of $\lvert D_k\cap\{1,\ldots,n\}\rvert$ for $3\leq k\leq 6$? For example, is it true that $\lvert D_6\cap \{1,\ldots,n\}\rvert \gg n$?
status: Studied by Erdős and Graham [ErGr76] (see also [LSS14]). It is known that no $D_k$ contains a prime, $D_2=\{ n^2 : n>1\}$, $\lvert D_3\cap \{1,\ldots,n\}\rvert = o(\lvert D_4\cap \{1,\ldots,n\}\rvert)$, the least element of $D_6$ is $527$, and $D_k=\emptyset$ for $k>6$.
solved_when: The order of growth of $\lvert D_k\cap\{1,\ldots,n\}\rvert$ is determined for $3\leq k\leq 6$, including in particular whether $\lvert D_6\cap \{1,\ldots,n\}\rvert \gg n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a long-standing entry in that catalog.

title: Erdős problem #375
open: If $n+1,\ldots,n+k$ are all composite, must there exist distinct primes $p_1,\ldots,p_k$ with $p_i\mid n+i$ for each $1\leq i\leq k$?
status: The case $k\leq 2$ is trivial. The conjecture is originally due to Grimm [Gr69]. Grimm proved it for $k\ll \log n/\log\log n$; Erdős and Selfridge improved this to $k\leq (1+o(1))\log n$; Ramachanda, Shorey, and Tijdeman [RST75] improved it to $k\ll\left(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\right)^3$. Laishram and Shorey [LaSh06] verified it for all $k\geq 1$ and all $n\leq 1.9\times 10^{10}$. It appears as problem B32 in Guy's collection [Gu04]; see also [860].
solved_when: Distinct primes $p_1,\ldots,p_k$ are proved to exist with $p_i\mid n+i$ for $1\leq i\leq k$ whenever $n+1,\ldots,n+k$ are all composite, for all $n,k\geq 1$ (or a counterexample is produced).
why: Resolving it affirmatively is extremely hard: it would in particular imply $p_{n+1}-p_n < p_n^{1/2-c}$ for some constant $c>0$, thereby resolving Legendre's conjecture.

title: Erdős problem #376
open: Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is coprime to $105$? Equivalently, are there infinitely many $n$ whose base-$3$ digits are only $0,1$, whose base-$5$ digits are only $0,1,2$, and whose base-$7$ digits are only $0,1,2,3$?
status: Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75] showed that for any two odd primes $p$ and $q$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is coprime to $pq$. Via Kummer's theorem, the problem is equivalent to asking for infinitely many $n$ with digits $0,1$ in base $3$, digits $0,1,2$ in base $5$, and digits $0,1,2,3$ in base $7$; such $n$ form sequence A030979 in the OEIS. The best result in this direction is due to Bloom and Croot [BlCr25], who proved that if $p_1,p_2,p_3$ are sufficiently large primes, then for all $\epsilon>0$ there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is coprime to $p_1p_2p_3$ except for a factor of size $\leq n^\epsilon$ — equivalently, almost all base-$p_i$ digits of such $n$ are $<p_i/2$. The problem is mentioned as B33 in Guy's collection [Gu04] and discussed in an article of Pomerance [Po15c]; Graham's \$1000 prize is noted in [Gu04] and [BeHa98].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that infinitely many $n$ satisfy $\gcd\bigl(\binom{2n}{n}, 105\bigr)=1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, offered with a \$1000 prize by Graham, and a solution would resolve a natural question about simultaneous digit restrictions across three prime bases.
aliases: Erdős #376; number theory / binomial coefficients / base representations

title: Erdős problem #377
open: Is there an absolute constant $C>0$ such that $\sum_{p\leq n,\ p\nmid \binom{2n}{n}} \frac{1}{p} \leq C$ for all $n$, where the sum runs over primes $p\leq n$ not dividing the central binomial coefficient $\binom{2n}{n}$?
status: The question is due to Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75], who proved that if $f(n)$ is the sum in question, then $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\leq x}f(n)=\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac{\log k}{2^k}=\gamma_0$ and $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\leq x}f(n)^2=\gamma_0^2$, so that for almost all integers $f(m)=\gamma_0+o(1)$. They also proved that for all large $n$, $f(n)\leq c\log\log n$ for some constant $c<1$ (it is trivial from Mertens estimates that $f(n)\leq (1+o(1))\log\log n$). The problem is mentioned as B33 in Guy's collection [Gu04] and is tracked at erdosproblems.com/377.
solved_when: An absolute constant $C>0$ is exhibited (or proved to exist) such that the bound $\sum_{p\leq n}1_{p\nmid \binom{2n}{n}}\frac{1}{p}\leq C$ holds for all $n$; a negative answer requires exhibiting, for every $C$, some $n$ violating the bound.
why: A positive answer would imply $\sum_{p\leq n}1_{p\mid \binom{2n}{n}}\frac{1}{p}=(1-o(1))\log\log n$, showing the central binomial coefficient is divisible by nearly all the prime mass one expects; Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus said there is 'no doubt' this latter claim is true.

title: Erdős problem #382
open: If $u\leq v$ are such that the largest prime dividing $\prod_{u\leq m\leq v}m$ appears with exponent at least $2$, must $v-u$ be small — specifically $v^{o(1)}$? Or can $v-u$ be arbitrarily large?
status: Erdős and Graham report it follows from results of Ramachandra that $v-u\leq v^{1/2+o(1)}$. Cambie observed that the first question reduces to old conjectures on prime gaps: by Cramér's conjecture, for every $\epsilon>0$ and every sufficiently large $u$ there is a prime between $u$ and $u+u^\epsilon$, so for $u+u^\epsilon<v$ the largest prime divisor of $\prod_{u\leq m\leq v}m$ appears with exponent $1$; since this is not the case in the question, Cramér implies $v-u=v^{o(1)}$. For the second question, Cambie gives a heuristic: the 'probability' that the largest prime divisor of $n$ is $<n^{1/2}$ is $1-\log 2>0$, so for any fixed $k$ there is positive 'probability' that there are $k$ consecutive integers around $q^2$ (for a prime $q$) all of whose prime divisors are bounded above by $q$, giving $v-u\geq k$. See [383] for a conjecture along these lines. A similar argument applies if multiplicity $2$ is replaced by multiplicity $r$ for any fixed $r\geq 2$. See also [380].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of whether $v-u=v^{o(1)}$ holds whenever the largest prime divisor of $\prod_{u\leq m\leq v}m$ has exponent at least $2$, and a determination of whether $v-u$ can be arbitrarily large.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles a natural question about how long runs of consecutive integers behave with respect to their large prime factors.

title: Erdős problem #383
open: Is it true that for every $k$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that the largest prime divisor of $\prod_{0\leq i\leq k}(p^2+i)$ is $p$ itself?
status: No resolution is recorded. Heuristically, the 'probability' that $n$ has no prime divisors $\geq n^{1/2}$ is $1-\log 2>0$, so standard heuristics predict the answer is yes. Tracked at erdosproblems.com/383.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every fixed $k$ infinitely many primes $p$ satisfy the condition; equivalently, an unconditional answer resolving Erdős problem #383.
why: A positive answer would resolve the second part of Erdős problem [382], and the problem is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #385
open: For each n, let F(n) be the maximum of m + p(m) over composite m < n, where p(m) is the least prime divisor of m. Is F(n) > n for all sufficiently large n, and does F(n) − n tend to infinity as n → ∞?
status: A question of Erdős, Eggleton, and Selfridge, who write that 'plausible conjectures on primes' imply that F(n) ≤ n for only finitely many n, and in fact it is possible that this quantity is always at least n + (1 − o(1))√n (note that it is trivially ≤ n + √n). Tao has discussed this problem in a blog post. Sarosh Adenwalla has observed that the first question is equivalent to problem [430]: if n is large and a_i is the sequence defined in the latter problem, then [430] implies that there is a composite a_j such that a_j − p(a_j) > n and hence F(n) > n. See also [463]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/385; Erdős references: [Er79d, p. 73].
solved_when: It is proved that F(n) > n for all sufficiently large n; the stronger question of whether F(n) − n → ∞ as n → ∞ may be treated as a further target, along with the conjectured lower bound F(n) ≥ n + (1 − o(1))√n.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would settle a natural question about the distribution of smooth composite numbers near n.

title: Erdős problem #386
open: For $2\leq k\leq n-2$, can the binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}$ equal a product of consecutive primes infinitely often? For example, $\binom{21}{2}=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7$.
status: Erdős and Graham write that 'a proof that this cannot happen infinitely often for $\binom{n}{2}$ seems hopeless; probably this can never happen for $\binom{n}{k}$ if $3\leq k\leq n-3$.' Weisenberg has provided four easy examples that show Erdős and Graham were too optimistic here: $\binom{7}{3}=5\cdot 7$, $\binom{10}{4}=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7$, $\binom{14}{4}=7\cdot 11\cdot 13$, and $\binom{15}{6}=5\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13$. The known values of $n$ for which $\binom{n}{2}$ is the product of consecutive primes are $4,6,15,21,715$ (see A280992).
solved_when: Either an infinite family of pairs $(n,k)$ with $2\leq k\leq n-2$ for which $\binom{n}{k}$ is a product of consecutive primes is exhibited, or it is proved that only finitely many such pairs exist.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #388
open: Can one classify all solutions of \[\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(m_1+i)=\prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2}(m_2+j)\] where $k_1,k_2>3$ and $m_1+k_1\leq m_2$? In particular, are there only finitely many such solutions?
status: Open, in the setting of number theory. More generally, it is conjectured that if $k_1>2$, then for fixed $a$ and $b$ the equation \[a\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(m_1+i)=b\prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2}(m_2+j)\] should have only a finite number of solutions. See also [363], [686], and [931].
solved_when: A complete classification of all solutions of the displayed equation with $k_1,k_2>3$ and $m_1+k_1\leq m_2$ is given, or, failing classification, a proof that only finitely many solutions exist.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolves a natural finiteness question about products of consecutive integers in number theory.

title: Erdős problem #389
open: Is it true that for every $n\geq 1$ there exists a $k$ such that $n(n+1)\cdots(n+k-1)\mid (n+k)\cdots(n+2k-1)$ — that is, the product of $k$ consecutive integers starting at $n$ divides the product of the next $k$ consecutive integers?
status: Asked by Erdős and Straus.
