Small cases are known: for $n=2$ one may take $k=5$, since $2\times 3\times 4\times 5\times 6 \mid 7\times 8\times 9\times 10\times 11$, and for $n=3$ one may take $k=4$, since $3\times 4\times 5\times 6 \mid 7\times 8\times 9\times 10$. Bhavik Mehta has computed the minimal such $k$ for $1\leq n\leq 18$, now available as A375071 on the OEIS.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that such a $k$ exists for every $n\geq 1$.

title: Erdős problem #390
open: Let $f(n)$ be the smallest $m$ such that $n! = a_1\cdots a_k$ for some integers $n < a_1 < \cdots < a_k = m$. Does the excess $f(n) - 2n$ grow like a constant times $\frac{n}{\log n}$, and if so, what is that constant?
status: Erdős, Guy, and Selfridge [EGS82] have shown that $f(n) - 2n \asymp \frac{n}{\log n}$, so the growth is known up to constant factors. Key works: erdosproblems.com/390.
solved_when: A constant $c$ is exhibited (or shown not to exist) such that $f(n) - 2n \sim c\frac{n}{\log n}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles the precise asymptotics of representing factorials as products of large factors.

title: Erdős problem #393
open: How narrow can the interval be from which the factors of a factorial are drawn? Formally, if $f(n)$ is the minimal $m\geq 1$ such that $n! = a_1\cdots a_t$ with $a_1 < \cdots < a_t = a_1+m$, what is the asymptotic behaviour of $f(n)$?
status: Erdős and Graham write that they do not even know whether $f(n)=1$ infinitely often, i.e. whether a factorial is the product of two consecutive integers infinitely often. Let $F_m(N)$ count the number of $n\leq N$ such that $f(n)=m$. Berend and Osgood [BeOs92] proved that, for each fixed $m$, $F_m(N)=o(N)$. Bui, Pratt, and Zaharescu [BPZ23] have shown that $F_m(N)\ll_m N^{33/34}$. A result of Luca [Lu02] implies, conditional on the ABC conjecture, that $f(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$.
solved_when: A determination of the growth of $f(n)$ as $n\to\infty$; in particular, an answer to whether $f(n)=1$ infinitely often.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and even the basic infinitude question (factorials as products of two consecutive integers) remains unsettled.

title: Erdős problem #394
open: Let $t_k(n)$ be the least $m$ such that $n$ divides the product $m(m+1)\cdots(m+k-1)$. How large is $\sum_{n\leq x} t_2(n)$ — in particular, is it $\ll x^2/(\log x)^c$ for some $c>0$ — and is it true that $\sum_{n\leq x} t_{k+1}(n) = o\!\left(\sum_{n\leq x} t_k(n)\right)$ for $k\geq 2$?
status: In [ErGr80] a conjecture of Erdős that the sum is $o(x^2)$ is mentioned; this was proved by Erdős and Hall [ErHa78], who in fact showed $\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\ll \frac{\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}x^2$. Erdős and Hall conjecture the sum is $o(x^2/(\log x)^c)$ for any $c<\log 2$. Since $t_2(p)=p-1$ for prime $p$, it is trivial that $\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\gg x^2/\log x$. Erdős and Hall [ErHa78] also note that $t_{n-1}(n!)=2$ and $t_{n-2}(n!)\ll n$, which $n=2^r$ shows is best possible. They ask about the behaviour of $t_{n-3}(n!)$, and whether for infinitely many $n$ one has $t_k(n!)<t_{k-1}(n!)-1$ for all $1\leq k<n$; they proved (with Selfridge) that this holds for $n=10$.
solved_when: A proof that $\sum_{n\leq x}t_2(n)\ll x^2/(\log x)^c$ for some $c>0$, or a proof or disproof that $\sum_{n\leq x}t_{k+1}(n)=o(\sum_{n\leq x}t_k(n))$ for $k\geq 2$, is established.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/394; settling it would pin down the average behaviour of the shortest length-$k$ product interval divisible by $n$, a basic multiplicative-structure quantity.

title: Erdős problem #396
open: Is it true that for every $k$ there exists $n$ such that $\prod_{0\leq i\leq k}(n-i) \mid \binom{2n}{n}$ — that is, can a run of $k+1$ consecutive integers ending at $n$ all divide the central binomial coefficient $\binom{2n}{n}$?
status: Erdős and Graham write that $n+1$ always divides $\binom{2n}{n}$ (indeed $\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ is the $n$th Catalan number), but it is quite rare that $n$ divides $\binom{2n}{n}$. Pomerance [Po14] has shown that for any $k\geq 0$ there are infinitely many $n$ such that $n-k\mid\binom{2n}{n}$, although the set of such $n$ has upper density $<1/3$. Pomerance also shows that the set of $n$ such that $\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)\mid \binom{2n}{n}$ has density $1$. The smallest $n$ for each $k$ are listed as A375077 on the OEIS.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every $k \geq 0$ there exists some $n$ with $\prod_{0\leq i\leq k}(n-i)$ dividing $\binom{2n}{n}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a basic question about the divisibility structure of central binomial coefficients.

title: Erdős problem #400
open: Is there a constant $c_k$ such that $\sum_{n\leq x} g_k(n) \sim c_k\,x\log x$, where $g_k(n)$ is the maximum of $(a_1+\cdots+a_k)-n$ over integers $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ with $a_1!\cdots a_k! \mid n!$? More precisely, is it true that for almost all $n<x$ one has $g_k(n)=c_k\log x+o(\log x)$?
status: Erdős and Graham write that it is easy to show $g_k(n) \ll_k \log n$ always, but the best possible constant is unknown. See also [401] (erdosproblems.com/400).
solved_when: Explicit constants $c_k$ are determined such that $\sum_{n\leq x}g_k(n)\sim c_k\,x\log x$, and it is shown that $g_k(n)=c_k\log x+o(\log x)$ for almost all $n<x$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and resolving it would pin down the sharp constant in the known bound $g_k(n)\ll_k\log n$, completing the asymptotic picture of how far factorial products can divide $n!$.

title: Erdős problem #404
open: For which integers $a \geq 1$ and primes $p$ is the set of $k$ for which one can find $a = a_1 < \cdots < a_n$ with $p^k \mid (a_1! + \cdots + a_n!)$ bounded above? Equivalently, letting $f(a,p)$ denote the greatest such $k$, determine for which pairs $(a,p)$ the function is finite and how it behaves; and decide whether there exist a prime $p$ and an infinite sequence $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots$ such that, with $p^{m_k}$ the highest power of $p$ dividing $\sum_{i \leq k} a_i!$, one has $m_k \to \infty$.
status: See also [403]. Lin [Li76] has shown that $f(2,2) \leq 254$.
solved_when: A complete characterization of the pairs $(a, p)$ for which such a finite upper bound exists, together with a determination (or sharp asymptotics) of $f(a, p)$, and a resolution of whether an infinite sequence $(a_i)$ and prime $p$ with $m_k \to \infty$ exist.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a concrete question about the $p$-divisibility of sums of factorials.

title: Erdős problem #406
open: Are there only finitely many powers of $2$ whose base-$3$ representation uses only the digits $0$ and $1$? Equivalently, is the set of $k$ such that $3^m$-free digit restrictions hold for $2^k$ finite — a question about the interaction of multiplicative independence and digit restrictions across bases?
status: The only known examples appear to be $1$, $4=1+3$, and $256=1+3+3^2+3^5$; if only digits $1$ and $2$ are allowed, $2^{15}$ seems to be the largest such power of $2$. Saye [Sa22] computed that $2^n$ contains every possible ternary digit for $16\leq n \leq 5.9\times 10^{21}$. Letting $N(x)$ count the $n\leq x$ such that $2^n$ has only the digits $0$ and $1$ in base $3$, Narkiewicz [Na80] proved $N(x)\leq 1.62 x^{\log_32}$. The problem appears as B33 in Guy's collection [Gu04], and many generalisations are possible — see, for example, [AbLa14] and [La09].
solved_when: A proof that only finitely many powers of $2$ have base-$3$ representations using only the digits $0$ and $1$ (ideally showing the only examples are $1$, $4$, and $256$), or an explicit construction of infinitely many such powers.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a positive answer would imply via Kummer's theorem that $3\mid \binom{2^{k+1}}{2^k}$ for all large $k$.

title: Erdős problem #408
open: If $\phi_k(n)$ denotes the $k$-fold iterate of the Euler totient function and $f(n) = \min\{k : \phi_k(n) = 1\}$ counts how many iterations are needed to reach 1, does the normalized quantity $f(n)/\log n$ have a distribution function, and is it almost always constant? More broadly, what can be said about the largest prime factor of $\phi_k(n)$ when $k$ is about $\log\log n$?
status: Pillai [Pi29] was the first to investigate this function, proving $\log_3 n < f(n) < \log_2 n$ for all large $n$. Shapiro [Sh50] proved that $f(n)$ is essentially multiplicative. Erdős, Granville, Pomerance, and Spiro [EGPS90] proved that the answer to the first two questions is yes, conditional on a form of the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture. It is likely true that if $k \to \infty$ however slowly with $n$, then for almost all $n$ the largest prime factor of $\phi_k(n)$ is $\leq n^{o(1)}$; this is discussed in problem B41 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $f(n)/\log n$ possesses a distribution function and is constant for almost all $n$, together with a characterization of the largest prime factor of $\phi_k(n)$ at $k = \log\log n$ — the expected behavior being that for $k \to \infty$ however slowly with $n$, the largest prime factor of $\phi_k(n)$ is $\leq n^{o(1)}$ for almost all $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would complete our understanding of how quickly iterating the totient function drives $n$ to 1.

title: Erdős problem #409
open: How many iterations of the map $n\mapsto \phi(n)+1$ are needed before a prime is reached? Sharpening this, one asks whether infinitely many $n$ can reach the same prime, what the density of $n$ reaching any fixed prime is, and — presumably the central question — for good upper bounds on $F(n)$, the count of iterations needed.
status: A problem of Finucane. $F(n)$, the number of iterations of $n\mapsto \phi(n)+1$ before reaching a prime, is sequence A039651 in the OEIS, where Cambie notes in the comments that $F(n)=o(n)$ is trivial and $F(n)=1$ infinitely often; the problem is somewhat ambiguously phrased, and presumably the intended question is to find good upper bounds for $F(n)$. One can ask similar questions about $n\mapsto \sigma(n)-1$: do iterates always reach a prime, and if so, how soon? (Iterates of this map cannot reach the same prime infinitely often, since they are non-decreasing.) The problem is discussed in problem B41 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A "good" (nontrivial, quantitative) upper bound on $F(n)$ is established; more precise goals include determining whether $F(n)=1$ beyond the known infinite family, whether a fixed prime is reached by infinitely many $n$, and the density of $n$ reaching any fixed prime.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would clarify the dynamics of a natural arithmetic iteration connecting the totient function to prime generation.

title: Erdős problem #410
open: If we repeatedly apply the divisor-sum function — starting from any integer $n\geq 2$, setting $\sigma_1(n)=\sigma(n)$ and $\sigma_k(n)=\sigma(\sigma_{k-1}(n))$ — must the $k$-th iterate grow faster than any exponential in $k$? Formally, is it true that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\sigma_k(n)^{1/k}=\infty$ for every $n\geq 2$?
status: The problem is discussed as problem B9 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\sigma_k(n)^{1/k}=\infty$ for every $n\geq 2$, or an explicit $n$ for which the limit fails.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/410; resolving it would settle a basic question about the growth of iterated arithmetic functions.

title: Erdős problem #411
open: For which starting values $n$ and which gaps $r$ does iterating the map $g(n)=n+\phi(n)$ eventually double exactly every $r$ steps — that is, $g_{k+r}(n)=2g_k(n)$ for all sufficiently large $k$?
status: The known solutions to $g_{k+2}(n)=2g_k(n)$ are $n=10$ and $n=94$. Selfridge and Weintraub found solutions to $g_{k+9}(n)=9g_k(n)$, and Weintraub found $g_{k+25}(3114)=729g_k(3114)$ for all $k\geq 6$. Steinerberger [St25] observed that for $r=2$ the problem is equivalent to solving $\phi(n)+\phi(n+\phi(n))=n$, and showed that then either the odd part of $n$ lies in $\{1,3,5,7,35,47\}$ or equals $8m+7$ or $6m+5$, where $8m+7\geq 10^{10}$ is prime and $\phi(6m+5)=4m+4$; whether infinitely many such $m$ exist relates to whether $\phi(n)=\frac{2}{3}(n+1)$ has infinitely many solutions. Cambie conjectures the only solutions have $r=2$ and $n=2^lp$ with $l\geq 1$ and $p\in\{2,3,5,7,35,47\}$, and reduced the problem to determining which $r,t\geq 1$ and primes $p\equiv 7\pmod{8}$ satisfy $g_k(2p^t)=4p^t$, conjecturing solutions occur only when $t=1$ and $p\in\{7,47\}$. Cambie also observed $g_{k+4}(738)=3g_k(738)$, $g_{k+4}(148646)=4g_k(148646)$, and $g_{k+4}(4325798)=4g_k(4325798)$ for all $k\geq 1$.
solved_when: A complete characterization is given of the pairs $(n,r)$ for which $g_{k+r}(n)=2g_k(n)$ holds for all large $k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle the structure of eventual doubling under iterated application of $n+\phi(n)$.

title: Erdős problem #412
open: Do any two orbits of the iterated sum-of-divisors function eventually meet? That is, defining $\sigma_1(n)=\sigma(n)$ and $\sigma_k(n)=\sigma(\sigma_{k-1}(n))$, is it true that for every $m,n\geq 2$ there exist $i,j$ with $\sigma_i(m)=\sigma_j(n)$?
status: In [Er79d] Erdős attributes the conjecture to van Wijngaarden, who told it to Erdős in the 1950s. Selfridge reports numerical evidence suggesting the answer is no, but Erdős and Graham write 'it seems unlikely that anything can be proved about this in the near future'. See also [413] and [414].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof, e.g., via an explicit pair $m,n\geq 2$ whose orbits never intersect) of the claim that all orbits of the iterated $\sigma$ function on integers $\geq 2$ eventually coincide.
why: A solution would determine whether there is eventually only one possible sequence on which iterates of the sum-of-divisors function can settle, settling one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #413
open: Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $m+\omega(m) \leq n$ for all $m<n$, where $\omega(n)$ counts the distinct prime divisors of $n$? More generally, can one show that there exists an $\epsilon>0$ such that infinitely many $n$ satisfy $m+\epsilon\omega(m)\leq n$ for all $m<n$?
status: In [Er79] Erdős calls such an $n$ a 'barrier' for $\omega$. Some other natural number theoretic functions (such as $\phi$ and $\sigma$) have no barriers because they increase too rapidly. Erdős believed that $\omega$ should have infinitely many barriers. In [Er79d] he proves that $F(n)=\prod k_i$, where $n=\prod p_i^{k_i}$, has infinitely many barriers (in fact the set of barriers has positive density in the integers). Erdős also believed that $\Omega$, the count of prime factors with multiplicity, should have infinitely many barriers; Selfridge found that the largest barrier for $\Omega$ below $10^5$ is $99840$. In [ErGr80] the problem is suggested as a way of showing that the iterated behaviour of $n\mapsto n+\omega(n)$ eventually settles into a single sequence regardless of the starting value (see also [412] and [414]). Erdős and Graham report it could be attacked by sieve methods, but 'at present these methods are not strong enough'. Lau [La26] (see [679]) has provided a positive answer to the second question, and proved a weaker version of the first: there exists a constant $C$ such that, for infinitely many $n$, $m+\omega(m)\leq n$ for all $1\leq m\leq n$.
solved_when: A proof that infinitely many such $n$ exist (barriers for $\omega$); partial progress is measured by proving the weakened versions stated above — the $\epsilon>0$ variant, or Lau's criterion of a constant $C$ with $m+\omega(m)\leq n+C$ for all $1\leq m\leq n$ for infinitely many $n$.
why: Resolving it would show that the iteration $n\mapsto n+\omega(n)$ eventually settles into a single sequence regardless of the starting value, one of Erdős's personally posed problems with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #414
open: Do the iterations of $h(n) = n + \tau(n)$ (where $\tau(n)$ is the number of divisors of $n$) eventually merge, in the sense that for any starting values $m$ and $n$ there exist $i$ and $j$ with $h_i(m) = h_j(n)$, where $h_1(n)=h(n)$ and $h_k(n)=h(h_{k-1}(n))$?
status: The question was asked by Spiro; Erdős and Graham believed the answer is yes. Similar questions can be asked about the iterates of many other functions. See also [412] and [413]. Tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com (erdosproblems.com/414).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for any $m, n$ there exist $i, j$ such that $h_i(m) = h_j(n)$ — i.e., that all orbits under iterates of $h$ eventually coincide.
why: A positive answer would show there is eventually only one possible sequence on which the iterations of $n \mapsto h(n)$ can settle, one of Erdős's personally posed problems.

title: Erdős problem #415
open: How large can the window be in which Euler's totient function realizes every possible ordering pattern? Formally, for $F(n)$ the largest $k$ such that each of the $k!$ orderings of $k$ consecutive values $\phi(m+1),\ldots,\phi(m+k)$ (with $m+k\leq n$) occurs somewhere up to $n$, determine the true order of $F(n)$; and clarify which patterns are the first to fail and how likely the 'natural' ordering mimicking $\phi(1),\ldots,\phi(k)$ is to appear.
status: In [ErGr80] it is left ambiguous whether an 'ordering pattern' involves strict inequalities or allows equality; Weisenberg has observed that the final question only makes sense if equality is allowed. [ErGr80] claims that Erdős [Er36b] proved $F(n)\asymp\log\log\log n$, and similarly with $\phi$ replaced by $\sigma$, $\tau$, $\nu$, or any 'decent' additive or multiplicative function, but this does not seem to be present in [Er36b], which only shows that the number of $m\leq n$ with $\phi(m)<\phi(m+1)$ is $\sim n/2$, and similarly for $\phi(m)>\phi(m+1)$. Pollack, Pomerance, and Treviño [PPT13] proved that if $G(n)$ is the maximum $k$ such that $\phi(m+1)>\phi(m+2)>\cdots>\phi(m+k)$ for some $m$ with $m+k\leq n$, then $G(n)\sim\frac{\log\log\log n}{\log\log\log\log\log\log n}$, with the same asymptotic if $>$ is replaced by $<,\leq,\geq$. Since $F(n)\leq G(n)$ trivially, this answers the first question in the negative. Chojecki and GPT-5.4 have sketched how the proof of [PPT13] can be adapted to obtain the same asymptotic for an arbitrary pattern of (strict) inequalities.
solved_when: The order of magnitude of $F(n)$ is determined (the record's original conjecture was $F(n)=(c+o(1))\log\log\log n$ for some constant $c$, which is now known to fail), together with identification of the first failing pattern (conjecturally the strictly decreasing pattern $\phi(m+1)>\cdots>\phi(m+k)$) and the status of the 'natural' ordering as most likely to appear.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolves how ordering structure of consecutive totient values degrades with window length.

title: Erdős problem #417
open: Does the ratio $V(x)/V'(x)$ converge to a limit, where $V'(x)$ counts the distinct values taken by Euler's totient $\phi(m)$ for $1\leq m\leq x$ and $V(x)$ counts the integers up to $x$ that occur as $\phi(m)$ for some $m$? In particular, does the limit exist, and if so, is it strictly greater than $1$ — possibly infinite?
status: It is trivial that $V'(x) \leq V(x)$. In [Er98] Erdős suggests the limit may be infinite. See also problem [416].
solved_when: The limit $\lim_{x\to\infty} V(x)/V'(x)$ is proven to exist, and its value is determined (at minimum, whether it is strictly greater than $1$, and whether it is infinite).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with its full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a basic structural question about the set of totient values — how distorted the counting is depending on whether one truncates the argument $m$ or the value $\phi(m)$.

title: Erdős problem #420
open: Is it true that $\lim_{n\to \infty} F((\log n)^C, n) = \infty$ for large enough $C$, where $F(f,n) = \frac{\tau((n+\lfloor f(n)\rfloor)!)}{\tau(n!)}$ and $\tau$ counts divisors? More precisely: is $F(\log n, n)$ everywhere dense in $(1,\infty)$, and generally, for any monotonic $f(n) \leq \log n$ with $f(n) \to \infty$, is $F(f,n)$ everywhere dense?
status: Erdős and Graham write that it is easy to show $\lim F(n^{1/2}, n) = \infty$, and in fact $n^{1/2}$ can be replaced by $n^{1/2-c}$ for some small constant $c > 0$. Erdős, Graham, Ivić, and Pomerance [EGIP96] proved that $\liminf F(c\log n, n) = 1$ for any $c > 0$, and $\lim F(n^{4/9}, n) = \infty$ (the exponent $4/9$ can be improved slightly). They also prove that if $f(n) = o((\log n)^2)$, then for almost all $n$, $F(f,n) \sim 1$. van Doorn notes in the comments that the existence of infinitely many bounded prime gaps implies $\limsup_{n\to\infty} F(g(n), n) = \infty$ for any $g(n) \to \infty$, and that Cramér's conjecture implies $\lim F(g(n)(\log n)^2, n) = \infty$ for any $g(n) \to \infty$.
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved) whether $\lim_{n\to\infty} F((\log n)^C, n) = \infty$ for large $C$, and whether $F(f,n)$ is everywhere dense for every monotonic $f(n) \leq \log n$ tending to infinity — including the special case $f(n) = \log n$ with density in $(1,\infty)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #422
open: Does the Hofstadter-type sequence defined by $f(1)=f(2)=1$ and $f(n) = f(n-f(n-1))+f(n-f(n-2))$ for $n>2$ miss infinitely many integers, and how does it behave asymptotically?
status: Asked by Hofstadter. The sequence begins $1,1,2,3,3,4,\ldots$ and is A005185 in the OEIS. It is not even known whether $f(n)$ is well-defined for all $n$. See erdosproblems.com/422.
solved_when: It is determined whether $f(n)$ is well-defined for all $n$, whether its range omits infinitely many integers, and a description of its growth/behaviour is given.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #424
open: Starting from $a_1=2$ and $a_2=3$, repeatedly append all values $a_ia_j-1$ with $i\neq j$ to the sequence; does the resulting set of integers have positive density? Formally, does there exist $c>0$ such that, for all large $x$, the sequence takes at least $cx$ distinct values in $[1,x]$?
status: The problem was asked by Hofstadter; the sequence begins $2,3,5,9,14,17,26,\ldots$ and is A005244 in the OEIS. It is also discussed in section E31 of Guy's book *Unsolved Problems in Number Theory*. In [ErGr80] (and in Guy's book) the problem as written asks whether almost all integers appear, but the answer is trivially no (as pointed out to Steinerberger): no integer $\equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ is ever in the sequence, since by induction $a,b\in\{0,2\}\pmod{3}$ implies $ab-1\in\{0,2\}\pmod{3}$, so the appearing set has density at most $2/3$. Presumably the intended question, as correctly asked in [Er77c], is whether a positive density of integers appear. See also Problem 63 of Green's open problems list.
solved_when: A constant $c>0$ is exhibited such that for all sufficiently large $x$, the number of values of $a_i$ lying in $[1,x]$ is at least $cx$ (i.e., positive lower density, since by 'positive density' Erdős most likely meant 'positive lower density').
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a long-standing question about whether this closure construction captures a positive fraction of the integers.

title: Erdős problem #425
open: How large can a multiplicative Sidon set be — that is, a subset $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ whose pairwise products $ab$ ($a<b$) are all distinct? More precisely, writing $F(n)$ for the maximum size of such a set, does there exist a constant $c$ with $F(n)=\pi(n)+(c+o(1))n^{3/4}(\log n)^{-3/2}$; and for the higher-order analogue where all products $a_1\cdots a_r$ ($a_1<\cdots<a_r$) are distinct, is $|A|\leq \pi(n)+O(n^{(r+1)/2r})$?
status: Erdős [Er68] proved that there exist constants $0<c_1\leq c_2$ with $\pi(n)+c_1 n^{3/4}(\log n)^{-3/2}\leq F(n)\leq \pi(n)+c_2 n^{3/4}(\log n)^{-3/2}$, the lower bound having been proved earlier in [Er38]. The real-number analogue asks for the largest $A\subset[1,x]$ such that $|ab-cd|\geq 1$ for all distinct $a,b,c,d\in A$. Erdős conjectured (see [Er73] and [Er77c]) that $|A|=o(x)$, but in [ErGr80] Erdős and Graham report that Alexander disproved this with a construction establishing $|A|\gg x$; Alexander's construction appears in [Er80]. Its simplified form takes a Sidon set $B\subseteq[1,X^2]$ of size $\gg X$ and sets $A=\{Xe^{b/X^2}:b\in B\}$; then $|ab-cd|\geq X^2|1-e^{1/X^2}|\gg 1$ for distinct $a,b,c,d\in A$, and after rescaling this gives a set of size $\gg X$ in an interval $[X,O(X)]$, with a simple modification making $A$ also $1$-separated. In [Er77c] Erdős considers a similar generalization.
solved_when: The asymptotic $F(n)=\pi(n)+(c+o(1))n^{3/4}(\log n)^{-3/2}$ is established for some explicit constant $c$, and the bound $|A|\leq \pi(n)+O(n^{(r+1)/2r})$ is proved for the $r$-product version.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would pin down the exact second-order term in the size of multiplicative Sidon sets beyond the primes.

title: Erdős problem #428
open: Does there exist a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that, for infinitely many $n$, every difference $n-a$ is prime for all $a\in A$ with $0<a<n$, and $\liminf\frac{\lvert A\cap[1,x]\rvert}{\pi(x)}>0$? In other words, can a set of positive lower density relative to the primes be simultaneously shifted into the primes at infinitely many positions $n$?
status: Erdős and Graham could show this is true, assuming the prime $k$-tuple conjecture, if the $\liminf$ is replaced by $\limsup$; the original $\liminf$ version remains unresolved. Full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/428.
solved_when: A specific set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is exhibited (or proven to exist) with $\liminf\frac{\lvert A\cap[1,x]\rvert}{\pi(x)}>0$ such that for infinitely many $n$, all $n-a$ are prime for every $a\in A$ with $0<a<n$; a negative answer would show no such set exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would clarify how thick a set of shifts can be while still landing in the primes infinitely often.

title: Erdős problem #430
open: Can this greedily constructed decreasing sequence of integers in $[1,n)$ — where $a_1=n-1$ and each subsequent term is the largest integer below the previous one whose prime factors all exceed $n-a_k$ — eventually fail to consist entirely of primes? Formally, is it true that for sufficiently large $n$, not every term of the sequence is prime?
status: Erdős and Graham write that "preliminary calculations made by Selfridge indicate that this is the case but no proof is in sight." For example, if $n=8$ then $a_1=7$ and $a_2=5$, and the sequence stops. Sarosh Adenwalla has observed that this problem is equivalent to (the first part of) [385]: assuming a positive answer to that, for all large $n$ there exists a composite $m<n$ such that all primes dividing $m$ are $>n-m$; it follows that such an $m$ equals some $a_i$ in the sequence defined for $[1,n)$, and $m$ is composite by assumption.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for all sufficiently large $n$, the sequence defined by $a_1=n-1$ and the greedy rule "all prime factors of $a_k$ exceed $n-a_k$" contains a composite term.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it settles the equivalent Erdős problem [385]: that for all large $n$ there exists a composite $m<n$ all of whose prime divisors exceed $n-m$.

title: Erdős problem #431
open: Can the set of primes be written as a sumset $A+B$ of two infinite sets, up to finitely many exceptions? This is Ostmann's "inverse Goldbach problem," and the expected answer is no: no two infinite sets $A$ and $B$ should satisfy $A+B = \mathbb{P}$ outside a finite error set.
status: A problem of Ostmann, sometimes known as the "inverse Goldbach problem"; in [Er80] Erdős dates it to about 25 years old, placing it at about 1955. The best result is due to Elsholtz and Harper [ElHa15], who showed that if such $A,B$ exist then for all large $x$, $\frac{x^{1/2}}{\log x\log\log x} \ll |A \cap [1,x]| \ll x^{1/2}\log\log x$, and similarly for $B$. Elsholtz [El01] proved there are no sets $A,B,C$ (all of size at least $2$) such that $A+B+C$ agrees with the primes up to finitely many exceptions. Granville [Gr90] proved, conditional on the prime $k$-tuples conjecture, that there are infinite sets $B$ and $C$ such that $\{\frac{b+c}{2}: b\in B, c\in C\}$ is a subset of the primes. Tao and Ziegler [TaZi23] gave an unconditional proof that there are infinite sets $B=\{b_1<\cdots\}$ and $C=\{c_1<\cdots\}$ such that $\{b_i+c_j : b_i\in B, c_j\in C, i<j\}$ is a subset of the primes. See also [429] and [432].
solved_when: A proof that no two infinite sets $A$ and $B$ exist with $A+B$ agreeing with the primes up to finitely many exceptions (or a construction of such sets).
why: It asks whether the primes, despite their pseudorandom structure, can decompose as a sumset — a basic structural question about additive decomposability that any proof resolving it would have to confront.

title: Erdős problem #432
open: If $A$ and $B$ are infinite sets of natural numbers whose sumset $A+B$ consists entirely of pairwise relatively prime elements, how dense can $A+B$ be?
status: The problem was asked by Straus and was inspired by a problem of Ostmann (see [431]); it remains open and is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/432.
solved_when: A sharp bound is established on the density of $A+B$ (e.g., its counting function or natural density) under the constraint that all elements of $A+B$ are pairwise coprime, with matching construction.
why: Resolving it would clarify the tension between additive structure and multiplicative coprimality constraints on sumsets, a recurring theme in Erdős-style additive number theory.

title: Erdős problem #436
open: Must there always be, for every exponent $k$, a bounded starting point beyond which one can find two consecutive $k$th power residues modulo any sufficiently large prime? Formally, with $r(k,m,p)$ the minimal $r$ such that $r,\ldots,r+m-1$ are all $k$th power residues mod $p$ and $\Lambda(k,m)=\limsup_{p\to\infty} r(k,m,p)$, is $\Lambda(k,3)$ finite for all odd $k$, and how large are these quantities?
status: The problem was asked by Lehmer and Lehmer [LeLe62], who noted that $\Lambda(2,2)=9$: $9$ is always a quadratic residue, and if $10$ isn't then either $2$ or $5$ is, so at least one of $1,2$ or $4,5$ or $9,10$ is a pair of consecutive quadratic residues (and there are infinitely many $p$ with no consecutive quadratic residues below $9,10$). A similar argument of Dunton [Du65] proves $\Lambda(3,2)=77$, and Bierstedt and Mills [BiMi63] proved $\Lambda(4,2)=1224$. Lehmer and Lehmer proved $\Lambda(k,3)=\infty$ for all even $k$ and $\Lambda(k,4)=\infty$ for all $k\leq 1048909$. Lehmer, Lehmer, and Mills [LLM63] proved $\Lambda(5,2)=7888$ and $\Lambda(6,2)=202124$. Brillhart, Lehmer, and Lehmer [BLL64] proved $\Lambda(7,2)=1649375$. Lehmer, Lehmer, Mills, and Selfridge [LLMS62] proved $\Lambda(3,3)=23532$. Graham [Gr64g] proved $\Lambda(k,l)=\infty$ for all $k\geq 2$ and $l\geq 4$. Hildebrand [Hi91] resolved the first question, proving $\Lambda(k,2)$ is finite for all $k$: for any $k\geq 2$, if $p$ is sufficiently large then there exists a pair of consecutive $k$th power residues modulo $p$ in $[1,O_k(1)]$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\Lambda(k,3)$ is finite for all odd $k$, together with sharp bounds or exact values for $\Lambda(k,2)$ and $\Lambda(k,3)$; the finiteness of $\Lambda(k,2)$ for all $k$ is already known.
why: It resolves the remaining half of a classical Lehmer–Lehmer question on runs of consecutive power residues, and quantitative bounds would reveal how small a modulus-independent guarantee can be for such runs.

title: Erdős problem #445
open: Does every sufficiently large prime $p$ have the property that, for any constant $c>1/2$ and any $n\geq 0$, one can find $a,b$ in the short interval $(n, n+p^c)$ with $ab\equiv 1 \pmod{p}$? Formally: for every $c>1/2$ there is a $p_0$ such that all primes $p>p_0$ admit such a pair $a,b$ in every interval of length $p^c$ starting at $n$.
status: Heilbronn (unpublished) proved the statement for $c$ sufficiently close to $1$. Heath-Brown [He00] used Kloosterman sums to prove it for all $c>3/4$. The problem is discussed in a MathOverflow question; see erdosproblems.com/445.
solved_when: A proof that for every $c>1/2$ there exists a prime $p_0$ such that for all primes $p>p_0$ and all integers $n\geq 0$, the interval $(n, n+p^c)$ contains $a,b$ with $ab\equiv 1 \pmod{p}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle the correct threshold exponent for short intervals containing modular inverses.

title: Erdős problem #450
open: How large must the interval length $y = y(\epsilon,n)$ be so that, among any $y$ consecutive integers starting at $x$, at most $\epsilon y$ of them have a divisor in the interval $(n,2n)$? Formally, determine the threshold $y$ for which the count of integers in $(x,x+y)$ having a divisor in $(n,2n)$ is at most $\epsilon y$.
status: It is not clear what the intended quantifier on $x$ is. Cambie has observed that if the statement is intended to hold for all $x$, then, provided $\epsilon(\log n)^\delta (\log\log n)^{3/2}\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, where $\delta=0.086\cdots$, there is no such $y$, by an averaging argument together with the work of Ford [Fo08]. On the other hand, Cambie has observed that if $\epsilon\ll 1/n$ then $y(\epsilon,n)\sim 2n$: indeed, if $y<2n$ then this is impossible, taking $x+n$ to be a multiple of the lowest common multiple of $\{n+1,\ldots,2n-1\}$. Conversely, for every fixed $\delta\in(0,1)$ and $n$ large, every $2(1+\delta)n$ consecutive elements contains many elements which are a multiple of an element in $(n,2n)$.
solved_when: An explicit determination of $y(\epsilon,n)$ — including clarification of the intended quantifier over $x$ — such that the number of integers in $(x,x+y)$ with a divisor in $(n,2n)$ is at most $\epsilon y$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #452
open: Let $\omega(n)$ count the number of distinct prime factors of $n$. How long can an interval $I\subseteq[x,2x]$ be if every $n\in I$ satisfies $\omega(n)>\log\log n$?
status: Erdős [Er37] proved that the density of integers $n$ with $\omega(n)>\log\log n$ is $1/2$. The Chinese remainder theorem implies that such an interval exists with $\lvert I\rvert \geq (1+o(1))\frac{\log x}{(\log\log x)^2}$. It could be true that there is such an interval of length $(\log x)^{k}$ for arbitrarily large $k$.
solved_when: The asymptotic maximal length of such an interval $I\subseteq[x,2x]$ is determined up to $o(1)$ factors; in particular, one decides whether lengths $(\log x)^{k}$ are achievable for arbitrarily large $k$, or whether the truth lies near $(1+o(1))\frac{\log x}{(\log\log x)^2}$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve a classic question about how uniformly the normal-order behavior of $\omega(n)$ can persist across consecutive integers.

title: Erdős problem #454
open: Is the minimum of $p_{n+i}+p_{n-i}$ over $i<n$ eventually much larger than twice the $n$th prime? Formally, with $f(n) = \min_{i<n}(p_{n+i}+p_{n-i})$, is $\limsup_n (f(n) - 2p_n) = \infty$?
status: Pomerance [Po79] has proved that the $\limsup$ is at least $2$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\limsup_n (f(n)-2p_n) = \infty$, where $f(n) = \min_{i<n}(p_{n+i}+p_{n-i})$ and $p_k$ is the $k$th prime.

title: Erdős problem #455
open: If a strictly increasing sequence of primes has gaps that never decrease, must the primes grow faster than quadratically in their index? Formally, must $\lim_n q_n/n^2=\infty$?
status: Richter [Ri76] proved that $\liminf_n q_n/n^2 > 0.352\cdots$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every prime sequence with nondecreasing gaps satisfies $\lim_n q_n/n^2=\infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/455.

title: Erdős problem #456
open: Is the smallest integer $m$ with $n\mid\phi(m)$ eventually smaller than the smallest prime $p_n\equiv 1\pmod{n}$ — and by how much? Formally, letting $p_n$ be the smallest prime $\equiv 1\pmod{n}$ and $m_n$ the smallest integer with $n\mid\phi(m_n)$: is $m_n<p_n$ for almost all $n$, does $p_n/m_n\to\infty$ for almost all $n$, and are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p-1$ is the only $n$ for which $m_n=p$?
status: Linnik's theorem implies $p_n\leq n^{O(1)}$, and trivially $m_n\leq p_n$ always; if $n=q-1$ for some prime $q$ then $m_n=p_n$. Erdős [Er79e] writes it is 'easy to show' that for infinitely many $n$ we have $m_n<p_n$, and that $m_n/n\to\infty$ for almost all $n$. van Doorn noted in the comments that if $n=2^{2k+1}$ then $m_n\leq 2n$ and $p_n\geq 2n+1$.
solved_when: It is proved that $m_n<p_n$ for almost all $n$; a stronger resolution establishes $p_n/m_n\to\infty$ for almost all $n$; and it is determined whether infinitely many primes $p$ satisfy that $p-1$ is the only $n$ with $m_n=p$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and answers would clarify the typical relationship between the multiplicative structure of $\phi$ and primes in arithmetic progressions.

title: Erdős problem #458
open: Let $[1,\ldots,n]$ denote the least common multiple of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, where $p_k$ is the $k$-th prime. Is it true that, for all $k\geq 1$,
status: Erdős and Graham write that the statement is "almost certainly" true but that the proof is beyond their ability for (at least) two reasons. First, one has to rule out the possibility of many primes $q$ with $p_k < q^2 < p_{k+1}$; there should be at most one such $q$, which would follow from $p_{k+1}-p_k < p_k^{1/2}$, itself essentially the notorious Legendre's conjecture. The small primes also cause trouble.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the inequality $[1,\ldots,p_{k+1}-1] < p_k[1,\ldots,p_k]$ for all $k \geq 1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (Erdős #458), with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/458; it concerns the fine structure of least common multiples relative to prime gaps.

title: Erdős problem #460
open: Does the reciprocal sum of the terms $a_i$ below $n$ grow without bound as $n\to\infty$, where $a_0=0$, $a_1=1$, and each $a_k$ is the least integer $>a_{k-1}$ with $(n-a_k,n-a_i)=1$ for all $0\leq i<k$? In particular, does $\sum_{0<a_i<n} 1/a_i \to \infty$, and does the answer persist when the sum is restricted to those $i$ for which $n-a_j$ is divisible by some prime $\leq a_j$, or to the complementary set?
status: This question arose in work of Eggleton, Erdős, and Selfridge, who proved $a_k < k^{2+o(1)}$ for $k$ large enough depending on $n$, but conjectured $a_k\ll k\log k$. The problem is from [Er77c] (see erdosproblems.com/460; Erdős references: [Er77c,p.64] [Er77c]). It is stated slightly differently in [ErGr80], with $a_0=n$ instead of $a_0=0$ and $1\leq i<k$ instead of $0\leq i<k$; the material difference is that the main formulation forces $(a_k,n)=1$ for all $k\geq 1$, which the second does not impose. Both [Er77c] and [ErGr80] state the problem without restricting the sum to $a_k<n$, though this was perhaps implicitly intended; without this condition the sum is infinite, since the sequence $a_k$ contains $n+p$ for all primes $p>n$ (an observation made by Svyable using ChatGPT). Although both sources mention a forthcoming paper of Eggleton, Erdős, and Selfridge, no candidate paper of theirs containing this problem can be found, so the motivation and precise intended problem remain unclear. Chojecki has noted in the comments that a positive solution to the main problem would fo[llow from consequences not fully recorded].
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved) whether $\sum_{0<a_i<n} 1/a_i\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, including the two variants restricting the sum to those $i$ such that $n-a_j$ is divisible by some prime $\leq a_j$, or to the complement of such $i$.
why: A positive solution would resolve one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and per Chojecki's comment would have further consequences; resolving it would also clarify the intended formulation of the Eggleton–Erdős–Selfridge program, whose motivation is currently unclear because no candidate paper of theirs containing this problem can be found.

title: Erdős problem #461
open: For each integer $t$, look at a window of $t$ consecutive integers $m\in[n+1,n+t]$ and record the part of each $m$ built from primes below $t$ (its $t$-smooth component $s_t(m)$). Do these $t$ integers realize at least a constant multiple of $t$ distinct such values — i.e., is $f(n,t)\gg t$ uniformly in both $n$ and $t$?
status: Erdős and Graham report they can show $f(n,t) \gg \frac{t}{\log t}$; the full strength $f(n,t)\gg t$ remains open (see erdosproblems.com/461).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given of the bound $f(n,t)\gg t$ holding uniformly for all $t$ and $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with its full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles a basic question about how distinct the small-prime parts of consecutive integers can be.

title: Erdős problem #462
open: Let $p(n)$ denote the least prime factor of $n$. Since the sum of $p(n)/n$ over composite $n<x$ grows like a constant times $x^{1/2}/(\log x)^2$, do these contributions spread out evenly — specifically, does a constant $C>0$ exist such that $\sum_{x\leq n\leq x+Cx^{1/2}(\log x)^2} p(n)/n \gg 1$ for all large $x$?
status: The problem remains open; it is catalogued with full history at erdosproblems.com/462. Additional thanks to: Zachary Chase.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that there exists a constant $C>0$ such that $\sum_{x\leq n\leq x+Cx^{1/2}(\log x)^2} \frac{p(n)}{n} \gg 1$ for all sufficiently large $x$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; solving it would resolve a concrete question about the distribution of least prime factors in short intervals, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #463
open: Is there a function $f$ with $f(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ such that, for all large $n$, one can find a composite number $m$ lying strictly between $n+f(n)$ and $n+p(m)$, where $p(m)$ denotes the least prime factor of $m$?
status: In [Er92e] Erdős asks about $F(n)=\min_{m>n}(m-p(m))$ and whether $n-F(n)\sim cn^{1/2}$ for some $c>0$. See also [385].
solved_when: Such a function $f$ tending to infinity is exhibited and proved to work for all sufficiently large $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with its full history at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution closes a specific entry in that catalog of open questions.

title: Erdős problem #468
open: For any $n$ let $D_n$ be the set of sums of the shape $d_1,d_1+d_2,d_1+d_2+d_3,\ldots$ where $1<d_1<d_2<\cdots$ are the divisors of $n$. What is the size of $D_n\backslash \cup_{m<n}D_m$? If $f(N)$ is the minimal $n$ such that $N\in D_n$ then is it true that $f(N)=o(N)$? Perhaps just for almost all $N$?
status: No proof expositions exist yet; contributors are invited to message a moderator or leave an exposition as a comment. The problem is tracked at erdosproblems.com/468.
solved_when: The problem is resolved by determining the size of $D_n\backslash \cup_{m<n}D_m$, and in particular by proving (or disproving) that $f(N)=o(N)$, or at least that this holds for almost all $N$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution would settle a long-standing entry in that collection concerning the additive structure of divisor sets.

title: Erdős problem #470
open: Does there exist an odd weird number — an odd abundant number that is not the sum of any subset of its proper divisors? And are there infinitely many primitive weird numbers, those with no weird proper divisor?
status: Weird numbers were investigated by Benkoski and Erdős [BeEr74], who proved that the set of weird numbers has positive density; the smallest weird number is $70$. Melfi [Me15] proved that there are infinitely many primitive weird numbers, conditional on $p_{n+1}-p_n<\frac{1}{10}p_n^{1/2}$ for all large $n$, which would follow from well-known conjectures concerning prime gaps. Fang [Fa22] has shown there are no odd weird numbers below $10^{21}$, and Liddy and Riedl [LiRi18] have shown that an odd weird number must have at least 6 prime divisors. If there are no odd weird numbers, then every weird number has abundancy index $<4$ (see [825]). The sequence of weird numbers is A006037 in the OEIS, and this is problem B2 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: An odd weird number is exhibited (earning the \$10 Erdős prize), or infinitely many primitive weird numbers are proved unconditionally; a proof that no odd weird number exists, or that only finitely many primitive weird numbers exist, would equally resolve the corresponding question.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a \$10 prize of his and tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; the existence of odd weird numbers is a basic structural question about abundant numbers left unsettled since the 1970s.

title: Erdős problem #472
open: Is there a finite starting sequence of primes from which Ulam's greedy prime recursion never dies — that is, primes $q_1<\cdots<q_m$ such that, defining $q_{n+1}$ to be the smallest prime of the form $q_n+q_i-1$ for some $i\le n$ (for $n\ge m$), the sequence continues forever?
status: A problem due to Ulam. For example, beginning with $3,5$ the sequence continues $3,5,7,11,13,17,\ldots$, and it is possible that this sequence is infinite. Reference: erdosproblems.com/472.
solved_when: An explicit initial finite sequence of primes $q_1<\cdots<q_m$ is exhibited (or proven to exist) for which the recursively defined sequence $q_{n+1}=\min\{q_n+q_i-1 : q_n+q_i-1 \text{ prime}\}$ is infinite.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a proof that such a sequence is infinite would resolve a long-standing question in prime-generating recursions.

title: Erdős problem #474
open: Under what set-theoretic assumptions does there exist a $3$-colouring of $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every uncountable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ contains a pair of each colour within $A^2$? Equivalently, when is $2^{\aleph_0}\not\to [\aleph_1]_3^2$?
status: A problem of Erdős from 1954. Sierpinski and Kurepa independently proved the statement for $2$ colours. Erdős proved it for $3$ colours under the continuum hypothesis $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_1$, and offered \$100 for deciding what happens if the continuum hypothesis is not assumed. Shelah [Sh88] proved, on the other hand, that it is consistent without the continuum hypothesis that $2^{\aleph_0}\to [\aleph_1]_3^2$, although with a very large value of $\mathfrak{c}$. It remains open whether it is consistent to have a negative answer assuming $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$; this specific question is asked in [Va99].
solved_when: The question of what happens when the continuum hypothesis is not assumed is decided — in particular, it is determined whether it is consistent to have a negative answer assuming $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_2$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a \$100 prize from Erdős and tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #475
open: Let $p$ be a prime. Given any finite set $A\subseteq \mathbb{F}_p\backslash \{0\}$, is there always a rearrangement $A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_t\}$ such that all partial sums $\sum_{1\leq k\leq m}a_{k}$ are distinct, for all $1\leq m\leq t$?
status: A problem of Graham, who proved it when $t=p-1$; a similar conjecture for arbitrary abelian groups was made by Alspach. Such an ordering is often called a valid ordering. It has been proved for $t\leq 12$ (see Costa and Pellegrini [CoPe20] and the references therein) and for $p-3\leq t\leq p-1$ (see Hicks, Ollis, and Schmitt [HOS19] and the references therein). It has been proved for all sufficiently large primes, via four types of result each handling a different range of $|A|$. Small $A$: Kravitz [Kr24] proved it for $t \leq \frac{\log p}{\log\log p}$ (independently observed earlier by Will Sawin in a MathOverflow post); Bedert and Kravitz [BeKr24] improved this to $t \leq e^{c(\log p)^{1/4}}$ for some constant $c>0$; Costa and Della Fiore [CoDe26] further improved this to $t \leq e^{c(\log p)^{1/3}}$. Medium $A$: Pham and Sauermann [PhSa26] proved it, for any $0<\alpha<1$, for all $1 \ll_\alpha t\leq p^{1-\alpha}$. Large $A$: Bedert, Bucić, Kravitz, Montgomery, and Müyesser [BBKMM25] proved it for all $p^{1-c}\leq t\leq (1-o(1))p$ for some
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every $A\subseteq \mathbb{F}_p\setminus\{0\}$ with $|A|=t$ admits a valid ordering, for all $t\leq p-1$ and all primes $p$ — equivalently, closure of the remaining gap between the small, medium, and large ranges currently covered.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (#475), with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a complete resolution settles Graham's question and Alspach's analogous conjecture for arbitrary abelian groups in the cyclic prime case.

title: Erdős problem #478
open: When the factorials $1!, 2!, \ldots, (p-1)!$ are reduced modulo a prime $p$, do they fill up a positive proportion of all residues? Erdős asked whether the set $A_p = \{ k! \pmod{p} : 1 \leq k < p \}$ satisfies $\lvert A_p\rvert \sim (1-\tfrac{1}{e})p$.
status: Since $A_p/A_p=\{1,\ldots,p-1\}$, it follows that $\lvert A_p\rvert \gg p^{1/2}$. The best known lower bound, due to Grebennikov, Sagdeev, Semchankau, and Vasilevskii [GSSV24], is $\lvert A_p\rvert \geq (\sqrt{2}-o(1))p^{1/2}$, which follows from proving that $\lvert A_pA_p\rvert = (1+o(1))p$. Wilson's theorem implies $(p-2)! \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$, hence $\lvert A_p\rvert \leq p-2$. Results on $\lvert A_p\rvert$ on average were obtained by Klurman and Munsch [KlMu17]. It is even open whether there are infinitely many primes $p$ with $\lvert A_p\rvert = p-2$, i.e. such that $2!,\ldots,(p-1)!$ are all distinct modulo $p$ (sometimes called socialist primes). Rokowska and Schinzel [RoSc60] proved that any socialist prime is $5 \pmod{8}$ and must satisfy $-(\tfrac{5}{p}) = (\tfrac{-23}{p}) = 1$, and that the congruence class missing from $2!,\ldots,(p-1)!$ must be $-(\tfrac{p-1}{2})!$. The only known socialist prime is $p=5$. Trudgian [Tr13] showed there are no other socialist primes $<10^9$, extended to $10^{11}$ by Andrejić and Tatarevic [AnTa16]. The problem is also discussed in problems A2 and F11 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved) that $\lvert A_p\rvert \sim (1-\tfrac{1}{e})p$ as $p \to \infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve a long-standing basic question about the distribution of factorial residues and, in the extremal direction, the existence of infinitely many socialist primes.

title: Erdős problem #479
open: Is it true that, for every integer $k\neq 1$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $2^n\equiv k\pmod{n}$?
status: This is a conjecture of Graham. It is easy to see that $2^n\not\equiv 1\mod{n}$ for all $n>1$, so the restriction $k\neq 1$ is necessary. Erdős and Graham report that Graham, Lehmer, and Lehmer proved the claim for $k=2^i$ with $i\geq 1$, or if $k=-1$, but no such paper could be found; Tang has written a short note giving a proof for this case. Indicative of the difficulty, for $k=3$ the smallest $n$ with $2^n\equiv 3\pmod{n}$ is $n=4700063497$. The minimal such $n$ for each $k$ is A036236 in the OEIS.
solved_when: For every $k\neq 1$, infinitely many $n$ satisfy $2^n\equiv k\pmod{n}$; equivalently, the set of such $n$ is shown infinite for each admissible $k$.
why: A conjecture of Graham and one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #486
open: Given a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and, for each $n\in A$, a chosen residue set $X_n\subseteq \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, consider the sifted set $B = \{ m\in \mathbb{N} : m\not\in X_n \pmod{n}$ for all $n\in A$ with $m>n\}$. Must $B$ have a logarithmic density, i.e. does the limit $\lim_{x\to \infty} \frac{1}{\log x}\sum_{\substack{m\in B\\ m<x}}\frac{1}{m}$ exist?
status: Davenport and Erdős [DaEr36] proved that the answer is yes when $X_n=\{0\}$ for all $n\in A$, with an alternative elementary proof later given in [DaEr51]. Erdős [Er80] wrote 'perhaps this question is not very difficult as far as I know it has not been attacked really seriously'. The problem is phrased in terms of logarithmic density since Besicovitch [Be34] showed examples exist without a natural density, even when $X_n=\{0\}$ for all $n\in A$. The problem generalizes the case $\lvert X_n\rvert=1$ for all $n\in A$, which is [25].
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that the logarithmic density of $B$ exists for every choice of $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ and every choice of residue sets $X_n\subseteq\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it generalizes the classical theory of sets of multiples, where the analogous density question is fundamental.

title: Erdős problem #488
open: Let $A$ be a finite set and $B=\{ n \geq 1 : a\mid n \text{ for some } a\in A\}$. Is it true that, for every $m>n\geq \max(A)$, $\frac{|B\cap [1,m]|}{m} < 2\frac{|B\cap [1,n]|}{n}$?
status: The constant $2$ would be best possible, witnessed by $A=\{a\}$, $n=2a-1$, $m=2a$. The problem is also discussed as problem E5 in Guy's collection [Gu04]. In [Er61] the problem appears with $a\mid n$ replaced by $a\nmid n$ in the definition of $B$ — most likely a typo, since the problem is stated as above in [Er66]. Several counterexamples are known for this alternate problem: Cambie observed that taking $A$ as the primes up to $n$ and $m=2n$ gives $\frac{|B\cap [1,m]|}{m}=\frac{\pi(2n)-\pi(n)+1}{2n}\sim \frac{1}{2\log n}$ while $\frac{|B\cap [1,n]|}{n}=\frac{1}{n}$. Further concrete counterexamples, found by Alexeev and Aristotle, are given in the comments section at erdosproblems.com/488. Key works: erdosproblems.com/488; Erdős references: [Er61,p.236] [Er66,p.150] [Er80,p.112] [Gu04] [Er61].
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the inequality $\frac{|B\cap [1,m]|}{m} < 2\frac{|B\cap [1,n]|}{n}$ for every finite set $A$ and every $m>n\geq \max(A)$; the constant $2$ is best possible, so any proof must use it.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles whether the density of multiples of a finite set can never double from one cutoff to a larger one.

title: Erdős problem #489
open: If $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has density $|A\cap[1,x]|=o(x^{1/2})$ and $B=\{n\geq 1: a\nmid n \text{ for all } a\in A\}$ is its set of avoided multiples, must the mean square gap $\lim \frac{1}{x}\sum_{b_i<x}(b_{i+1}-b_i)^2$ of the elements $b_1<b_2<\cdots$ of $B$ exist and be finite?
status: This is a number theory problem. In the example $A=\{p^2: p \text{ prime}\}$, $B$ is the set of squarefree numbers, and the existence of this limit was proved by Erdős. See also [208]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/489; Erdős references: [Er61].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, for every $A$ with $|A\cap[1,x]|=o(x^{1/2})$, the limit $\lim \frac{1}{x}\sum_{b_i<x}(b_{i+1}-b_i)^2$ exists and is finite.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #495
open: Let $\alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{R}$. Is it true that $\liminf_{n\to \infty} n \| n\alpha \| \| n\beta \| =0$, where $\|x\|$ denotes the distance from $x$ to the nearest integer?
status: This is the infamous Littlewood conjecture, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com (erdosproblems.com/495); Erdős references: [Er61].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof with explicit counterexample $\alpha,\beta$) of the stated limit inferior being zero for all real $\alpha,\beta$.
why: This is the infamous Littlewood conjecture, one of Erdős's personally posed problems; a solution would resolve a central question in simultaneous Diophantine approximation.

title: Erdős problem #500
open: What is the maximum number of triples one can place on $n$ vertices while avoiding a complete $3$-uniform hypergraph on 4 vertices? Formally, determine the Turán number $\mathrm{ex}_3(n,K_4^3)$, where $K_4^3$ is a set of 4 vertices carrying all 4 possible 3-edges.
status: This is a problem of Turán, who observed that dividing the vertices into three equal parts $X_1,X_2,X_3$ and taking as edges the triples with exactly one vertex in each part, or two vertices in $X_i$ and one in $X_{i+1}$ (where $X_4=X_1$), gives $\mathrm{ex}_3(n,K_4^3)\geq\left(\frac{5}{9}+o(1)\right)\binom{n}{3}$; this is probably the truth. The current best upper bound is $\mathrm{ex}_3(n,K_4^3)\leq 0.5611666\binom{n}{3}$, due to Razborov [Ra10]. See [712] for the general case. Key works: erdosproblems.com/500; Erdős references: [Er61] [Er71,p.104] [Er74c,p.81] [Er81].
solved_when: The value of $\mathrm{ex}_3(n,K_4^3)$ is determined asymptotically; the conjectured answer, matching Turán's construction, is $\left(\frac{5}{9}+o(1)\right)\binom{n}{3}$.
why: This is Turán's original hypergraph extremal problem, one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with a $500 Erdős prize attached), and a solution would resolve the most famous open case of the general Turán conjecture for hypergraphs.
aliases: Erdős #500; graph theory / hypergraphs / turan number

title: Erdős problem #501
open: For every real $x$, let $A_x\subset\mathbb{R}$ be a bounded set of outer measure $<1$. Must there exist an infinite independent set — that is, an infinite $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ such that $x\not\in A_y$ for all distinct $x,y\in X$? A sharper variant asks: if the $A_x$ are closed with measure $<1$, must there exist an independent set of size $3$?
status: Under the assumptions of the second question, Gladysz [Gl62] proved the existence of an independent set of size $2$, and Newelski, Pawlikowski, and Seredyński [NPS87] proved the existence of an infinite independent set, a strong affirmative answer to the second question. For the first question: Erdős and Hajnal [ErHa60] proved the existence of arbitrarily large finite independent sets; Hechler [He72] proved the answer is no assuming the continuum hypothesis; Newelski, Pawlikowski, and Seredyński [NPS87] proved the answer is yes under the stronger assumption that all $A_x$ are closed; Lee proved the answer is yes assuming the existence of an extension of the Lebesgue measure to all subsets of $\mathbb{R}$; and Glazer (using GPT 5.6 Sol, Fable 5, and Opus 4.8) proved the answer to the first question is independent of ZFC.
solved_when: The first question is settled by a proof in ZFC, or a proof of independence from ZFC, of the existence of such an infinite independent set; the second by a ZFC proof of an independent set of size $3$ for closed sets of measure $<1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #503
open: What is the largest possible size of a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ such that every three points from $A$ determine an isosceles triangle? That is, for any three points $x,y,z$ from $A$, at least two of the distances $\lvert x-y\rvert,\lvert y-z\rvert,\lvert x-z\rvert$ are equal.
status: When $d=2$ the answer is $6$ (due to Kelly [ErKe47] — an alternative proof is given by Kovács [Ko24c]). When $d=3$ the answer is $8$ (due to Croft [Cr62]). The best upper bound known in general is due to Blokhuis [Bl84], who showed that $\lvert A\rvert \leq \binom{d+2}{2}$. Alweiss has observed a lower bound of $\binom{d+1}{2}$ follows from considering the subset of $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ formed of all vectors $e_i+e_j$ where $e_i,e_j$ are distinct coordinate vectors; this set can be viewed as a subset of some $\mathbb{R}^d$ and is easily checked to have the required property. Weisenberg observed in the comments that an additional point can be added to Alweiss' construction, giving a lower bound of $\binom{d+1}{2}+1$. The fact that the truth for $d=3$ is $8$ suggests that neither of these bounds is the truth. See also [1088] for a generalisation.
solved_when: The exact maximum size of such a set is determined as a function of $d$, i.e., the gap between the known lower bound $\binom{d+1}{2}+1$ and Blokhuis's upper bound $\binom{d+2}{2}$ is closed.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a classical extremal distance-geometry question about the constraints imposed by forbidding scalene triangles.

title: Erdős problem #506
open: What is the minimum number of circles determined by any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, not all on a circle?
status: There is clearly some non-degeneracy condition intended here — probably either that not all the points are on a line, or the stronger condition that no three points are on a line. The problem was addressed by Elliott [El67], who claimed that (assuming not all points are on a circle or a line), provided $n>393$, the points determine at least $\binom{n-1}{2}$ distinct circles. An error in this was observed by Purdy and Smith [PuSm], who noted that Elliott's proof actually gives a lower bound of $\binom{n-1}{2}+1-\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor$, again for all $n>393$. This is best possible, as witnessed by a circle with $n-1$ points and a single point off the circle. The corrected lower bound was also reported by Bálint and Bálintová [BaBa94], although without any explanation. The problem appears to remain open for small $n$. Segre observed that projecting a cube onto a plane shows that the lower bound $\binom{n-1}{2}$ is false for $n=8$. See also [104] and [831].
solved_when: The exact minimum number of distinct circles determined by $n$ points (under the intended non-degeneracy condition) is determined for all $n$, in particular settling the remaining small values of $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it completes a classical extremal-geometry question about how many distinct circles a point set must determine.

title: Erdős problem #508
open: What is the chromatic number of the plane? That is, what is the smallest number of colours required to colour $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that no two points of the same colour are distance $1$ apart?
status: This is the Hadwiger–Nelson problem. Let $\chi$ be the chromatic number of the plane. An equilateral triangle trivially shows that $\chi\geq 3$. Several small graphs show $\chi\geq 4$, in particular the Moser spindle and Golomb graph. The best bounds currently known are $5 \leq \chi \leq 7$; the lower bound is due to de Grey [dG18], and the upper bound follows from colouring the plane by tessellating with hexagons of diameter slightly less than $1$. Matolcsi, Ruzsa, Varga, and Zsámboki have proved that the fractional chromatic number of the plane is at least $4$, and Croft [Cr67] proved it is at most $4.359\cdots$. See also [704], [705], and [706]. The independence number of a finite unit distance graph is the topic of [1070]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/508; Erdős references: [Er61,p.246] [Er75f,p.107] [Er81].
solved_when: The exact value of $\chi$, the chromatic number of the plane, is determined; currently known only to satisfy $5 \leq \chi \leq 7$.

title: Erdős problem #509
open: Let $f(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z]$ be a monic non-constant polynomial. Can the sublevel set $\{ z\in \mathbb{C} : \lvert f(z)\rvert \leq 1\}$ always be covered by a set of circles the sum of whose radii is at most $2$?
status: Cartan proved the covering holds with $2$ replaced by $2e$, improved to $2.59$ by Pommerenke [Po61]. Pommerenke [Po59] proved that $2$ is achievable when the set is connected (see [1046]). A higher-dimensional generalisation was asked by Erdős as Problem 4.23 in [Ha74].
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the constant $2$: either every monic non-constant $f\in\mathbb{C}[z]$ has its sublevel set $\{z : |f(z)|\le 1\}$ coverable by circles with total radius $\le 2$, or an example shows this fails.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and sits at the interface of polynomial lemniscates and covering estimates in the plane; closing the gap between the known bounds would settle the sharp constant.

title: Erdős problem #510
open: Given any finite set $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ of size $N$, must there exist an angle $\theta$ and an absolute constant $c>0$ such that $\sum_{n\in A}\cos(n\theta) < -cN^{1/2}$?
status: This is Chowla's cosine problem. Ruzsa [Ru04], improving on an earlier result of Bourgain [Bo86], proved an upper bound of $-\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N}))$. Polynomial bounds were proved independently by Bedert [Be25c] and Jin, Milojević, Tomon, and Zhang [JMTZ25]. The best bound follows from the method of Bedert [Be25c], which proved the existence of some $c>0$ such that, for all $A$ of size $N$, $\sum_{n\in A}\cos(n\theta) < -cN^{1/7}$. The example $A=B-B$, where $B$ is a Sidon set, shows that $N^{1/2}$ would be the best possible here. This problem is Problem 81 on Green's open problems list and is related to [256].
solved_when: Explicit constants $c>0$ (and $\theta$) are exhibited such that for every finite $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ of size $N$, $\sum_{n\in A}\cos(n\theta) < -cN^{1/2}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a negative-type answer of order $N^{1/2}$ would be optimal, as shown by the Sidon-set example $A=B-B$.

title: Erdős problem #513
open: For a transcendental entire function $f=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nz^n$, how large can the ratio of the biggest Taylor coefficient scaled at radius $r$ to the full maximum modulus be, infinitely often as $r\to\infty$? Formally, what is the greatest possible value of $\liminf_{r\to \infty} \frac{\max_n|a_nr^n|}{\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|}$?
status: It is trivial that $B\in[1/2,1]$. Kövári (unpublished) observed $B>1/2$. Gray and Shah [GrSh63] give an argument of Clunie showing $B\leq 2/\pi$. Clunie and Hayman [ClHa64] improved both bounds to $4/7< B \leq 2/\pi-c$ for an absolute constant $c>0$. He and Tang [HeTa26] improved the lower bound to $B> 0.5850724$ (with $4/7\approx 0.57143$), and this was further improved slightly to $0.5850788$ by GPT (as prompted by Sothanaphan). Note $2/\pi\approx 0.63662$. See also [227].
solved_when: The exact value of the supremum $B$ over all transcendental entire functions of this liminf is determined.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a long-standing question on how far Taylor coefficients can fall short of the maximum modulus.

title: Erdős problem #514
open: Given an entire transcendental function $f(z)$, must there exist a path to infinity along which $|f(z)/z^n| \to \infty$ for every $n$ simultaneously? And can one say more — estimating the length of such a path in terms of $M(r)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$, or finding a path along which $|f(z)|$ grows faster than some fixed function of $M(r)$, such as $M(r)^\epsilon$?
status: Boas (unpublished) has proved the first part, that such a path must exist. The remaining quantitative questions about path length and growth relative to $M(r)$ are open.
solved_when: The existence part is settled by establishing (or refuting) such a path; the problem is fully resolved when quantitative bounds are proved for the path's length in terms of $M(r)$, and it is determined whether a path exists along which $|f(z)|$ tends to $\infty$ faster than $M(r)^\epsilon$.

title: Erdős problem #517
open: If an entire function $f(z)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_kz^{n_k}$ (with all $a_k\neq 0$) has exponents so sparse that $n_k/k\to \infty$, must it assume every value infinitely often?
status: The problem originates in a conjecture of Fejér and Pólya. Fejér [Fe08] proved that if $\sum\frac{1}{n_k}<\infty$ then $f(z)$ assumes every value at least once, and Biernacki [Bi28] strengthened this: under the same condition $\sum\frac{1}{n_k}<\infty$, $f(z)$ assumes every value infinitely often. Pólya [Po29] proved that if $f$ has finite order and $\limsup (n_{k+1}-n_k)=\infty$, then $f(z)$ assumes every value infinitely often.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that $n_k/k\to \infty$ implies every value is assumed infinitely often by such an entire function.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, and would settle the Fejér–Pólya line of conjecture on value-taking by gap series.

title: Erdős problem #520
open: Does a random Rademacher multiplicative function — where each prime independently gets $f(p)\in\{-1,1\}$ uniformly and square-free values multiply accordingly — satisfy a law of the iterated logarithm? That is, does there exist a constant $c>0$ such that, almost surely, $\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)}{\sqrt{N\log\log N}}=c$?
status: Without multiplicativity — assigning $f(m)=\pm 1$ at random — the statement holds with $c=\sqrt{2}$ by the law of the iterated logarithm. Wintner [Wi44] proved that, almost surely, $\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2+o(1)}$, and Erdős improved the bound to $N^{1/2}(\log N)^{O(1)}$. Lau, Tenenbaum, and Wu [LTW13] showed that, almost surely, $\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{2+o(1)}$, and Caich [Ca24b] improved this to $\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{3/4+o(1)}$. Harper [Ha13] showed the sum is almost surely not $O(N^{1/2}/(\log\log N)^{5/2+o(1)})$, and conjectured that Erdős' conjecture is false, with almost surely $\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2}(\log\log N)^{1/4+o(1)}$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, for some constant $c>0$, almost surely $\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)}{\sqrt{N\log\log N}}=c$; in particular this settles whether the conjectured normalization $\sqrt{N\log\log N}$ is correct.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; it probes whether multiplicativity changes the fluctuations of random multiplicative sums compared to independent random signs.

title: Erdős problem #521
open: For a random polynomial $f_n(z)=\sum_{0\leq k\leq n}\epsilon_k z^k$ whose coefficients $\epsilon_k$ are independently and uniformly chosen from $\{-1,1\}$, if $R_n$ counts the number of real roots, is it true that, almost surely, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{R_n}{\log n}=\frac{2}{\pi}$?
status: Erdős and Offord [EO56] showed that the number of real roots of a random degree $n$ polynomial with $\pm 1$ coefficients is $(\frac{2}{\pi}+o(1))\log n$. It is ambiguous in [Er61] whether Erdős intended the coefficients to be uniformly chosen from $\{-1,1\}$ or $\{0,1\}$; in the latter case, the constant $\frac{2}{\pi}$ should be $\frac{1}{\pi}$ (see the discussion in the comments). In the $\{-1,1\}$ case, Do [Do24] proved that if $R_n[-1,1]$ counts the number of roots in $[-1,1]$, then, almost surely, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{R_n[-1,1]}{\log n}=\frac{1}{\pi}$. See also [522].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, almost surely, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{R_n}{\log n}=\frac{2}{\pi}$ for uniformly random $\pm 1$ coefficients.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles the precise almost-sure asymptotics for real roots of random Littlewood-type polynomials.

title: Erdős problem #522
open: If $f(z)=\sum_{0\leq k\leq n} \epsilon_k z^k$ is a random polynomial whose coefficients $\epsilon_k\in \{-1,1\}$ are independent and uniformly random, and $R_n$ counts the roots of $f$ in the unit disk $\{ z\in \mathbb{C} : \lvert z\rvert \leq 1\}$, is it true that $R_n/(n/2)\to 1$ almost surely?
status: Random polynomials with i.i.d. coefficients are sometimes called Kac polynomials; this problem concerns Rademacher coefficients, i.e. independent uniform $\pm 1$ values. Erdős and Offord [EO56] showed the number of real roots of a random degree $n$ polynomial with $\pm 1$ coefficients is $(\frac{2}{\pi}+o(1))\log n$. A weaker version was solved by Yakir [Ya21], who proved $R_n/(n/2)\to 1$ in probability — a weaker claim also asked by Erdős and appearing in a book of Hayman [Ha67]. More precisely, $\lim_{n\to \infty} \mathbb{P}(\lvert R_n-n/2\rvert \geq n^{9/10}) =0$. There is some ambiguity whether Erdős intended coefficients in $\{-1,1\}$ or $\{0,1\}$ (see the comments section). See also [521].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $R_n/(n/2)\to 1$ almost surely for random polynomials with independent uniform $\pm 1$ coefficients.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving the almost-sure limit upgrades the known convergence in probability to the strongest natural mode.

title: Erdős problem #524
open: For a typical choice of signs, how large must the maximum of a Littlewood-type polynomial on $[-1,1]$ be? Formally, writing $t=\sum_{k=1}^\infty \epsilon_k(t)2^{-k}$ with $\epsilon_k(t)\in\{0,1\}$, what is the correct order of magnitude, for almost all $t\in(0,1)$, of \[M_n(t)=\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\left\lvert \sum_{k\leq n}(-1)^{\epsilon_k(t)}x^k\right\rvert?\]
status: A problem of Salem and Zygmund [SaZy54]. Chung showed that, for almost all $t$, there exist infinitely many $n$ such that \[M_n(t) \ll \left(\frac{n}{\log\log n}\right)^{1/2}.\] Erdős (unpublished) showed that for almost all $t$ and every $\epsilon>0$ we have $\lim_{n\to \infty}M_n(t)/n^{1/2-\epsilon}=\infty$.
solved_when: The almost-sure order of magnitude of $M_n(t)$ as $n\to\infty$ is determined, up to matching constants, in the sense that upper and lower bounds of the same power of $n$ (and matching logarithmic factors, if present) are proved for almost all $t\in(0,1)$.
why: Resolving it would settle a classic question of Salem and Zygmund on random sign polynomials that Erdős himself posed and tracked, closing the gap between the known upper and lower behavior of these maxima.

title: Erdős problem #528
open: Does the connective constant $C_k$ of the $\mathbb{Z}^k$ lattice admit a closed-form determination? That is, letting $f(n,k)$ count self-avoiding walks of $n$ steps starting at the origin in $\mathbb{Z}^k$, determine $C_k=\lim_{n\to\infty}f(n,k)^{1/n}$.
status: The constant $C_k$ is sometimes known as the connective constant. Hammersley and Morton [HM54] showed that the limit exists, and it is trivial that $k \leq C_k \leq 2k-1$. Kesten [Ke63] proved that $C_k = 2k-1-1/2k+O(1/k^2)$, and more precise asymptotics are given by Clisby, Liang, and Slade [CLS07]. Conway and Guttmann [CG93] showed $C_2 \geq 2.62$, and Alm [Al93] showed $C_2 \leq 2.696$. Jacobsen, Scullard, and Guttmann [JSG16] computed the first few decimal places: $C_2 = 2.6381585303279\cdots$. See also [529].
solved_when: An exact determination (or sharp characterization) of $C_k$ is obtained; the central case is a rigorous evaluation of $C_2$, currently only known numerically as $C_2 = 2.6381585303279\cdots$, with bounds $2.62 \leq C_2 \leq 2.696$.

title: Erdős problem #529
open: For a self-avoiding walk of $n$ steps on the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^k$, does the expected distance $d_2(n)$ from the origin grow faster than $n^{1/2}$ in the plane, i.e. is $\lim_{n\to\infty} d_2(n)/n^{1/2}=\infty$? And in higher dimensions, is $d_k(n)\ll n^{1/2}$ for $k\geq 3$?
status: Slade [Sl87] proved that, for $k$ sufficiently large, $d_k(n)\sim Dn^{1/2}$ for some constant $D>0$ (independent of $k$). Hara and Slade ([HaSl91], [HaSl92]) extended this to all $k\geq 5$. For $k=2$, Duminil-Copin and Hammond [DuHa13] proved $d_2(n)=o(n)$. It is now conjectured that $d_k(n)\ll n^{1/2}$ is false for $k=3$ and $k=4$, and more precisely (see for example Section 1.4 of [MaSl93]) that $d_2(n)\sim Dn^{3/4}$, $d_3(n)\sim n^{\nu}$ with $\nu\approx 0.59$, and $d_4(n)\sim D(\log n)^{1/8}n^{1/2}$. Madras and Slade [MaSl93] have a monograph on self-avoiding walks. See also [528].
solved_when: The limit statement $d_2(n)/n^{1/2}\to\infty$ is proved, and $d_k(n)\ll n^{1/2}$ is proved or disproved for each $k\geq 3$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would determine the basic fluctuation scale of self-avoiding walks across dimensions.

title: Erdős problem #530
open: How large a Sidon subset must every finite set of real numbers contain? Formally, determine the order of $\ell(N)$, the maximal size such that any $A\subset\mathbb{R}$ with $|A|=N$ contains a Sidon subset of size $\ell(N)$; in particular, is $\ell(N)\sim N^{1/2}$?
status: Originally asked by Riddell [Ri69]. Erdős noted the bounds $N^{1/3} \ll \ell(N) \leq (1+o(1))N^{1/2}$ (the upper bound following from the case $A=\{1,\ldots,N\}$). The lower bound was improved to $N^{1/2}\ll \ell(N)$ by Komlós, Sulyok, and Szemerédi [KSS75]. The correct constant is unknown, but it is likely that the upper bound is true, so that $\ell(N)\sim N^{1/2}$. In [AlEr85] Alon and Erdős make the stronger conjecture that perhaps $A$ can always be written as the union of at most $(1+o(1))N^{1/2}$ many Sidon sets (this is easily verified for $A=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ using standard constructions of Sidon sets). This is discussed in problem C9 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. See also [1088] and [1208] for a higher-dimensional generalisation.
solved_when: The order of $\ell(N)$ is determined; the natural target is proving (or disproving) that $\ell(N)\sim N^{1/2}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles the correct scale of the largest Sidon subset guaranteed in an arbitrary real set.

title: Erdős problem #531
