open: How large must $N$ be so that any two-colouring of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ guarantees a $k$-element set $A$ all of whose nonempty subset sums are monochromatic? Estimate the minimal such $N$, namely $F(k)$.
status: The existence of $F(k)$ was established by Sanders and Folkman, and it also follows from Rado's theorem; it is commonly known as Folkman's theorem. Erdős and Spencer [ErSp89] proved $F(k)\geq 2^{ck^2/\log k}$ for some constant $c>0$. Balogh, Eberhard, Narayanan, Treglown, and Wagner [BENTW17] improved this to $F(k)\geq 2^{2^{k-1}/k}$.
solved_when: Sharp asymptotic bounds on $F(k)$ are obtained, matching the known lower bounds up to constants in the exponent.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and the gap between the Folkman-type existence bounds and the known lower bounds is wide open.

title: Erdős problem #535
open: How large can a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be if no $r$ elements of it share the same pairwise greatest common divisor? Formally, for $r \geq 3$, estimate $f_r(N)$, the maximum size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ in which no $r$-element subset has all pairwise gcds equal.
status: Erdős [Er64] proved $f_r(N) \leq N^{\frac{3}{4}+o(1)}$, and Abbott and Hanson [AbHa70] improved the exponent to $1/2$. For the lower bound, Erdős [Er64] showed $f_r(N) > N^{\frac{c_r}{\log\log N}}$ for any $r \geq 3$ and some constant $c_r>0$, and conjectured this should also be an upper bound. The problem is intimately connected with the sunflower problem [20]: Erdős [Er64] noted that a positive solution to [20] would imply $f_r(N) \leq N^{\frac{C_r}{\log\log N}}$ for some constant $C_r>0$. The recent sunflower bounds of Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang [ALWZ20] yield $f_r(N) \leq N^{C_r\frac{\log\log\log N}{\log\log N}}$, in particular $f_r(N) \leq N^{o(1)}$. Abbott and Hanson [AbHa67] gave an alternative description of the details of these lower and upper bounds (a similar detailed calculation appears in the comments by Hrishi). See also [536]. Tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/535.
solved_when: $f_r(N)$ is determined up to $N^{o(1)}$ factors — specifically, matching upper and lower bounds of the form $N^{\Theta_r(1/\log\log N)}$, confirming Erdős's conjecture that $f_r(N) \leq N^{C_r/\log\log N}$ for some constant $C_r > 0$.
why: Resolving this would settle one of Erdős's personally posed problems and, given its intimate connection to the sunflower problem, would mark substantial progress on that famous question as well.

title: Erdős problem #536
open: Let $f(N)$ be the largest size of a subset $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ containing no distinct $a,b,c$ with all pairwise least common multiples equal, i.e. $[a,b]=[b,c]=[a,c]$. Is it true that $f(N)=o(N)$, and more generally what is the correct order of $f(N)$?
status: The analogous quantity is $\gg N$ if one asks for four elements with the same pairwise least common multiple, as shown by Erdős [Er62], with a proof given in [Er70]; Erdős also asked this at the 1991 problem session of West Coast Number Theory. Abbott and Gardner [AbGa67] proved $f(N) \geq (1-o(1))(\log\log N)\frac{N}{\log N}$. In the comments, Weisenberg sketches a proof that, for some function $\omega(N)\to \infty$ as $N\to\infty$, $(\log\log N)^{\omega(N)}\frac{N}{\log N}\ll f(N) \leq \left(\frac{221}{225}+o(1)\right)N$. See also [535], [537], and [856]; a related combinatorial problem is asked at [857].
solved_when: The asymptotic behavior of $f(N)$ is determined — in particular, a proof or disproof that $f(N)=o(N)$, ideally pinning down where $f(N)$ lies between the known lower bound $(\log\log N)^{\omega(N)}\frac{N}{\log N}$ (with $\omega(N)\to\infty$) and the upper bound $\left(\frac{221}{225}+o(1)\right)N$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a natural extremal question about lcm-equality structures in dense sets of integers.

title: Erdős problem #538
open: If $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ has the property that, for every $m$, the equation $m=pa$ with $p$ prime and $a\in A$ has at most $r$ solutions, how large can the harmonic sum $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ be? That is, determine the best possible upper bound for $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ in terms of $r$ and $N$.
status: Erdős observed that $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{p\leq N}\frac{1}{p}\leq r\sum_{m\leq N^2}\frac{1}{m}\ll r\log N$, and hence $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n} \ll r\frac{\log N}{\log\log N}$. See also [536] and [537]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/538; Erdős references: [Er73].
solved_when: An upper bound for $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$ matching the true order of magnitude is proved, together with a construction showing it is best possible.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; settling it resolves a question in multiplicative number theory about how sparse a set must be when its prime multiples have bounded multiplicity.

title: Erdős problem #545
open: Let $G$ be a graph with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices. Is the Ramsey number $R(G)$ maximised when $G$ is "as complete as possible"? Formally, if $m=\binom{n}{2}+t$ with $0\leq t<n$, is $R(G)\leq R(H)$, where $H$ is formed by connecting a new vertex to $t$ vertices of $K_n$?
status: A question of Erdős and Graham. The weaker bound $R(G) \leq 2^{O(m^{1/2})}$ is the subject of [546], and is true, proved by Sudakov [Su11]. LouisD in the comments has noted the conjecture fails for small $m$ (in particular for $2\leq m\leq 5$ and $7\leq m\leq 9$). This is problem #10 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection. Tracked at erdosproblems.com/545; Erdős references: [Er84b,p.11] [Su11].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every graph $G$ with $m=\binom{n}{2}+t$ edges, $0\leq t<n$, and no isolated vertices, $R(G)\leq R(H)$, where $H$ joins a new vertex to $t$ vertices of $K_n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with Graham), and it identifies the extremal graph shape for Ramsey numbers of fixed-edge-count graphs; its resolution would pin down the maximum possible $R(G)$ over all $m$-edge graphs.

title: Erdős problem #550
open: Does the classical Chvátal bound for tree Ramsey numbers extend from cliques to complete multipartite graphs? Formally, for $m_1\leq\cdots\leq m_k$ and sufficiently large $n$, if $T$ is a tree on $n$ vertices and $G$ is the complete multipartite graph with vertex class sizes $m_1,\ldots,m_k$, prove that $R(T,G)\leq (\chi(G)-1)(R(T,K_{m_1,m_2})-1)+m_1$.
status: Chvátal [Ch77] proved that $R(T,K_m)=(m-1)(n-1)+1$. This problem is #16 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: The inequality $R(T,G)\leq (\chi(G)-1)(R(T,K_{m_1,m_2})-1)+m_1$ is proved for all trees $T$ on $n$ vertices, all $m_1\leq\cdots\leq m_k$, and all sufficiently large $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would extend the exact tree Ramsey formula to the multipartite setting.

title: Erdős problem #551
open: Is the Ramsey number of a cycle versus a clique given exactly by the classical off-diagonal formula? That is, does \(R(C_k,K_n)=(k-1)(n-1)+1\) hold for all \(k\geq n\geq 3\), with the single exception \(n=k=3\)?
status: Asked by Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp, who also ask for the smallest value of \(k\) such that this identity holds for fixed \(n\), and, for fixed \(n\), for the minimum value of \(R(C_k,K_n)\). The identity was proved for \(k>n^2-2\) by Bondy and Erdős [BoEr73]. Nikiforov [Ni05] extended this to \(k\geq 4n+2\). Keevash, Long, and Skokan [KLS21] proved the identity when \(k\geq C\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\) for some constant \(C\), establishing the conjecture for sufficiently large \(n\). This is problem #18 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: The identity \(R(C_k,K_n)=(k-1)(n-1)+1\) is proved for all \(k\geq n\geq 3\) except \(n=k=3\).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would complete the exact determination of cycle–clique Ramsey numbers.

title: Erdős problem #552
open: Determine the Ramsey number $R(C_4,S_n)$, where $S_n=K_{1,n}$ is the star on $n+1$ vertices. In particular, is it true that, for any $c>0$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $R(C_4,S_n)\leq n+\sqrt{n}-c$?
status: A problem of Burr, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp [BEFRS89]. Erdős often asked about $R(C_4,S_n)$ in the equivalent formulation of a bound on the minimum degree of a graph guaranteeing a $C_4$ (see [85]). It is known that $n+\sqrt{n}-6n^{11/40}\leq R(C_4,S_n)\leq n+\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil+1$; the lower bound is due to [BEFRS89], the upper bound to Parsons [Pa75]. The lower bound of [BEFRS89] is related to gaps between primes, and assuming e.g. Cramer's conjecture on gaps between primes their lower bound would be $n+\sqrt{n}-n^{o(1)}$. In [Er96] Erdős asks (an equivalent formulation of) whether $R(C_4,S_n)\geq n+\sqrt{n}-O(1)$, but says this is probably 'too optimistic'. They also ask, if $f(n)=R(C_4,S_n)$, whether $f(n+1)=f(n)$ infinitely often, whether the density of such $n$ is $0$, and whether $f(n+1)\leq f(n)+2$ for all $n$; a similar question about an equivalent function is the subject of [85]. Parsons [Pa75] proved that $R(C_4,S_n)=n+\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil$ whenever $n=q^2+1$ for a prime power $q$, and $R(C_4,S_n)=n+\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil+1$ [in the complementary cases of his determination].
solved_when: The value of $R(C_4,S_n)$ is determined (or equivalently a bound on the minimum degree guaranteeing a $C_4$ is obtained), resolving whether for any $c>0$ there are infinitely many $n$ with $R(C_4,S_n)\leq n+\sqrt{n}-c$; Erdős offered \$100 for a proof or disproof of this second question.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, and it sits at the intersection of Ramsey theory and additive number theory — the known lower bound is tied to gaps between primes.

title: Erdős problem #555
open: In a $k$-colouring of the edges of a complete graph, how large must the graph be to force a monochromatic cycle of length $2n$? That is, determine the value of $R_k(C_{2n})$, the minimal $m$ such that every $k$-colouring of $K_m$ contains a monochromatic copy of $C_{2n}$.
status: A problem of Erdős and Graham. Erdős [Er81c] gives the bounds $k^{1+\frac{1}{2n}}\ll R_k(C_{2n})\ll k^{1+\frac{1}{n-1}}$. Chung and Graham [ChGr75] showed $R_k(C_4)>k^2-k+1$ when $k-1$ is a prime power, and $R_k(C_4)\leq k^2+k+1$ for all $k$. This problem is #24 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: The exact value of $R_k(C_{2n})$ is determined (as a function of $k$ and $n$).

title: Erdős problem #556
open: In a 3-colouring of the edges of a complete graph, how large must the graph be to force a monochromatic cycle of length $n$? Formally, prove that $R_3(C_n) \leq 4n - 3$, where $R_3(G)$ is the minimal $m$ such that every 3-colouring of $K_m$ contains a monochromatic copy of $G$.
status: A problem of Bondy and Erdős; the inequality is best possible for odd $n$. Łuczak [Lu99] showed $R_3(C_n) \leq (4+o(1))n$ for all $n$, and in fact $R_3(C_n) \leq 3n + o(n)$ for even $n$. Kohayakawa, Simonovits, and Skokan [KSS05] proved the conjecture when $n$ is sufficiently large and odd. Benevides and Skokan [BeSk09] proved that if $n$ is sufficiently large and even then $R_3(C_n) = 2n$. The problem is #25 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection. Key works: erdosproblems.com/556; Erdős references: [Er81] [Er81c] [Lu99].
solved_when: The inequality $R_3(C_n) \leq 4n - 3$ is proved (this bound is best possible for odd $n$); equivalently, the exact asymptotic $R_3(C_n) \leq (4+o(1))n$ is improved to the sharp constant.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with Bondy), and resolving the remaining cases would complete a classical Ramsey-theoretic determination of the exact 3-colour Ramsey number of cycles, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #558
open: How large must a complete graph be so that every $k$-colouring of its edges forces a monochromatic copy of the complete bipartite graph $K_{s,t}$? Formally, determine $R_k(K_{s,t})$ as a function of $k$, $s$, and $t$.
status: Chung and Graham [ChGr75] prove the general bounds \[(2\pi\sqrt{st})^{\frac{1}{s+t}}\left(\frac{s+t}{e^2}\right)k^{\frac{st-1}{s+t}}\leq R_k(K_{s,t})\leq (t-1)(k+k^{1/s})^s\] and determined $R_k(K_{2,2})=(1+o(1))k^2$. Alon, Rónyai, and Szabó [ARS99] proved $R_k(K_{3,3})=(1+o(1))k^3$ and that if $s\geq (t-1)!+1$ then $R_k(K_{s,t})\asymp k^t$. The problem is #27 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection; it is tracked at erdosproblems.com/558 (Erdős reference [Er81c]).
solved_when: An exact determination (or sharp asymptotic formula) for $R_k(K_{s,t})$ for general $k$, $s$, $t$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and a solution would resolve a basic multicolour Ramsey question for bipartite graphs where current general bounds are far apart.

title: Erdős problem #560
open: What is the size Ramsey number of the complete bipartite graph — the fewest edges a graph can have while still forcing a monochromatic copy of $K_{n,n}$ under every 2-colouring? Formally, determine $\hat{R}(K_{n,n})$, where $\hat{R}(G)$ is the minimum number of edges $m$ of a graph $H$ such that any 2-colouring of $E(H)$ contains a monochromatic copy of $G$.
status: The best known bounds are $\frac{1}{60}n^2 2^n < \hat{R}(K_{n,n}) < \frac{3}{2}n^3 2^n$. The lower bound, valid for $n \geq 6$, is due to Erdős and Rousseau [ErRo93]; the upper bound was proved by Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp [EFRS78b] and independently by Nešetřil and Rödl [NeRo78]. Conlon, Fox, and Wigderson [CFW23] showed that for any $s \leq t$, $\hat{R}(K_{s,t}) \gg s^{2-\frac{s}{t}}t\,2^s$, and proved $\hat{R}(K_{s,t}) \asymp s^2 t\,2^s$ whenever $t \gg s\log s$; they conjecture this asymptotic holds for all $s \leq t$, which in particular would give $\hat{R}(K_{n,n}) \asymp n^3 2^n$. This problem is #29 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection and is tracked at erdosproblems.com/560.
solved_when: (quantitative targets from the record) closing the gap between the known bounds $\frac{1}{60}n^2 2^n < \hat{R}(K_{n,n}) < \frac{3}{2}n^3 2^n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and a resolution — particularly of the conjectured $\hat{R}(K_{n,n}) \asymp n^3 2^n$ — would settle the general size Ramsey behaviour of complete bipartite graphs, where the best known bounds differ by a factor of order $n$.

title: Erdős problem #561
open: Is there an exact formula for the size Ramsey number of a union of stars versus a union of stars? Formally, with $F_1=\cup_{i\leq s} K_{1,n_i}$ and $F_2=\cup_{j\leq t} K_{1,m_j}$ where $n_1\geq \cdots \geq n_s\geq 1$ and $m_1\geq \cdots \geq m_t\geq 1$, prove that $\hat{R}(F_1,F_2) = \sum_{2\leq k\leq s+t}l_k$, where $l_k=\max\{n_i+m_j-1 : i+j=k\}$.
status: Burr, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp [BEFRS78] proved the formula when all the $n_i$ are identical and all the $m_i$ are identical. Győri and Schelp [GySc02] proved it under the condition $\binom{l_k}{2}> \sum_{k\leq i\leq s+t}l_i$ for all $2\leq k\leq s+t$. Davoodi, Javadi, Kamranian, and Raeisi [DJKR25] proved further special cases: all cases when $s=1$, or $s=2$ and $n_1=n_2$, or all $n_i$ and $m_j$ are odd, or all $n_i$ are an identical odd number and $m_1$ is odd. The problem is #30 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: The displayed formula $\hat{R}(F_1,F_2) = \sum_{2\leq k\leq s+t}l_k$ with $l_k=\max\{n_i+m_j-1 : i+j=k\}$ is proved for arbitrary star forests $F_1$ and $F_2$ as above.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; an exact formula for the size Ramsey number of star forests would resolve a basic open case of the general size Ramsey problem.

title: Erdős problem #562
open: Does the $r$-uniform hypergraph Ramsey number $R_r(n)$ — the least $m$ such that any $2$-colouring of the edges of the complete $r$-uniform hypergraph on $m$ vertices forces a monochromatic $K_n^{(r)}$ — grow like a tower of exponentials of height $r-1$ in $n$? Formally, prove that for $r \geq 3$, $\log_{r-1} R_r(n) \asymp_r n$, where $\log_{r-1}$ is the $(r-1)$-fold iterated logarithm.
status: A problem of Erdős, Hajnal, and Rado [EHR65]; a generalisation of problem [564]. It is listed as problem #38 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection, and is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/562.
solved_when: Positive constants $c_r, C_r$ are established such that, for all sufficiently large $n$ and every $r \geq 3$, $c_r n \leq \log_{r-1} R_r(n) \leq C_r n$; equivalently, $R_r(n)$ is pinned down up to constant factors in the exponent as a tower of $2$'s of height $r-1$.
why: This would determine the asymptotic order of the fundamental hypergraph Ramsey numbers for all uniformities $r \geq 3$, resolving one of Erdős's personally posed problems; without it, the exact tower-height structure of higher-uniformity Ramsey growth remains unconfirmed beyond the known bounds.
aliases: Erdős #562; graph theory / ramsey theory / hypergraphs

title: Erdős problem #563
open: Does every large complete graph admit a two-colouring whose every large vertex subset is close to balanced between the colours? Formally, let $F(n,\alpha)$ be the smallest $m$ such that some $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ gives every $X\subseteq[n]$ with $|X|\geq m$ more than $\alpha\binom{|X|}{2}$ edges of each colour; prove that for every $0\leq\alpha<1/2$, $F(n,\alpha)\sim c_\alpha\log n$ for a constant $c_\alpha$ depending only on $\alpha$.
status: The probabilistic method easily gives $F(n,\alpha)\asymp_\alpha\log n$ for every $0\leq\alpha<1/2$, so the correct order of growth is known and only the constant is in question. When $\alpha=0$ the problem asks for a $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_n$ with no monochromatic clique of size $m$, recovering the classical Ramsey numbers. A generalisation to hypergraphs appears in [161]. The problem is #39 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection; see erdosproblems.com/563 and Erdős references [Er90b,p.21].
solved_when: The asymptotic $F(n,\alpha)\sim c_\alpha\log n$ is established for every $0\leq\alpha<1/2$, with $c_\alpha$ depending only on $\alpha$.
aliases: Erdős #563; graph theory / ramsey theory / hypergraphs

title: Erdős problem #564
open: Let $R_3(n)$ be the minimal $m$ such that every $2$-colouring of the edges of the complete $3$-uniform hypergraph on $m$ vertices contains a monochromatic copy of the complete $3$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices. Is there a constant $c>0$ with $R_3(n) \geq 2^{2^{cn}}$, i.e., does the doubly exponential lower bound hold?
status: This is a special case of [562]. Erdős, Hajnal, and Rado [EHR65] proved the bounds $2^{cn^2} < R_3(n) < 2^{2^{n}}$ for some constant $c>0$. Erdős, Hajnal, Máté, and Rado [EHMR84] proved a doubly exponential lower bound for the corresponding problem with $4$ colours. The problem is #37 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection, and is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/564.
solved_when: Explicit constants $c>0$ and $n_0$ are exhibited with a proof that $R_3(n) \geq 2^{2^{cn}}$ for all $n \geq n_0$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with a $500 prize) and resolving it would settle a basic gap in our knowledge of hypergraph Ramsey numbers, between the known singly exponential lower bound and the doubly exponential upper bound.
aliases: Erdős #564; graph theory / ramsey theory / hypergraphs

title: Erdős problem #566
open: Is every graph $G$ in which each $k$-vertex subgraph has at most $2k-3$ edges Ramsey size linear? That is, must $R(G,H)\ll m$ hold for every graph $H$ with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices?
status: The property fails for a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $2n-2$ edges, for example with $H=K_n$. Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp [EFRS93] have shown that any graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and at most $n+1$ edges is Ramsey size linear. This problem is #31 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection. Key work: erdosproblems.com/566.
solved_when: A proof, or counterexample, is given to the assertion that every such $G$ (with all $k$-vertex subgraphs having at most $2k-3$ edges) satisfies $R(G,H)\ll m$ for all $H$ with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it asks for the exact sparsity threshold at which Ramsey numbers become linear in the size of the host graph, and it implies problem [567].

title: Erdős problem #567
open: Is each of the graphs $Q_3$, $K_{3,3}$, and $H_5$ (obtained from $C_5$ by adding two vertex-disjoint chords) Ramsey size linear? That is, is it true that $R(G,H)\ll m$ whenever $H$ is a graph with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices?
status: In [Er95] Erdős specifically asks about the case $G=K_{3,3}$. The graph $H_5$ can also be described as $K_4^*$, obtained from $K_4$ by subdividing one edge ($K_4$ itself is not Ramsey size linear, since $R(4,n)\gg n^{3-o(1)}$, see [166]). Bradać, Gishboliner, and Sudakov [BGS23] have shown that every subdivision of $K_4$ on at least $6$ vertices is Ramsey size linear, and also that $R(H_5,H)\ll m$ whenever $H$ is a bipartite graph with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices. This problem is #32 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $R(G,H)\ll m$ for each of $G=Q_3$, $G=K_{3,3}$, and $G=H_5$, for every $H$ with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, a special case of [566], tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it probes where Ramsey size linearity begins below $K_4$.

title: Erdős problem #568
open: If a fixed graph $G$ satisfies $R(G,T_n)\ll n$ for every $n$-vertex tree $T_n$ and $R(G,K_n)\ll n^2$, must $G$ also satisfy $R(G,H)\ll m$ for every graph $H$ with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices? Equivalently, must such a $G$ be Ramsey size linear?
status: The problem is restated by the record itself as asking whether $G$ is Ramsey size linear. It appears as #33 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection, and its full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/568.
solved_when: A proof that the two hypotheses $R(G,T_n)\ll n$ and $R(G,K_n)\ll n^2$ imply $R(G,H)\ll m$ for all $H$ with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices, or a counterexample exhibiting such a $G$ and an $H$ violating the bound.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and resolving it would settle a basic structural question about when Ramsey numbers are controlled by edge count rather than vertex count.

title: Erdős problem #569
open: For each $k\geq 1$, how large can the Ramsey number $R(C_{2k+1},H)$ be forced to be by a graph $H$ with no isolated vertices? Formally, what is the best possible constant $c_k$ such that $R(C_{2k+1},H)\leq c_k m$ for every graph $H$ on $m$ edges without isolated vertices?
status: The problem is #34 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection, and is tracked at erdosproblems.com/569 (Erdős problem #569). No further results are recorded.
solved_when: For each $k\geq 1$, the optimal constant $c_k$ is determined: matching upper and lower bounds are established for $R(C_{2k+1},H)\leq c_k m$ over all graphs $H$ on $m$ edges without isolated vertices.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution settles a long-standing entry in that collection.

title: Erdős problem #572
open: Is the maximum number of edges in an $n$-vertex graph of girth greater than $2k$ at least a constant times $n^{1+1/k}$? Formally: show that for $k\geq 3$, $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k})\gg n^{1+\frac{1}{k}}$.
status:
It is easy to see that $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k+1})=\lfloor n^2/4floor$ for any $k\geq 1$ (and $n>2k+1$), since no bipartite graph contains an odd cycle. Erdős and Klein [Er38] proved $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_4)\asymp n^{3/2}$. Erdős [Er64c] and Bondy and Simonovits [BoSi74] showed that $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k})\ll kn^{1+ rac{1}{k}}$. Benson [Be66] has proved the conjecture for $k=3$ and $k=5$. Lazebnik, Ustimenko, and Woldar [LUW95] have shown that, for arbitrary $k\geq 3$, $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k})\gg n^{1+ rac{2}{3k-3+
u}}$, where $
u=0$ if $k$ is odd and $
u=1$ if $k$ is even. See [LUW99] for further history and references; see also [765].
solved_when: For every $k\geq 3$, there exist constants $c_k>0$ and $n_k$ such that $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k})\geq c_k\, n^{1+1/k}$ for all $n\geq n_k$, matching the known upper bound $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_{2k})\ll kn^{1+\frac{1}{k}}$ up to constant factors.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (#46 in Extremal Graph Theory of the graphs problem collection, #572 overall), tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it would settle the correct order of the extremal number for even cycles.
aliases: Erdős #572; graph theory / turan number / cycles

title: Erdős problem #573
open: Is it true that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;\{C_3,C_4\})\sim (n/2)^{3/2}?\]
status: A problem of Erdős and Simonovits, who proved that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;\{C_4,C_5\})=(n/2)^{3/2}+O(n).\]Kövári, Sós, and Turán [KST54] proved that the extremal number of edges for containing either $C_4$ or an odd cycle of any length is $\sim (n/2)^{3/2}$. This problem is therefore asking whether the threshold is the same if we just forbid odd cycles of length $3$. See also [574] for the general case, and [765] for $\mathrm{ex}(n;C_4)$. This problem is #48 in Extremal Graph Theory in the graphs problem collection.

title: Erdős problem #576
open: How large can a graph on $n$ vertices be before it must contain the $k$-dimensional hypercube $Q_k$ (which has $2^k$ vertices and $k2^{k-1}$ edges) as a subgraph? Formally, determine the asymptotic behaviour of the extremal number $\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_k)$, with the case $k=3$ being the central open instance.
status: Erdős and Simonovits [ErSi70] proved $(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))n^{3/2}\leq \mathrm{ex}(n;Q_3)\ll n^{8/5}$, and they mention that Erdős had originally conjectured $\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_3)\gg n^{5/3}$. They also proved that if $G$ is $Q_3$ with a missing edge, then $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\asymp n^{3/2}$. In [Er74c], [Er81], and [Er93] Erdős asked whether $\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_3)\asymp n^{8/5}$. A theorem of Sudakov and Tomon [SuTo22] implies $\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_k)=o(n^{2-\frac{1}{k}})$, which Janzer and Sudakov [JaSu22] improved to $\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_k)\ll_k n^{2-\frac{1}{k-1}+\frac{1}{(k-1)2^{k-1}}}$. See also [1035]. The problem is #52 in Extremal Graph Theory in the graphs problem collection, tracked at erdosproblems.com/576.
solved_when: The order of magnitude of $\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_3)$ is determined (in particular resolving whether $\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_3)\asymp n^{8/5}$), or more generally the correct asymptotics of $\mathrm{ex}(n;Q_k)$ are established for each $k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, a benchmark case in extremal graph theory for understanding which graphs force the extremal number to jump between the $n^{3/2}$ and $n^2$ scales; a solution would clarify the general theory of extremal numbers of degenerate bipartite graphs.

title: Erdős problem #579
open: Is it true that for every $\delta>0$ there is a constant $c(\delta)>0$ such that any sufficiently large $n$-vertex graph with no $K_{2,2,2}$ and at least $\delta n^2$ edges contains an independent set of size at least $c(\delta)\,n$?
status: A problem of Erdős, Hajnal, Sós, and Szemerédi, who proved the statement for $\delta>1/8$. See also [533] and the entry in the graphs problem collection. Tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/579; Erdős references: [Er90] [Er91] [Er93,p.340].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given of the statement above: for every $\delta>0$, all sufficiently large $n$-vertex $K_{2,2,2}$-free graphs with at least $\delta n^2$ edges have an independent set of size $\gg_\delta n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and resolving it would settle a natural Ramsey-type question about how sparsity constraints force large independent sets in dense graphs.

title: Erdős problem #583
open: Can every connected graph on $n$ vertices be partitioned into at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$ edge-disjoint paths? This is the Erdős–Gallai path-partition conjecture, one of Erdős's personally posed problems.
status: A problem of Erdős and Gallai. Dropping the edge-disjoint condition, the conjecture was proved by Fan [Fa02]; see also [Er71,p.101]. For a connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices: Lovász [Lo68] proved $G$ can be partitioned into at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ edge-disjoint paths and cycles, hence into at most $n-1$ paths, which implies the conjecture if $G$ has at most one vertex of even degree. Chung [Ch78] proved a partition into at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$ edge-disjoint trees. Pyber [Py96] proved $G$ can be covered by at most $n/2+O(n^{3/4})$ (not necessarily edge-disjoint) paths, and proved the conjecture when the subgraph induced by even-degree vertices is a forest. Bonamy and Perrett [BoPe19] proved it for maximum degree $\leq 5$; Blanché, Bonamy, and Bonichon [BBB21] for planar graphs; Anto and Basavaraju [AnBa23] for $2$-degenerate graphs (every subgraph has a vertex of degree $\leq 2$); and Chu, Fan, and Zhou [CFZ26] for graphs whose induced subgraph condition as stated in the record.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that every connected graph on $n$ vertices admits a partition into at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$ edge-disjoint paths.
why: It is a natural sharp bound on how few paths can decompose a connected graph; solving it would settle a long-standing Erdős problem tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/583.

title: Erdős problem #584
open: If a graph on $n$ vertices has $\delta n^{2}$ edges, can we always find a subgraph with many edges in which any two edges lie together on a short cycle? More precisely, are there subgraphs $H_1,H_2\subseteq G$ such that $H_1$ has $\gg \delta^3n^2$ edges and every two edges in $H_1$ are contained in a cycle of length at most $6$ — with two edges sharing a vertex lying on a cycle of length $4$ — and $H_2$ has $\gg \delta^2n^2$ edges and every two edges in $H_2$ are contained in a cycle of length at most $8$?
status: A problem of Erdős, Duke, and Rödl. Duke and Erdős [DuEr82] proved the first statement if $n$ is sufficiently large depending on $\delta$. Duke, Erdős, and Rödl [DER84] proved the first statement with a $\delta^5$ in place of a $\delta^3$. Fox and Sudakov [FoSu08b] proved the second statement when $\delta > n^{-1/5}$. The real challenge remains proving the first statement when $\delta = n^{-c}$ for some $c>0$. See also the entry in the graphs problem collection (erdosproblems.com/584).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the stated decomposition: $H_1$ with $\gg \delta^3 n^2$ edges whose every two edges lie on a cycle of length at most $6$ (cycles of length $4$ when the two edges share a vertex), and $H_2$ with $\gg \delta^2 n^2$ edges whose every two edges lie on a cycle of length at most $8$ — ideally in the sparse regime $\delta = n^{-c}$ for some $c > 0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and the sparse regime $\delta = n^{-c}$ is the real challenge that would complete it.

title: Erdős problem #585
open: What is the maximum number of edges in an $n$-vertex graph that does not contain two edge-disjoint cycles with the same vertex set? More precisely, does the true order of magnitude lie closer to the known lower bound of $n\log\log n$ or to the near-polynomial upper bounds currently available?
status: Pyber, Rödl, and Szemerédi [PRS95] constructed such a graph with $\gg n\log\log n$ edges. Chakraborti, Janzer, Methuku, and Montgomery [CJMM24] showed such a graph has at most $n(\log n)^{O(1)}$ edges; indeed, they prove there is a constant $C>0$ such that for any $k\geq 2$ there is a $c_k$ such that any $n$-vertex graph with at least $c_k n(\log n)^{C}$ edges contains $k$ pairwise edge-disjoint cycles with the same vertex set.
solved_when: The extremal function is determined up to constant factors (or at least its order of magnitude, e.g., settling whether it is $n(\log\log n)^{O(1)}$, $n(\log n)^{C}$, or something in between).
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolves the gap between the $n\log\log n$ construction and the quasi-polynomial upper bound.

title: Erdős problem #588
open: Let $f_k(n)$ be the smallest number such that any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no $k+1$ collinear points determine at most $f_k(n)$ lines containing at least $k$ points. Is it true that $f_k(n) = o(n^2)$ for $k \geq 4$?
status: The problem generalizes [101], which asks the case $k=4$. The restriction to $k \geq 4$ is necessary: Sylvester showed $f_3(n) = n^2/6 + O(n)$, and constructions of Burr, Grünbaum, and Sloane [BGS74] and Füredi and Palásti [FuPa84] show $f_3(n) \geq (1/6 + o(1))n^2$. For $k \geq 4$, Kárteszi [Ka63] proved $f_k(n) \gg_k n \log n$, resolving a conjecture of Erdős that $f_k(n)/n \to \infty$. Grünbaum [Gr76] improved this to $f_k(n) \gg_k n^{1+\frac{1}{k-2}}$, and Erdős speculated this might be the correct order of magnitude; however, Solymosi and Stojaković [SoSt13] gave a construction showing $f_k(n) \gg_k n^{2-O_k(1/\sqrt{\log n})}$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given that $f_k(n) = o(n^2)$ for every $k \geq 4$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with a $100 prize from Erdős), tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it asks whether excluding $k+1$ collinear points sharply limits the number of rich lines.

title: Erdős problem #589
open: How large a subset with no three points on a line must every set of $n$ points in the plane with no four points on a line contain? Formally, if $g(n)$ is the maximal size guaranteed by such a set, estimate $g(n)$.
status: A trivial greedy algorithm gives $g(n)\gg n^{1/2}$. Erdős thought $g(n)\gg n$, but in fact $g(n)=o(n)$, which follows from the density Hales-Jewett theorem proved by Furstenberg and Katznelson [FuKa91] (see [185]). Füredi [Fu91b] proved $n^{1/2}\log n\ll g(n)=o(n)$. Balogh and Solymosi [BaSo18] improved the upper bound to $g(n)\ll n^{5/6+o(1)}$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/589; Erdős references: [Er84].
solved_when: Sharp asymptotic bounds for $g(n)$ are determined, separating it from the currently known regime $n^{1/2}\log n \ll g(n) \ll n^{5/6+o(1)}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it anchors the general question of finding subsets with no $l$ points on a line inside sets with no $k$ points on a line for $3\leq l<k$.

title: Erdős problem #592
open: Which countable ordinals $\beta$ have the property that, setting $\alpha = \omega^{\beta}$, every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_\alpha$ yields either a red $K_\alpha$ or a blue $K_3$?
status: Ordinals $\alpha$ with $\alpha \to (\alpha,3)^2$ are called partition ordinals. Specker [Sp57] proved the property holds for $\beta=2$ and fails for $3 \leq \beta < \omega$; Chang [Ch72] proved it for $\beta = \omega$. Galvin and Larson [GaLa74] showed that any $\beta \geq 3$ with the property must be additively indecomposable, so in particular $\beta = \omega^\gamma$ for some countable $\gamma$, and they conjecture that every $\beta \geq 3$ of this form has the property. Schipperus [Sc10] proved it holds for $\beta = \omega^\gamma$ when $\gamma$ is a countable ordinal that is the sum of one or two indecomposable ordinals, and fails when $\gamma$ is the sum of four or more indecomposable ordinals. The remaining open case is when $\gamma$ is the sum of three indecomposable ordinals. The case $\beta = \omega$ is the subject of [590], and $\beta = \omega^2$ is the subject of [591]; see also [118], and [1169] for the case $\alpha = \omega_1^2$.
solved_when: A complete characterization is given of the countable ordinals $\beta$ such that $\alpha = \omega^{\beta}$ satisfies $\alpha \to (\alpha,3)^2$ — in particular, settling the remaining case where $\gamma$ is the sum of three indecomposable ordinals (i.e., whether $\beta = \omega^\gamma$ then has the property), thereby confirming or refuting the Galvin–Larson conjecture that every additively indecomposable $\beta \geq 3$ works.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with a $1000 prize), and a full resolution would complete the classification of the ordinal partition relation $\alpha \to (\alpha,3)^2$, a core question of ordinal Ramsey theory.

title: Erdős problem #593
open: Which finite 3-uniform hypergraphs are unavoidable in every 3-uniform hypergraph of uncountable chromatic number? Formally, characterize those finite 3-uniform hypergraphs that appear in every 3-uniform hypergraph with chromatic number $>\aleph_0$.
status: Similar problems were investigated by Erdős, Galvin, and Hajnal [EGH75]. Erdős claims that for graphs the problem is completely solved: a graph of chromatic number $\geq \aleph_1$ must contain all finite bipartite graphs but need not contain any fixed odd cycle.
solved_when: A complete characterization is given of the finite 3-uniform hypergraphs contained in every 3-uniform hypergraph of chromatic number $>\aleph_0$, with proof.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (carrying his $500 prize), and the answer would extend to 3-uniform hypergraphs the divisibility phenomenon known for graphs, where uncountable chromatic number forces exactly the finite bipartite graphs.
aliases: Erdős #593; set theory / graph theory / hypergraphs / chromatic number

title: Erdős problem #595
open: Does there exist an infinite $K_4$-free graph that cannot be written as the union of countably many triangle-free graphs? Equivalently, can the finite Ramsey-type obstructions of Erdős and Hajnal's problem be pushed to a single countable counterexample?
status: This is a problem of Erdős and Hajnal. Folkman [Fo70] and Nešetřil and Rödl [NeRo75] proved that for every $n \geq 1$ there is a graph $G$ containing no $K_4$ that is not the union of $n$ triangle-free graphs. See also [582] and [596]. Full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/595, with Erdős references [Er87] and [Fo70].
solved_when: An explicit or existence proof of an infinite graph containing no $K_4$ that is not the union of countably many triangle-free graphs; alternatively, a proof that every $K_4$-free graph is such a countable union.
why: Resolving it would clarify how finite vertex-Ramsey behavior scales to infinity, and it carries a $250 prize offered by Erdős himself.

title: Erdős problem #596
open: Which pairs of graphs $G_1, G_2$ have the property that for every $n \geq 1$ there is a $G_1$-free graph $H$ such that any $n$-colouring of its edges yields a monochromatic copy of $G_2$, while at the same time every $G_1$-free graph admits an $\aleph_0$-colouring of its edges with no monochromatic $G_2$?
status: Erdős and Hajnal originally conjectured that there are no such $G_1, G_2$, but in fact $G_1 = C_4$ and $G_2 = C_6$ is an example: Nešetřil and Rödl established the first property for this pair, and Erdős and Hajnal the second (indeed, every $C_4$-free graph is a countable union of trees). Whether the property holds for $G_1 = K_4$ and $G_2 = K_3$ is the content of problem [595]. See erdosproblems.com/596; Erdős reference [Er87].
solved_when: A complete characterization of the pairs $(G_1, G_2)$ satisfying both the finite-colour Ramsey property and the countable-colour avoidance property described above is given.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; a solution would clarify the interplay between forbidden subgraphs, finite Ramsey thresholds, and countable colourings, with the full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.
aliases: Erdős #596; graph theory / ramsey theory / set theory

title: Erdős problem #597
open: If a graph $G$ on at most $\aleph_1$ vertices contains neither a $K_4$ nor a $K_{\aleph_0,\aleph_0}$, must the partition relation $\omega_1^2 \to (\omega_1\omega, G)^2$ hold? In particular, does this remain true when $G$ is finite?
status: Erdős and Hajnal proved that $\omega_1^2 \to (\omega_1\omega,3)^2$. Erdős originally asked this with just the assumption that $G$ is $K_4$-free, but Baumgartner proved that $\omega_1^2 \not\to (\omega_1\omega, K_{\aleph_0,\aleph_0})^2$, ruling out the original formulation. References: erdosproblems.com/597; Erdős references: [Er87] [Va99,7.84].
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of whether $\omega_1^2 \to (\omega_1\omega, G)^2$ for every graph $G$ on at most $\aleph_1$ vertices that is both $K_4$-free and $K_{\aleph_0,\aleph_0}$-free, including an answer for finite $G$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would clarify how forbidden-subgraph assumptions drive partition relations at $\omega_1$.
aliases: Erdős #597; graph theory / ramsey theory / set theory

title: Erdős problem #598
open: Let $m$ be an infinite cardinal and $\kappa$ be the successor cardinal of $2^{\aleph_0}$. Can one colour the countable subsets of $m$ using $\kappa$ many colours so that every $X\subseteq m$ with $\lvert X\rvert=\kappa$ contains subsets of all possible colours?
status: No proof expositions are available yet; contributors are invited to message a moderator or leave an exposition as a comment. Key works: erdosproblems.com/598; Erdős references: [Er87].
solved_when: An explicit colouring $c:[m]^{\aleph_0}\to\kappa$ is constructed (or proved impossible) such that every $X\subseteq m$ with $\lvert X\rvert=\kappa$ contains countable subsets of every colour.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it advances the cardinal-arithmetic edge of Ramsey theory.

title: Erdős problem #600
open: Let $e(n,r)$ be the least number such that every graph on $n$ vertices with at least $e(n,r)$ edges, each of which lies in a triangle, must contain an edge lying in at least $r$ triangles. For $r \geq 2$, is it true that $e(n,r+1) - e(n,r) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$? Is it true that $e(n,r+1)/e(n,r) \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$?
status: Ruzsa and Szemerédi [RuSz78] proved that $e(n,r) = o(n^2)$ for any fixed $r$. See also [80].
solved_when: For every fixed $r \geq 2$, it is proved (or disproved) that $e(n,r+1) - e(n,r) \to \infty$ and that $e(n,r+1)/e(n,r) \to 1$ as $n \to \infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #601
open: For which limit ordinals $\alpha$ must every graph whose vertex set is $\alpha$ contain either an infinite path or an independent set whose vertices have order type $\alpha$? Equivalently, determine the class of limit ordinals for which this Ramsey-type dichotomy holds.
status: The problem was posed by Erdős, Hajnal, and Milner [EHM70], who proved the statement true for $\alpha < \omega_1^{\omega+2}$. In [Er82e] Erdős offers \$250 for showing what happens when $\alpha=\omega_1^{\omega+2}$ and \$500 for settling the general case. Larson [La90] proved the statement true for all $\alpha<2^{\aleph_0}$ assuming Martin's axiom.
solved_when: The ordinal $\alpha = \omega_1^{\omega+2}$ is settled (worth \$250), and the general case for all limit ordinals $\alpha$ is settled (worth \$500).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems with cash prizes attached, and it sits at the interface of graph theory and set theory, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #602
open: Let $(A_i)$ be a countably infinite family of countably infinite sets, pairwise intersecting in a finite set that never has exactly one element. Must there be a $2$-colouring of $\cup A_i$ such that no $A_i$ is monochromatic?
status: A problem of Komjáth. The existence of such a $2$-colouring is sometimes known as Property B. Key works: erdosproblems.com/602; Erdős references: [Er87].
solved_when: A proof, or a counterexample family $(A_i)$ with $\lvert A_i\rvert=\aleph_0$ and $\lvert A_i\cap A_j\rvert$ finite and $\neq 1$ for $i\neq j$, that admits no such $2$-colouring.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and its resolution would clarify when countable almost-disjoint families necessarily admit Property B colourings.

title: Erdős problem #604
open: Given any set of $n$ distinct points in the plane, must there be one point of the set from which the other points determine nearly $n^{1-o(1)}$ distinct distances? More sharply, must some point $x\in A\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfy $\#\{d(x,y):y\in A\}\gg n/\sqrt{\log n}$?
status: The problem is a stronger form of the distinct distances problem [89]. The integer grid shows $n/\sqrt{\log n}$ is best possible. It may be true that $\gg n$ points work (Hunter noted in the comments this trivially follows from a single such point), or that the bound holds on average: in [Er75f] Erdős conjectured $\sum_{x\in A}d(x)\gg n^2/\sqrt{\log n}$. In [Er97e] Erdős offered \$500 for a solution, though it is unclear whether for a single such point or $\gg n$ many. In [Er97e] Erdős wrote he initially 'overconjectured' that the answer matches the number of distinct distances between all pairs (see [89]), but this was disproved by Harborth; the answers could still agree up to an additive $n^{o(1)}$. The best known bound is $\gg n^{c-o(1)}$ due to Katz and Tardos [KaTa04], where $c=\frac{48-14e}{55-16e}=0.864137\cdots$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every $n$-point set $A\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ contains a point $x$ with $\#\{d(x,y):y\in A\}\gg n/\sqrt{\log n}$ — the bound shown best possible by the integer grid. The original target $n^{1-o(1)}$ also resolves the problem.
why: This is the pinned-distance analogue of Erdős's distinct distances problem, one of his personally posed questions with a $500 prize, and a full solution would reveal how pinned distances relate to total distinct distances (conceivably equal up to an additive $n^{o(1)}$ factor).

title: Erdős problem #609
open: Let $f(n)$ be the minimal $m$ such that any $n$-colouring of the edges of $K_{2^n+1}$ forces a monochromatic odd cycle of length at most $m$. How fast does $f(n)$ grow?
status: A problem of Erdős and Graham. The edges of $K_{2^n}$ can be $n$-coloured to avoid odd cycles of any length, and it can be shown that $C_5$ and $C_7$ can be avoided for large $n$. Chung [Ch97] asked whether $f(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$; Day and Johnson [DaJo17] proved this is true, showing $f(n)\geq 2^{c\sqrt{\log n}}$ for some constant $c>0$. The trivial upper bound is $2^n$. Girão and Hunter [GiHu24] proved $f(n)\ll \frac{2^n}{n^{1-o(1)}}$, and Janzer and Yip [JaYi25] improved this to $f(n)\ll n^{3/2}2^{n/2}$. See also the entry in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: An asymptotic estimate of $f(n)$ is obtained — in particular, closing the gap between the lower bound $f(n)\geq 2^{c\sqrt{\log n}}$ (for some constant $c>0$) and the upper bound $f(n)\ll n^{3/2}2^{n/2}$, with the trivial upper bound being $2^n$.
why: A sharp estimate would resolve one of Erdős's personally posed Ramsey-theoretic problems (Erdős #609), clarifying how large a monochromatic odd cycle is forced just past the $2^n$ threshold where no odd cycle need appear at all.

title: Erdős problem #611
open: If every maximal clique of an $n$-vertex graph $G$ is large — say at least $cn$ vertices — must there be a small set of vertices hitting every maximal clique, of size $o_c(n)$? Formally, letting $\tau(G)$ denote the clique transversal number, is $\tau(G)=o_c(n)$ under this assumption, and for $c>0$ how small can the threshold $k_c(n)$ be so that requiring every maximal clique to have at least $k_c(n)$ vertices forces $\tau(G)<(1-c)n$?
status: A problem of Erdős, Gallai, and Tuza [EGT92], who proved $k_c(n) \geq n^{c'/\log\log n}$ for some $c'>0$, and that if every clique has size at least $k$ then $\tau(G) \leq n-(kn)^{1/2}$. Bollobás and Erdős proved that if every maximal clique has at least $n+3-2\sqrt{n}$ vertices then $\tau(G)=1$, and this threshold is best possible. See also [610] and the entry in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that all maximal cliques having at least $cn$ vertices implies $\tau(G)=o_c(n)$, together with an estimate of the minimal $k_c(n)$ guaranteeing $\tau(G)<(1-c)n$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolves the quantitative relationship between clique size and clique transversal number.

title: Erdős problem #612
open: How small can the diameter of a connected graph be forced to be by its minimum degree once cliques of bounded size are forbidden? Formally, following the amended conjecture of Czabarka, Singgih, and Székely: if $G$ is a connected graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $d$ containing no $K_{k+1}$, is the diameter of $G$ at most $(3-\tfrac{2}{k})\frac{n}{d}+O(1)$?
status: The original problem, posed by Erdős, Pach, Pollack, and Tuza [EPPT89], conjectured that if $G$ is connected on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $d$ and diameter $D$, contains no $K_{2r}$, and $(r-1)(3r+2)\mid d$, then $D\leq \frac{2(r-1)(3r+2)}{2r^2-1}\frac{n}{d}+O(1)$, and if $G$ contains no $K_{2r+1}$ and $3r-1\mid d$, then $D\leq \frac{3r-1}{r}\frac{n}{d}+O(1)$; they gave constructions showing these bounds would be sharp and proved the case $2r+1=3$. It is known (see [EPPT89]) that any connected graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $d$ has diameter $D\leq 3\frac{n}{d+1}+O(1)$. The $K_{2r}$-free case with $r\geq 2$ was disproven by Czabarka, Singgih, and Székely [CSS21], who constructed arbitrarily large connected graphs on $n$ vertices containing no $K_{2r}$, with minimum degree $d$ and diameter $\frac{6r-5}{(2r-1)d+2r-3}n+O(1)$, contradicting the conjecture for each fixed $r$ as $d\to\infty$. They proposed the amended single-case conjecture that a connected $K_{k+1}$-free graph with minimum degree $d$ has diameter at most $(3-\tfrac{2}{k})\frac{n}{d}+O(1)$; this bound is known under the weaker assumption of $k$-colourability for $k=3$ and $k=4$, shown by Czabarka, Dankelmann, and Székely [CDS09] and Czabarka, Smith, and Székely [CSS23]. Cambie and Jooken [CaJo25] have given an example that shows the diameter for $K_4$-free
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the bound $D\leq(3-\tfrac{2}{k})\frac{n}{d}+O(1)$ for connected $K_{k+1}$-free graphs on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $d$, with the constant $3-\tfrac{2}{k}$ matching the constructions showing sharpness.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolves the correct quantitative trade-off between minimum degree, forbidden clique size, and diameter.

title: Erdős problem #614
open: Let $f(n,k)$ be the minimal number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices such that every set of $k+2$ vertices induces a subgraph of maximum degree at least $k$. What is the exact value, or good bounds, on $f(n,k)$?
status: The problem remains open; it is recorded in the graphs problem collection, with full history maintained at erdosproblems.com/614.
solved_when: The function $f(n,k)$ is determined, or tight asymptotic bounds are established, for general $n$ and $k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution resolves a long-standing question in extremal graph theory.

title: Erdős problem #616
open: Given an $r$-uniform hypergraph ($r\geq 3$) in which every subgraph on at most $3r-3$ vertices has covering number at most $1$, how large can the covering number of the whole hypergraph be? Formally, determine the best possible $t$ such that $\tau(G)\leq t$ for every $r$-uniform hypergraph $G$ with $\tau(G')\leq 1$ for all subgraphs $G'$ on at most $3r-3$ vertices.
status: Erdős, Hajnal, and Tuza [EHT91] proved that the answer satisfies $\frac{3}{16}r+\frac{7}{8}\leq t \leq \frac{1}{5}r$. The problem is tracked at erdosproblems.com/616, with Erdős references [Er99].
solved_when: The exact value of $t$ as a function of $r$ is determined; in particular, the gap between the known bounds $\frac{3}{16}r+\frac{7}{8} \leq t \leq \frac{1}{5}r$ is closed.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/616; resolving it would settle a natural local-to-global question about covering numbers in uniform hypergraphs.

title: Erdős problem #617
open: Must every $r$-colouring of the edges of $K_{r^2+1}$, for $r \geq 3$, contain $r+1$ vertices whose induced $K_{r+1}$ misses at least one colour?
status: This is a conjecture of Erdős and Gyárfás [ErGy99], who proved it for $r=3$ and $r=4$, observed it is false for $r=2$, and showed the property fails for infinitely many $r$ if $r^2+1$ is replaced by $r^2$. The problem is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/617 (Erdős references: [Er99]).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given that for every $r \geq 3$, every $r$-colouring of the edges of $K_{r^2+1}$ contains $r+1$ vertices with at least one colour missing on the induced $K_{r+1}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, asking whether a "balanced" colouring — one where every $K_{r+1}$ uses all $r$ colours — is impossible; a resolution settles a natural extremal question in edge-colourings of complete graphs.

title: Erdős problem #620
open: If $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices without a $K_4$, how large a triangle-free induced subgraph must $G$ contain?
status: The question was first asked by Erdős and Rogers [ErRo62] and is generally known as the Erdős-Rogers problem. It is now known that $f(n)=n^{1/2+o(1)}$. Bollobás and Hind [BoHi91] proved $n^{1/2} \ll f(n) \ll n^{7/10+o(1)}$. Krivelevich [Kr94] improved this to $n^{1/2}(\log\log n)^{1/2} \ll f(n) \ll n^{2/3}(\log n)^{1/3}$. Wolfovitz [Wo13] proved $f(n) \ll n^{1/2}(\log n)^{120}$. The best bounds currently known are $n^{1/2}\frac{(\log n)^{1/2}}{\log\log n}\ll f(n)\ll n^{1/2}\log n$, where the lower bound follows from results of Shearer [Sh95] and the upper bound was proved by Mubayi and Verstraete [MuVe24].
solved_when: The function $f(n)$, defined as the largest integer such that every $K_4$-free graph on $n$ vertices contains a triangle-free induced subgraph on at least $f(n)$ vertices, is determined up to a constant or polylogarithmic factor — ideally resolving whether the truth lies closer to $n^{1/2}$ or $n^{1/2}\log n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/620; a solution would settle a classical Ramsey-type extremal question about how much triangle-freeness is forced inside $K_4$-freeness.

title: Erdős problem #623
open: Let $X$ be a set of cardinality $\aleph_\omega$ and $f$ a function from the finite subsets of $X$ to $X$ with $f(A)\notin A$ for all finite $A$. Must there exist an infinite $Y\subseteq X$ that is independent, meaning $f(B)\notin Y$ for every finite $B\subset Y$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Hajnal [ErHa58], who proved that if $|X|<\aleph_\omega$ then the answer is no. Erdős suggests in [Er99] that this problem is 'perhaps undecidable'.
solved_when: A proof that such an infinite independent $Y\subseteq X$ always exists for $|X|=\aleph_\omega$, or a counterexample showing one need not; equivalently, a resolution of the independence-completeness question at $\aleph_\omega$ given the known negative answer below $\aleph_\omega$.
why: It completes the boundary of the Erdős–Hajnal independence question, determining whether $\aleph_\omega$ is the first cardinal where free sets must exist — with likely connections to independence phenomena in set theory.

title: Erdős problem #624
open: Must every choice function on the subsets of an $n$-point set require essentially more than $\log_2 n$ points in a set $Y$ to cover all $n$ values? Formally, let $H(n)$ be the least $m$ such that there exists $f:\{A:A\subseteq X\}\to X$ with $\{f(A):A\subseteq Y\}=X$ for every $Y\subseteq X$ with $|Y|\geq m$, where $|X|=n$; prove that $H(n)-\log_2 n\to\infty$.
status: A problem of Erdős and Hajnal [ErHa68], who proved $\log_2 n \leq H(n) < \log_2 n + (3+o(1))\log_2\log_2 n$. Erdős said even the weaker statement that for $n=2^k$ we have $H(n)\geq k+1$ is open, but Alon gave a simple proof: by the pigeonhole principle there are $\frac{n-1}{2}$ two-element subsets $A_i$ with the same $f(A_i)$, and any $Y$ of size $k$ containing at least $k/2$ of them has at most $2^k-\lfloor k/2\rfloor+1<2^k=n$ distinct elements in $\bigcup_{A\subseteq Y}\{f(A)\}$. For this weaker statement, Erdős and Gyárfás conjectured the stronger form that if $|X|=2^k$ then, for any $f:\{A:A\subseteq X\}\to X$, there must exist $Y\subset X$ of size $k$ with $\#\{f(A):A\subseteq Y\}<2^k-k^C$ for every $C$ (with $k$ sufficiently large depending on $C$). This was proved by Alon (personal communication) in the stronger form that there exists an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, for $k$ large enough, some $Y\subset X$ of size $k$ has $\#\{f(A):A\subseteq Y\}<(1-c)2^k$. Alon also proved that, provided $k$ is large enough, if $|X|=2^{ The record as given is truncated at this point.
solved_when: It is proved that $H(n)-\log_2 n\to\infty$, showing the answer to the covering threshold differs from $\log_2 n$ by an unbounded amount.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles the sharp order of the covering threshold for arbitrary choice functions.

title: Erdős problem #626
open: Does the maximal girth of an $n$-vertex graph with chromatic number $k \geq 4$ grow linearly in $\log n$ — that is, does $\lim_{n\to\infty} g_k(n)/\log n$ exist? Equivalently, does $\lim_{n\to\infty} \log h^{(m)}(n)/\log n$ exist for the maximal chromatic number $h^{(m)}(n)$ of an $n$-vertex graph of girth $>m$, and what is its value?
status: It is known that $\frac{1}{4\log k}\log n \leq g_k(n) \leq \frac{2}{\log(k-2)}\log n + 1$, the lower bound due to Kostochka [Ko88] and the upper bound to Erdős [Er59b]. Erdős [Er59b] proved that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\log h^{(m)}(n)}{\log n} \gg \frac{1}{m}$ and, for odd $m$, that the limit is at most $\frac{2}{m+1}$, and conjectured this is sharp. He had no good guess for the value of the limit for even $m$, other than that it should lie in $[\frac{2}{m+2}, \frac{2}{m}]$, but could not prove this even for $m=4$. See also the entry in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: The existence (or non-existence) of $\lim_{n\to\infty} g_k(n)/\log n$ is settled for $k \geq 4$, or of $\lim_{n\to\infty} \log h^{(m)}(n)/\log n$ for general $m$, together with the value of the limit when it exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it asks for the fundamental relationship between chromatic number and girth in finite graphs.
aliases: Erdős #626; graph theory / chromatic number / cycles

title: Erdős problem #627
open: Let $f(n)$ be the largest ratio $\chi(G)/\omega(G)$ attained by an $n$-vertex graph $G$, where $\chi$ is the chromatic number and $\omega$ the clique number. Does the limit $\lim_{n\to\infty} f(n)/(n/(\log_2 n)^2)$ exist?
status: Tutte and Zykov [Zy52] independently proved that for every $k$ there is a graph with $\omega(G)=2$ and $\chi(G)=k$. Erdős [Er61d] proved that for every $n$ there is a graph on $n$ vertices with $\omega(G)=2$ and $\chi(G)\gg n^{1/2}/\log n$, whence $f(n) \gg n^{1/2}/\log n$. Erdős [Er67c] proved that $f(n) \asymp \frac{n}{(\log_2 n)^2}$ and that the limit in question, if it exists, must lie in $[1/4,4]$ (he states the upper bound as $1$, but [AFM25] note the method actually gives $4$). Araujo, Filipe, and Miyazaki [AFM25] prove that if $\lim \frac{\log R(k)}{k}$ exists and equals $C$ (see [77]), and also $R(s,t)\leq R(k)$ for all $st\leq k^2$, then the limit in this question also exists and equals $C^2$; using this connection they improve the upper bound from $4$ to $\approx 3.7$. See also the entry in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: The existence (or non-existence) of $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{f(n)}{n/(\log_2 n)^2}$ is settled; if it exists, its value is determined (known to lie in $[1/4, 4]$, improved to $\approx 3.7$ as an upper bound).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it calibrates how far apart chromatic and clique numbers can be on $n$ vertices.

title: Erdős problem #628
open: If a graph with chromatic number $k$ contains no $K_k$, and $a,b\geq 2$ with $a+b=k+1$, must it contain two disjoint subgraphs with chromatic numbers at least $a$ and at least $b$ respectively?
status: The property is sometimes called being $(a,b)$-splittable, and the question is often called the Erdős–Lovász Tihany conjecture. Erdős [Er68b] originally asked about $a=b=3$, which was proved by Brown and Jung [BrJu69], who in fact prove that $G$ must contain two vertex disjoint odd cycles. Balogh, Kostochka, Prince, and Stiebitz [BKPS09] proved the full conjecture for quasi-line graphs and graphs with independence number $2$. Further partial results are covered in Song's comprehensive survey [So22]; see also the entry in the graphs problem collection (erdosproblems.com/628).
solved_when: For every such graph $G$ and every $a,b\geq 2$ with $a+b=k+1$, the two disjoint subgraphs of the stated chromatic numbers are shown to exist.
why: This is the Erdős–Lovász Tihany conjecture, one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a proof would settle a long-standing structural question about how chromatic number is distributed across $K_k$-free graphs.

title: Erdős problem #629
open: What is the smallest bipartite graph whose list chromatic number exceeds $k$? Formally, determine $n(k)$, the minimal number of vertices of a bipartite graph $G$ with $\chi_L(G)>k$.
status: A problem of Erdős, Rubin, and Taylor [ERT80], who proved $2^{k-1}<n(k)<k^22^{k+2}$, and also showed that if $m(k)$ is the size of the smallest family of $k$-sets without property B (the smallest number of $k$-sets in a graph with chromatic number $3$), then $m(k)\leq n(k)\leq m(k+1)$; bounds on $m(k)$ are the subject of [901]. The lower bounds on $m(k)$ by Radhakrishnan and Srinivasan [RaSr00] imply $2^k \left(\frac{k}{\log k}\right)^{1/2}\ll n(k)$. Erdős, Rubin, and Taylor [ERT80] proved $n(2)=6$, and Hanson, MacGillivray, and Toft [HMT96] proved $n(3)=14$ and $n(k)\leq kn(k-2)+2^k$. See also the entry in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: An exact formula for $n(k)$ is determined (or asymptotically tight bounds closing the exponential gap), with the known exact values $n(2)=6$ and $n(3)=14$ matched by the general theory.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and a solution would settle a fundamental question about how small a bipartite graph can be while forcing list-chromatic number above any given threshold; the problem is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #634
open: Which integers $n$ have the property that some triangle can be dissected into exactly $n$ congruent triangles? Equivalently, determine the set of $n$ for which there exists a triangle cutting into $n$ mutually congruent pieces.
status: Erdős's question was reported by Soifer [So09c]. It is easy to see that all square numbers have this property (in fact for square numbers any triangle will do), and Soifer [So09c] showed that numbers of the form $2n^2, 3n^2, 6n^2, n^2+m^2$ also have it. Beeson has shown that $7$ and $11$ do not have this property; it is possible that no prime of the form $4n+3$ has it, and in particular it is unknown whether $19$ congruent triangles can be assembled into a triangle. Soifer proved [So09] that under relaxation of congruence to similarity, every triangle can be cut into $N$ similar triangles when $N\neq 2,3,5$; and if the smaller triangles are required to be similar to the larger one, the only possible values of $N$ are $n^2, n^2+m^2, 3n^2$, as proved by Snover, Waiveris, and Williams [SWW91]. Zhang [Zh25], among other results, has proved that for any integers $a \geq b$.
solved_when: A complete characterization of the integers $n$ admitting a dissection of some triangle into $n$ congruent triangles is given — in particular, resolving whether $19$ (and generally primes of the form $4n+3$ such as $7$ and $11$) has the property.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a $25 prize, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a characterization would settle a natural question at the interface of combinatorics and Euclidean geometry.

title: Erdős problem #635
open: Let $t\geq 1$ and $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be such that whenever $a,b\in A$ with $b-a\geq t$ we have $b-a\nmid b$. How large can $\lvert A\rvert$ be? Is it true that\[\lvert A\rvert \leq \left(\frac{1}{2}+o_t(1)\right)N?\]
status: Asked by Erdős in a letter to Ruzsa in around 1980. Erdős observed that when $t=1$ the maximum is $\lvert A\rvert=\lfloor(N+1)/2\rfloor$, achieved by the odd numbers. When $t=2$ he observed there exists such an $A$ with $\lvert A\rvert \geq \frac{N}{2}+c\log N$ for some constant $c>0$, namely the odd numbers together with numbers of the shape $2^k$ for $k$ odd. The second question has been resolved in the affirmative by ChatGPT-5.2 (prompted by Leeham); Tao has since observed that a positive answer also follows fairly quickly from an inequality due to Elliott [El79].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every fixed $t\geq 1$ any $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ satisfying the divisibility condition above has $\lvert A\rvert \leq \left(\frac{1}{2}+o_t(1)\right)N$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, posed in a letter to Ruzsa around 1980, and is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle the exact asymptotic density of such divisor-avoiding sets.

title: Erdős problem #638
open: If a family $S$ of finite graphs has, for every $n$, some member $G_n$ whose every $n$-colouring of the edges yields a monochromatic triangle, must there exist, for every infinite cardinal $\aleph$, a graph $G$ all of whose finite subgraphs lie in $S$ and whose every $\aleph$-colouring of the edges yields a monochromatic triangle?
status: Erdős writes 'if the answer is affirmative many extensions and generalisations will be possible'. Barreto notes in the comments that (as is often the case with problems of this kind) presumably $S$ is intended to also be closed under taking subgraphs, or else a sparse family of complete graphs gives a trivial counterexample.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the statement above, for every family $S$ (presumably closed under taking subgraphs) and every infinite cardinal $\aleph$.

title: Erdős problem #640
open: For each $k\geq 3$, is there a function $f(k)$ such that every graph of chromatic number at least $f(k)$ must contain an odd cycle whose vertices span a subgraph of chromatic number at least $k$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Hajnal. It is trivial when $k=3$, since any non-bipartite graph contains an odd cycle, and all odd cycles have chromatic number $3$. Steiner has observed in the comments that the problem is equivalent to the variant in which 'odd cycle' is replaced with 'path'. Key works: erdosproblems.com/640; Erdős references: [Er97d,p.84].
solved_when: For every $k\geq 3$, an explicit or existence-proof bound $f(k)$ is established such that $\chi(G)\geq f(k)$ forces an odd cycle in $G$ spanning a subgraph of chromatic number at least $k$.

title: Erdős problem #642
open: Let $f(n)$ be the maximum number of edges in a graph on $n$ vertices in which every cycle has more vertices than chords. Is $f(n)$ bounded by a constant times $n$?
status: A problem of Hamburger and Szegedy, where a chord is an edge between two vertices of a cycle that are not consecutive on it. Chen, Erdős, and Staton [CES96] proved $f(n) \ll n^{3/2}$. Draganić, Methuku, Munhá Correia, and Sudakov [DMMS24] improved this to $f(n) \ll n(\log n)^8$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the bound $f(n) \ll n$; equivalently, determining whether $f(n)$ is linear in $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it settles a natural extremal question about cycle–chord structure in graphs.

title: Erdős problem #643
open: How many edges force a $t$-uniform hypergraph to contain two disjoint pairs of edges with the same union? Formally, let $f(n;t)$ be the minimal number of edges such that every $t$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices with at least $f(n;t)$ edges contains four edges $A,B,C,D$ with $A\cup B=C\cup D$ and $A\cap B=C\cap D=\emptyset$; estimate $f(n;t)$, and in particular decide whether $f(n;t)=(1+o(1))\binom{n}{t-1}$ for $t\geq 3$.
status: For $t=2$ the problem asks for the maximal number of edges in a $C_4$-free graph, so $f(n;2)=(1/2+o(1))n^{3/2}$. Füredi [Fu84] proved $f(n;3)\ll n^2$ and $f(n;3)>\binom{n}{2}$ for infinitely many $n$. Pikhurko and Verstraëte [PiVe09] proved $f(n;3)\leq \frac{13}{9}\binom{n}{2}$ for all $n$. More generally, Füredi [Fu84] proved $\binom{n-1}{t-1}+\lfloor\frac{n-1}{t}\rfloor\leq f(n;t)<\frac{7}{2}\binom{n}{t-1}$ and conjectured the lower bound is sharp for $t\geq 4$. Pikhurko and Verstraëte [PiVe09] proved $1\leq \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(n;t)}{\binom{n}{t-1}}\leq \min\left(\frac{7}{4},1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}\right)$ for all $t\geq 3$. Füredi [Fu84] proved that $f(n;3)/\binom{n}{2}$ converges as $n\to\infty$, but the existence of the limit for $t\geq 4$ is unknown.
solved_when: The order of magnitude and asymptotics of $f(n;t)$ are determined — ideally proving or refuting $f(n;t)=(1+o(1))\binom{n}{t-1}$ for $t\geq 3$, or at minimum establishing the existence (and value) of $\lim_{n\to\infty} f(n;t)/\binom{n}{t-1}$ for all $t\geq 3$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com); resolving it would settle a basic extremal question about how much union-structure can be avoided in uniform hypergraphs, extending the classical $C_4$-free extremal problem to higher uniformity.

title: Erdős problem #644
open: Let $f(k,r)$ be the smallest integer such that whenever $A_1,A_2,\ldots$ is a family of $k$-element sets with the property that every $r$ of the $A_i$'s share a common pair $\{x,y\}$, some single set of size $f(k,r)$ intersects every $A_i$. Is it true that $f(k,7)=(1+o(1))\frac{3}{4}k$, and more generally that for any $r\geq 3$ there exists a constant $c_r$ such that $f(k,r)=(1+o(1))c_rk$?
status: A problem of Erdős, Fon-Der-Flaass, Kostochka, and Tuza [EFKT92], who proved that $f(k,3)=2k$, $f(k,4)=\lfloor 3k/2\rfloor$, $f(k,5)=\lfloor 5k/4\rfloor$, and further that $f(k,6)=k$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/644; Erdős references: [Er97d].
solved_when: The asymptotics of $f(k,7)$ are determined, in particular confirming or refuting $f(k,7)=(1+o(1))\frac{3}{4}k$; and, for the general question, that for each $r\geq 3$ a constant $c_r$ is shown to exist with $f(k,r)=(1+o(1))c_rk$ (or a counterexample is given).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would settle the asymptotic behavior of a basic extremal piercing function for set systems.

title: Erdős problem #647
open: Does there exist an integer $n>24$ for which every smaller $m$ satisfies $m+\tau(m)\leq n+2$, where $\tau(m)$ counts the divisors of $m$? Formally: is there some $n>24$ such that $\max_{m<n}(m+\tau(m))\leq n+2$?
status: This is a problem of Erdős and Selfridge. The inequality holds for $n=24$, and the bound $n+2$ is best possible since $\max(\tau(n-1)+n-1,\tau(n-2)+n-2)\geq n+2$. In [Er79] Erdős said 'it is extremely doubtful' that there are infinitely many such $n$, and in fact suggested that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\max_{m<n}(\tau(m)+m-n)=\infty$. In [Er79d] Erdős said it 'seems certain' that for every $k$ there are infinitely many $n$ for which $\max_{n-k<m<n}(m+\tau(m))\leq n+2$, but 'this is hopeless with our present methods', although it follows from Schinzel's Hypothesis H. In [Er92e] Erdős offered £25 (converted to \$44 using approximate 1992 exchange rates) for an example of such an $n>24$, writing 'I am being rather stingy but we old people are stingy.' Tao has observed in the comments that, since $\tau(m)$ is similar to $2^{\omega(m)}$, this problem is similar to (but slightly weaker than) the first part of [679], but much stronger than [413] or [248]. See also [413].
solved_when: An explicit integer $n>24$ with $\max_{m<n}(m+\tau(m))\leq n+2$ is exhibited (this would claim Erdős's £25, i.e. \$44, prize), or a proof that no such $n$ exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, offered with a cash prize in [Er92e] and tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a long-standing question about how large $m+\tau(m)$ can get relative to a nearby integer.

title: Erdős problem #653
open: Given $n$ points in the plane, order them by the number of distinct distances from each point to the others, $R(x_1)\leq\cdots\leq R(x_n)$, and let $g(n)$ be the maximum number of distinct values these counts can take. Is it true that $g(n) \geq (1-o(1))n$?
status: Erdős and Fishburn proved $g(n)>\frac{3}{8}n$ and Csizmadia improved this to $g(n)>\frac{7}{10}n$. Both groups also proved the upper bound $g(n) < n-cn^{2/3}$ for some constant $c>0$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $g(n)\ge(1-o(1))n$, i.e. that the number of distinct values among the $R(x_i)$ is asymptotically $n$.

title: Erdős problem #654
open: If $n$ points in the plane have no four on a circle, must some point determine a nearly linear number of distinct distances to the others? Formally, letting $f(n)$ be the largest value such that every such configuration contains a point with at least $f(n)$ distinct distances to the other points, is $f(n) > (1-o(1))n$, or at least $f(n) > (1/3+c)n$ for some constant $c>0$ and all large $n$?
status: It is trivial that $f(n) \geq (n-1)/3$. In [Er97e] Erdős asks whether $f(n)>(1-o(1))n$, but says this is 'perhaps too optimistic but I am sure that [the trivial bound] can be significantly improved'. In [Er87b] and [ErPa90] Erdős and Pach ask this under the additional assumption that there are no three points on a line (so that the points are in general position), although they only ask the weaker question whether there is a lower bound of the shape $(\tfrac{1}{3}+c)n$ for some constant $c>0$. They suggest the lower bound $(1-o(1))n$ is true under the assumption that any circle around a point $x_i$ contains at most $2$ other $x_j$. The strongest form of this conjecture was disproved by Aletheia [Fe26], which constructed a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, no four on a circle, such that there are at most $\frac{3}{4}n$ distinct distances from any single point (although this construction has all the points on the union of two lines, so does not help with the stronger version with the points in general position).
solved_when: A bound $f(n) > (1/3+c)n$ for some absolute $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$ is proved (or refuted); the stronger conjecture $f(n) > (1-o(1))n$ remains the ambitious target, with the general-position variants (no three on a line) as further cases.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems with a full tracked history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a long-standing question about how forbidding four concyclic points forces distance diversity.

title: Erdős problem #655
open: If $n$ points in the plane, in suitable general position (e.g. no three on a line and no four on a circle), are such that no circle centered at one of the points contains three other points, must the point set determine strictly more than $n/2$ distinct distances? Formally, are there at least $(1+c)\frac{n}{2}$ distinct distances for some constant $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$?
status: This is a problem of Erdős and Pach. It is easy to see that the assumption implies at least $\frac{n-1}{2}$ distinct distances from every point. Zach Hunter observed that taking $n$ equally spaced points on a circle disproves the conjecture as stated; presumably some general-position assumption (e.g. no three on a line and no four on a circle), in the spirit of related conjectures of Erdős and others, was intended.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, under an appropriate general-position assumption added to the stated circle condition, the number of distinct distances is at least $(1+c)\frac{n}{2}$ for some constant $c>0$ and all $n$ sufficiently large; or an explicit construction showing no such $c$ exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would clarify how local center-based incidence conditions force global distance diversity in planar point sets.

title: Erdős problem #657
open: If a set $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ of $n$ points has no isosceles triangles — every $3$ points determine $3$ distinct distances — must $A$ determine at least $f(n)n$ distinct distances for some $f(n)\to\infty$?
status: In [Er73] Erdős attributes this problem (more generally in $\mathbb{R}^k$) to himself and Davies; in [Er97e] he does not mention Davis, but says it was investigated by himself, Füredi, Ruzsa, and Pach. In [Er73] Erdős says it is not even known in $\mathbb{R}$ whether $f(n)\to\infty$. Sarosh Adenwalla observed this is equivalent to minimising the number of distinct differences in a set $A\subset\mathbb{R}$ of size $n$ without three-term arithmetic progressions. Dumitrescu [Du08] proved that, in these terms, $(\log n)^c \leq f(n) \leq 2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$ for some constant $c>0$. Hunter observed in the comments that a result of Ruzsa coupled with standard tools of additive combinatorics (with details given by Alfaiz and Tang) and recent progress on the size of subsets without three-term arithmetic progressions (see [BlSi23], which improves slightly on the bounds due to Kelley and Meka [KeMe23]) yield $2^{c(\log n)^{1/9}}\leq f(n)$ for some constant $c>0$. Straus has observed that if $2^k\geq n$ then there exist $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^k$ containing no isosceles triangle and determining at most $n-1$ distances. See also [135].
solved_when: One proves that any such set of $n$ points determines at least $f(n)n$ distinct distances for some function $f(n)\to\infty$, or exhibits a construction where this fails.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a basic question about how much the absence of isosceles triangles forces distance diversity.

title: Erdős problem #660
open: Must the vertices of a convex polyhedron with $n$ vertices in $\mathbb{R}^3$ determine $(1-o(1))\frac{n}{2}$ distinct pairwise distances?
status: For the analogous planar problem in $\mathbb{R}^2$, there are always at least $n/2$ distinct distances, as proved by Altman [Al63] (see [93]). In [Er75f], Erdős claims that Altman proved the vertices determine $\gg n$ distinct distances, but gives no reference.
