solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that any $n$ vertices of a convex polyhedron in $\mathbb{R}^3$ determine at least $(1-o(1))\frac{n}{2}$ distinct distances.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would complete a basic extremal geometry question about distance sets in three dimensions.

title: Erdős problem #661
open: For all large $n$, can one find points $x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_n\in \mathbb{R}^2$ such that the number of distinct distances $d(x_i,y_j)$ is $o\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right)$?
status: The analogous question can be asked for points in $\mathbb{R}^3$. In $\mathbb{R}^4$, Lenz observed that taking the points on two orthogonal circles gives $x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_n\in \mathbb{R}^4$ with $d(x_i,y_j)=1$ for all $i,j$. A related general question: if $F(2n)$ is the minimal number of such distances and $f(2n)$ is the minimal number of distinct distances between any $2n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, is $F = o(f)$? See also [89]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/661; Erdős references: [Er92e] [Er97e] [Er97f].
solved_when: An explicit construction (for all large $n$) of two $n$-point sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose bipartite distinct-distance count $d(x_i,y_j)$ is $o(n/\sqrt{\log n})$, or a proof that no such construction exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying his $50 prize and tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve a natural bipartite variant of his distinct distances problem.

title: Erdős problem #662
open: Among $n$ points in the plane with all pairwise distances at least $1$, is the number of distances at most $t$ bounded above by $f(t)$, the corresponding count for the triangular lattice (e.g. $f(1)=6$, $f(\sqrt{3})=12$, $f(3)=18$), once $n$ is large enough in terms of $t$ — with equality perhaps attained only by the triangular lattice? In particular, must the number of distances $\leq \sqrt{3}-\epsilon$ be less than $1$?
status: A problem of Erdős, Lovász, and Vesztergombi, stated essentially verbatim in [Er97e,p.532], but as written it does not make sense and must contain at least one typo; suggestions about the intended formulation are welcome. Erdős further proposed a stronger conjecture: letting $t_1<t_2<\cdots$ be the distances occurring in the triangular lattice ($t_1=1$, $t_2=\sqrt{3}$, $t_3=3$, $t_4=5$, etc.), that there is an $\epsilon_n$ so that for every set $y_1,\ldots,$ with $d(y_i,y_j)\geq 1$ the number of distances $d(y_i,y_j)<t_n$ is less than $f(t_n)$ — which is also nonsense interpreted literally, and Erdős's intent is unclear.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for $n$ sufficiently large depending on $t$, any set $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $d(x_i,x_j)\geq 1$ has at most $f(t)$ distances $\leq t$, with equality only for the triangular lattice; including the special case that the number of distances $\leq \sqrt{3}-\epsilon$ is less than $1$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would settle the extremal behavior of short-distance counts among separated point sets, where the triangular lattice plays the conjectured extremal role.

title: Erdős problem #663
open: For fixed $k\geq 2$, let $q(n,k)$ be the least prime not dividing $\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)$. Is $q(n,k)<(1+o(1))\log n$ once $n$ is sufficiently large?
status: A problem of Erdős and Pomerance. The bound $q(n,k)<(1+o(1))k\log n$ is easy. It may be true that the improved bound holds even up to $k=o(\log n)$. A heuristic argument in favour of this is provided by Tao in the comments. See also [457].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, for each fixed $k\geq 2$, $q(n,k)<(1+o(1))\log n$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a natural question about prime divisors of short intervals of consecutive integers.

title: Erdős problem #665
open: Does every large point set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ admit a pairwise balanced design — a collection of sets $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $2\leq |A_i|<n$ such that every pair of distinct elements lies in exactly one $A_i$ — all of whose blocks satisfy $|A_i| > n^{1/2}-C$ for some absolute constant $C>0$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Larson [ErLa82]. Erdős asks in [ErLa82] and [Er97f, p.3] for the slowest growing function $h$ such that, for all large $n$, a pairwise balanced design exists with $|A_i|>n^{1/2}-h(n)$ for all blocks; the problem above asks whether $h(n)\ll 1$. Erdős and Larson prove $h(n)\ll n^{1/2-c}$ for some constant $c>0$, and note this improves to $h(n)\ll (\log n)^2$ assuming Cramér-type bounds on gaps between consecutive primes. Shrikhande and Singhi [ShSi85] proved the answer is no conditional on the conjecture that the order of every projective plane is a prime power, by showing that every pairwise balanced design on $n$ points with all blocks of size $\geq n^{1/2}-c$ embeds in a projective plane of order $n+i$ for some $i\leq c+2$ when $n$ is sufficiently large (see [723]). In general, if $H(n)$ is the largest prime gap $\leq n$, then assuming the prime power conjecture the above results show $H(n)\asymp h(n)$.
solved_when: For some constant $C>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, a pairwise balanced design on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ is constructed with $|A_i| > n^{1/2}-C$ for every $1\leq i\leq m$; equivalently, the slowest growing admissible $h$ in the requirement $|A_i|>n^{1/2}-h(n)$ satisfies $h(n)\ll 1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling whether the block-size deficit from $\sqrt n$ must grow resolves the general question of how close to projective-plane-like uniformity such designs can be forced.

title: Erdős problem #667
open: Let $p,q\geq 1$ be fixed integers. We define $H(n)=H(N;p,q)$ to be the largest $m$ such that any graph on $n$ vertices where every set of $p$ vertices spans at least $q$ edges must contain a complete graph on $m$ vertices. Is\[c(p,q)=\liminf \frac{\log H(n)}{\log n}\]a strictly increasing function of $q$ for $1\leq q\leq \binom{p-1}{2}+1$?
status: A problem of Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp. When $q=1$ this corresponds exactly to the classical Ramsey problem, and hence for example $\frac{1}{p-1}\leq c(p,1)\leq \frac{2}{p+1}$. It is easy to see that if $q=\binom{p-1}{2}+1$ then $c(p,q)=1$. Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp have shown that $c(p,\binom{p-1}{2})\leq 1/2$.
solved_when: The function $c(p,q)=\liminf \frac{\log H(n)}{\log n}$ is proved (or disproproved) to be strictly increasing in $q$ over the range $1\leq q\leq \binom{p-1}{2}+1$ for fixed integers $p,q\geq 1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would clarify how local density conditions on $p$-sets force clique growth, generalizing the classical Ramsey problem.

title: Erdős problem #668
open: Is the number of incongruent configurations of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ that maximize the number of unit distances unbounded as $n\to\infty$? More sharply, is it always greater than $1$ for $n>3$?
status: The count is in fact $=1$ also for $n=4$, the unique example being two equilateral triangles joined by an edge. Computational evidence of Engel, Hammond-Lee, Su, Varga, and Zsámboki [EHSVZ25] and Alexeev, Mixon, and Parshall [AMP25] suggests the count is $=1$ for various other $5\leq n\leq 21$, although these calculations checked only up to graph isomorphism rather than congruency. The actual maximal number of unit distances is the subject of [90].
solved_when: It is proved that the number of incongruent maximizing configurations of $n$ points tends to infinity as $n\to\infty$ (or, at minimum, that it exceeds $1$ for every $n>3$).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would clarify the structure of extremal unit-distance configurations, a central theme of the Erdős unit distance problem.

title: Erdős problem #669
open: How many distinct lines can be forced through $k$ or more of $n$ points in the plane? Formally, with $F_k(n)$ the maximum number of lines containing at least $k$ of the points and $f_k(n)$ the maximum number of lines containing exactly $k$ of them, determine $\lim F_k(n)/n^2$ and $\lim f_k(n)/n^2$.
status: Trivially $f_k(n)\leq F_k(n)$ and $f_2(n)=F_2(n)=\binom{n}{2}$. The case $k=3$ is the classical 'Orchard problem' of Sylvester: Burr, Grünbaum, and Sloane [BGS74] proved $f_3(n)=\frac{n^2}{6}-O(n)$ and $F_3(n)=\frac{n^2}{6}-O(n)$. A trivial counting bound gives $F_k(n) \leq \binom{n}{2}/\binom{k}{2}$, hence $\lim F_k(n)/n^2 \leq \frac{1}{k(k-1)}$. See also [101].
solved_when: The limits $\lim F_k(n)/n^2$ and $\lim f_k(n)/n^2$ are determined (in particular settling the estimates of $f_k(n)$ and $F_k(n)$ up to $O(n)$ error terms, as the $k=3$ case achieves).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full solution history tracked at erdosproblems.com; determining the limits resolves a quantitative extremal question in combinatorial geometry that generalizes the classical Orchard problem.

title: Erdős problem #671
open: Does there exist a sequence of interpolation nodes $a_i^n \in [-1,1]$ (with the $p_i^n$ the associated Lagrange basis polynomials) and a point $x\in[-1,1]$ where the Lebesgue-type sum $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sum_{1\le i\le n}|p_i^n(x)|=\infty$, and yet the Lagrange interpolation polynomials $\mathcal{L}^n f$ converge to $f(x)$ for every continuous $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}$? More strongly, can this divergence of the sum hold at *every* $x\in[-1,1]$ while $\mathcal{L}^n f \to f$ pointwise for every continuous $f$?
status: Bernstein [Be31] proved that for any choice of nodes $a_i^n$ there exists $x_0\in[-1,1]$ such that $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sum_{1\le i\le n}|p_i^n(x_0)|=\infty$. Erdős and Vértesi [ErVe80] proved that for any choice of $a_i^n$ there exists a continuous $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $\limsup_{n\to\infty}|\mathcal{L}^n f(x)|=\infty$ for almost all $x\in[-1,1]$. Tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/671; Erdős references: [Er82e] [Er97f] [Va99,2.40] [Be31].
solved_when: An explicit sequence of nodes $a_i^n\in[-1,1]$ is produced for which, for every continuous $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb{R}$, the interpolants $\mathcal{L}^n f$ converge pointwise to $f$ on $[-1,1]$, despite $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sum_{1\le i\le n}|p_i^n(x)|=\infty$ at some $x$ (or at every $x$, for the stronger form); or a proof that no such sequence exists.
why: It probes the exact relationship between the growth of the Lebesgue-type sums and pointwise convergence of Lagrange interpolation — whether unbounded interpolation "constants" necessarily destroy convergence for some continuous function. A $250 prize (Erdős) is attached.

title: Erdős problem #672
open: Can the product of the terms of an arithmetic progression $n, n+d, \ldots, n+(k-1)d$ of positive integers of length $k\geq 4$, with $(n,d)=1$, be a perfect power? In other words, does there exist such a progression whose product equals an $\ell$th power for some $\ell\geq 2$?
status: Erdős believed the answer is no. Erdős and Selfridge [ErSe75] proved that the product of consecutive integers is never a perfect power. The theory of Pell equations implies that there are infinitely many pairs $n,d$ with $(n,d)=1$ such that $n(n+d)(n+2d)$ is a square. For the question of whether the product of an arithmetic progression of length $k$ can equal an $\ell$th power: Euler proved this is impossible when $k=4$ and $\ell=2$, and Obláth [Ob51] proved impossibility for $(k,\ell)=(5,2),(3,3),(3,4),(3,5)$. Marszalek [Ma85] showed it is possible only for $k\ll_d 1$, where $d$ is the common difference. Györy, Hajdu, and Saradha [GHS04] proved impossibility for $4\leq k\leq 5$; Bennett, Bruin, Györy, and Hajdu [BBGH06] extended this to $4\leq k\leq 11$, and also proved impossibility for $k$ sufficiently large depending only on the number of prime divisors of $d$; Györy, Hajdu, and Pintér [GHP09] proved impossibility for $4\leq k\leq 34$; and Bennett and Siksek [BeSi20] proved impossibility for all $k$ sufficiently large and $\ell > e^{10^k}$ prime. Jakob Führer has observed this is possible for intege
solved_when: A proof that for all $k\geq 4$ and all $(n,d)=1$, the product $n(n+d)\cdots(n+(k-1)d)$ is never a perfect power (or an explicit example where it is).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, extending his celebrated theorem with Selfridge to arithmetic progressions, and its resolution would settle a natural generalization of one of the most classical Diophantine questions about perfect powers.

title: Erdős problem #675
open: Does the set of sums of two squares have the translation property — that is, for every $n$, is there a shift $t_n \geq 1$ such that membership in $A$ is unchanged for all $1 \leq a \leq n$ upon adding $t_n$? More broadly: if the primes are split into two parts $P \sqcup Q$, each containing $\gg x/\log x$ primes up to $x$ for all large $x$, can the set of integers divisible only by primes from $P$ have the translation property; and for the set of squarefree numbers, how fast must the minimal $t_n$ grow — is it true that $t_n > \exp(n^c)$ for some constant $c > 0$?
status: Elementary sieve theory implies that the set of squarefree numbers has the translation property. More generally, Brun's sieve proves that if $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a set of pairwise coprime integers with $\sum_{b<x}\frac{1}{b}=o(\log\log x)$, then $A=\{ n: b\nmid n \textrm{ for all } b\in B \}$ has the translation property. Erdős did not know what happens if the condition on $\sum_{b<x}\frac{1}{b}$ is weakened or dropped altogether.
solved_when: The translation property is established or refuted for the set of sums of two squares and for the $P$-smooth-type sets arising from the prime partition described above; and for the squarefree numbers, the growth of the minimal $t_n$ is determined, in particular whether $t_n > \exp(n^c)$ for some constant $c > 0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it probes how far elementary sieve methods reach before failing: Erdős himself did not know what happens when the coprimality/reciprocal-sum hypothesis is weakened or dropped.

title: Erdős problem #676
open: Is every sufficiently large integer representable as $ap^2+b$ with $p$ prime, $a\geq 1$ an integer, and $0\leq b<p$? A sharpened variant asks for the minimal $c_n$ such that $n=ap^2+b$ with $0\leq b<c_np$ for some $p\leq\sqrt{n}$: is $c_n\leq 1$ eventually, or even $c_n<n^{o(1)}$?
status: In number theory, the sieve of Eratosthenes implies almost all integers are of this form, and the Brun–Selberg sieve gives $\ll x/(\log x)^c$ exceptions in $[1,x]$ for some constant $c>0$. Erdős [Er79] believed it "rather unlikely" that all large integers are of this form. If the condition that $p$ is prime is dropped, Selfridge and Wagstaff made a "preliminary computer search" and suggested infinitely many $n$ are not of this form even then; it "should be true" that the exceptions in $[1,x]$ number $<x^c$ for some $c<1$. Erdős also posed the general question of sufficient conditions on $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ and $f:A\to\mathbb{N}$ guaranteeing every (or almost every) large number equals $am^2+b$ with $m\in A$, $a\geq 1$, $0\leq b<f(m)$, and the $c_n$ variant, where in [Er79d] he suggests $\limsup c_n=\infty$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/676; [Er79], [Er79d], [Er80,p.107].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every sufficiently large integer $n$ admits a representation $n=ap^2+b$ with $p$ prime, $a\geq 1$, and $0\leq b<p$; quantitative targets from the record include whether the number of exceptions in $[1,x]$ is $<x^c$ for some $c<1$, and whether $\limsup c_n=\infty$ (as Erdős suggests in [Er79d]) versus $c_n\leq 1$ eventually or $c_n<n^{o(1)}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, and it opens a general framework asking which sets $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ and functions $f:A\to\mathbb{N}$ guarantee that all (or almost all) large numbers are of the form $am^2+b$ with $m\in A$, $a\geq 1$, $0\leq b<f(m)$.

title: Erdős problem #677
open: Can two disjoint blocks of the same length have the same least common multiple — that is, must $M(n,k)=\mathrm{lcm}\{n+1,\ldots,n+k\}$ differ from $M(m,k)$ whenever $m\geq n+k$?
status: The Thue-Siegel theorem implies that for fixed $k$ there are only finitely many pairs $m,n$ with $m\geq n+k$ and $M(n,k)=M(m,k)$. The only solutions Erdős knew were $M(4,3)=M(13,2)$ and $M(3,4)=M(19,2)$. In [Er79d] Erdős conjectures the stronger fact that, aside from finitely many exceptions, if $k>2$ and $m\geq n+k$ then $\prod_{i\leq k}(n+i)$ and $\prod_{i\leq k}(m+i)$ cannot have the same set of prime factors. The problem is discussed as B35 in Guy's collection [Gu04]; see also [678], [686], and [850].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $M(n,k)\neq M(m,k)$ for all $m\geq n+k$; any such answer should also address the more general count of solutions to $M(n,k)=M(m,l)$ with $m\geq n+k$ and $l>1$, which Erdős expected to be very few and none when $l\geq k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history maintained at erdosproblems.com, and a clean answer would settle a basic question about how lcms of consecutive integers encode their location.

title: Erdős problem #679
open: Are there infinitely many integers $n$ such that $n-k$ is unusually poor in prime factors for every $k<n$, in the sense that $\omega(n-k) < (1+\epsilon)\frac{\log k}{\log\log k}$ holds for all sufficiently large $k<n$ (with the threshold depending only on $\epsilon$)? And is the stronger bound $\omega(n-k) < \frac{\log k}{\log\log k}+O(1)$ in fact false?
status: One can ask similar questions for $\Omega$, the number of prime factors with multiplicity, where $\log k/\log\log k$ is replaced by $\log_2 k$. In the comments DottedCalculator has disproved the stronger version, proving that in fact for all large $n$ there exists $k<n$ such that $\omega(n-k)\geq \frac{\log k}{\log\log k} + c\frac{\log k}{(\log\log k)^2}$ for some constant $c>0$. Lau [La26] has proved that there exists a constant $C>0$ such that, for infinitely many $n$, $\omega(n-k) \leq \Omega(n-k)\leq C\log k$ for all $1<k<n$. Lau conjectures that, for $\omega$, this can only be improved in the constant factor, and thus the original question has a negative answer. See also [248], [413], and [1203]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/679; Erdős references: [Er79d].
solved_when: Either infinitely many $n$ are shown to satisfy $\omega(n-k) < (1+\epsilon)\frac{\log k}{\log\log k}$ for all sufficiently large $k<n$, or it is shown that only finitely many such $n$ exist.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would settle whether integers can uniformly fall near the typical size of $\omega$ across their entire translated interval.

title: Erdős problem #680
open: Is it true that for all sufficiently large $n$ there exists some $k$ such that $p(n+k) > k^2+1$, where $p(m)$ denotes the least prime factor of $m$? Dually, can one prove the statement fails if $k^2+1$ is replaced by $e^{(1+\epsilon)\sqrt{k}} + C_\epsilon$, for all $\epsilon>0$ and some constant $C_\epsilon > 0$?
status: The $k^2+1$ claim follows from plausible assumptions on the distribution of primes (as does the question with $k^2$ replaced by $k^d$ for any $d$); the challenge is to prove it unconditionally. Erdős observed that Cramér's conjecture $\limsup_{k\to\infty} \frac{p_{k+1}-p_k}{(\log k)^2}=1$ implies that for all $\epsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$ there exists some $k$ with $p(n+k) > e^{(1-\epsilon)\sqrt{k}}$. However, there is now evidence that Cramér's conjecture is false: a more refined heuristic by Granville [Gr95] suggests the $\limsup$ is $2e^{-\gamma}\approx 1.119\cdots$, so perhaps the $1+\epsilon$ in the second question should be replaced by $2e^{-\gamma}+\epsilon$. See also [681] and [682].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for all sufficiently large $n$ there exists $k$ with $p(n+k) > k^2+1$, together with an unconditional proof or refutation of the bound with $e^{(1+\epsilon)\sqrt{k}}+C_\epsilon$ in place of $k^2+1$ for all $\epsilon>0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it probes the limits of how long runs of large least prime factors can be forced unconditionally versus under prime-distribution heuristics.

title: Erdős problem #681
open: Is it true that for all sufficiently large $n$ there exists some $k$ such that $n+k$ is composite yet has no small prime factor — specifically, its least prime factor $p(n+k)$ exceeds $k^2$? In other words, can one always reach a composite number near $n$ whose least prime factor is large relative to the shift $k$?
status: The problem is related to questions of Erdős, Eggleton, and Selfridge. It is speculated that the statement may remain true with $k^2$ replaced by $k^d$ for any $d$. See also problems [680] and [682]. Reference: [Er79d]; tracked at erdosproblems.com/681.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the statement: for all large $n$ there exists $k$ with $n+k$ composite and $p(n+k) > k^2$, where $p(m)$ denotes the least prime factor of $m$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a standing question about the distribution of large least prime factors in short shifted intervals.

title: Erdős problem #683
open: Is there an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, for every $1\leq k\leq n$, the largest prime divisor $P(\binom{n}{k})$ of the binomial coefficient satisfies $P(\binom{n}{k})\geq \min(n-k+1, k^{1+c})$?
status: A theorem of Sylvester and Schur (see [Er34]) states that $P(\binom{n}{k})>k$ if $k\leq n/2$. Erdős [Er55d] proved that there exists some $c>0$ such that, whenever $k\leq n/2$, $P(\binom{n}{k})\gg k\log k$. Erdős [Er79d] writes it 'seems certain' that the proposed bound holds for every $c>0$, with only a finite number of exceptions (depending on $c$). Standard heuristics on prime gaps suggest that for $k\leq n/2$ the largest prime divisor is in fact $>e^{c\sqrt{k}}$ for some constant $c>0$; this is essentially equivalent to [961].
solved_when: An explicit constant $c>0$ is exhibited for which the inequality $P(\binom{n}{k})\geq \min(n-k+1, k^{1+c})$ holds for all $1\leq k\leq n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a proof would give strong, uniform lower bounds on prime divisors of binomial coefficients, well beyond the currently known linear-in-$k$ and $k\log k$ estimates.
aliases: Erdős #683; number theory / primes / binomial coefficients

title: Erdős problem #684
open: For each $0\leq k\leq n$, split $\binom{n}{k}=uv$ so that all primes dividing $u$ lie in $[2,k]$ and all primes dividing $v$ lie in $(k,n]$, and let $f(n)$ be the smallest $k$ with $u>n^2$. How fast does $f(n)$ grow with $n$ — what are sharp upper and lower bounds?
status: A classical theorem of Mahler states that for any $\epsilon>0$ and integers $k$ and $l$, writing $(n+1)\cdots(n+k)=ab$ with primes of $a$ at most $l$ and primes of $b$ greater than $l$, one has $a<n^{1+\epsilon}$ for all sufficiently large $n$ (depending on $\epsilon,k,l$). Mahler's theorem implies $f(n)\to\infty$ but is ineffective, giving no bounds on the growth of $f(n)$. Tang and ChatGPT proved $f(n)\leq n^{30/43+o(1)}$; the same proof would give $f(n)\leq n^{2/3+o(1)}$ assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (or Density Hypothesis). A heuristic by Sothanaphan and ChatGPT in the comments suggests that, at least for most $n$, $f(n)\sim 2\log n$. An internal OpenAI model [APSSV26] gave an elementary argument showing $f(n)\ll(\log n)^2$ and constructing arbitrarily large $n$ with $f(n)\geq (1/2-o(1))\log n$. One can similarly ask for estimates on the smallest integer $f(n,k)$ such that the factor of $\binom{n}{k}$ containing all primes $\leq f(n,k)$ exceeds $n^2$. Reference: [Er79d].
solved_when: Explicit upper and lower bounds for $f(n)$ are established; the natural quantitative target, suggested by current heuristics, is determining whether $f(n)\sim 2\log n$ for most $n$, with the unconditional elementary bound $f(n)\ll(\log n)^2$ and the lower bound $f(n)\geq(1/2-o(1))\log n$ for arbitrarily large $n$ as benchmarks.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/684; settling it would resolve a basic question about how the small-prime and large-prime parts of binomial coefficients balance.
aliases: Erdős #684; number theory / primes / binomial coefficients

title: Erdős problem #685
open: Let $\epsilon>0$ and $n$ be large depending on $\epsilon$. Is it true that for all $n^\epsilon<k\leq n^{1-\epsilon}$ the number of distinct prime divisors of $\binom{n}{k}$ is \[(1+o(1))k\sum_{k<p<n}\frac{1}{p}?\] Or perhaps even when $k \geq (\log n)^c$?
status: It is trivial that the number of prime factors is \[>\frac{\log \binom{n}{k}}{\log n},\] and this inequality becomes (asymptotic) equality if $k>n^{1-o(1)}$. Full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/685; Erdős references: [Er79d].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, for every $\epsilon>0$ and all $n^\epsilon<k\leq n^{1-\epsilon}$ with $n$ sufficiently large in terms of $\epsilon$, the number of distinct prime divisors of $\binom{n}{k}$ equals $(1+o(1))k\sum_{k<p<n}\frac{1}{p}$; ideally extended down to $k \geq (\log n)^c$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a basic question about the multiplicative structure of binomial coefficients.
aliases: Erdős #685; number theory / primes / binomial coefficients

title: Erdős problem #686
open: Can every integer $N\geq 2$ be written as \[N=\frac{\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(m+i)}{\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)}\] for some $k\geq 2$ and $m\geq n+k$? A subquestion: when $n$ and $k$ are fixed, what can be said about the set of integers so represented?
status: Number theory. The problem remains open; the record notes the subquestion of what can be said about the set of integers represented when $n$ and $k$ are fixed, and refers to related problems [388] and [677]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/686; Erdős references: [Er79d].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every integer $N\geq 2$ admits such a representation with $k\geq 2$ and $m\geq n+k$, or a characterization of the integers representable for fixed $n$ and $k$.

title: Erdős problem #688
open: How small must a modulus be for a suitably chosen system of prime congruence classes to cover every integer up to $n$? Formally, let $\epsilon_n$ be maximal such that one can choose a congruence class $a_p$ for each prime $n^{\epsilon_n}<p\leq n$ so that every integer in $[1,n]$ satisfies at least one of the congruences $\equiv a_p \pmod{p}$; estimate $\epsilon_n$ — in particular, is $\epsilon_n = o(1)$?
status: Erdős could prove $\epsilon_n \gg \frac{\log\log\log n}{\log\log n}$. See also [687], [689], and [1200]. References: erdosproblems.com/688; [Er79d], [Er80, p.106].
solved_when: An asymptotic estimate of $\epsilon_n$ is obtained, resolving in particular whether $\epsilon_n = o(1)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #689
open: For sufficiently large $n$, can one assign to each prime $2 \leq p \leq n$ a congruence class $a_p \pmod{p}$ so that every integer in $[1,n]$ satisfies at least two of the congruences $\equiv a_p \pmod{p}$?
status: The natural generalization replaces $2$ by any fixed integer $r$ (with $n$ sufficiently large depending on $r$); see also [687] and [688]. Replacing primes with all integers gives problem [1205]. The variant with $2$ replaced by $10$ appears as Problem 45 on Green's open problems list. References: [Er79d], [Er80, p.108].
solved_when: An explicit choice of classes $a_p$ (or a proof of existence) is given for which every integer in $[1,n]$ satisfies at least two of the congruences, for all sufficiently large $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a long-standing question about covering systems built from prime moduli.

title: Erdős problem #691
open: Given $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$, let $M_A=\{ n \geq 1 : a\mid n \textrm{ for some } a\in A\}$ be the set of multiples of $A$. Find a necessary and sufficient condition on $A$ for $M_A$ to have density $1$.
status: A sequence $A$ for which $M_A$ has density $1$ is called a Behrend sequence. If $A$ is a set of prime numbers (or, more generally, a set of pairwise coprime integers without $1$), a necessary and sufficient condition is $\sum_{p\in A}\frac{1}{p}=\infty$. The general situation is more complicated. Suppose $A$ is the union of $(n_k,(1+\eta_k)n_k)\cap \mathbb{Z}$ where $1\leq n_1<n_2<\cdots$ is lacunary (a block sequence). If $\sum \eta_k<\infty$ then the density of $M_A$ exists and is $<1$; if $\eta_k=1/k$, so $\sum \eta_k=\infty$, the density still exists and is $<1$. Erdős writes it 'seems certain' that there is some threshold $\alpha\in(0,1)$ such that, if $\eta_k=k^{-\beta}$, then the density of $M_A$ is $1$ if $\beta<\alpha$ and $<1$ if $\beta>\alpha$. Tenenbaum notes in [Te96] that this is certainly not true as written, since if the $n_j$ grow sufficiently quickly the sequence is never Behrend, for any choice of $\eta_k$; he writes 'we understand from subsequent discussions with Erdős that he had actually in mind a two-sided condition on' $n_{j+1}/n_j$. Tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/691; Erdős references: [Er79e,p.77].
solved_when: A characterization of those sets $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ for which $M_A$ has natural density $1$ is proved (for pairwise coprime $A$ without $1$, the criterion $\sum_{a\in A} 1/a = \infty$ already suffices).
why: A sequence $A$ with $M_A$ of density $1$ is a Behrend sequence, a central notion in the multiplicative structure of integers; a complete characterization would settle when unions of integer intervals in lacunary blocks cover almost all integers in density, including Erdős's conjectured threshold $\alpha\in(0,1)$ for $\eta_k = k^{-\beta}$.

title: Erdős problem #693
open: Let $k\geq 2$ and let $n$ be sufficiently large depending on $k$. If $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ is the set of integers in $[n,n^k]$ having a divisor in $(n,2n)$, how large are the gaps between consecutive elements of $A$? Formally, estimate $\max_i (a_{i+1}-a_i)$; is it at most $(\log n)^{O(1)}$?
status: See also [446]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/693; Erdős references: [Er79e].
solved_when: A bound (or proof of impossibility) on $\max_i(a_{i+1}-a_i)$ for the integers in $[n,n^k]$ with a divisor in $(n,2n)$ is established; in particular, an affirmative answer establishes $\max_i(a_{i+1}-a_i)\leq(\log n)^{O(1)}$ for $n$ sufficiently large depending on $k\geq 2$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution resolves a long-standing question about the distribution of integers with divisors in a prescribed interval.

title: Erdős problem #695
open: If $p_1<p_2<\cdots$ is a chain of primes with $p_{i+1}\equiv 1\pmod{p_i}$, must $p_k$ grow faster than any exponential in $k$, in the sense that $\lim_k p_k^{1/k}=\infty$? And can one in fact construct such a chain with $p_k \leq \exp(k(\log k)^{1+o(1)})$?
status: Such sequences are sometimes called prime chains. The greedy chain, starting $p_1=2$ and taking $p_{i+1}$ as the smallest prime $\equiv 1\pmod{p_i}$, satisfies $p_k \leq e^{e^{O(k)}}$ by Linnik's theorem. It is conjectured that for any prime $p$ there is a prime $p'\leq p(\log p)^{O(1)}$ with $p'\equiv 1\pmod{p}$, which would imply $p_k\leq \exp(k(\log k)^{1+o(1)})$. An extensive study of the growth of finite prime chains was carried out by Ford, Konyagin, and Luca [FKL10]. See also [696].
solved_when: A proof (or construction) resolving whether $\lim_k p_k^{1/k}=\infty$ for every prime chain with $p_{i+1}\equiv 1\pmod{p_i}$, and a determination of whether a chain exists with $p_k \leq \exp(k(\log k)^{1+o(1)})$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle the fundamental growth rate of prime chains.

title: Erdős problem #699
open: Must every pair of binomial coefficients $\binom{n}{i}$ and $\binom{n}{j}$ with $1\leq i<j\leq n/2$ share a prime factor at least $i$? Formally: is there always a prime $p\geq i$ dividing $\gcd\left(\binom{n}{i},\binom{n}{j}\right)$?
status: This is a problem of Erdős and Szekeres. The theorem of Sylvester and Schur says that for any $1\leq i\leq n/2$ there exists some prime $p>i$ which divides $\binom{n}{i}$. GPT 5.6 (prompted by Price) has proved the present claim when $j\leq \frac{3}{2}i$ or $n=2j$. It is easy to prove (see the comments) that only finitely many $n$ can form a counterexample with any fixed $i<j$. Erdős and Szekeres further conjectured that $p\geq i$ can be improved to $p>i$ except in a few special cases; this fails in particular when $i=2$ and $n$ is some particular powers of $2$. They found some counterexamples when $i=3$, but only one counterexample when $i\geq 4$: $\gcd\left(\binom{28}{5},\binom{28}{14}\right)=2^3\cdot 3^3\cdot 5$. The problem is mentioned as B31 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the statement that for every $1\leq i<j\leq n/2$ there exists a prime $p\geq i$ with $p\mid \gcd\left(\binom{n}{i},\binom{n}{j}\right)$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and refines the classical Sylvester–Schur theorem on prime divisors of binomial coefficients to common divisors of pairs.

title: Erdős problem #700
open: Which composite numbers $n$ make the binomial coefficients $\binom{n}{k}$ as coprime to $n$ as possible? Formally, with $f(n)=\min_{1<k\leq n/2}\gcd\left(n,\binom{n}{k}\right)$ and $P(n)$ the largest prime factor of $n$, characterise the composite $n$ with $f(n)=n/P(n)$, decide whether infinitely many composite $n$ satisfy $f(n)>n^{1/2}$, and determine whether $f(n) \ll_A n/(\log n)^A$ for every $A>0$ and every composite $n$.
status: This is a problem of Erdős and Szekeres. It is easy to see that $f(n)\leq n/P(n)$ for composite $n$, since if $j=p^k$ where $p^k\mid n$ and $p^{k+1}\nmid n$ then $\gcd\left(n,\binom{n}{j}\right)=n/p^k$; this implies $f(n) \leq (1+o(1))n/\log n$. It is known that $f(n)=n/P(n)$ when $n$ is the product of two primes, and another example is $n=30$. For the second question, $f(n)\geq p(n)$ (the smallest prime dividing $n$) for any $n$, so infinitely many $n$ (those $=p^2$) satisfy $f(n)\geq n^{1/2}$. A positive answer to the second question was provided by GPT 5.6 Sol Pro (prompted by Price): it proves that there exist infinitely many $n$ (products of three primes) such that $f(n)\sim n^{2/3}$. See erdosproblems.com/700.
solved_when: A complete characterisation of the composite $n$ with $f(n)=n/P(n)$ is given, together with resolutions of whether infinitely many composite $n$ have $f(n)>n^{1/2}$ and whether $f(n) \ll_A n/(\log n)^A$ holds for every $A>0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/700; settling it would clarify how large the common divisors of $n$ and its binomial coefficients must be.

title: Erdős problem #701
open: Is there always an element $x$ that witnesses the maximum size of an intersecting subfamily of a downset? That is, for every family $\mathcal{F}$ closed under taking subsets, does there exist $x$ such that every intersecting subfamily $\mathcal{F}'\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ satisfies $|\mathcal{F}'|\leq|\{A\in\mathcal{F}: x\in A\}|$?
status: The problem originates with Chvátal [Ch74], who proved the analogous statement under a stronger condition than closure under subsets: assuming all sets lie in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the family must contain $B$ whenever $A\in\mathcal{F}$ and there is an injection $f:B\to A$ with $x\leq f(x)$ for all $x\in B$. Sterboul [St74] proved the statement when, for $\mathcal{G}$ the maximal sets of $\mathcal{F}$ under inclusion, all sets in $\mathcal{G}$ have the same size, $|A\cap B|\leq 1$ for all distinct $A,B\in\mathcal{G}$, and at least two sets in $\mathcal{G}$ intersect. Frankl and Kupavskii [FrKu23] proved it when $\mathcal{F}$ has covering number $2$. Borg [Bo11] proposed a weighted generalisation, which he proves under certain additional assumptions. Erdős references: [Er81,p.26] [Ch74] [St74]; erdosproblems.com/701.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that for every subset-closed family $\mathcal{F}$ there exists an element $x$ such that every intersecting subfamily $\mathcal{F}'\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ has $|\mathcal{F}'|\leq|\{A\in\mathcal{F}: x\in A\}|$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/701; settling it resolves a natural generalization of the classical EKR-type extremal question to arbitrary downsets.

title: Erdős problem #704
open: How does the chromatic number of the unit distance graph in $\mathbb{R}^n$ grow with the dimension $n$? In particular, does $\chi(G_n)$ grow exponentially in $n$, and does the limit $\lim_{n\to\infty}\chi(G_n)^{1/n}$ exist?
status: This is a generalisation of the Hadwiger–Nelson problem (which addresses $n=2$). Frankl and Wilson [FrWi81] proved exponential growth: $\chi(G_n)\geq(1+o(1))1.2^n$. This was improved to $\chi(G_n)\geq(1.239\cdots+o(1))^n$ by Raigorodsky [Ra00]. The trivial colouring (by tiling with cubes) gives $\chi(G_n)\leq(2+\sqrt{n})^n$. Larman and Rogers [LaRo72] improved this to $\chi(G_n)\leq(3+o(1))^n$, and conjecture the truth may be $(2^{3/2}+o(1))^n$ (note that $2^{3/2}\approx 2.828$). Prosanov [Pr20] has given an alternative proof of this upper bound. See also [508], [705], and [706].
solved_when: The growth rate of $\chi(G_n)$ is determined up to $1+o(1)$ in the exponential base — that is, the limit $\lim_{n\to\infty}\chi(G_n)^{1/n}$ is shown to exist and its value is determined.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, a natural higher-dimensional generalisation of the Hadwiger–Nelson problem; settling it resolves a long-tracked open question with full history at erdosproblems.com.
aliases: Erdős #704; graph theory / geometry / chromatic number

title: Erdős problem #706
open: How large must the chromatic number be for a graph whose vertices are a finite set of points in the plane, with edges joining pairs at distances drawn from a prescribed set $A\subset(0,\infty)$ of size $r$? Formally, if $L(r)$ is the least bound on $\chi(G)$ for all such graphs, estimate $L(r)$ — in particular, is $L(r)\leq r^{O(1)}$?
status: The case $r=1$ is the Hadwiger–Nelson problem, for which it is known that $5\leq L(1)\leq 7$. See also [508], [704], and [705].
solved_when: An estimate of $L(r)$ is obtained; the highlighted quantitative target is proving (or refuting) $L(r)\leq r^{O(1)}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it generalizes the classic Hadwiger–Nelson problem on coloring the plane.

title: Erdős problem #708
open: Given any $n$-element set $A$ of integers at least $2$ and any interval of $\max(A)$ consecutive integers, how large a subset $B$ of that interval suffices to ensure the product of its elements is divisible by $\prod_{a\in A} a$? Formally, if $g(n)$ is the minimal such size, is $g(n)\leq (2+o(1))n$, or perhaps even $g(n)\leq 2n$?
status: The problem is due to Erdős and Surányi [ErSu59], who proved $g(n)\geq (2-o(1))n$ and $g(3)=4$; their lower-bound construction takes $A=\{p_ip_j: i\neq j\}$ for primes $p_1<\cdots<p_\ell$ with $2p_1^2>p_\ell^2$. Gallai first considered problems of this type, observing $g(2)=2$ and $g(3)\geq 4$. In [Er92c] Erdős offers '100 dollars or 1000 rupees', whichever is more, for a proof or disproof (in 1992, 1000 rupees was worth approximately \$38.60). Erdős and Surányi also asked for the smallest $c_n\geq 1$ such that any interval $I\subset [0,\infty)$ of length $c_n\max(A)$ contains $B$ with $|B|=n$ and $\prod_{a\in A} a \mid \prod_{b\in B} b$; they proved $c_2=1$ and $c_3=\sqrt{2}$, but have no good general upper or lower bounds. See also [709].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $g(n)\leq (2+o(1))n$, ideally the sharper $g(n)\leq 2n$, is established; this would match the known lower bound $g(n)\geq (2-o(1))n$ of Erdős and Surányi [ErSu59].
why: It determines the exact asymptotic order of the minimal multiplier set in this divisibility problem, closing one of Erdős's personally posed questions, which carries his $100 prize offer and is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #710
open: How large must an interval of integers be to guarantee it contains distinct $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ with $k\mid a_k$ for every $1\le k\le n$? Formally, letting $f(n)$ be the least $f$ such that $(n,n+f)$ admits such a choice, obtain an asymptotic formula for $f(n)$.
status: The problem originates with Erdős and Pomerance [ErPo80], who proved $(2/\sqrt{e}+o(1))n(\log n/\log\log n)^{1/2}\leq f(n)\leq (1.7398\cdots+o(1))n(\log n)^{1/2}$. In [Er92c], Erdős offered 2000 rupees (about $78, converted at 1992 exchange rates) for an asymptotic formula. See also problem [711].
solved_when: An asymptotic formula for $f(n)$ is established, closing the gap between the lower bound $(2/\sqrt{e}+o(1))n(\log n/\log\log n)^{1/2}$ and the upper bound $(1.7398\cdots+o(1))n(\log n)^{1/2}$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a monetary prize and full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/710; resolving it would settle a classical divisibility-selection question of Erdős and Pomerance.

title: Erdős problem #712
open: What fraction of all $r$-tuples of an $n$-vertex set can carry an $r$-edge while no $k$ vertices are completely covered by edges? Formally, determine, for any $k>r>2$, the value of $\mathrm{ex}_r(n,K_k^r)/\binom{n}{r}$, where $\mathrm{ex}_r(n,K_k^r)$ is the largest number of $r$-edges placeable on $n$ vertices so that no set of $k$ vertices carries all $\binom{k}{r}$ possible $r$-edges.
status: Turán proved that, when $r=2$, the limit is $\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{k-1}\right)$. Erdős [Er81] offered \$500 for the determination of this value for any fixed $k>r>2$, and \$1000 for 'clearing up the whole set of problems'. See also [500] for the case $r=3$ and $k=4$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/712; Erdős references: [Er71,p.104] [Er74c,p.76] [Er81] [Er81].
solved_when: The value of the limit $\mathrm{ex}_r(n,K_k^r)/\binom{n}{r}$ is determined for any fixed $k>r>2$; Erdős offered \$500 for this and \$1000 for 'clearing up the whole set of problems'.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would settle a central case of the hypergraph Turán problem.
aliases: Erdős #712; graph theory / turan number / hypergraphs

title: Erdős problem #713
open: For every bipartite graph $G$, does its Turán number grow like a pure power of $n$ — that is, do there exist $\alpha\in[1,2)$ and $c>0$ with $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\sim cn^\alpha$? And must the exponent $\alpha$ necessarily be rational?
status: A problem of Erdős and Simonovits; Erdős sometimes asked it in the weaker form $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\asymp n^{\alpha}$. Erdős [Er67d] initially conjectured that for any bipartite graph $G$, $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\sim cn^{\alpha}$ for some $c>0$ and $\alpha$ of the shape $1+\frac{1}{k}$ or $2-\frac{1}{k}$ for an integer $k\geq 2$; this was disproved by Erdős and Simonovits [ErSi70]. The analogous statement fails for hypergraphs: Frankl and Füredi [FrFu87] proved that if $G$ is the $5$-uniform hypergraph on $8$ vertices with edges $\{12346,12457,12358\}$, then $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)=o(n^5)$ but $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\neq O(n^c)$ for any $c<5$. Füredi and Gerbner [FuGe21] gave a simplified proof and extended it to a counterexample for all $k\geq 5$; whether it holds for $k=3$ and $k=4$ remains open, though Füredi and Gerbner conjecture it does not. See also [571].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every bipartite graph $G$ there exist $\alpha\in[1,2)$ and $c>0$ such that $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\sim cn^\alpha$, together with an answer to whether $\alpha$ must be rational.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a $500 prize, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; it concerns the basic question of whether extremal numbers of bipartite graphs always have clean power-law asymptotics.

title: Erdős problem #714
open: Can a graph on $n$ vertices with no $K_{r,r}$ subgraph have on the order of $n^{2-1/r}$ edges for every fixed $r$? Formally: is it true that $\mathrm{ex}(n; K_{r,r}) \gg n^{2-1/r}$?
status: Kövári, Sós, and Turán [KST54] proved $\mathrm{ex}(n; K_{r,r}) \ll n^{2-1/r}$ for all $r \geq 2$. Brown [Br66] and, independently, Erdős, Rényi, and Sós [ERS66] proved the conjectured lower bound when $r=3$. When $r=2$ it is known that $\mathrm{ex}(n;K_{2,2}) = \left(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\right)n^{3/2}$ (see [768], since $K_{2,2}=C_4$). See also [147]. The generalisation to hypergraphs is [1158].
solved_when: A construction (for general $r$) of $K_{r,r}$-free graphs with $\gg n^{2-1/r}$ edges is given, matching the Kövári–Sós–Turán upper bound $\mathrm{ex}(n; K_{r,r}) \ll n^{2-1/r}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would complete the order of magnitude of the extremal number of complete bipartite graphs, a foundational quantity in extremal graph theory.

title: Erdős problem #719
open: Is every $r$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices the union of at most $\mathrm{ex}_{r}(n;K_{r+1}^r)$ copies of $K_r^r$ and $K_{r+1}^r$, no two of which share a $K_r^r$? Formally, writing $\mathrm{ex}_r(n;K_{r+1}^r)$ for the maximum number of $r$-edges on $n$ vertices avoiding a $K_{r+1}^r$, the question asks whether this extremal number bounds the size of such a decomposition.
status: The problem is posed as a conjecture of Erdős and Sauer; it remains open, with the record given at erdosproblems.com/719 and the Erdős reference [Er81].
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every $r$-hypergraph $G$ on $n$ vertices decomposes into at most $\mathrm{ex}_{r}(n;K_{r+1}^r)$ copies of $K_r^r$ and $K_{r+1}^r$ with no two copies sharing a $K_r^r$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution would settle a long-standing item from that catalog.

title: Erdős problem #723
open: If there is a finite projective plane of order $n$ then must $n$ be a prime power? A finite projective plane of order $n$ is a collection of subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n^2+n+1\}$ of size $n+1$ such that every pair of elements is contained in exactly one set.
status: These always exist if $n$ is a prime power. The conjecture has been proved for $n\leq 11$, but it is open whether there exists a projective plane of order $12$. Bruck and Ryser [BrRy49] have proved that if $n\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ or $n\equiv 2\pmod{4}$ then $n$ must be the sum of two squares, which for example rules out $n=6$ or $n=14$. The case $n=10$ was ruled out by computer search [La97].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every finite projective plane has prime-power order; in particular, resolving whether a projective plane of order 12 exists.

title: Erdős problem #724
open: Must there be at least a constant times $\sqrt{n}$ mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order $n$, for every order $n$? Formally, writing $f(n)$ for the maximum number of mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order $n$, is it true that $f(n) \gg n^{1/2}$?
status: Euler conjectured that $f(n)=1$ when $n\equiv 2 \pmod{4}$, but this was disproved by Bose, Parker, and Shrikhande [BPS60], who proved $f(n)\geq 2$ for $n\geq 7$. Chowla, Erdős, and Straus [CES60] proved $f(n) \gg n^{1/91}$. Wilson [Wi74] proved $f(n) \gg n^{1/17}$. Beth [Be83c] proved $f(n) \gg n^{1/14.8}$. The sequence of $f(n)$ is A001438 in the OEIS.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $f(n) \gg n^{1/2}$; any resolution establishing explicit lower bounds matching the $n^{1/2}$ order resolves it.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would settle a long-standing question on the size of complete sets of orthogonal Latin squares.

title: Erdős problem #725
open: Can one give an asymptotic formula for the number of $k\times n$ Latin rectangles? In other words, determine the asymptotics of this count as $n$ grows, for as wide a range of $k$ as possible.
status: Erdős and Kaplansky [ErKa46] proved the count is $\sim e^{-\binom{k}{2}}(n!)^k$ when $k=o((\log n)^{3/2-\epsilon})$. Yamamoto [Ya51] extended this to $k\leq n^{1/3-o(1)}$. The count of such Latin rectangles is A001009 in the OEIS.
solved_when: An asymptotic formula for the number of $k\times n$ Latin rectangles is established, valid for $k$ growing faster than the currently known range (beyond $k\leq n^{1/3-o(1)}$), ideally up to $k$ comparable to $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and settling it would resolve a long-standing question on the enumeration of basic combinatorial designs.

title: Erdős problem #726
open: Does the residue of a large integer $n$, taken modulo each prime $p\leq n$, fall in the upper half of the residues — that is, $n\equiv r\pmod p$ for some $p/2<r<p$ — often enough that the weighted count matches half of the primes' harmonic density? Formally, is it true that as $n\to\infty$,
status: A conjecture of Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75]. For comparison, the classical estimate of Mertens states that $\sum_{p\leq n}\frac1p\sim\log\log n$. Here $n\in(p/2,p)\pmod p$ means $n\equiv r\pmod p$ for some integer $r$ with $p/2<r<p$. The problem is tracked at erdosproblems.com/726.
solved_when: The asymptotic $\sum_{p\leq n}1_{n\in(p/2,p)\pmod{p}}\frac1p \sim \frac{\log\log n}{2}$ is proved, with no quantitative rate required beyond the asymptotic itself.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would clarify how the residues of a fixed integer distribute across the upper half of prime moduli, a natural refinement of the classical Mertens estimate for $\sum_{p\leq n}1/p$.

title: Erdős problem #727
open: For a fixed integer $k\geq 2$, are there infinitely many $n$ such that $(n+k)!^2$ divides $(2n)!$? In other words, does $\binom{2n}{n}$ remain divisible by $(n+k)!^2$ infinitely often?
status: The conjecture is due to Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75], and it remains open even for $k=2$. Balakran [Ba29] proved the $k=1$ case, i.e. that $(n+1)^2\mid \binom{2n}{n}$ for infinitely many $n$; it is a classical fact that $(n+1)\mid \binom{2n}{n}$ for all $n$ (see Catalan numbers). Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus observed that Balakran's method further shows there are infinitely many $n$ with $(n+k)!(n+1)!\mid (2n)!$ (in fact this holds whenever $k<c\log n$ for some small constant $c>0$). Erdős [Er68c] proved that if $a!b!\mid n!$ then $a+b\leq n+O(\log n)$.
solved_when: For some fixed $k\geq 2$, it is proved that $(n+k)!^2 \mid (2n)!$ for infinitely many $n$; the case $k=2$ alone would resolve the problem as stated.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/727; resolving it would settle a natural divisibility question about central binomial coefficients that has resisted attack even in its smallest open case.

title: Erdős problem #731
open: For almost all integers $n$, what is the typical size of the least integer $m$ that does not divide the central binomial coefficient $\binom{2n}{n}$? More precisely, find a reasonable function $f(n)$ such that, for almost all $n$, this least $m$ satisfies $m \sim f(n)$.
status: The problem was posed by Erdős, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus [EGRS75], who say it is 'not hard to show that', for almost all $n$, the minimal such $m$ satisfies $m = \exp((\log n)^{1/2+o(1)})$.
solved_when: An explicit function $f(n)$ is given and proved to satisfy $m \sim f(n)$ for almost all integers $n$, where $m$ is the least integer with $m \nmid \binom{2n}{n}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; determining the typical order of the first non-divisor of the central binomial coefficient refines our understanding of the divisibility structure of $\binom{2n}{n}$.

title: Erdős problem #734
open: For every large $n$, can one construct a pairwise balanced block design on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ whose block sizes are distributed so that no single size occurs too often — specifically, at most $O(n^{1/2})$ blocks of any given size $t$?
status: A pairwise balanced block design requires every pair in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ to be contained in exactly one block $A_i$. Erdős [Er81] writes 'this will be probably not be very difficult to prove but so far I was not successful'. Erdős and de Bruijn [dBEr48] proved that any such design has $m\geq n$, which implies some size $t$ must occur $\gg n^{1/2}$ times, so the $O(n^{1/2})$ target is essentially best possible up to constants.
solved_when: For all sufficiently large $n$, a non-trivial pairwise balanced block design $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ is given such that for all $t$, the number of $i$ with $|A_i|=t$ is $O(n^{1/2})$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/734; settling it would resolve a long-standing question in combinatorial design theory.

title: Erdős problem #736
open: If a graph $G$ has chromatic number $\aleph_1$, must there exist, for every cardinal $m$, a graph $G_m$ of chromatic number $m$ all of whose finite subgraphs are subgraphs of $G$?
status: The question originates as a conjecture of Walter Taylor, and the more general problem replaces $\aleph_1$ with any uncountable cardinal $\kappa$; more generally, Erdős asks to characterise families $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ of finite graphs such that there is a graph of chromatic number $\aleph_\alpha$ all of whose finite subgraphs are in $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$. Komjáth [KoSh05] proved that it is consistent that the answer is no: there exists a graph $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that if $H$ is any graph all of whose finite subgraphs are subgraphs of $G$, then $H$ has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_2$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/736; Erdős references: [Er81] [Er93,p.343].
solved_when: The question is answered affirmatively or negatively for graphs $G$ of chromatic number $\aleph_1$; equivalently, the general problem of characterising families $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ of finite graphs for which there exists a graph of chromatic number $\aleph_\alpha$ all of whose finite subgraphs lie in $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ is resolved.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would clarify how strongly an uncountable chromatic number constrains the finite subgraphs a graph can realise.

title: Erdős problem #738
open: If a graph has infinite chromatic number and contains no triangle, must it contain every tree as an induced subgraph?
status: Open. The statement is a conjecture of Gyárfás; the problem is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/738, with Erdős reference [Er81].
solved_when: A proof that every triangle-free graph of infinite chromatic number contains each fixed tree as an induced subgraph, or a counterexample exhibiting one such graph and one tree it omits.
why: Resolving it would clarify how high chromatic number forces substructure in sparse graphs — a central theme of the Erdős school — and settle one of Erdős's personally posed problems.

title: Erdős problem #739
open: If a graph has infinite chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$, must it contain subgraphs realizing every smaller infinite chromatic number? Formally: given a graph $G$ with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$, is it true that for every infinite cardinal $\mathfrak{n}<\mathfrak{m}$ there exists a subgraph of $G$ with chromatic number $\mathfrak{n}$?
status: The question is due to Galvin [Ga73], who proved it true for $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_0$; he also showed that the stronger version where the subgraph is induced implies $2^{\mathfrak{k}}<2^{\mathfrak{n}}$ for all cardinals $\mathfrak{k}<\mathfrak{n}$. Komjáth [Ko88b] proved it consistent that $2^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_1}=2^{\aleph_2}=\aleph_3$ and that graphs failing the property exist (with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_2$ and $\mathfrak{n}=\aleph_1$). Shelah [Sh90] proved, assuming the axiom of constructibility, that the answer is yes with $\mathfrak{m}=\aleph_2$ and $\mathfrak{n}=\aleph_1$. It remains open whether the answer is yes under the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis, for example. Erdős references: [Er81] [Ga73] [Ko88b].
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) is given of the statement that every graph of chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$ contains, for every infinite cardinal $\mathfrak{n}<\mathfrak{m}$, a subgraph of chromatic number $\mathfrak{n}$; in particular, an answer is known under the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (tracked at erdosproblems.com/739), and its answer is independent of ZFC in ways that tie the structure of infinite chromatic graphs directly to cardinal arithmetic.

title: Erdős problem #740
open: Must every graph of infinite chromatic number contain, for each fixed $r \geq 1$, a subgraph of the same chromatic number that avoids all odd cycles of length at most $r$? Formally, for an infinite cardinal $\mathfrak{m}$ and a graph $G$ with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$, must $G$ contain a subgraph with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$ and no odd cycle of length $\leq r$?
status: This is a question of Erdős and Hajnal. Rödl proved the statement true for $\mathfrak{m} = \aleph_0$ and $r = 3$ (see [108] for the finitary version). More generally, Erdős and Hajnal asked whether for every cardinal $\mathfrak{m}$ and integer $r$ there exists some $f_r(\mathfrak{m})$ such that every graph with chromatic number $\geq f_r(\mathfrak{m})$ contains a subgraph with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$ and no odd cycle of length $\leq r$. Erdős [Er95d] claimed that even the $r = 3$ case is open: must every graph with sufficiently large chromatic number contain a triangle-free graph with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$? In [Er81] Erdős also asks the same question with girth in place of odd-girth, i.e. the subgraph contains no cycle at all of length $\leq C$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/740; Erdős references: [Er69b] [Er71,p.100] [Er81] [Er95d].
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) settles the question for every infinite cardinal $\mathfrak{m}$ and every $r \geq 1$; in particular, an answer to the $r = 3$ case — whether every graph with sufficiently large chromatic number contains a triangle-free subgraph of chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$ — and to the general form asking for a function $f_r(\mathfrak{m})$ such that every graph with chromatic number $\geq f_r(\mathfrak{m})$ contains a subgraph with chromatic number $\mathfrak{m}$ and no odd cycle of length $\leq r$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and touches the core interaction between chromatic number and local cycle structure in infinite graphs.

title: Erdős problem #743
open: Can every sequence of trees $T_2,\ldots,T_n$, where $T_k$ has exactly $k$ vertices, be packed edge-disjointly into $K_n$? Equivalently, is $K_n$ always expressible as an edge-disjoint union of the $T_k$?
status: This is a conjecture of Gyárfás, known as the tree packing conjecture. Gyárfás and Lehel [GyLe78] proved it holds if all but at most $2$ of the trees are stars, or if all the trees are stars or paths. Fishburn [Fi83] proved it for $n\le 9$. Bollobás [Bo83] proved that the smallest $\lfloor n/\sqrt{2}\rfloor$ many trees can always be packed greedily into $K_n$. Joos, Kim, Kühn, and Osthus [JKKO19] proved the conjecture when the trees have bounded maximum degree. Allen, Böttcher, Clemens, Hladký, Piguet, and Taraz [ABCHPT21] proved it when all the trees have maximum degree $\le c\frac{n}{\log n}$ for some constant $c>0$. Janzer and Montgomery [JaMo24] proved that there exists some $c>0$ such that the largest $cn$ trees can be packed into $K_n$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every $n$ and every choice of trees $T_k$ on $k$ vertices ($2\le k\le n$), the complete graph $K_n$ decomposes as an edge-disjoint union of $T_2,\ldots,T_n$.
why: This is the tree packing conjecture of Gyárfás, one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #749
open: Let $\epsilon>0$. Does there exist $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that the lower density of $A+A$ is at least $1-\epsilon$ and yet $1_A\ast 1_A(n) \ll_\epsilon 1$ for all $n$?
status: It is unclear from [Er94b] whether Erdős believed the answer should be yes or no. He also asked a similar question for upper density, for which he seemed more certain the answer should be yes. He wrote that both he and Sárközy believed that if $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\leq C$ for all $n$ then the upper density of $A+A$ is at most $1-\epsilon_C$, where $\epsilon_C>0$ may depend on $C$. The upper density variant has been resolved by Bhalla, with the assistance of GPT 5.4: for any $\epsilon>0$, Bhalla constructs a set $A$ for which the upper density of $A+A$ is at least $1-\epsilon$ and yet $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\ll \epsilon^{-1}$ for all $n$. See also [28].
solved_when: For every $\epsilon>0$, an explicit construction of a set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is given with lower density of $A+A$ at least $1-\epsilon$ and $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\ll_\epsilon 1$ for all $n$ — or a proof that no such $A$ exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles a basic question on how large a sumset can be while representation counts stay uniformly bounded.

title: Erdős problem #757
open: Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}$ be a set of size $n$ such that every subset $B\subseteq A$ with $\lvert B\rvert =4$ has $\lvert B-B\rvert\geq 11$. What is the best constant $c>0$ such that $A$ must always contain a Sidon set of size $\geq cn$?
status: For comparison, a Sidon set $B$ has $\lvert B-B\rvert=13$, so the condition says at most one difference is 'missing' from $B-B$. Equivalently, one can view $A$ as a set such that every four points determine at least five distinct distances, and ask for a subset with all distances distinct; without loss of generality, one may assume $A\subset \mathbb{N}$. Erdős and Sós proved $c\geq 1/2$. Gyárfás and Lehel [GyLe95] proved $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{141\cdot 76}\leq c\leq\frac{3}{5}$, where the upper bound comes from the set of the first $n$ Fibonacci numbers. Ma and Tang [MaTa26] have improved these bounds to $\frac{9}{17}\leq c\leq \frac{4}{7}$.
solved_when: Exact constants are determined: a proof that some specific $c$ works for all such $A$, matching a construction showing no larger constant is possible.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; determining the exact constant resolves the quantitative link between the local four-point difference condition and the existence of large Sidon subsets.

title: Erdős problem #761
open: Must every graph of large chromatic number also have large dichromatic number, and must every graph of large cochromatic number contain a subgraph of large dichromatic number? Here the dichromatic number is the minimum number of colours for which some orientation admits a colouring with no monochromatic oriented cycle, and the cochromatic number is the minimum number of colours whose classes each induce a complete or empty graph.
status: The first question is due to Erdős and Neumann-Lara. The second question is due to Erdős and Gimbel. A positive answer to the second question implies a positive answer to the first via the bound mentioned in [760].
solved_when: Affirmative answers are established to both questions — that is, a proof that large chromatic number forces large dichromatic number, and a proof that large cochromatic number forces containment of a graph with large dichromatic number.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; the second question implies the first via the bound mentioned in [760], so settling it would resolve both.

title: Erdős problem #766
open: How small can the Turán number be forced to be by fixing the vertex and edge count of the excluded graph? Formally, let $f(n;k,l)=\min \mathrm{ex}(n;G)$ over all graphs $G$ with $k$ vertices and $l$ edges, and ask for good estimates of $f(n;k,l)$ in the range $k<l\leq k^2/4$; for fixed $k$ and large $n$, is $f(n;k,l)$ strictly monotone in $l$?
status: Dirac and Erdős independently proved that when $l=\lfloor k^2/4\rfloor+1$, $f(n;k,l)\leq \lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1$.
solved_when: Good estimates for $f(n;k,l)$ are obtained throughout the range $k<l\leq k^2/4$, and the strict monotonicity of $f(n;k,l)$ in $l$ (for fixed $k$ and large $n$) is decided.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution would close a long-standing entry in that catalogue and advance extremal graph theory around Turán numbers.

title: Erdős problem #768
open: Is the density of integers $n$ with the property that for every prime $p\mid n$ there is some divisor $d>1$ of $n$ with $d\equiv 1\pmod{p}$ asymptotically $\exp(-(c+o(1))\sqrt{\log N}\log\log N$ in $[1,N]$? Formally, for $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ the set of such $n$, is there a constant $c>0$ such that for all large $N$, $\frac{|A\cap[1,N]|}{N}=\exp(-(c+o(1))\sqrt{\log N}\log\log N)$?
status: Erdős proved that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that for all large $N$, $\exp(-c\sqrt{\log N}\log\log N)\leq \frac{|A\cap[1,N]|}{N}$, and also that $\frac{|A\cap[1,N]|}{N}\leq \exp(-(1+o(1))\sqrt{\log N\log\log N})$. The correct asymptotic between these bounds remains unknown. Tracked at erdosproblems.com/768; Erdős references: [Er74b].
solved_when: One proves (or disproves) the existence of a constant $c>0$ such that for all large $N$, $\frac{|A\cap[1,N]|}{N}=\exp(-(c+o(1))\sqrt{\log N}\log\log N)$, matching Erdős's conjectured shape.
why: $|A\cap[1,N]|$ gives an upper bound for the number of integers $n\leq N$ for which there is a non-cyclic simple group of order $n$, so pinning down its asymptotics directly controls that count; it is also one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #769
open: How many homothetic cubes are needed before the $n$-dimensional unit cube can be decomposed into exactly $k$ of them, for all large $k$? Formally, for $c(n)$ the minimal threshold with this property, give good bounds — in particular, is it true that $c(n) \gg n^n$?
status: First investigated by Hadwiger, who proved the lower bound $c(n) \geq 2^n + 2^{n-1}$. It is easy to see that $c(2)=6$, and Meier conjectured $c(3)=48$. Burgess and Erdős [Er74b] proved $c(n) \ll n^{n+1}$. Erdős wrote "I am certain that if $n+1$ is a prime then $c(n) > n^n$." Hudelson [Hu98] proved that if $(2^n-1, 3^n-1)=1$ then $c(n) < 6^n$, and in general $c(n) \ll (2n)^{n-1}$. Connor and Marmorino [CoMa18] proved $c(n) \geq 2^{n+1}-1$ for all $n \geq 3$, $c(n) \leq 1.8n^{n+1}$ if $n+1$ is prime, and $c(n) \leq e^2 n^n$ otherwise.
solved_when: Sharp bounds on $c(n)$ are obtained; the headline question is whether $c(n) \gg n^n$ (with Erdős's stronger suggestion that $c(n) > n^n$ when $n+1$ is prime).

title: Erdős problem #770
open: Let $h(n)$ be the least integer such that the numbers $2^n-1,3^n-1,\ldots,h(n)^n-1$ are mutually coprime — how does $h(n)$ behave? In particular, for every prime $p$, does the density $\delta_p$ of integers $n$ with $h(n)=p$ exist, is $\liminf h(n)=\infty$, and is it true that whenever $p$ is the greatest prime with $p-1\mid n$ and $p>n^\epsilon$, one has $h(n)=p$?
status: It is easy to see that $h(n)=n+1$ if and only if $n+1$ is prime, and that $h(n)$ is unbounded for odd $n$. It is probably true that $h(n)=3$ for infinitely many $n$. See also [820]. (Erdős references: [Er74b])
solved_when: The behavior of $h(n)$ is characterized: for every prime $p$ the density $\delta_p$ of integers $n$ with $h(n)=p$ is shown to exist (or not), and the questions of whether $\liminf h(n)=\infty$ and whether $h(n)$ equals the greatest prime $p$ with $p-1\mid n$ and $p>n^\epsilon$ are resolved.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution settles a long-standing entry in that collection.

title: Erdős problem #773
open: How large can a Sidon subset of the squares $\{1,2^2,\ldots,N^2\}$ be — in particular, is the answer $N^{1-o(1)}$?
status: The question is due to Alon and Erdős [AlEr85], who proved via a random subset that $|A| \geq N^{2/3-o(1)}$ is possible, and observed the upper bound $|A| \ll \frac{N}{(\log N)^{1/4}}$, since (as shown by Landau) the density of the sums of two squares decays like $(\log N)^{-1/2}$. Croot, Mao, and Yip (see the comments) improved the upper bound to $|A| \leq N^{1-\frac{c}{\log\log N}}$ for some constant $c>0$. The lower bound was improved to $|A| \gg N^{2/3}$ by Lefmann and Thiele [LeTh95]. In [Er80] Erdős further defines $g(A)$ to be the maximal size of a Sidon set of $\{a^2 : a\in A\}$ and asks whether $g(A)\geq g(\{1,\ldots,N\})$ where $N=|A|$ (see [530] for the linear analogue). He further asks the infinite analogue: is there an infinite set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ such that $|A\cap [1,N]| \geq N^{1-o(1)}$ for all large $N$ and $\{a^2 : a \in A\}$ is a Sidon set? See [1206] for a similar question for higher powers.
solved_when: The maximum size of a Sidon subset $A\subseteq\{1,2^2,\ldots,N^2\}$ is determined up to $N^{o(1)}$ factors; specifically, a proof (or disproof) that the maximum is $N^{1-o(1)}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and sits at the interface of Sidon sets and additive properties of the squares.
aliases: Erdős #773; number theory / sidon sets / squares

title: Erdős problem #774
open: Must every proportionately dissociated set of natural numbers be expressible as a union of finitely many dissociated sets? Formally, if every finite subset $B\subset A$ contains a dissociated subset of size $\gg |B|$, must $A = A_1\cup\dots\cup A_k$ with each $A_i$ dissociated?
status: The question appears in a paper of Alon and Erdős [AlEr85], though the general topic was first considered by Pisier [Pi83], who observed that the converse holds and proved that being proportionately dissociated is equivalent to being a 'Sidon set' in the harmonic analysis sense: whenever $f:A\to\mathbb{C}$ there exists some $\theta\in[0,1]$ such that $\|f\|_1 \ll \left|\sum_{n\in A} f(n)e(\theta)\right|$, where $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$. Alon and Erdős write that it 'seems unlikely that [this] is also sufficient'. They also note the same question can be asked replacing dissociated with Sidon (in the additive combinatorial sense) (see [328]); that variant was resolved in the negative by Nešetřil, Rödl, and Sales [NRS24].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every proportionately dissociated $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ is a finite union of dissociated sets — equivalently, a construction of a proportionately dissociated set that is not such a finite union.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it sits at the interface of additive combinatorics and harmonic analysis, asking whether a density-type condition forces a finite coloring-type structure.

title: Erdős problem #776
open: How large must the ground set be, as a function of $r$, before one can build an antichain $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ whose realized set sizes number exactly $n-3$, with the constraint that every occurring size $t$ is realized by at least $r$ distinct sets? Formally, determine $n_0(r)$, the threshold past which an antichain in $2^{[n]}$ with $n-3$ distinct set sizes exists subject to this multiplicity condition.
status: A problem of Erdős and Trotter. For $r=1$ and $n>3$ the maximum possible is $n-2$; for $r>1$ and $n$ sufficiently large, $n-3$ is achievable but $n-2$ is never achievable. He and Tang [HeTa26b] (with ChatGPT) proved that $n_0(2)=3$, $n_0(3)=8$, and for all $r\geq 4$ that $2r+2\leq n_0(r)\leq 2r+2\log_2 r+O(\log\log r)$, hence $n_0(r)\sim 2r$ as $r\to\infty$.
solved_when: $n_0(r)$ is determined exactly for all $r\geq 2$, where $n_0(r)$ is the least value such that for all $n>n_0(r)$ such a family with $n-3$ distinct set sizes exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (posed with Trotter), and pinning down $n_0(r)$ completes the quantitative picture of how the multiplicity requirement trades off against the number of distinct antichain sizes.

title: Erdős problem #778
open: In the clique-building game on $K_n$, where Alice and Bob alternately colour edges red and blue (Alice first) and Alice wins if the largest red clique exceeds every blue clique, does Bob have a winning strategy for every $n\geq 3$? Related variants ask the same when Bob colours two edges per move of Alice's one but must build the strictly larger clique for $n>3$, and when the winner is decided by comparing maximum degrees of the two colour subgraphs.
status: Malekshahian and Spiro [MaSp24] proved, for the first game, that the set of $n$ for which Bob wins has density at least $3/4$; in fact, if Alice wins at $n$ then Bob wins at $n+1,n+2,n+3$. For the third game they prove that the set of $n$ for which Bob wins has density at least $2/3$, and more strongly that if Alice wins at $n$ then Bob wins at $n+1,n+2$.
solved_when: A determination of the winner, with strategy, for each of the three games — specifically whether Bob wins the first game for all $n\geq 3$, whether Bob wins the two-edges-per-move variant for all $n>3$, and who wins the maximum-degree variant (for all $n$).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, so a complete resolution would close a long-standing entry in that collection.

title: Erdős problem #779
open: Let $n>1$ and let $p_1<\cdots<p_n$ be the first $n$ primes, with $P=\prod_{1\leq i\leq n}p_i$. Does there always exist a prime $p$ with $p_n<p<P$ such that $P+p$ is prime?
status: A problem of Deaconescu. Erdős expects the least such prime to be much smaller than $P$, in fact $p\leq n^{O(1)}$, and Deaconescu has verified the conjecture for $n\leq 1000$. The usual heuristic gives $P+p$ prime with 'probability' $\approx 1/\log P$, so the chance of failure is $\ll (1-1/\log P)^{P-p_n}\ll \exp(-n^{-cn})$, using $P=n^{(1+o(1))n}$; as Cambie points out, 'the chances of failing are ridiculously small'. Key works: erdosproblems.com/779; Erdős references: [Gu83].
solved_when: For every $n>1$ there exists a prime $p$ with $p_n<p<P$ and $P+p$ prime; the conjectured strengthening that the least such $p$ satisfies $p\leq n^{O(1)}$ is the expected target.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would settle a basic question about primes just beyond a primorial.

title: Erdős problem #782
open: Do the squares contain arbitrarily long quasi-progressions? That is, does there exist some constant $C>0$ such that, for any $k$, the squares contain a sequence $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ where, for some $d$ and all $1\leq i<k$, $x_i+d\leq x_{i+1}\leq x_i+d+C$? And do the squares contain arbitrarily large cubes of the form $a+\{\sum_i \epsilon_ib_i : \epsilon_i\in\{0,1\}\}$?
status: This is a question of Brown, Erdős, and Freedman [BEF90]. It is a classical fact that the squares do not contain arithmetic progressions of length 4. An affirmative answer to the first question implies an affirmative answer to the second. Solymosi [So07] conjectured the answer to the second question is no. Cilleruelo and Granville [CiGr07] have observed that the answer to the second question is no conditional on the Bombieri-Lang conjecture.
solved_when: A resolution of either question: a proof that for some constant $C>0$ and every $k$ the squares contain a quasi-progression of length $k$ (or a proof that no such $C$ exists), and likewise a determination of whether the squares contain arbitrarily large sets of the form $a+\{\sum_i \epsilon_ib_i : \epsilon_i\in\{0,1\}\}$.
why: It probes how far the rigid structure of the squares departs from containing genuine arithmetic progressions, since the squares famously contain no 4-term arithmetic progression; an answer would sharpen our understanding of additive patterns inside nonlinear sequences.

title: Erdős problem #786
open: Is there, for every $\epsilon>0$, a set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ of density greater than $1-\epsilon$ whose elements are multiplicative-independent in the sense that any equality $a_1\cdots a_r=b_1\cdots b_s$ with $a_i,b_j\in A$ forces $r=s$? Equivalently, can one always find such a set $A\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$ of size at least $(1-o(1))N$?
status: The integers $\equiv 2\pmod{4}$ give an example with density $1/4$. Selfridge constructed such a set with density $1/e-\epsilon$ for any $\epsilon>0$: let $p_1<\cdots<p_k$ be large consecutive primes with $\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{1}{p_i}<1<\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\frac{1}{p_i}$, and let $A$ be the integers divisible by exactly one of $p_1,\ldots,p_k$. For the finite question, the integers with a prime factor $>N^{1/2}$ give a set of size $\geq(\log 2)N$; Erdős could improve this constant slightly, and Tao, in the comments at erdosproblems.com/786, improved it further by taking $A$ to be the integers with exactly one prime factor $>N^{\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{e}}}$, which has size $\approx 0.8285N$. In [Er65] Erdős reports that Ruzsa proved the maximal size of such an $A$ is $\leq(1-c)N$ for some constant $c>0$ for large $N$, but the proof 'is not yet published'; the proof is presumably via the associated additive function $f(a_1\cdots a_r)=r$, so $A=\{n: f(n)=1\}$, together with a result of Erdős, Ruzsa, and Sárkzösy [ERS73]. References: [Er65] [Er69,p.81] [Er73,p.132] [Er80,p.114]; erdosproblems.com/786.
solved_when: For every $\epsilon>0$, an explicit set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ of density $>1-\epsilon$ (equivalently, in the finite version, a set $A\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$ of size $\geq(1-o(1))N$) is constructed with the property that $a_1\cdots a_r=b_1\cdots b_s$ with $a_i,b_j\in A$ implies $r=s$; or, in the opposite direction, a proof that no such set exists for some fixed $\epsilon>0$.
why: A solution determines how large a multiplicative-independence property can coexist with near-full density in the integers, resolving one of Erdős's personally posed problems tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #787
