open: How large a sum-free-within-$A$ subset must every $n$-element set of reals contain: if $g(n)$ is the largest integer such that every $A\subset\mathbb{R}$ with $|A|=n$ has a subset $B$ of size at least $g(n)$ with $b_1+b_2\notin A$ for all distinct $b_1,b_2\in B$, what is the true order of growth of $g(n)$?
status: The function was considered by Erdős and Moser. Choi observed that without loss of generality one may assume $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$. Klarner proved $g(n)\gg\log n$ (indeed, a greedy construction suffices). Choi [Ch71] proved $g(n)\ll n^{2/5+o(1)}$. The current best bounds are $(\log n)^{1+c}\ll g(n)\ll\exp(\sqrt{\log n})$ for some constant $c>0$, the lower bound due to Sanders [Sa21] and the upper bound due to Ruzsa [Ru05]. Beker [Be25] improved the lower bound to $(\log n)^{1+1/68+o(1)}\ll g(n)$.
solved_when: $g(n)$ is determined up to the order of magnitude implied by matching upper and lower bounds — in particular, closing the gap between the current lower bounds of order $(\log n)^{1+c}$ and the upper bound $\exp(\sqrt{\log n})$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems with a tracked full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would settle a basic extremal question about how far any set of reals is from forcing additive structure on all its large subsets.

title: Erdős problem #788
open: How large can the quantity $f(n)$ be, where $f(n)$ is the maximal value such that for every $B\subset (2n,4n)\cap\mathbb{N}$ there exists $C\subset (n,2n)\cap\mathbb{N}$ with $c_1+c_2\not\in B$ for all distinct $c_1\neq c_2\in C$ and $|C|+|B|\geq f(n)$? In particular, is it true that $f(n)\leq n^{1/2+o(1)}$?
status: The problem originates with a conjecture of Choi [Ch71], who proved $f(n)\ll n^{3/4}$. Adenwalla in the comments gave a simple construction proving $f(n)\gg n^{1/2}$, and Hunter in the comments sketched an argument giving $f(n)\ll n^{2/3+o(1)}$. Baltz, Schoen, and Srivastav [BSS00] proved $f(n)\ll (n\log n)^{2/3}$. Hunter's argument shows more generally that if a random Cayley graph with edge probability $p$ has (almost surely) independence number $\ll p^{-c-o(1)}$, then $f(n)\leq n^{\frac{c}{c+1}+o(1)}$; the work of Alon and Pham [AlPh25] on random Cayley graphs therefore implies $f(n)\leq n^{3/5+o(1)}$, and the conjectured bound of $\leq p^{-1+o(1)}$ for the independence number would yield $f(n)\leq n^{1/2+o(1)}$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the bound $f(n)\leq n^{1/2+o(1)}$, together with an estimate of $f(n)$ up to $n^{o(1)}$ factors.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (number 788, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com), and resolving it settles Choi's conjecture on the interplay between a set and a large sum-avoiding partner set.

title: Erdős problem #789
open: How large a subset $B$ can every $n$-element set of integers $A$ be guaranteed to contain, if $B$ must have no nontrivial additive relation among its elements — that is, whenever $a_1+\cdots+a_r=b_1+\cdots+b_s$ with $a_i,b_i\in B$, we must have $r=s$? Formally, if $h(n)$ is the maximal value such that every $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ with $|A|=n$ contains such a $B$ with $|B|\geq h(n)$, estimate $h(n)$.
status: Erdős [Er62c] proved $h(n)\ll n^{5/6}$, and Straus [St66] improved this to $h(n)\ll n^{1/2}$. From below, Erdős noted $h(n)\gg n^{1/3}$ by taking $B=\{a:\{\alpha a\}\in n^{-1/3}+\tfrac{1}{2}(-n^{-2/3},n^{-2/3})\}$ for a random $\alpha\in[0,1]$; [Er62c] and Choi [Ch74b] improved this to $h(n)\gg (n\log n)^{1/3}$. See also [186] and [874].
solved_when: The order of magnitude of $h(n)$ as a function of $n$ is determined up to constants, closing the gap between the lower bound $h(n)\gg (n\log n)^{1/3}$ and the upper bound $h(n)\ll n^{1/2}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full solution history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would sharpen our understanding of how much additive structure can be avoided inside any finite set of integers.

title: Erdős problem #790
open: How large a sum-free subset must every set of $n$ integers contain? Formally, if $l(n)$ is the largest number such that every $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ with $|A|=n$ has a sum-free $B\subseteq A$ (no solutions to $a_1=a_2+\cdots+a_r$ with all $a_i\in B$ distinct) with $|B|\geq l(n)$, estimate $l(n)$ — in particular, is $l(n)n^{-1/2}\to\infty$, and is $l(n)<n^{1-c}$ for some $c>0$?
status: Erdős observed $l(n)\geq (n/2)^{1/2}$, which Choi improved to $l(n)>(1+c)n^{1/2}$ for some $c>0$. Erdős [Er73] thought he could prove $l(n)=o(n)$ but had 'difficulties in reconstructing [his] proof' (in [Er65] he wrote 'by complicated arguments we can show $l(n)=o(n)$'). Choi, Komlós, and Szemerédi [CKS75] proved $\left(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}n\right)^{1/2}\ll l(n)\ll \frac{n}{\log n}$, and further conjecture that $l(n)\geq n^{1-o(1)}$. See also [876].
solved_when: $l(n)$ is determined up to constants (or asymptotically); at minimum, deciding whether $l(n)n^{-1/2}\to\infty$ and whether $l(n)<n^{1-c}$ for some $c>0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; it sits at the heart of estimating guaranteed sum-free subsets of arbitrary integer sets.

title: Erdős problem #791
open: Let $g(n)$ be the smallest size of a set $A\subseteq \{0,\ldots,n\}$ whose sumset $A+A$ covers $\{0,\ldots,n\}$. What is the asymptotic behavior of $g(n)$ — in particular, is it true that $g(n)\sim 2n^{1/2}$?
status: Such a set is called a finite additive $2$-basis; the problem originates with Rohrbach, who proved in [Ro37] that $(2+c)n \leq g(n)^2 \leq 4n$ for some small constant $c>0$. The conjecture $g(n)\sim 2n^{1/2}$ was disproved by Mrose [Mr79], whose construction implies $g(n)^2 \leq \frac{7}{2}n$. The current best-known bounds are $(2.181\cdots+o(1))n \leq g(n)^2 \leq (3.458\cdots+o(1))n$, the lower bound due to Yu [Yu15] and the upper bound due to Kohonen [Ko17]. The problem is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/791.
solved_when: An asymptotic estimate of $g(n)$ is obtained; success would be deciding whether $g(n)\sim 2n^{1/2}$, or otherwise narrowing the gap between the known constants in the bounds $(2.181\cdots+o(1))n \leq g(n)^2 \leq (3.458\cdots+o(1))n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and determining $g(n)$ resolves the long-standing question (of Rohrbach) of how small a finite additive $2$-basis for $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ can be.

title: Erdős problem #792
open: How large a sum-free subset must every set of $n$ integers contain? Formally, if $f(n)$ is the largest integer such that every $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ with $|A|=n$ has a sum-free $B\subseteq A$ with $|B|\geq f(n)$ (i.e., no solutions to $a+b=c$ with $a,b,c\in B$), estimate $f(n)$.
status: Erdős [Er65] gave a simple proof showing $f(n)\geq n/3$. Alon and Kleitman [AlKl90] improved this to $f(n)\geq \frac{n+1}{3}$, and Bourgain [Bo97] further improved it to $\frac{n+2}{3}$. The best lower bound known is $f(n)\geq \frac{n}{3}+c\log\log n$ for some constant $c>0$, due to Bedert [Be25b]. The best upper bound known is $f(n)\leq \frac{n}{3}+o(n)$, due to Eberhard, Green, and Manners [EGM14]. This is Problem 1 on Green's open problems list.
solved_when: The asymptotic behavior of $f(n)$ is determined — in particular, the gap between the known lower bound $f(n)\geq \frac{n}{3}+c\log\log n$ and the upper bound $f(n)\leq \frac{n}{3}+o(n)$ is closed.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would settle a central question in additive combinatorics about the unavoidable size of sum-free structure in arbitrary integer sets.

title: Erdős problem #796
open: For $k\geq 2$, let $g_k(n)$ be the largest size of a set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that no integer $m$ has $k$ or more representations $m=a_1a_2$ with $a_1<a_2\in A$. Is it true that $g_3(n)=\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+(c+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}$ for some constant $c$ — that is, does the second-order term of $g_3(n)$ exist with a linear-in-$\log n$ denominator?
status: Erdős [Er64d] proved that if $2^{r-1}<k\leq 2^r$ then $g_k(n)\sim\frac{(\log\log n)^{r-1}}{(r-1)!\log n}n$ (the asymptotic count of integers $\leq n$ with $r$ distinct prime factors), so the first-order asymptotics of $g_k(n)$ are known. In [Er69b] Erdős discussed the second-order terms, and this question is implicit there, especially compared to the explicit question [425] he asked on several occasions. In [Er69] the question appears with a denominator of $(\log n)^2$ in the second term; moreover, for $k=3$ he claims he could prove $\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_1\frac{n}{(\log n)^2}\leq g_3(n)\leq\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_2\frac{n}{(\log n)^2}$ for some $0<c_1\leq c_2$. This is strange, since in [Er64d] his upper and lower bound techniques in fact prove $\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_1\frac{n}{\log n}\leq g_3(n)\leq\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+c_2\frac{n}{\log n}$ for some $0<c_1\leq c_2$; the $(\log n)^2$ in [Er69] is likely a repeated typo with $\log n$ intended in both the reported bounds and the main question.
solved_when: The asymptotic $g_3(n)=\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}n+(c+o(1))\frac{n}{\log n}$ is proven for some explicit constant $c$ (equivalently, the second-order term with denominator $\log n$ is pinned down, correcting the likely typo of $(\log n)^2$ in [Er69]).
why: The leading-order asymptotics of $g_k(n)$ are already known, so this asks for the fine second-order structure of multiplication tables under Erdős's original restriction — a personally posed Erdős problem whose full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #802
open: Must every $K_r$-free graph on $n$ vertices with average degree $t$ contain an independent set on $\gg_r \frac{\log t}{t}n$ vertices?
status: A conjecture of Ajtai, Erdős, Komlós, and Szemerédi [AEKS81], who proved that there must exist an independent set on $\gg_r \frac{\log\log(t+1)}{t}n$ many vertices. Shearer [Sh95] improved this to $\gg_r \frac{\log t}{\log\log(t+1)t}n$. Ajtai, Komlós, and Szemerédi [AKS80] proved the conjectured bound when $r=3$. Alon [Al96b] proved the conjectured bound, but replacing the $K_r$-free assumption with the stronger assumption that the induced graph on every vertex neighbourhood has chromatic number $\leq r-2$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the bound: every $K_r$-free graph on $n$ vertices with average degree $t$ has an independent set of size $\gg_r \frac{\log t}{t}n$.

title: Erdős problem #805
open: For which functions $g(n)$ with $n>g(n)\geq (\log n)^2$ does there exist a graph on $n$ vertices in which every induced subgraph on $g(n)$ vertices contains both a clique of size at least $\log n$ and an independent set of size at least $\log n$? In particular, is there such a graph for $g(n)=(\log n)^3$?
status: This is a problem of Erdős and Hajnal, who thought that there is no such graph for $g(n)=(\log n)^3$. Alon and Sudakov [AlSu07] proved that there is no such graph with $g(n)=\frac{c}{\log\log n}(\log n)^3$ for some constant $c>0$. Alon, Bucić, and Sudakov [ABS21] constructed such a graph with $g(n)\leq 2^{2^{(\log\log n)^{1/2+o(1)}}}$. See also [804].
solved_when: A complete characterization of the functions $g(n)$ with $n>g(n)\geq(\log n)^2$ for which such a graph exists is given, or at minimum the case $g(n)=(\log n)^3$ is settled.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling the threshold determines how uniformly small induced subgraphs can force large homogeneous sets.

title: Erdős problem #809
open: Must every graph on $n$ vertices with $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1$ edges admit, for some $r$ on the order of $n^2/8$, an edge-colouring with $r$ colours in which every copy of an odd cycle $C_{2k+1}$ is rainbow? Formally, is it true that, for all $k\geq 3$, $\chi_S(n, \lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1, C_{2k+1})\sim n^2/8$?
status: The problem originates with Burr, Erdős, Graham, and Sós [BEGS89], who proved $\chi_S(n, \lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1, C_{2k+1})\gg_k n^2$. Bucić, Chen, and Ma [BCM26] solved it affirmatively for all $k\geq 4$. The cases $C_3$ and $C_5$ behave quite differently: it is easy to see $\chi_S(n, \lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1, C_3)=3$, and Erdős and Simonovits proved (as reported in [BEGS89]) that $\chi_S(n, \lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1, C_5)=\lfloor n/2\rfloor+3$ for all large $n$. See also [810].
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved) that $\chi_S(n, \lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1, C_{2k+1})\sim n^2/8$ for all $k\geq 3$; since the case $k\geq 4$ is settled, the remaining target is the asymptotic constant $1/8$ for $k=3$ — though note $\chi_S(n, \lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1, C_3)=3$ exactly, so the open instances are precisely the asserted asymptotics for the remaining $k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it completes the picture of anti-Ramsey behaviour of odd cycles just past the extremal edge count.

title: Erdős problem #810
open: Does some positive constant $\epsilon$ exist such that, for all sufficiently large $n$, there is a graph on $n$ vertices with at least $\epsilon n^2$ edges whose edges can be colored with $n$ colors so that every $C_4$ receives $4$ distinct colors? Equivalently, is there an $\epsilon>0$ with $\chi_S(n,\epsilon n^2,C_4)\leq n$ for all large $n$, where $\chi_S(n,e,G)$ is the anti-Ramsey number — the smallest $r$ such that some $n$-vertex, $e$-edge graph admits an $r$-edge-colouring in which every copy of $G$ has entirely distinct edge colours?
status: The problem is due to Burr, Erdős, Graham, and Sós [BEGS89], who believed the answer is no. In [BEGS89] they prove there does not exist such an $\epsilon$ if $C_4$ is replaced by $P_4$. They also posed the stronger question of whether, for fixed $\epsilon>0$, $\chi_S(n,\epsilon n^2,G)/n\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ for all connected bipartite $G$ that is not a star; Sárközy and Selkow [SaSe06] proved this for all such $G$ except complete bipartite graphs, leaving $C_4$ open in particular. In [BEGS89] they also observe that, for some constant $c>0$, $\chi_S(n, cg(n;7,4),C_4)\leq n$, where $g(n;7,4)$ is the maximum number of edges in a $3$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices in which no $7$ vertices contain $4$ edges; it is unknown, though likely, that $g(n;7,4)=o(n^2)$ (see [1178]). See also [809]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/810; Erdős references: [Er91,p.399].
solved_when: An explicit $\epsilon>0$ is exhibited such that $\chi_S(n,\epsilon n^2,C_4)\leq n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, or it is proved that no such $\epsilon$ exists. The stronger question is settled by determining whether, for fixed $\epsilon>0$, $\chi_S(n,\epsilon n^2,C_4)/n\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it is the remaining open case of the general question of Burr, Erdős, Graham, and Sós on anti-Ramsey numbers of bipartite graphs.

title: Erdős problem #812
open: Does the Ramsey number $R(n)$ grow with genuinely increasing speed — specifically, is $R(n+1)/R(n) \geq 1+c$ for some constant $c>0$ and all large $n$? A stronger conjectured form asks whether $R(n+1)-R(n) \gg n^2$.
status: Burr, Erdős, Faudree, and Schelp [BEFS89] proved that $R(n+1)-R(n) \geq 4n-8$ for all $n\geq 2$. The lower bound of [165] implies that $R(n+2)-R(n) \gg n^{2-o(1)}$.
solved_when: A proof that there exists a constant $c>0$ such that $R(n+1)/R(n) \geq 1+c$ for all sufficiently large $n$; alternatively (stronger form), a proof that $R(n+1)-R(n) \gg n^2$.

title: Erdős problem #813
open: Let $h(n)$ be the smallest number such that every graph on $n$ vertices in which every set of $7$ vertices contains a triangle must contain a clique on at least $h(n)$ vertices. How fast does $h(n)$ grow — in particular, do there exist constants $c_1,c_2>0$ with $n^{1/3+c_1}\ll h(n)\ll n^{1/2-c_2}$?
status: This is a problem of Erdős and Hajnal, who proved $n^{1/3}\ll h(n)\ll n^{1/2}$. Bucić and Sudakov [BuSu23] have since proved $h(n)\gg n^{5/12-o(1)}$.
solved_when: The growth rate of $h(n)$ is pinned down, or at least constants $c_1,c_2>0$ are exhibited such that $n^{1/3+c_1}\ll h(n)\ll n^{1/2-c_2}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a classic extremal question about how local triangle density in 7-sets forces large cliques.

title: Erdős problem #817
open: Given $k\geq 3$, let $g_k(n)$ be the smallest $N$ such that $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ contains an $n$-element set $A$ whose subset-sum set $\langle A\rangle = \{\sum_{a\in A}\epsilon_a a: \epsilon_a\in\{0,1\}\}$ is free of non-trivial $k$-term arithmetic progressions. How fast does $g_k(n)$ grow — in particular, is $g_3(n)\gg 3^n$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Sárközy, who proved $g_3(n)\gg \frac{3^n}{n^{O(1)}}$. History and references are tracked at erdosproblems.com/817; Erdős references: [Er91].
solved_when: An estimate of $g_k(n)$ is obtained, and in particular the lower bound $g_3(n)\gg 3^n$ is proved (or refuted).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would resolve a concrete question at the intersection of additive combinatorics and subset-sum structure.

title: Erdős problem #819
open: How large can the restricted sumset $A+A$ be inside $[1,N]$ when $A$ is a set of about $\sqrt{N}$ integers from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$? Formally, letting $f(N)$ be the maximum of $\lvert (A+A)\cap[1,N]\rvert$ over all $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $\lvert A\rvert=\lfloor N^{1/2}\rfloor$, estimate $f(N)$.
status: In additive combinatorics, Erdős and Freud [ErFr91] proved $\left(\frac{3}{8}-o(1)\right)N \leq f(N) \leq \left(\frac{1}{2}+o(1)\right)N$, and noted that the problem is closely connected to the size of the largest quasi-Sidon set (see [840]).
solved_when: $f(N)$ is determined up to $(1+o(1))$ — equivalently, the gap between the constants $3/8$ and $1/2$ in the known bounds is closed by matching upper and lower bounds of the form $(c-o(1))N \leq f(N) \leq (c+o(1))N$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and settling it would also sharpen our understanding of the closely related question of the size of the largest quasi-Sidon set; its full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #820
open: Is $H(n)=3$ infinitely often — i.e., are $(2^n-1,3^n-1)=1$ for infinitely many $n$ — where $H(n)$ is the smallest $l$ for which some $k<l$ satisfies $(k^n-1,l^n-1)=1$? More broadly, estimate $H(n)$: does some constant $c>0$ exist such that, for every $\epsilon>0$, $H(n) > \exp(n^{(c-\epsilon)/\log\log n})$ infinitely often while $H(n) < \exp(n^{(c+\epsilon)/\log\log n})$ for all large enough $n$? And does a similar upper bound hold for the smallest $k$ with $(k^n-1,2^n-1)=1$?
status: Erdős [Er74b] proved that there exists a constant $c>0$ such that $H(n) > \exp(n^{c/(\log\log n)^2})$ for infinitely many $n$. van Doorn, in the comments, sketches a proof of the stronger lower bound: there exists a constant $c>0$ and infinitely many $n$ such that $H(n) > \exp(n^{c/\log\log n})$. The values of $H(n)$ for $1\leq n\leq 10$ are $3,3,3,6,3,18,3,6,3,12$. The sequence of $n$ for which $(2^n-1,3^n-1)=1$ is OEIS A263647. See also [770].
solved_when: The order of magnitude of $H(n)$ is pinned down: either it is shown that $H(n)=3$ infinitely often (that is, $(2^n-1,3^n-1)=1$ infinitely often) or a sharp estimate of $H(n)$ is given — in particular, resolving whether for some constant $c>0$ and all $\epsilon>0$, $H(n) > \exp(n^{(c-\epsilon)/\log\log n})$ for infinitely many $n$ and $H(n) < \exp(n^{(c+\epsilon)/\log\log n})$ for all sufficiently large $n$, and analogously for the smallest $k$ such that $(k^n-1,2^n-1)=1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with its full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle basic questions about how coprime the values $k^n-1$ can be.

title: Erdős problem #821
open: For a positive integer $n$, let $g(n)$ count how many $m$ satisfy $\phi(m)=n$, where $\phi$ is Euler's totient function. Is it true that, for every $\epsilon>0$, there exist infinitely many $n$ such that $g(n) > n^{1-\epsilon}$?
status: Pillai proved that $\limsup g(n)=\infty$, and Erdős [Er35b] proved that there exists some constant $c>0$ such that $g(n) > n^c$ for infinitely many $n$. The conjecture would follow if we knew that, for every $\epsilon>0$, there are $\gg_\epsilon \frac{x}{\log x}$ many primes $p<x$ such that all prime factors of $p-1$ are $<p^\epsilon$. The best known bound, due to Lichtman [Li22], is that there are infinitely many $n$ such that $g(n) > n^{0.71568\cdots}$, obtained as a consequence of proving that there are $\geq \frac{x}{(\log x)^{O(1)}}$ many primes $p\leq x$ such that all prime factors of $p-1$ are $\leq x^{0.2843\cdots}$, improving a number of previous exponents, most recently those of Baker and Harman [BaHa98]. The average size of $g(n)$ was investigated by Luca and Pollack [LuPo11]. See also [416].
solved_when: For every $\epsilon>0$, infinitely many $n$ satisfy $g(n) > n^{1-\epsilon}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; a solution would resolve a long-standing question about how often the totient function takes the same value, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #824
open: Let $h(x)$ count pairs of integers $1\leq a<b<x$ with $(a,b)=1$ and $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)$, where $\sigma$ is the sum-of-divisors function. Is it true that $h(x)>x^{2-o(1)}$?
status: Erdős [Er74b] proved that $\limsup h(x)/x=\infty$ and claimed a similar proof for this problem; a complete proof that $h(x)/x\to\infty$ was provided by Pollack and Pomerance [PoPo16]. A similar question can be asked replacing the condition $(a,b)=1$ with the condition that $a$ and $b$ are squarefree. Weisenberg suggests another variant, requiring that there are no proper factors $u\mid a$ and $v\mid b$ such that $\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)$ and $(u,a/u)=(v,b/v)=1$, which is the weakest restriction one can impose that is still strong enough to eliminate trivial duplicates.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $h(x)>x^{2-o(1)}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a positive answer would show that equal divisor sums among coprime pairs occur essentially as often as possible.

title: Erdős problem #826
open: Are there infinitely many $n$ such that the divisor function satisfies $\tau(n+k)\ll k$ for all $k\geq 1$ — that is, can the entire shifted tail of one number's divisor counts be simultaneously linear in the shift?
status: In the number-theoretic literature this is viewed as a stronger form of [248]. Lau [La26] has proved that there exists an absolute constant $C$ such that, for infinitely many $n$, $\tau(n+k)\ll k^C$ for all $k\geq 1$.
solved_when: A proof that infinitely many $n$ satisfy $\tau(n+k)\ll k$ for every $k\geq 1$ (or a proof that only finitely many such $n$ exist).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked publicly at erdosproblems.com/826.

title: Erdős problem #827
open: For each $k$, is there a number $n_k$ such that any $n_k$ points in general position in $\mathbb{R}^2$ contain a $k$-point subset whose $\binom{k}{3}$ triples determine circles of pairwise distinct radii — and if so, what is the exact value of $n_k$?
status: In [Er75h] Erdős asks whether $n_k$ exists. In [Er78c] he gave a simple argument proving that it does, in fact $n_k \leq k+2\binom{k-1}{2}\binom{k-1}{3}$, but this argument is incorrect, as explained by Martinez and Roldán-Pensado [MaRo15], who give a corrected argument proving $n_k\ll k^9$. A simple probabilistic argument, given in the comments by FlaredRain, improves this to $n_k\ll k^5$.
solved_when: The value of $n_k$ is determined (or asymptotically tightly bounded).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would pin down a basic Ramsey-type parameter in combinatorial geometry.

title: Erdős problem #828
open: Is it true that for every integer $a$ there are infinitely many $n$ such that Euler's totient function divides $n+a$ — that is, $\phi(n) \mid n+a$?
status: The statement is a conjecture of Graham. Lehmer has conjectured that $\phi(n)\mid n-1$ if and only if $n$ is prime, and it is an easy exercise to show that $\phi(n) \mid n$ if and only if $n=2^a3^b$ for some $a,b\geq 0$. The problem is discussed as B37 in Guy's collection [Gu04] (see also [Er83]).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for any fixed $a\in\mathbb{Z}$ the congruence $\phi(n)\mid n+a$ holds for infinitely many $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and a resolution would clarify the divisibility structure of $\phi(n)$ relative to shifts of $n$; it is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #829
open: Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be the set of cubes. Is it true that\[1_A\ast 1_A(n) \ll (\log n)^{O(1)}?\]
status: number theory Mordell proved that\[\limsup_{n\to \infty} 1_A\ast 1_A(n)=\infty\]and Mahler [Ma35b] proved\[1_A\ast 1_A(n) \gg (\log n)^{1/4}\]for infinitely many $n$. Stewart [St08] improved this to\[1_A\ast 1_A(n) \gg (\log n)^{11/13}.\]

title: Erdős problem #830
open: Are there infinitely many pairs of natural numbers $a,b$ with $\sigma(a)=\sigma(b)=a+b$ — amicable pairs, such as $220$ and $284$? More precisely, if $A(x)$ counts amicable pairs $1\leq a\leq b\leq x$, is it true that $A(x)>x^{1-o(1)}$?
status: Erdős [Er55b] proved $A(x)=o(x)$. Pomerance [Po81] improved this to $A(x) \leq x \exp(-(\log x)^{1/3})$, and later [Po15] to $A(x) \leq x \exp(-(\tfrac{1}{2}+o(1))(\log x\log\log x)^{1/2})$. This is problem B4 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that there are infinitely many amicable pairs; the quantitative target is whether $A(x) > x^{1-o(1)}$ as $x\to\infty$.

title: Erdős problem #831
open: How many distinct radii must be forced by any $n$ points in the plane in general position (no three collinear, no four concyclic), in the sense of circles through triples of the points? Formally, letting $h(n)$ denote the maximum such that every configuration of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no three on a line and no four on a circle admits at least $h(n)$ circles of pairwise different radii through three of the points, estimate $h(n)$.
status: The problem is recorded in the geometry section of Erdős's problems, with cross-references [104] and [506]; see erdosproblems.com/831, with Erdős references [Er75h] and [Er92e].
solved_when: An asymptotically tight estimate of $h(n)$ is obtained — that is, matching (up to constants) upper and lower bounds on the number of distinct radii guaranteed for $n$ points in general position as above.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would resolve a long-standing entry in that catalog of his geometry questions.

title: Erdős problem #835
open: Does any $k>2$ admit a colouring of the $k$-subsets of $\{1,\ldots,2k\}$ with $k+1$ colours such that every $(k+1)$-subset contains $k$-subsets of all $k+1$ colours? Equivalently, is the chromatic number of the Johnson graph $J(2k,k)$ ever equal to $k+1$ for $k>2$?
status: Trivially possible for $k=2$; Erdős and Rosenfeld were not sure about $k=6$. The chromatic number of $J(2k,k)$ is always at least $k+1$ and at most $2k$. The chromatic numbers listed at erdosproblems.com show the answer is false for $3\leq k\leq 8$. Ma and Tang proved that $\chi(J(2k,k))>k+1$ for all $k>2$ not of the form $p-1$ for prime $p$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/835; Erdős references: [Er74d,p.283].
solved_when: Either an example of some $k>2$ with $\chi(J(2k,k))=k+1$ is given, or it is proved that $\chi(J(2k,k))>k+1$ for every $k>2$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with Rosenfeld), tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles the chromatic number of Johnson graphs at its natural lower bound.

title: Erdős problem #836
open: Let $r\geq 2$ and $G$ be an $r$-uniform hypergraph with chromatic number $3$ (that is, there is a $3$-colouring of the vertices of $G$ such that no edge is monochromatic). Suppose any two edges of $G$ have a non-empty intersection. Must $G$ contain $O(r^2)$ many vertices? Must there be two edges which meet in $\gg r$ many vertices?
status: A problem of Erdős and Shelah. The Fano geometry gives an example where there are no two edges which meet in $r-1$ vertices, and it is open whether there are any other such examples. Erdős and Lovász [ErLo75] proved that there must be two edges which meet in $\gg \frac{r}{\log r}$ many vertices. Alon provided a counterexample to the first question: take two sets $X$ and $Y$ of sizes $2r-2$ and $\frac{1}{2}\binom{2r-2}{r-1}$ respectively, where $Y$ corresponds to all partitions of $X$ into two equal parts; the edges are all subsets of $X$ of size $r$, together with all sets consisting of a subset of $X$ of size $r-1$ and the unique element of $Y$ corresponding to the induced partition of $X$. This hypergraph is intersecting, has chromatic number $3$, and has $\asymp 4^r/\sqrt{r}$ many vertices. Key works: erdosproblems.com/836; Erdős references: [Er74d].
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for each of the two questions: whether such an intersecting $3$-chromatic $r$-uniform hypergraph must have $O(r^2)$ vertices, and whether it must contain two edges meeting in $\gg r$ vertices (improving the known $\gg \frac{r}{\log r}$ bound).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it probes the extremal structure of intersecting hypergraphs with low chromatic number.
aliases: Erdős #836; graph theory / hypergraphs / chromatic number

title: Erdős problem #837
open: For $k\geq 2$, let $A_k\subseteq[0,1]$ be the set of $\alpha$ such that there exists some $\beta(\alpha)>\alpha$ with the following property: whenever $G_1,G_2,\ldots$ is a sequence of $k$-uniform hypergraphs with $\liminf e(G_n)/\binom{|G_n|}{k}>\alpha$, there exist subgraphs $H_n\subseteq G_n$ with $|H_n|\to\infty$ and $\liminf e(H_n)/\binom{|H_n|}{k}>\beta$ — and further, this property need not hold if $>\alpha$ is replaced by $\geq\alpha$. What is $A_3$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Simonovits. It is known that $A_2=\{1-1/k:k\geq 1\}$. (See erdosproblems.com/837; Erdős references: [Er74d].)
solved_when: The set $A_3$ is explicitly determined, matching the style of the known description $A_2=\{1-1/k:k\geq 1\}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with Simonovits), tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a description of $A_3$ would settle the first open uniformity level of the problem.

title: Erdős problem #838
open: Given $n$ points in the plane with no three collinear, how many distinct convex subsets must they determine? If $f(n)$ denotes the minimum possible number, does $\log f(n)$ grow like a constant times $(\log n)^2$, i.e. does there exist a constant $c$ such that $\lim \frac{\log f(n)}{(\log n)^2}=c$?
status: A question of Erdős and Hammer. Erdős proved in [Er78c] that there exist constants $c_1,c_2>0$ such that $n^{c_1\log n}<f(n)<n^{c_2\log n}$. See also [107].
solved_when: The limit $\lim \frac{\log f(n)}{(\log n)^2}$ is shown to exist (and ideally its value determined); equivalently, the known bounds $n^{c_1\log n}<f(n)<n^{c_2\log n}$ are tightened to matching order.
why: Resolving it would settle the exact asymptotic order of the number of convex subsets in general-position point sets, a natural extremal-geometric measure of combinatorial richness; it is one of Erdős's personally posed problems with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #839
open: If an increasing sequence of integers $1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots$ has the property that no $a_i$ is the sum of consecutive earlier terms $a_j$ ($j<i$), must the sequence be genuinely sparse — specifically, must $\limsup a_n/n=\infty$? Or, more weakly, must $\lim \frac{1}{\log x}\sum_{a_n<x}\frac{1}{a_n}=0$?
status: Erdős notes it is easy to see that $\liminf a_n/n<\infty$ is possible, and that one can have $\sum_{a_n<x} 1/a_n \gg \log\log x$. The upper density of such a sequence can be $1/2$, and Erdős thought it probably could not exceed $1/2$; this is false — Freud [Fr93] constructed a sequence with upper density $19/36$. See also [359] and [867].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given of either $\limsup \frac{a_n}{n}=\infty$ or $\lim \frac{1}{\log x}\sum_{a_n<x}\frac{1}{a_n}=0$ for every sequence with the stated property.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with its full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would clarify how strongly the "no consecutive-sum" constraint forces sparsity of a sequence.

title: Erdős problem #840
open: Let $f(N)$ be the size of the largest quasi-Sidon subset $A\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$, where we say that $A$ is quasi-Sidon if $\lvert A+A\rvert=(1+o(1))\binom{\lvert A\rvert}{2}$. How does $f(N)$ grow?
status: The problem was considered by Erdős and Freud [ErFr91], who proved $\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+o(1)\right)N^{1/2} \leq f(N) \leq \left(2+o(1)\right)N^{1/2}$, though both bounds had already been given by Erdős in [Er81h]. Here $2/\sqrt{3}=1.15\cdots$. The lower bound comes from taking a genuine Sidon set $B\subset [1,N/3]$ of size $\sim N^{1/2}/\sqrt{3}$ and taking the union with $\{N-b : b\in B\}$. Pikhurko [Pi06] improved the upper bound to $f(N) \leq \left(\left(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{(\pi+2)^2}\right)^{-1/2}+o(1)\right)N^{1/2}$, where the constant is $1.863\cdots$. The analogous question with $A-A$ in place of $A+A$ is simpler, and there the maximal size is $\sim N^{1/2}$, as proved by Cilleruelo. See also [30], [819], and [864].
solved_when: The asymptotic behavior of $f(N)$ is determined, i.e., the unknown constant $c$ in $f(N) = (c+o(1))N^{1/2}$ is identified (or shown not to exist), improving on the current bounds $\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+o(1)\right)N^{1/2} \leq f(N) \leq \left(\left(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{(\pi+2)^2}\right)^{-1/2}+o(1)\right)N^{1/2}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; closing the gap between $1.15\cdots$ and $1.863\cdots$ in the leading constant would resolve a basic question about how weakly the Sidon property can be relaxed while still limiting a set to order $N^{1/2}$.

title: Erdős problem #848
open: Is the maximum size of a subset $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $ab+1$ never squarefree (for all $a,b\in A$) achieved by taking those $n\equiv 7\pmod{25}$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Sárközy. Van Doorn gave an argument showing $|A| \leq (0.108\cdots + o(1))N$: the condition forces $a^2+1$ divisible by $p^2$ for some prime $p$ for every $a\in A$, and since $a^2+1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$ has $2$ or $0$ solutions according as $p\equiv 1$ or $3 \pmod 4$, every $a\in A$ lies in one of $2$ residue classes for some prime $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$, giving $|A|/N \leq 2\sum_{p\equiv 1\pmod 4} 1/p^2 \approx 0.108$ as $N\to\infty$. Weisenberg noted the proof gives a slightly better constant of $\approx 0.105$ (see the comments section). Sawhney solved this for all sufficiently large $N$ in this note, proving something slightly stronger: there exists $c>0$ such that if $|A| \geq (\frac{1}{25}-c)N$ and $N$ is large, then $A$ is contained in either $\{n\equiv 7\pmod{25}\}$ or $\{n\equiv 18\pmod{25}\}$. See also [844]. (Key works: erdosproblems.com/848; Erdős references: [Er92b,p.239])
solved_when: The extremal size of $A$ is determined, matching (or refuting) the residue class construction $n\equiv 7\pmod{25}$, which has density $1/25$; equivalently, a proof that the maximum is exactly the size of that class for all (or all sufficiently large) $N$.

title: Erdős problem #849
open: Is it true that, for every integer $t\geq 1$, there exists an integer $a$ such that the equation $\binom{n}{k}=a$ (with $1\leq k\leq n/2$) has exactly $t$ solutions? Equivalently, does every possible multiplicity of a value in Pascal's triangle actually occur?
status: Erdős [Er96b] credits this problem to himself and Gordon 'many years ago', but it is more commonly known as Singmaster's conjecture. For $t=3$ one can take $a=120$, and for $t=4$ one can take $a=3003$; no examples are known for $t\geq 5$. Both Erdős and Singmaster believed the answer is no, and in fact that there is an absolute upper bound on the number of solutions. Matomäki, Radziwill, Shao, Tao, and Teräväinen [MRSTT22] have proved that, assuming $a$ is sufficiently large depending on $\epsilon>0$, there are always at most two solutions if $k$ is restricted to $k\geq \exp((\log n)^{2/3+\epsilon})$.
solved_when: For every integer $t\geq 1$ an integer $a$ is exhibited (or proven to exist) such that $\binom{n}{k}=a$ with $1\leq k\leq n/2$ has exactly $t$ solutions; the problem is settled in the negative by a proof that some $t$ occurs as no value's multiplicity, or by an absolute upper bound on the number of solutions.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it touches the core of Singmaster's conjecture on how often values can repeat in Pascal's triangle.

title: Erdős problem #850
open: Can there exist two distinct integers $x$ and $y$ such that $x$ and $y$ have the same prime factors, $x+1$ and $y+1$ have the same prime factors, and $x+2$ and $y+2$ also have the same prime factors?
status: This is sometimes known as the Erdős-Woods conjecture. For just $x,y$ and $x+1,y+1$ one can take $x=2(2^r-1)$ and $y=x(x+2)$. Erdős also asked whether there are any other examples. Makowski [Ma68] observed that $x=75$ and $y=1215$ is another example, since $75=3\cdot 5^2$ and $1215=3^5\cdot 5$, while $76=2^2\cdot 19$ and $1216=2^6\cdot 19$. (This example was also found independently by Matthew Bolan, and by Dubickas, who posed it as part of the 2024 team selection test in Lithuania.) No other examples are known; the sequence is listed as A343101 at the OEIS. Shorey and Tijdeman [ShTi16] have shown that, assuming a strong form of the ABC conjecture due to Baker, the answer to the original problem is no. See also [677]. The case of $x,y$ and $x+1,y+1$ appeared as Problem 1 in the Third Benelux Mathematical Olympiad 2011. The problem is discussed as problem B19 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: The question is answered definitively: either an explicit pair of distinct integers $x,y$ satisfying the three simultaneous same-prime-factors conditions is exhibited, or it is proved that no such pair exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, sometimes known as the Erdős-Woods conjecture, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #852
open: Consider the consecutive gaps $d_n = p_{n+1}-p_n$ between successive primes. How long a run of consecutive gaps, starting below some bound $x$, can be found with all gaps distinct? Formally, if $h(x)$ is the largest $h$ such that $d_n, d_{n+1}, \ldots, d_{n+h-1}$ are all distinct for some $n < x$, estimate $h(x)$ — in particular, is it true that $h(x) > (\log x)^c$ for some constant $c>0$, and that $h(x) = o(\log x)$?
status: Brun's sieve implies $h(x) \to \infty$ as $x \to \infty$ (see erdosproblems.com/852; Erdős reference [Er85c]).
solved_when: An asymptotic estimate of $h(x)$ is obtained; minimally, a proof or disproof of $h(x) > (\log x)^c$ for some constant $c>0$ together with a determination of whether $h(x) = o(\log x)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/852, so resolving it closes a numbered entry in that collection.

title: Erdős problem #853
open: Let $d_n = p_{n+1} - p_n$ denote the gap between consecutive primes, and let $r(x)$ be the smallest even integer $t$ that does not occur as a prime gap $d_n = t$ for any $n \le x$. Does $r(x) \to \infty$, or even $r(x)/\log x \to \infty$?
status: In [Er85c] Erdős states the problem but omits the condition that $t$ be even, which is clearly necessary.
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved) whether $r(x) \to \infty$, and ideally whether the stronger bound $r(x)/\log x \to \infty$ holds.
why: A positive answer would show that small prime gaps are eventually all "used up" below any fixed threshold, sharpening our understanding of the distribution of consecutive prime gaps; it is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #854
open: For the $k$th primorial $n_k$, list the integers $1=a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_{\phi(n_k)}=n_k-1$ coprime to $n_k$ and consider the gaps $a_{i+1}-a_i$, which are all even — how well can one estimate the smallest even integer that never occurs as such a gap? More formally, are there $\gg \max_i (a_{i+1}-a_i)$ many even integers representable as $a_{j+1}-a_j$?
status: This was asked by Erdős in Oberwolfach, most likely in 1986. Erdős first thought that (for large enough $k$) all even $t\leq \max(a_{i+1}-a_i)$ can be written as $t=a_{j+1}-a_j$ for some $j$, but in [Ob1] writes 'perhaps this is false', and reports computations of Lacampagne and Selfridge showing this fails for $n_k=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13$, which 'show some doubt on [his] conjecture'; he says it could fail for all or infinitely many $k$. In [Ob1] he also asks about the set of $j$ for which $a_{j+1}-a_j=\max(a_{i+1}-a_i)$, in particular requesting estimates on the number of such $j$ and the minimal value of such a $j$.
solved_when: An estimate is obtained for the smallest even integer not of the form $a_{i+1}-a_i$, together with an answer to whether $\gg \max_i (a_{i+1}-a_i)$ many even integers occur as gaps $a_{j+1}-a_j$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems about the structure of reduced residue systems of primorials, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would clarify how evenly the gap sizes of integers coprime to $n_k$ are distributed.

title: Erdős problem #855
open: Is it true that for all large $x$ and $y$, the number of primes up to $x+y$ is at most $\pi(x)+\pi(y)$, where $\pi(x)$ counts the primes in $[1,x]$? That is, does $\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)$ hold eventually?
status: Commonly known as the second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture. In [Er85c] Erdős describes it as 'an old conjecture of mine which was probably already stated by Hardy and Littlewood'. It is probably false: Hensley and Richards [HeRi73] have shown it is false assuming the Hardy–Littlewood prime tuples conjecture; indeed, under that conjecture, for every large $y$ there are infinitely many $x$ such that $\pi(x+y)>\pi(x)+\pi(y)+(\log 2-o(1))\frac{y}{(\log y)^2}$, where the $o(1)$ term tends to $0$ as $y\to\infty$. Erdős [Er85c] reports Straus as remarking that the 'correct way' of stating the conjecture would have been $\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+2\pi(y/2)$, but Clark and Jarvis [ClJa01] have shown this is also incompatible with the prime tuples conjecture. In [Er85c] Erdős conjectures the weaker result (which in particular follows from the conjecture of Straus) that $\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)+O\left(\frac{y}{(\log y)^2}\right)$, which the Hensley and Richards result shows (conditionally) would be best possible. Richards conjectured that this weaker statement is false. Erdős and Richards further conjectured that the original inequality is true almost always — that is, the set of exceptions is small.
solved_when: A proof or disproof of the inequality $\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)$ for all sufficiently large $x$ and $y$; alternatively, a resolution of Erdős's weaker conjecture $\pi(x+y) \leq \pi(x)+\pi(y)+O\left(\frac{y}{(\log y)^2}\right)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, commonly known as the second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture; it sits in direct tension with the prime tuples conjecture, so resolving it clarifies which of these central beliefs about the distribution of primes can survive.

title: Erdős problem #856
open: Let $k\geq 3$ and $f_k(N)$ be the maximum value of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$, where $A$ ranges over all subsets of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ which contain no subset of size $k$ with the same pairwise least common multiple. Estimate $f_k(N)$.
status: Erdős [Er70] notes that $f_k(N) \ll \frac{\log N}{\log\log N}$. Indeed, for such a set $A$, for every $t$ there are $<k$ solutions to $t=ap$ with $a\in A$ and $p$ prime, whence $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{p<N}\frac{1}{p}< k \sum_{t<N^2}\frac{1}{t} \ll \log N$, and the bound follows since $\sum_{p<N}\frac{1}{p}\gg \log\log N$. Improved bounds have been given by Tang and Zhang [TaZh25b], who proved $(\log N)^{b_k-o(1)}\leq f_k(N)\leq (\log N)^{c_k+o(1)}$ for some constants $0<b_k\leq c_k\leq 1$, and in particular $(\log N)^{0.438}\leq f_3(N)\leq (\log N)^{0.889}$ for all large $N$. The exponents here are related to progress in the sunflower conjecture [857], to which this problem is closely related: the exponents $c_k$ are $<1$ (so the upper bound is non-trivial) if and only if [857] holds for $k$-sunflowers. The analogous question with natural density in place of logarithmic density (measuring $\lvert A\rvert$ instead of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$) is the subject of [536]; in particular Erdős [Er70] constructed $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $\lvert A\rvert \gg$ (record truncated here).
solved_when: The order of magnitude of $f_k(N)$ is determined — in particular, matching upper and lower bounds of the form $(\log N)^{\alpha+o(1)}$ for each fixed $k\geq 3$ (e.g., closing the gap between $(\log N)^{0.438}$ and $(\log N)^{0.889}$ for $k=3$).
why: The exponents governing $f_k(N)$ are tied to progress on the sunflower conjecture [857]: the upper bound is non-trivial if and only if [857] holds for $k$-sunflowers, so a solution would resolve a question tightly linked to a major open problem in combinatorics.

title: Erdős problem #857
open: Let $m=m(n,k)$ be the least integer such that any collection of sets $A_1,\ldots,A_m\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ must contain a sunflower of size $k$ — a subcollection of $k$ of the $A_i$ whose pairwise intersections all coincide. Can $m(n,k)$ be estimated, or even given an asymptotic formula?
status: The problem belongs to combinatorics and is related to problems [536] and [856]. In [Er70] Erdős asks it in the equivalent formulation with intersection replaced by union; it is sometimes known as the weak sunflower problem (see [20] for the strong sunflower problem). When $k=3$ it is strongly connected to the cap set problem — finding the maximal size of subsets of $\mathbb{F}_3^n$ with no three-term arithmetic progressions — as observed by Alon, Shpilka, and Umans [ASU13]. Naslund and Sawin [NaSa17] proved $m(n,3) \leq (3/2^{2/3})^{(1+o(1))n}$.
solved_when: An estimate — ideally an asymptotic formula — for $m(n,k)$ is obtained for general $n$ and $k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and for $k=3$ it is strongly connected to the cap set problem, so progress here feeds directly into that central area.

title: Erdős problem #859
open: Let $t\geq 1$ and let $d_t$ be the density of the set of integers $n\in\mathbb{N}$ for which $t$ can be represented as the sum of distinct divisors of $n$. Do there exist constants $c_1,c_2>0$ such that $d_t \sim \frac{c_1}{(\log t)^{c_2}}$ as $t\to\infty$?
status: Erdős [Er70] proved that $d_t$ always exists, and that there exist constants $c_3,c_4>0$ with $\frac{1}{(\log t)^{c_3}} < d_t < \frac{1}{(\log t)^{c_4}}$.
solved_when: Explicit constants $c_1,c_2>0$ are exhibited with a proof that $d_t \sim \frac{c_1}{(\log t)^{c_2}}$ as $t\to\infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling the asymptotic order of $d_t$ would complete the picture beyond Erdős's power-of-log bounds.

title: Erdős problem #860
open: How short can an interval be that, for every $m \geq 1$, contains integers divisible by each of the first $\pi(n)$ primes, one integer per prime? Formally, estimate the minimal $h(n)$ such that $(m, m+h(n))$ always contains distinct $a_i$ with $p_i \mid a_i$ for $1 \leq i \leq \pi(n)$.
status: A problem of Erdős and Pomerance [ErPo80], who proved $h(n) \ll \frac{n^{3/2}}{(\log n)^{1/2}}$. Erdős and Selfridge proved $h(n) > (3-o(1))n$, and Ruzsa proved $h(n)/n \to \infty$. The problem is discussed as B32 in Guy's collection [Gu04]; see also [375].
solved_when: The order of magnitude of $h(n)$ is determined (up to constants), improving on the known bounds $h(n) > (3-o(1))n$, $h(n)/n \to \infty$, and $h(n) \ll n^{3/2}/(\log n)^{1/2}$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #864
open: How large can a set $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be if at most one integer $n$ has more than one representation as $n=a+b$ with $a\leq b\in A$? In particular, is the maximal size of $|A|$ at most $(1+o(1))\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}N^{1/2}$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Freud, who prove the matching lower bound $\lvert A\rvert \geq (1+o(1))\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}N^{1/2}$, by taking a genuine Sidon set $B\subset [1,N/3]$ of size $\sim N^{1/2}/\sqrt{3}$ and taking the union with $\{N-b : b\in B\}$. For the analogous question with $n=a-b$ they prove that $\lvert A\rvert\sim N^{1/2}$. This is a weaker form of [840]. (See erdosproblems.com/864; Erdős references: [Er92c].)
solved_when: An upper bound $\lvert A\rvert \leq (1+o(1))\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}N^{1/2}$ is proved for all such sets $A$, or the asymptotics of the maximal size are otherwise determined.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and sits in the classical study of near-Sidon sets in additive combinatorics.
aliases: Erdős #864; number theory / sidon sets / additive combinatorics

title: Erdős problem #866
open: Let $k\geq 3$ and let $g_k(N)$ be the smallest integer such that any $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,2N\}$ with $\lvert A\rvert \geq N+g_k(N)$ must contain all $\binom{k}{2}$ pairwise sums of some integers $b_1,\ldots,b_k$ (the $b_i$ themselves need not lie in $A$). What is the true order of growth of $g_k(N)$?
status: The problem is due to Choi, Erdős, and Szemerédi. The set of odd numbers in $\{1,\ldots,2N\}$ admits no such $b_i$, so $g_k(N)\geq 0$ always; taking $A$ to be the odds together with the powers of $2$ shows $g_5(N)\gg \log N$. Choi, Erdős, and Szemerédi proved $g_3(N)=2$ and $g_4(N)\ll 1$; van Doorn has shown $g_4(N)\leq 2032$. They also proved $g_5(N)\asymp \log N$ and $g_6(N)\asymp N^{1/2}$, and in general $g_k(N)\ll_k N^{1-2^{-k}}$, while for every $\epsilon>0$, if $k$ is sufficiently large then $g_k(N) > N^{1-\epsilon}$.
solved_when: Sharp estimates for $g_k(N)$ are obtained — in particular, determining the exact value of $g_4(N)$ (known to be bounded, in fact $g_4(N)\leq 2032$), and closing the gap for general $k$ between the upper bound $g_k(N) \ll_k N^{1-2^{-k}}$ and the lower bound $g_k(N) > N^{1-\epsilon}$ for all sufficiently large $k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, posed with Choi and Szemerédi, and solving it would settle a natural extremal question about forced additive structure in dense sets; the full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #870
open: Must every additive basis of order $k \geq 3$ with sufficiently many representations contain a minimal basis of the same order? Formally: for $k \geq 3$ and $A$ an additive basis of order $k$, does there exist a constant $c = c(k) > 0$ such that if $r(n) \geq c \log n$ for all large $n$ then $A$ must contain a minimal basis of order $k$, where $r(n)$ counts representations of $n$ as a sum of at most $k$ elements of $A$?
status: The question is due to Erdős and Nathanson [ErNa79], who proved the analogous statement for $k=2$ under the stronger hypothesis $1_A \ast 1_A(n) > (\log \frac{4}{3})^{-1}\log n$ for all large $n$. Härtter [Ha56] and Nathanson [Na74] showed that additive bases containing no minimal additive basis exist. See also [868].
solved_when: For each $k \geq 3$, a constant $c = c(k) > 0$ is exhibited (or shown not to exist) such that every additive basis $A$ of order $k$ with $r(n) \geq c\log n$ for all large $n$ contains a minimal basis of order $k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it probes the boundary between bases rich enough to contain minimal sub-bases and those, shown to exist, that contain none.

title: Erdős problem #872
open: In the two-player saturation game where players alternately select integers from $\{2,3,\ldots,n\}$ into a common primitive set (no chosen element divides another) until no legal move remains, with one player trying to prolong the game and the other to end it quickly, how long can the game be guaranteed to last? In particular, does it last at least $\epsilon n$ moves for some $\epsilon>0$ and $n$ sufficiently large?
status: The problem is a number-theoretic variant of a combinatorial game of Hajnal, in which players alternately add edges to a graph while keeping it triangle-free; that graph-theoretic game trivially ends in at most $n^2/4$ moves, Füredi and Seress [FuSe91] proved it can be guaranteed to last for $\gg n\log n$ moves, and Biró, Horn, and Wildstrom [BPW16] proved it must end in at most $(\frac{26}{121}+o(1))n^2<0.215n^2$ moves; such games are known as saturation games. Erdős does not specify which player goes first, which may result in different answers. GPT-5.2 Pro, prompted by Price, showed the final question has a negative answer: assuming the 'Prolonger' goes first, the 'Shortener' can guarantee that it ends in at most $(\frac{23}{48}+o(1))n$ moves; this constant has been refined (see the comment section for the latest). Since all primes in $(n/2,n]$ must eventually be chosen, the game must last for at least $\gg \frac{n}{\log n}$ moves.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the game lasts at least $\epsilon n$ moves for some $\epsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$; the stronger question of whether it lasts at least $(1-\epsilon)\frac{n}{2}$ moves has already been answered negatively in the prolonger-first variant.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would determine the true order of a natural primitive-set saturation game.

title: Erdős problem #873
open: Given an infinite increasing sequence of natural numbers $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$, let $F(A,X,k)$ count the indices $i$ for which the least common multiple $[a_i,a_{i+1},\ldots,a_{i+k-1}]$ is less than $X$. Is it true that, for every $\epsilon>0$, one can choose $k$ so that $F(A,X,k)<X^\epsilon$ uniformly over all $A$ and $X$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Szemerédi, who proved that for every $A$, $F(A,X,3)\ll X^{1/3}\log X$, and constructed an $A$ with $F(A,X,3)\gg X^{1/3}\log X$ for infinitely many $X$. It is possible that some sequence attains this bound for every $X$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/873; Erdős references: [Er92c].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given that for every $\epsilon>0$ there exists $k$ (depending only on $\epsilon$) such that $F(A,X,k)<X^\epsilon$ for every sequence $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ and every $X$; a counterexample exhibits an $A$ for which no such $k$ exists for some $\epsilon$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a basic question about how sparse small-lcm blocks must be in arbitrary sequences.

title: Erdős problem #875
open: How slowly can an infinite set $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\subset\mathbb{N}$ grow if its order-specific sumsets $S_r=\{a_1+\cdots+a_r:a_1<\cdots<a_r\in A\}$ are pairwise disjoint for distinct $r\geq 1$? In particular, for which exponents $c$ can the gaps satisfy $a_{n+1}-a_n\leq n^c$?
status: This is a problem of Deshouillers and Erdős, an infinite version of [874]; such sets are sometimes called admissible. Erdős writes 'it [is not] completely trivial to find such a sequence for which $a_{n+1}/a_n\to 1$', and it is not clear from this whether Deshouillers and Erdős knew of such a sequence.
solved_when: The set of exponents $c$ for which there exists such a set (often called admissible) with $a_{n+1}-a_n\leq n^c$ is determined, together with the corresponding growth-rate and gap lower bounds.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution settles a named open question in additive combinatorics.

title: Erdős problem #876
open: Let $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\subset \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite sum-free set — that is, there are no solutions to $a=b_1+\cdots+b_r$ with $b_1<\cdots<b_r<a\in A$. How small can the gap $a_{n+1}-a_n$ be; in particular, is it possible that $a_{n+1}-a_n<n$?
status: Erdős [Er98] writes that Graham 'recently proved' that there is such a sequence for which $a_{n+1}-a_n<n^{1+o(1)}$, and that Melfi proved a somewhat weaker result. Erdős [Er62c] proved that a sum-free set has density zero. Deshouillers, Erdős, and Melfi [DEM99] constructed a sum-free set that grows like $a_n\sim n^{3+o(1)}$. Luczak and Schoen [LuSc00] have proved that, for all large $N$, $\lvert A\cap [1,N]\rvert\ll (N\log N)^{1/2}$, and that there exists a sum-free set $B$ such that $\lvert B\cap [1,N]\rvert \gg \frac{N^{1/2}}{(\log N)^{1/2+o(1)}}$ for all large $N$. In [Er75b] and [Er77c] Erdős asks to determine the maximum possible value of $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}$: Erdős had proved this is $<100$, Sullivan had shown that this is $<4$, and Sullivan conjectured the maximum is slightly larger than $2$. See also [790].
solved_when: A construction of such a sum-free set with $a_{n+1}-a_n<n$ is given, or it is proved that no such set exists.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and would settle the extremal density of sum-free subsets of the naturals.

title: Erdős problem #878
open: Do the two arithmetic functions $f$ and $F$ associated to the prime factorisation of $n$ — where $f(n)=\sum p_i^{\ell_i}$ with $\ell_i$ chosen so that $n\in[p_i^{\ell_i},p_i^{\ell_i+1})$, and $F(n)$ is the maximum of $\sum_i a_i$ over pairwise coprime distinct $a_i\leq n$ whose prime factors all divide $n$ — behave, for almost all $n$, as $f(n)=o(n\log\log n)$ and $F(n)\gg n\log\log n$? In particular, is $\max_{n\leq x}f(n)\sim \frac{x\log x}{\log\log x}$, is $\max_{n\leq x}f(n)=\max_{n\leq x}F(n)$ (for all, or perhaps just all large, $x$), does an asymptotic formula exist for the number of $n<x$ with $f(n)=F(n)$, and does an asymptotic formula exist for $H(x)=\sum_{n<x}\frac{f(n)}{n}$, for which it is asked whether $H(x)\ll x\log\log\log\log x$?
status: Erdős [Er84e] proved that $\max_{n\leq x}f(n)\sim \frac{x\log x}{\log\log x}$ along a sequence of $x\to\infty$, and that $x\log\log\log\log x\ll H(x)\ll x\log\log\log x$. It is trivial that $f(n)\leq F(n)$ for all $n$. It may be true that, for almost all $n$, $F(n)\sim\frac{1}{2}n\log\log n$. Erdős notes that $f(n)/n$ 'almost behaves as a conventional additive function', but unusually $f(n)/n$ does not have a mean value — indeed $\limsup \frac{1}{x}\sum_{n<x}\frac{f(n)}{n}=\infty$ while $\liminf \frac{1}{x}\sum_{n<x}\frac{f(n)}{n}<\infty$. Barreto has noted in the comments that the upper bound for $H(x)$ implies $f(n)=o(n\log\log n)$ for almost all $n$, and also that $\max_{n\leq x}f(n)=\max_{n\leq x}F(n)$ is false at $x=210$. See also [879].
solved_when: Each of the above questions is resolved: almost-all bounds $f(n)=o(n\log\log n)$ and $F(n)\gg n\log\log n$, the asymptotic $\max_{n\leq x}f(n)\sim \frac{x\log x}{\log\log x}$, the equality $\max_{n\leq x}f(n)=\max_{n\leq x}F(n)$ (for all $x$, or for all large $x$), asymptotic formulas for $\#\{n<x: f(n)=F(n)\}$ and for $H(x)=\sum_{n<x}\frac{f(n)}{n}$, and the bound $H(x)\ll x\log\log\log\log x$.
why: The function $f(n)/n$ almost behaves as a conventional additive function yet fails to have a mean value, so resolving these questions would illuminate how such borderline additive behavior distributes; it is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #879
open: How close can the maximum weight of an admissible set in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ — a set of pairwise coprime integers — come to the natural upper bound $H(n)=\sum_{p<n}p + n\pi(n^{1/2})$? Formally, is it true that $G(n) > H(n) - n^{1+o(1)}$, and is it true that for every $k\geq 2$ the extremal admissible set contains an integer with at least $k$ prime factors once $n$ is large enough?
status: Erdős and Van Lint proved that $H(n)-n^{3/2-o(1)} < G(n) < H(n)$ and that $(H(n)-G(n))/n \to \infty$. They established $G(n) > H(n) - n^{1+o(1)}$ assuming 'plausible (but hopeless) assumptions about the distribution of primes', and proved the second claim for $k=2$. See also problem [878]. The problem is tracked at erdosproblems.com/879, with Erdős references [Er84e] [Er98].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $G(n) > H(n) - n^{1+o(1)}$, and a proof that for every $k \geq 2$ and all sufficiently large $n$, the admissible set maximizing $G(n)$ contains at least one integer with at least $k$ prime factors.
why: It determines the precise order of the gap $H(n)-G(n)$ between a natural upper bound and the truth for a classic extremal coprimality problem, and settles structural features of the extremal sets themselves.

title: Erdős problem #881
open: If an additive basis of order $k$ is minimal — removing any infinite subset destroys its property of being a basis of order $k$ — must it nevertheless be possible to remove some infinite subset and still have a basis of order $k+1$?
status: No proof expositions related to this problem have been contributed yet; the problem remains tracked at erdosproblems.com/881, with Erdős reference [Er98].
solved_when: A proof, or a counterexample, showing for every minimal additive basis $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ of order $k$ either that some infinite $B\subset A$ leaves $A\setminus B$ a basis of order $k+1$, or that such a $B$ need not exist.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would clarify how much redundancy minimal additive bases must retain.

title: Erdős problem #883
open: Given a set $A \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$, form the graph $G(A)$ joining two integers when they are coprime: must $G(A)$ contain all odd cycles of length $\leq \frac{n}{3}+1$ once $|A| > \lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor + \lfloor\frac{n}{3}\rfloor - \lfloor\frac{n}{6}\rfloor$? Equivalently, must the same threshold force, for every $\ell \geq 1$ and all sufficiently large $n$, a complete $(1,\ell,\ell)$ tripartite graph on $2\ell+1$ vertices in $G(A)$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Sárkőzy [ErSa97], who proved that if $|A| > \lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor + \lfloor\frac{n}{3}\rfloor - \lfloor\frac{n}{6}\rfloor$ then $G(A)$ contains all odd cycles of length $\leq cn$ for some constant $c>0$. This threshold is best possible: taking $A$ to be the set of $m \leq n$ divisible by $2$ or $3$ yields a $G(A)$ with no triangles. The second question was solved by Sárközy [Sa99], who proved that for large $n$, if $|A|$ exceeds the given threshold then $G(A)$ contains a complete $(1,\ell,\ell)$ tripartite graph with $\ell \gg \frac{\log n}{\log\log n}$.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that, for $|A| > \lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor + \lfloor\frac{n}{3}\rfloor - \lfloor\frac{n}{6}\rfloor$, the graph $G(A)$ contains all odd cycles of length $\leq \frac{n}{3}+1$; and correspondingly that for every $\ell \geq 1$, sufficiently large $n$, and $|A|$ above the same threshold, $G(A)$ contains a complete $(1,\ell,\ell)$ tripartite graph on $2\ell+1$ vertices.
why: Resolving it would determine the exact forcing behavior of the extremal threshold in the coprimality graph; without it we know only that some odd cycles of linear length appear, not the full range up to $\frac{n}{3}+1$ or the full tripartite hierarchy.

title: Erdős problem #885
open: Given an integer $n\geq 1$, define its factor difference set $D(n) = \{|a-b| : n=ab\}$. Is it true that, for every $k\geq 1$, there exist integers $N_1<\cdots<N_k$ such that $|\cap_i D(N_i)| \geq k$?
status: The question is due to Erdős and Rosenfeld [ErRo97], who proved it true for $k=2$. Jiménez-Urroz [Ji99] proved it for $k=3$, and Bremner [Br19] proved it for $k=4$; the general case remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given of the statement that for every $k\geq 1$ there exist integers $N_1<\cdots<N_k$ whose factor difference sets have a common intersection of size at least $k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a complete answer would settle the general pattern of which $k$ such intersections can always be achieved.

title: Erdős problem #886
open: Let $\epsilon>0$. Is it true that, for all large $n$, the number of divisors of $n$ in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+n^{1/2-\epsilon})$ is $O_\epsilon(1)$?
status: Erdős attributes this conjecture to Ruzsa. Erdős and Rosenfeld [ErRo97] proved that there are infinitely many $n$ such that there are four divisors of $n$ in $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+16n^{1/4})$. They also proved that, for any constant $C>0$, all large $n$ have at most $1+C^2$ many divisors in $[n^{1/2}, n^{1/2}+Cn^{1/4}]$. See also [887].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every fixed $\epsilon>0$ there is a constant $C(\epsilon)$ such that all sufficiently large $n$ have at most $C(\epsilon)$ divisors in the interval $(n^{1/2},n^{1/2}+n^{1/2-\epsilon})$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would clarify how divisors can cluster just above $\sqrt{n}$.

title: Erdős problem #887
open: Is there an absolute constant $K$ such that, for every $C>0$, if $n$ is sufficiently large then $n$ has at most $K$ divisors in the interval $(n^{1/2}, n^{1/2}+C n^{1/4})$?
status: The question is due to Erdős and Rosenfeld [ErRo97], who proved that infinitely many $n$ have $4$ divisors in $(n^{1/2}, n^{1/2}+n^{1/4})$, and asked whether $4$ is best possible. They also showed that for $n$ large enough depending on $C$, $n$ has at most $1+C^2$ divisors in $(n^{1/2}, n^{1/2}+C n^{1/4})$. Chan [Ch14] resolved the case when $n$ is a square, proving that a square $n$ has at most $5$ divisors in $[n^{1/2}-n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/7}, n^{1/2}+n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/7}]$. In [Ch15], Chan further proves that if $n=(N-a)(N-b)$ for some $0\leq a\leq b\leq \exp((\log n)^{2/7})$, then $n$ has at most $18$ divisors in $[n^{1/2}-n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/14}, n^{1/2}+n^{1/4}(\log n)^{1/14}]$. See also [886].
solved_when: An absolute constant $K$ is exhibited such that for every $C>0$, all sufficiently large $n$ (depending on $C$) have at most $K$ divisors in $(n^{1/2}, n^{1/2}+C n^{1/4})$. Equivalently, since $4$ divisors in this interval are known to occur infinitely often (with $C=1$), the sharp value would show whether $4$ is best possible.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles how tightly divisors can cluster just above $\sqrt{n}$.

title: Erdős problem #889
open: Do the consecutive integers $n, n+1, n+2, \dots$ eventually contain terms with arbitrarily many "new" prime factors? Formally, for $k\geq 0$ let $v(n,k)$ count the prime factors of $n+k$ that do not divide any $n+i$ for $0\leq i<k$ (equivalently, the prime factors of $n+k$ exceeding $k$); is it true that $v_0(n)=\max_{k\geq 0}v(n,k)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$?
status: The question is due to Erdős and Selfridge [ErSe67], who could only show that $v_0(n)\geq 2$ for $n\geq 17$. More generally, they conjecture that $v_l(n)=\max_{k\geq l}v(n,k)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ for every fixed $l$, but could not even prove that $v_1(n)\geq 2$ for all large $n$. The problem appears as B27 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: It is proved that $v_0(n)=\max_{k\geq 0}v(n,k)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$; the record states no further quantitative target.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it probes how prime factors distribute among consecutive integers — a basic structure the current methods barely touch.

title: Erdős problem #890
open: In any block of $k$ consecutive integers, must the total count of prime factors exceeding $k$ be small infinitely often? Formally, writing $\omega_k(n)$ for the number of distinct prime factors of $n$ greater than $k$, is it true that, for every $k\geq 1$, \[\liminf_{n\to \infty}\sum_{0\leq i<k}\omega_k(n+i)\leq k?\] And, without the size restriction, is it true that \[\limsup_{n\to \infty}\left(\sum_{0\leq i<k}\omega(n+i)\right)\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}=1,\] where $\omega$ counts all distinct prime factors?
status: The question is due to Erdős and Selfridge [ErSe67], who observed that $\liminf_{n\to \infty}\sum_{0\leq i<k}\omega_k(n+i)\geq k-1$ for every $k$; this follows from Pólya's theorem that the set of $k$-smooth integers has unbounded gaps, since for large $n$ all but at most one of $n,n+1,\ldots,n+k-1$ has a prime factor $>k$. It is classical that $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\omega(n)\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}=1$. (There appears to be an error in [ErSe67], who ask the first question with $\omega_k$ replaced by $\omega$ and a bound of $k+\pi(k)$ rather than $k$; as explained by Meza and Tao in the comments this formulation is obviously false, and the version given here is most likely what was intended.)
solved_when: Both displayed statements are proved for every $k\geq 1$: the liminf of $\sum_{0\leq i<k}\omega_k(n+i)$ is at most $k$, and the limsup of $\left(\sum_{0\leq i<k}\omega(n+i)\right)\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}$ equals $1$.

title: Erdős problem #891
open: Let $2=p_1<p_2<\cdots$ be the primes and $k\geq 2$. Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $n$, there must exist an integer in $[n,n+p_1\cdots p_k)$ with more than $k$ prime factors?
status: Schinzel deduced from Pólya's theorem [Po18] (that the sequence of $k$-smooth integers has unbounded gaps) that the statement is true with $p_1\cdots p_k$ replaced by $p_1\cdots p_{k-1}p_{k+1}$. The problem remains open even for $k=2$, i.e. whether every interval of $6$ (sufficiently large) consecutive integers contains an integer with at least $3$ prime factors. Weisenberg observed that Dickson's conjecture implies the answer is no if $p_1\cdots p_k$ is replaced by $p_1\cdots p_k-1$: letting $L_k$ be the lcm of all integers at most $p_1\cdots p_k$, Dickson's conjecture gives infinitely many $n'$ with $\frac{L_k}{m}n'+1$ prime for all $1\leq m<p_1\cdots p_k$, so for $n=L_kn'+1$ all integers in $[n,n+p_1\cdots p_k-1)$ have at most $k$ prime factors.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, for every $k\geq 2$, all sufficiently large $n$ admit an integer in $[n,n+p_1\cdots p_k)$ with $>k$ prime factors — including the first open case $k=2$, where every interval of $6$ sufficiently large consecutive integers should contain an integer with at least $3$ prime factors.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a natural question about the local density of highly composite integers in short intervals.

title: Erdős problem #892
open: Given a strictly increasing sequence of integers $b_1<b_2<\cdots$, when does there exist a primitive sequence $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ (no element dividing another) with $a_n \ll b_n$ for all $n$? Formally, is a necessary and sufficient condition available — and in particular, does the absence of non-trivial solutions to $(b_i,b_j)=b_k$ suffice? Similarly, find necessary and sufficient conditions on a sequence $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ ensuring a primitive set $A$ with $|A\cap[1,2^{n_i}]|\gg 2^{n_i}$ for every $i$.
status: A problem of Erdős, Sárközi, and Szemerédi [ESS68]. It is known that $\sum \frac{1}{b_n\log b_n}<\infty$ and $\sum_{b_n<x}\frac{1}{b_n}=o\left(\frac{\log x}{\sqrt{\log\log x}}\right)$ are both necessary (the former is due to Erdős [Er35], the latter to Erdős, Sárközy, and Szemerédi [ESS67]). A similar question can be asked for sequences of real numbers, as in [143]. In [Er80] Erdős suggests the first question is 'difficult and perhaps has no reasonable solution', and that perhaps the final question is more reasonable. Key works: erdosproblems.com/892; Erdős references: [Er80,p.101] [Er98] [Er35].
solved_when: A characterization is given of the sequences $b_1<b_2<\cdots$ admitting a primitive sequence $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ with $a_n\ll b_n$ for all $n$ (in particular resolving whether the gcd condition — no non-trivial solutions to $(b_i,b_j)=b_k$ — is sufficient), together with a characterization of the sequences $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ admitting a primitive set $A$ with $|A\cap[1,2^{n_i}]|\gg 2^{n_i}$ for every $i$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would complete the classification of when sequences can be dominated by primitive sets, a basic question about primitive sets.

title: Erdős problem #893
open: Does the ratio $f(2n)/f(n)$ tend to a limit, where $f(n)=\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\tau(2^k-1)$ and $\tau$ counts the divisors of an integer? Formally, one asks whether $\lim_{n\to\infty} f(2n)/f(n)$ exists, and — as the evidence now suggests — whether in fact it diverges to infinity.
status: Erdős [Er98] said that "probably there is no simple asymptotic formula for $f(n)$ since $f(n)$ increases too fast." Kovač and Luca [KoLu25], building on a heuristic independently found by Cambie (personal communication), have shown that there is no finite limit, in that $\limsup_{n\to\infty} f(2n)/f(n)=\infty$, and provide both theoretical and numerical evidence suggesting $\lim f(2n)/f(n)=\infty$.
solved_when: The limit behavior of $f(2n)/f(n)$ is determined unconditionally; the natural criterion here is a proof that $\lim_{n\to\infty} f(2n)/f(n)=\infty$, which the known heuristic and numerics support but do not prove.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve a long-standing question about the growth of the divisor sums attached to the numbers $2^k-1$.

title: Erdős problem #901
open: How few edges can an $n$-uniform hypergraph have while still not being $2$-colorable? Formally, if $m(n)$ is the minimal number of edges in a $3$-chromatic $n$-uniform hypergraph, determine or tightly estimate $m(n)$.
status: The hypergraph in question lacks Property B, meaning there is a set $S$ intersecting every edge while containing no edge. It is known that $m(2)=3$, $m(3)=7$, and $m(4)=23$. Erdős proved $2^n \ll m(n) \ll n^2 2^n$ (the lower bound in [Er63b] and the upper bound in [Er64e]). Erdős conjectured that $m(n)/2^n\to \infty$, proved by Beck [Be77], who showed $m(n)\gg (\log n)2^n$, and later [Be78] improved this to $n^{1/3-o(1)}2^n \ll m(n)$. Radhakrishnan and Srinivasan [RaSr00] improved this to $\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}2^n \ll m(n)$. Pluhar [Pl09] gave a very short proof that $m(n) \gg n^{1/4}2^n$. In [ErLo75] Erdős and Lovász speculate that $n2^n$ is the correct order of magnitude for $m(n)$.
solved_when: The asymptotic order of $m(n)$ is determined up to constant (or $1+o(1)$) factors; in particular, this would confirm or refute the conjecture of Erdős and Lovász [ErLo75] that $m(n)$ has order $n2^n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems with a full tracked history, and its resolution would settle the fundamental question of the minimum size of a non-$2$-colorable uniform hypergraph, closing a decades-long line of successive lower-bound improvements.

title: Erdős problem #902
open: How large must a tournament be so that every set of $n$ vertices is simultaneously dominated by some single outside vertex? Formally, if $f(n)$ is the minimal number of vertices of a tournament in which every $n$-set is dominated by at least one other vertex, what is the order of magnitude of $f(n)$?
status: Schütte asked Erdős this question in the early 1960s. It is easy to check that $f(1)=3$ and $f(2)=7$. Erdős [Er63c] proved $2^{n+1}-1 \leq f(n) \ll n^2 2^n$. Szekeres and Szekeres [SzSz65] proved that $f(3)=19$ and $n2^n \ll f(n)$.
solved_when: The growth rate of $f(n)$ is determined up to constant (or near-constant) factors — in particular, closing the gap between the lower bound $2^{n+1}-1$ and $n2^n$ and the upper bound $\ll n^2 2^n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, posed to him by Schütte, and its full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/902.

title: Erdős problem #906
open: Does there exist a non-zero entire function $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ such that, for any infinite sequence $n_1<n_2<\cdots$, the set $\{z: f^{(n_k)}(z)=0 \text{ for some } k\geq 1\}$ is everywhere dense?
status: Erdős [Er82e] writes that this was solved in the affirmative 'more than ten years ago', but gives no reference or indication who solved it. From context he seems to attribute this to Barth and Schneider [BaSc72], but that paper contains no such result. Tang points out that the problem is trivial if $f$ is a polynomial, so presumably the intended function $f$ is transcendental. Key references: erdosproblems.com/906; Erdős references: [Er56d] [Er82e,p.72] [Er82e].
solved_when: An affirmative construction of such a transcendental entire function $f$ (or a proof that none exists) is given.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it also clarifies a misattributed claim in the literature.

title: Erdős problem #911
open: Can a graph with many edges force a superlinear blow-up in its size Ramsey number? Formally, is there a function $f$ with $f(x)/x \to \infty$ as $x \to \infty$ such that, for all large $C$, every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $e \geq Cn$ edges satisfies $\hat{R}(G) > f(C)\,e$, where $\hat{R}(G)$ is the minimal number of edges in a graph Ramsey for $G$?
status: The problem remains open with no proof expositions recorded; the record cites erdosproblems.com/911 and Erdős's reference [Er82e, p. 78].
solved_when: An $f$ with $f(x)/x \to \infty$ as $x \to \infty$ is exhibited and it is proved that for all large $C$, every $n$-vertex graph with $e \geq Cn$ edges satisfies $\hat{R}(G) > f(C)\,e$; or the conjecture is refuted by constructing, for arbitrarily large $C$, dense graphs $G$ with $\hat{R}(G)$ at most linear in $e$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; a resolution would clarify how density governs the Ramsey behavior of sparse-host Ramsey theory, and the problem is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #912
open: When $n!$ is factored into prime powers, how many distinct exponents appear? Writing $n! = \prod_i p_i^{k_i}$ and letting $h(n)$ count the distinct values among the $k_i$, prove that $h(n) \sim c\,(n/\log n)^{1/2}$ as $n \to \infty$ for some constant $c>0$.
status: A problem of Erdős and Selfridge, who proved (see [Er82c]) that $h(n) \asymp (n/\log n)^{1/2}$. A heuristic of Tao using the Cramér model for the primes (detailed in the comments) suggests the asymptotic holds with $c = \sqrt{2\pi} = 2.506\cdots$.
