solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $h(n) \sim c\,(n/\log n)^{1/2}$ as $n\to\infty$ for some explicit constant $c>0$; the heuristic prediction is $c = \sqrt{2\pi} = 2.506\cdots$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle the precise asymptotic behavior of the exponent multiset of factorials.

title: Erdős problem #913
open: Are there infinitely many $n$ for which the prime factorisation $n(n+1) = \prod_i p_i^{k_i}$ into distinct primes has all exponents $k_i$ pairwise distinct?
status: It is likely that there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $8p^2-1$ is also prime, in which case the answer is affirmative with exponents $\{1,2,3\}$, taking $n=8p^2-1$. The problem has been formalised in Lean as part of the Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures project. Key works: erdosproblems.com/913; Erdős references: [Er82c,p.28].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that infinitely many such $n$ exist; the conjectured route would exhibit infinitely many primes $p$ such that $8p^2 - 1$ is also prime, giving instances with exponents $\{1,2,3\}$ via $n = 8p^2 - 1$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #917
open: Among all $k$-chromatic critical graphs on $n$ vertices, how many edges can one force? Writing $f_k(n)$ for the maximum number of edges in such a graph, Erdős asked whether $f_k(n) \gg_k n^2$ for $k\geq 4$ and, more precisely, whether $f_k(n) \sim \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{\lfloor k/3\rfloor}\right)n^2$ for $k\geq 6$ (with the first case being $f_6(n)\sim n^2/4$).
status: Erdős [Er93] wrote 'I learned of this definition from Dirac in 1949 and immediately asked whether $f_k(n)=o(n^2)$. To my great surprise Dirac constructed a $6$ critical graph on $n$ vertices with more than $\frac{n^2}{4}$ edges.' Dirac [Di52] proved $f_6(4n+2) \geq 4n^2+8n+3$, witnessed by two disjoint copies of $C_{2n+1}$ with all edges between them. Erdős [Er69b] observed that Dirac's construction generalises: if $3\mid k$, there are infinitely many $n$ (of the shape $mk/3$ with $m$ odd) such that $f_k(n) \geq \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{k/3}\right)n^2 + n$. Toft [To70] proved $f_k(n)\gg_k n^2$ for $k\geq 4$. Stiebitz [St87] constructed, for $k\geq 6$, infinitely many $n$ with $f_k(n) \geq \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{\lfloor k/3\rfloor+\delta_k}\right)n^2$, where $\delta_k=0$ if $k\equiv 0\pmod{3}$, $\delta_k=1/7$ if $k\equiv 1\pmod{3}$, and $\delta_k\equiv 24/69$ if $k\equiv 2\pmod{3}$; this disproves Erdős's conjectured asymptotic for $k\not\equiv 0\pmod{3}$. Stiebitz also proved the general upper bound $f_k(n) < \mathrm{ex}(n;K_{k-1})\sim \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{k-2}\right)n^2$.
solved_when: The correct asymptotic behaviour of $f_k(n)$ for $k\geq 4$ is determined, in particular resolving whether $f_k(n)\gg_k n^2$, whether $f_6(n)\sim n^2/4$, and what the true leading constant is for each $k\geq 6$.

title: Erdős problem #918
open: Can a graph have large chromatic number while all its small subgraphs stay countably colorable? Specifically, is there a graph with $\aleph_2$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_2$ such that every subgraph on $\aleph_1$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$, and is there a graph with $\aleph_{\omega+1}$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that every subgraph on $\aleph_\omega$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$?
status: The problem is due to Erdős and Hajnal [ErHa68b], who proved that for every finite $k$ there is a graph with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ where each subgraph on less than $\aleph_k$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_0$. In [Er69b] the question is asked with chromatic number $=\aleph_0$, but in the comments louisd observes this is (assuming subgraph and not induced subgraph was intended) trivially impossible, and hence presumably the problem was intended as written here, which is how it is posed in [ErHa68b].
solved_when: Explicit constructions (or proofs of existence or non-existence) of: (i) a graph with $\aleph_2$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_2$ whose every subgraph on $\aleph_1$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$, and (ii) a graph with $\aleph_{\omega+1}$ vertices and chromatic number $\aleph_1$ whose every subgraph on $\aleph_\omega$ vertices has chromatic number $\leq\aleph_0$.
why: It probes how chromatic number can concentrate at large cardinalities rather than appearing in smaller subgraphs; a solution extends the Erdős–Hajnal construction paradigm beyond chromatic number $\aleph_1$.

title: Erdős problem #919
open: Does there exist a graph on the vertex set $\omega_2^2$ with chromatic number $\aleph_2$ such that every subgraph whose vertex set has lesser type has chromatic number at most $\aleph_0$? And what if the target chromatic number is instead $\aleph_1$?
status: The question was inspired by a theorem of Babai: if $G$ is a graph on a well-ordered set with chromatic number $\geq \aleph_0$, there is a subgraph on vertices of order-type $\omega$ with chromatic number $\aleph_0$. Erdős and Hajnal showed this does not generalise to higher cardinals: they (see [Er69b]) constructed a graph on $\omega_1^2$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that every strictly smaller subgraph has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_0$; its vertices are the pairs $(x_\alpha,y_\beta)$ for $1\leq \alpha,\beta <\omega_1$, ordered lexicographically, with $(x_{\alpha_1},y_{\beta_1})$ connected to $(x_{\alpha_2},y_{\beta_2})$ if and only if $\alpha_1<\alpha_2$ and $\beta_1<\beta_2$. A similar construction produces a graph on $\omega_2^2$ with chromatic number $\aleph_2$ such that every smaller subgraph has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_1$.
solved_when: A graph $G$ on $\omega_2^2$ is exhibited with chromatic number $\aleph_2$ (respectively $\aleph_1$ in the variant), such that every subgraph whose vertices have a lesser type has chromatic number $\leq \aleph_0$; or such a graph is proven not to exist.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it probes the limits of how chromatic number can concentrate on large well-ordered vertex sets.

title: Erdős problem #928
open: Let $\alpha,\beta\in (0,1)$ and let $P(n)$ denote the largest prime divisor of $n$. Does the density of integers $n$ such that $P(n)<n^{\alpha}$ and $P(n+1)<(n+1)^\beta$ exist?
status: Dickman [Di30] showed the density of smooth $n$, with largest prime factor $<n^\alpha$, is $\rho(1/\alpha)$ where $\rho$ is the Dickman function. Erdős also asked whether infinitely many such $n$ even exist, but Meza has observed that this follows immediately from Schinzel's result [Sc67b] that for infinitely many $n$ the largest prime factor of $n(n+1)$ is at most $n^{O(1/\log\log n)}$. Erdős asked whether the events $P(n)<n^\alpha$ and $P(n+1)<(n+1)^\beta$ are independent, in the sense that the density of $n$ satisfying both conditions is equal to $\rho(1/\alpha)\rho(1/\beta)$. Teräväinen [Te18] has proved the logarithmic density exists and is equal to $\rho(1/\alpha)\rho(1/\beta)$. Wang [Wa21] has proved the density is $\rho(1/\alpha)\rho(1/\beta)$ assuming the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture for friable integers. In [Er76e] Erdős conjectured that the density of the set of $n$ such that all of $n,\ldots,n+r-1$ are $n^{\alpha}$ smooth (i.e. $P(n+i)\leq n^{\alpha}$ for $0\leq i<r$) is $\rho(1/\alpha)^r$. See also [370].
solved_when: The natural density of integers $n$ with $P(n)<n^{\alpha}$ and $P(n+1)<(n+1)^\beta$ is shown to exist (and, as conjectured, to equal $\rho(1/\alpha)\rho(1/\beta)$, where $\rho$ is the Dickman function).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; resolving it would settle the conjectured independence of consecutive smoothness conditions, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/928.

title: Erdős problem #929
open: How small can the sieve level be and still guarantee that arbitrarily long runs of consecutive integers each have a small prime factor? Formally, for large $k\geq 2$, let $S(k)$ be the minimal $x$ such that a positive density set of $n$ has $n+1,\dots,n+k$ all divisible by primes $\leq x$; estimate $S(k)$, and in particular, is $S(k)\geq k^{1-o(1)}$?
status: Rosser's sieve gives $S(k) > k^{1/2-o(1)}$. Trivially $S(k)\leq k+1$, e.g. by taking $n\equiv 1 \pmod{(k+1)!}$. The best bound on large gaps between primes due to Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard, and Tao [FGKMT18] (see [4]) implies $S(k) \ll k \frac{\log\log\log k}{\log\log k\, \log\log\log\log k}$. Tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/929; Erdős references: [Er76d].
solved_when: An asymptotic estimate of $S(k)$ is obtained — in particular, the conjectured lower bound $S(k)\geq k^{1-o(1)}$ is proved or refuted.
why: A solution would sharpen our understanding of how large prime gaps and small prime factors interact, improving on what sieve methods and the best large-gap results currently give.

title: Erdős problem #930
open: Is it true that for every number of intervals $r$ there is a length threshold $k$ such that the product of integers over $r$ disjoint intervals, each of length at least $k$, is never a perfect power? Formally: for every $r$, does there exist $k$ such that if $I_1,\ldots,I_r$ are disjoint intervals of consecutive integers, all of length at least $k$, then $\prod_{1\leq i\leq r}\prod_{m\in I_i}m$ is not a perfect power?
status: Erdős and Selfridge [ErSe75] proved that the product of consecutive integers is never a power (establishing the case $r=1$). The condition that the intervals be large in terms of $r$ is necessary for $r=2$ — see the constructions in [363]. See also [363] for the case of squares. Tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/930; Erdős references: [Er76d].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the stated assertion: for every $r$, the existence of a $k$ such that the product of integers over any $r$ disjoint intervals of consecutive integers, each of length at least $k$, is not a perfect power.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and it extends his celebrated theorem with Selfridge on products of consecutive integers to multiple intervals; a solution would clarify how the "no perfect powers" phenomenon behaves once the consecutive integers are split into separated blocks.

title: Erdős problem #932
open: For infinitely many $r$, does the interval between consecutive primes $p_r$ and $p_{r+1}$ contain at least two integers $n$ (with $p_r<n<p_{r+1}$) all of whose prime factors are $<p_{r+1}-p_r$?
status: Erdős thought the statement was true but that there are very few such $r$; he could show that the density of $r$ for which at least one such $n$ exists is $0$. The problem has been formalised in Lean as part of the Google DeepMind Formal Conjectures project. Key references: erdosproblems.com/932; Erdős references: [Er76d].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that such integers $n$ exist within the interval $(p_r, p_{r+1})$ for infinitely many $r$, with all prime factors of each such $n$ strictly less than the prime gap $p_{r+1}-p_r$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a question he believed true but expected to occur only very rarely.

title: Erdős problem #933
open: If $n(n+1)=2^k3^lm$ with $(m,6)=1$, must the largest prime-power part supported on $\{2,3\}$ exceed $n\log n$ by an unbounded factor? Formally, is it true that $\limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{2^k3^l}{n\log n}=\infty$?
status: Mahler proved a more general result implying in particular that $2^k3^l < n^{1+o(1)}$. Erdős [Er76d] wrote "it is easy to see" that for infinitely many $n$, $2^k3^l > n\log n$. Steinerberger has noted a simple proof of this fact follows from taking $n=2^{3^r}$ for any integer $r\geq 1$, when $k=3^r$ and $l=r+1$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{2^k3^l}{n\log n}=\infty$ for $n(n+1)=2^k3^lm$ with $(m,6)=1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a concrete question about how much of $n(n+1)$ can be carried by the primes 2 and 3 alone.

title: Erdős problem #934
open: How many edges can a graph of maximum degree $d$ have before it must contain two edges whose shortest path between them has length at least $t$? Formally, estimate $h_t(d)$, the minimal number of edges forcing such a pair in any graph with maximal degree $\leq d$.
status: A problem of Erdős and Nešetřil. Erdős [Er88] wrote "This problem seems to be interesting only if there is a nice expression for $h_t(d)$." It is easy to see that $h_t(d) \leq 2d^t$ always and $h_1(d) = d+1$. Erdős and Nešetřil and Bermond, Bond, Paoli, and Peyrat [BBPP83] independently conjectured that $h_2(d) \leq \tfrac{5}{4}d^2 + 1$, with equality for even $d$ (see [149]); this was proved by Chung, Gyárfás, Tuza, and Trotter [CGTT90]. Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, de Joannis de Verclos, and Kang [CCJK22] conjectured $h_3(d) \leq d^3 - d^2 + d + 2$, with equality if and only if $d = p^k + 1$ for some prime power $p^k$, and proved $h_3(3) = 23$. The same authors conjecture that, for all $t \geq 3$, $h_t(d) \geq (1-o(1))d^t$ for infinitely many $d$ and $h_t(d) \leq (1+o(1))d^t$ for all $d$ (with $o(1) \to 0$ as $d \to \infty$). They also prove that, if $t$ is large, there are infinitely many $d$ such that $h_t(d) \geq 0.629^t d^t$, and that for all $t \geq 1$, $h_t(d) \leq \tfrac{3}{2}d^t + 1$.
solved_when: A sharp (or asymptotically sharp) estimate of $h_t(d)$ is obtained for general $t$ and $d$ — in the direction of the conjectured asymptotics $h_t(d) \geq (1-o(1))d^t$ for infinitely many $d$ and $h_t(d) \leq (1+o(1))d^t$ for all $d$, with $o(1)\to 0$ as $d\to\infty$; in particular, resolution of the conjecture $h_3(d) \leq d^3 - d^2 + d + 2$ with equality iff $d = p^k+1$ for a prime power $p^k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and as Erdős himself noted, it is interesting precisely if $h_t(d)$ admits a nice closed expression.

title: Erdős problem #935
open: How large can the powerful part of a product of consecutive integers be? Formally, writing $Q_2(n)=\prod_{p: k_p\geq 2} p^{k_p}$ for the powerful part of $n=\prod p^{k_p}$, is it true that for every $\epsilon>0$ and $\ell\geq 1$, all sufficiently large $n$ satisfy $Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))<n^{2+\epsilon}$; and, for $\ell\geq 2$, is $\limsup_{n\to\infty} Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))/n^2$ infinite while $\lim_{n\to\infty} Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))/n^{\ell+1}=0$?
status: Erdős [Er76d] writes that if this is true then it 'seems very difficult to prove'. A result of Mahler implies, for every $\ell\geq 1$, $\limsup_{n\to\infty} Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))/n^2 \geq 1$. All these questions can be asked replacing $Q_2$ by $Q_r$ for $r>2$, keeping only prime powers with exponent $\geq r$. The second part is essentially the same (up to constants) as [367]; the construction given there by van Doorn (also given by Aletheia [Fe26]) proves it in the affirmative, since solutions to the Pell equation $x^2-8y^2=1$ imply $\limsup_{n\to\infty} Q_2(n(n+1)(n+2))/n^2=\infty$. In [Fe26] it is similarly noted that the ABC conjecture implies a positive answer to the third question.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given of the bound $Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))<n^{2+\epsilon}$ for all sufficiently large $n$, for every $\epsilon>0$ and $\ell\geq 1$, together with answers to the two $\ell\geq 2$ limit questions: whether $\limsup_{n\to\infty} Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))/n^2$ is infinite, and whether $\lim_{n\to\infty} Q_2(n(n+1)\cdots(n+\ell))/n^{\ell+1}=0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems with a full tracked history at erdosproblems.com; it probes how much square-powered structure can concentrate in a short interval of consecutive integers, a basic question about multiplicative structure in intervals.

title: Erdős problem #936
open: Are $2^n \pm 1$ and $n! \pm 1$ powerful numbers — meaning every prime $p$ dividing $m$ satisfies $p^2 \mid m$ — for only finitely many $n$?
status: Cushing and Pascoe [CuPa16] showed the answer to the second question is yes assuming the abc conjecture — in fact, for any fixed $k \geq 0$, there are only finitely many $n$ and powerful $x$ such that $|x - n!| \leq k$. CrowdMath [Cr20] showed that the answer to the first question is yes, also assuming the abc conjecture.
solved_when: One proves unconditionally (or refutes) that the set of $n$ for which $2^n \pm 1$ is powerful, and the set of $n$ for which $n! \pm 1$ is powerful, are both finite.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it resolves a long-standing question at the interface of factorial/exponential sequences and multiplicative structure.

title: Erdős problem #938
open: Are there only finitely many three-term arithmetic progressions among consecutive terms of the sequence of powerful numbers, where a number is powerful if every prime dividing it divides it at least twice? Formally, writing the powerful numbers as $n_1<n_2<\cdots$, must the equality $n_{k+1}-n_k = n_{k+2}-n_{k+1}$ hold for only finitely many $k$?
status: The problem remains open. Erdős also conjectured (see [364]) that there are no triples of powerful numbers of the shape $n, n+1, n+2$. The problem is tracked at erdosproblems.com/938 with reference [Er76d].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the equation $n_{k+1}-n_k=n_{k+2}-n_{k+1}$ has only finitely many solutions in consecutive powerful numbers; a disproof would exhibit infinitely many such triples.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a concrete structural question about the gaps in one of the classical multiplicative sequences.

title: Erdős problem #939
open: Let $r\geq 2$. An $r$-powerful number $n$ is one such that if $p\mid n$ then $p^r\mid n$. Formally: for $r\geq 4$, can the sum of $r-2$ coprime $r$-powerful numbers ever be itself $r$-powerful, and if so, are there at most finitely many such solutions?
status: Nitaj [Ni95] proved there are infinitely many triples of coprime $3$-powerful numbers $a,b,c$ with $a+b=c$, such as $2^3\cdot 3^5\cdot 73^3+271^3 = 919^3$; in his construction at least two of $a,b,c$ are perfect cubes. Cohn [Co98] constructed infinitely many such triples, none of which are perfect cubes, and Walsh [Wa24] gave an alternative construction. Euler had conjectured that the sum of $k-1$ many $k$th powers is never a $k$th power, but this is false for $k=5$, as Lander and Parkin [LaPa67] found $27^5+84^5+110^5+133^5=144^5$. Cambie found several examples of the sum of $r-2$ coprime $r$-powerful numbers being itself $r$-powerful, e.g. for $r=5$: $3^761^5=2^83^{10}5^7+2^{12}23^6+11^513^5$, as well as solutions for $r=7$ and $r=8$ (the latter even with the sum of $5$ $8$-powerful numbers being $8$-powerful). Kitamura gave another example in the comments. GPT-5.5. Pro (prompted by Price) gave a simple construction in the comments showing that for $r\geq 6$ there are infinitely many $r$-powerful numbers which are the sum of $(r-2)$ (in fact $\lceil r/2\rceil+1$) many coprime $r$-powerful numbers.
solved_when: A proof that for every $r\geq 4$ there are at most finitely many solutions to the sum of $r-2$ coprime $r$-powerful numbers being $r$-powerful, or a construction showing infinitely many such solutions for some $r\geq 4$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #940
open: Are there infinitely many integers that cannot be written as a sum of at most $r$ $r$-powerful numbers (where $r\geq 3$ and $n$ is $r$-powerful if $p^r\mid n$ whenever $p\mid n$)? More sharply, does the set of integers representable as a sum of at most $r$ $r$-powerful numbers have density $0$?
status: Erdős [Er76d] claimed the density-$0$ statement is 'easy' for $r=2$ (a potential 'easy argument' appears in the comments by Tao; it was first proved in the literature by Baker and Brüdern [BaBr94]). For $r=3$ it is not even known whether the integers that are the sum of at most three cubes have density $0$; in the Oberwolfach problem book this is recorded in 1986 as a problem of Erdős and Ivić. In [Er76d] Erdős claimed that 'a simple counting argument' implies infinitely many integers are not the sum of at most $r$ $r$-powerful numbers, but Schinzel pointed out he made a mistake. Heath-Brown [He88] proved that all large numbers are the sum of at most three $2$-powerful numbers, see [941]. See also [1081] for a more refined question concerning $r=2$, and [1107] for the case of $r+1$ summands.
solved_when: For some $r\geq 3$, it is proved that infinitely many integers are not the sum of at most $r$ $r$-powerful numbers; the stronger form asks whether the representable set has density $0$ (a natural refinement: even the density-$0$ statement for sums of at most three cubes, $r=3$, would resolve a major case).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (#940), and the case $r=3$ is not even known at the level of sums of three cubes, so any progress directly advances the additive theory of powerful numbers.

title: Erdős problem #942
open: How many powerful integers (those divisible by $p^2$ whenever divisible by $p$) can lie in a single interval $[n^2,(n+1)^2)$? Formally, letting $h(n)$ count such integers, does there exist a constant $c>0$ with $h(n) < (\log n)^{c+o(1)}$ always, and $h(n) > (\log n)^{c-o(1)}$ for infinitely many $n$?
status: Erdős writes it is not hard to prove that $\limsup h(n)=\infty$, and that the density $\delta_l$ of integers with $h(n)=l$ exists with $\sum \delta_l=1$; a proof that $h(n)$ is unbounded is given by van Doorn in the comments. De Koninck and Luca [DeLu04] proved that for infinitely many $n$, $h(n) \gg \left(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\right)^{1/3}$, and gave the density ($\approx 0.275$) of those $n$ with $h(n)=1$. Hughes (with AI assistance) observed that the argument of [DeLu04] makes two inefficient choices; optimised as described in the comments, the construction of [DeLu04] (see also [DLS05]) yields infinitely many $n$ with $h(n) \gg \frac{\log n}{\log\log n\log\log\log n}$.
solved_when: An asymptotic estimate for $h(n)$ is obtained; in particular, the polylogarithmic upper and lower bounds above are established (or refuted) for some constant $c>0$.

title: Erdős problem #943
open: Is the number of representations of every integer $n$ as a sum of two powerful numbers small compared to any power of $n$? Formally, if $A$ is the set of powerful numbers (those $n$ with $p\mid n \Rightarrow p^2\mid n$), does the convolution $1_A \ast 1_A(n) = n^{o(1)}$ hold for every $n$?
status: The problem remains open; no proof expositions related to it have been contributed to date, and the record lists no partial results. It is tracked at erdosproblems.com/943, with Erdős reference [Er76d].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $1_A \ast 1_A(n) = n^{o(1)}$ for every $n$, where $A$ denotes the set of powerful numbers.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve a long-standing question about the additive structure of the powerful numbers.

title: Erdős problem #944
open: A vertex or edge set is critical if deleting it lowers the chromatic number. Given $k\geq 4$ and $r\geq 1$, must there exist a graph of chromatic number $k$ in which every vertex is critical, yet no set of $r$ or fewer edges is critical?
status: The question was conjectured by Dirac in 1970 for $k\geq 4$ and $r=1$. Dirac's conjecture was proved for $k=5$ by Brown [Br92]. Lattanzio [La02] proved such graphs exist for all $k$ such that $k-1$ is not prime, and independently Jensen [Je02] gave an alternative construction for all $k\geq 5$. Martinsson and Steiner [MaSt25] proved the statement for every $r\geq 1$ if $k$ is sufficiently large depending on $r$, and Skottova and Steiner [SkSt25] improved this to all $k\geq 5$ and $r\geq 1$, leaving only the case $k=4$ open (even $k=4$ with $r=1$ remains open). For the quantitative form, where $f_k(n)$ is the largest $r\geq 1$ such that there exists a $k$-vertex-critical graph on $n$ vertices with no critical set of at most $r$ edges, Skottova and Steiner [SkSt25] proved $f_k(n)\to\infty$ for $k\geq 5$, establishing $n^{1/3}\ll_k f_k(n) \ll_k \frac{n}{(\log n)^{C}}$ for all $k\geq 5$, where $C>0$.
solved_when: For every $k\geq 4$ and $r\geq 1$, a $k$-vertex-critical graph is constructed in which every critical set of edges has size $>r$; equivalently, $f_k(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, with quantitative bounds of the form $n^{1/3}\ll_k f_k(n) \ll_k \frac{n}{(\log n)^{C}}$ for $C>0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it completes the last case ($k=4$) of Dirac's 1970 conjecture and its Erdős strengthening.

title: Erdős problem #945
open: How long can a run of consecutive integers be if each has a distinct number of divisors? Formally, if $F(x)$ is the maximal $k$ such that some $n+1,\ldots,n+k\leq x$ have pairwise distinct values of $\tau$, is it true that $F(x)\leq(\log x)^{O(1)}$ — i.e., that some constant $C>0$ forces every interval $[x,x+(\log x)^C]$ to contain two integers with the same number of divisors?
status: The problem originates with Erdős and Mirsky [ErMi52], who proved $\frac{(\log x)^{1/2}}{\log\log x}\ll F(x)\ll \exp\left(O\left(\frac{(\log x)^{1/2}}{\log\log x}\right)\right)$. Erdős [Er85e] claimed the lower bound could be improved via their method 'with some more work' to $(\log x)^{1-o(1)}$. Beker improved the upper bound to $F(x)\ll \exp\left(O\left((\log x)^{1/3+o(1)}\right)\right)$. Cambie observed that Cramér's conjecture implies $F(x)\ll(\log x)^2$, and that if every interval in $[x,2x]$ of length $\gg\log x$ contains a squarefree number (see [208]), then every interval of length $\gg(\log x)^2$ contains two numbers with the same number of divisors, whence $F(x)\ll(\log x)^2$. See [1004] for the analogous problem with the Euler totient function. The problem is discussed as B18 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: An estimate of $F(x)$ resolving the polylogarithmic question is given: specifically, a proof (or refutation) that $F(x)\leq(\log x)^{C}$ for some constant $C>0$ and all large $x$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling the polylogarithmic bound (or breaking it) would determine the true order of runs of distinct divisor counts.

title: Erdős problem #949
open: If $S\subset \mathbb{R}$ is a sum-free set (containing no solutions to $a+b=c$), must there exist a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$ of cardinality continuum such that $A+A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$? In other words, can a sum-free set never block the real line from hosting a continuum-sized "translate-avoiding" sumset inside its complement?
status: Erdős suggested that if the answer is no, one could consider the variant where $S$ is assumed Sidon (all sums $a+b$ with $a,b\in S$ distinct, aside from trivial coincidences). In the comments, Dillies gives a positive proof of this Sidon variant, found by AlphaProof: if $S\subset\mathbb{R}$ is Sidon, then there exists $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\backslash S$ of cardinality continuum with $A+A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\backslash S$. The original sum-free question remains open. (Key works: erdosproblems.com/949; Erdős references: [Er77c])
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) is given for the existence, for every sum-free $S\subset\mathbb{R}$, of a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$ with $|A|$ equal to the continuum and $A+A\subseteq \mathbb{R}\backslash S$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution closes a named entry in that catalog of open questions.

title: Erdős problem #950
open: For each integer $n$, consider $f(n)=\sum_{p<n}\frac{1}{n-p}$, the sum over primes $p$ below $n$ of the reciprocal of the gap $n-p$. Is it true that $\liminf f(n)=1$ and $\limsup f(n)=\infty$, and that $f(n)=o(\log\log n)$ for all $n$?
status: The function was considered by de Bruijn, Erdős, and Turán, who showed $\sum_{n<x}f(n)\sim \sum_{n<x}f(n)^2\sim x$; they give no proofs, but a proof of the (harder) second claim is given by Gorodetsky here. The existence of some $c>0$ such that there are $\gg n^c/\log n$ many primes in $[n,n+n^c]$ implies that $\liminf f(n)>0$. Erdős writes that a 'weaker conjecture which is perhaps not quite inaccessible' is that, for every $\epsilon>0$, if $x$ is sufficiently large there exists $y<x$ such that $\pi(x)<\pi(y)+\epsilon \pi(x-y)$ (compare this to [855]). He notes that if $\pi(x)<\pi(y)+O\left(\frac{x-y}{\log x}\right)$ for all $y<x-(\log x)^C$ for some constant $C>0$, then $f(n)\ll \log\log\log n$. The study of $f(p)$ is even harder, and Erdős could not prove that $\sum_{p<x}f(p)^2\sim \pi(x)$. See also [1210].
solved_when: It is proved that $\liminf f(n)=1$, $\limsup f(n)=\infty$, and $f(n)=o(\log\log n)$ for all $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and concerns the fine-scale distribution of primes as seen through harmonic proximity sums.

title: Erdős problem #951
open: Suppose $1<a_1<\cdots$ is a sequence of real numbers whose finite products $\prod_i a_i^{k_i}$ are pairwise separated by at least $1$. Must such a sequence have at most $\pi(x)$ elements up to $x$ — that is, no more than the primes themselves?
status: Erdős [Er77c] said this question was asked 'during [his] lecture at Queens College [by] one member of the audience (perhaps S. Shapiro)' (though in [Er80] he seemed sure it was Shapiro, while also recalling he had himself asked it in [Er69]). In [Er80] he further asks whether equality holds if and only if the $a_i$ are the set of primes. Such a sequence is sometimes called a set of Beurling prime numbers, with the products called the associated generalised integers. Beurling conjectured that if the number of reals in $[1,x]$ of the form $\prod a_i^{k_i}$ is $x+o(\log x)$ then the $a_i$ must be the primes; it is unclear whether this is intended for all $x$ or only sufficiently large $x$. The former version can be disproved by finite calculation, since any finite sequence of $a_i$ can be extended to a suitable infinite sequence via a greedy algorithm, and a finite counterexample for $x=10$ was found by ChatGPT-5.2 Pro (prompted by Leeham).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every such sequence satisfies $\#\{a_i \leq x\} \leq \pi(x)$ for all $x$; a resolution may also address Erdős's further question in [Er80] of whether equality holds if and only if the $a_i$ are the set of primes.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would clarify how rigidly the multiplicative separation condition forces a sequence to be at most as dense as the primes.

title: Erdős problem #952
open: Does there exist an infinite sequence of distinct Gaussian primes $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ with bounded gaps, i.e. $\lvert x_{n+1} - x_n\rvert \ll 1$ for all $n$? This is the Gaussian moat problem: can one walk to infinity in the Gaussian integers stepping only on Gaussian primes, with each step of uniformly bounded length?
status: This is the Gaussian moat problem, and despite the attribution it is not actually a problem of Erdős; it has been erroneously attributed to him in the past. As Erdős recalls in [Er77c]: 'The conjecture was told me by Motzkin at the Pasadena number theory meeting 1963 November and it was apparently raised by Basil Gordon and Motzkin. I naturally liked it very much and told it right away to many people, naturally attributing it to Motzkin, but this was later forgotten. Thus the problem is returned to its rightful owners.' In [Er80] Erdős writes 'the answer is almost certainly negative'. The problem is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/952, with Erdős references [Er77c] and [Er80, p.114].
solved_when: Either an infinite sequence of distinct Gaussian primes with $\lvert x_{n+1}-x_n\rvert \ll 1$ is exhibited, or such a sequence is proven not to exist.
why: It is the Gaussian-integer analogue of asking whether Gaussian primes admit bounded-gap chains, and a negative answer would confirm the widely held belief that any prime-walk in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ must cross an arbitrarily wide prime-free "moat."

title: Erdős problem #953
open: How large can a measurable set in the plane be if no two of its points are an integer distance apart? Formally, for $A\subset \{ x\in \mathbb{R}^2 : \lvert x\rvert <r\}$ with $\lvert a-b\rvert \not\in \mathbb{Z}$ for any distinct $a,b\in A$, what is the supremum of the measure of $A$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Sárközi. Erdős [Er77c] writes that 'Sárközi has the sharpest results, but nothing has been published yet'. The trivial upper bound is $O(r)$. Koizumi and Kovac have observed in the comments that Sárközy's lower bound in [466] can be adapted to give a lower bound of $\gg_\epsilon r^{1/2-\epsilon}$ for all $\epsilon>0$. See also [465] for a similar problem concerning upper bounds and [466] for a similar problem concerning lower bounds.
solved_when: The maximal measure of such a set $A$ is determined, up to matching upper and lower bounds, as a function of $r$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and the sharp results claimed by Sárközi have never been published — settling it would resolve a long-standing gap in the record.

title: Erdős problem #954
open: For Rosen's sequence, defined by $a_0=0$, $a_1=1$, and $a_{k+1}$ the smallest $n$ such that the count of solutions to $a_i+a_j\leq n$ (with $0\leq i\leq j\leq k$, $j\geq 1$) is less than $n$, is the number of solutions to $a_i+a_j\leq x$ equal to $x+O(x^{1/4+o(1)})$?
status: This sequence was constructed by Rosen. The number of solutions to $a_i+a_j\leq x$ is always at least $x$ by construction, but Erdős and Rosen could not even prove whether it is at most $(1+o(1))x$. The sequence begins $0,1,3,5,9,13,17,24,31,38,45,\ldots$ Reference: [Er77c,p.71]; see erdosproblems.com/954.
solved_when: The asymptotic $N(x)=x+O(x^{1/4+o(1)})$ is proved for the number of solutions $N(x)$ to $a_i+a_j\leq x$; a major partial advance would be proving $N(x)\leq(1+o(1))x$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and even the basic question of whether the solution count exceeds the trivial lower bound $x$ by more than $o(x)$ remains unanswered.

title: Erdős problem #955
open: If a set of natural numbers has density zero, must the set of numbers whose sum of proper divisors lands in it also have density zero? Formally, for $s(n)=\sigma(n)-n$, does $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ of density $0$ force $s^{-1}(A)$ to have density $0$?
status: This is a conjecture of Erdős, Granville, Pomerance, and Spiro [EGPS90]. The converse direction can fail: $s(A)$ may have positive density even when $A$ has zero density (e.g., $A$ the product of two distinct primes). Erdős [Er73b] proved that there are sets $A$ of positive density such that $s^{-1}(A)$ is empty. Pollack [Po14b] proved the conjecture when $A$ is the set of primes. Troupe [Tr15] proved it when $A$ is the set of integers with unusually many prime factors, and Troupe [Tr20] when $A$ is the set of integers that are the sum of two squares. Pollack, Pomerance, and Thompson [PPT18] proved that if $\epsilon(x)=o(1)$ and $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ has size at most $x^{1/2+\epsilon(x)}$, then $\#\{n\leq x: s(n)\in A\}=o(x)$ as $x\to\infty$; combined with $s(n)\ll n\log\log n$, this implies $s^{-1}(A)$ has density $0$ whenever $|A\cap[1,x]|\leq x^{1/2+o(1)}$. Alanen calls $k$ with no solutions to $s(n)=k$ untouchable; these are discussed in problem B10 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ of natural density $0$, the set $s^{-1}(A)=\{n: s(n)\in A\}$ also has natural density $0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a basic question about the distribution of values of the sum-of-proper-divisors function.

title: Erdős problem #956
open: How many unit distances can arise between $n$ disjoint translates of a compact convex set in the plane? Formally, with $\delta(C,D)=\inf_{c\in C, d\in D}\|c-d\|$, let $h(n)$ be the maximal $m$ such that some compact convex $C\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ and a set $X$ of size $n$ have all translates $(C+x)_{x\in X}$ disjoint and $m$ pairs $x_1,x_2\in X$ with $\delta(C+x_1,C+x_2)=1$; determine $h(n)$, and in particular prove there exists a constant $c>0$ such that $h(n)>n^{1+c}$ for all large $n$.
status: A problem of Erdős and Pach [ErPa90], who proved $h(n)\ll n^{4/3}$. They also consider the related function for $n$ disjoint convex sets (not necessarily translates), giving an upper bound of $\ll n^{7/5}$. It is trivial that $h(n)\geq f(n)$, where $f(n)$ is the maximal number of unit distances determined by $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (see [90]).
solved_when: The growth rate of $h(n)$ is determined, or at minimum it is proved that $h(n)>n^{1+c}$ for some constant $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would extend the classical unit-distance problem from points to convex translates.

title: Erdős problem #959
open: For a set $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ of size $n$, order the distinct distances $d_1,\ldots,d_k$ it determines by their multiplicities $f(d_1)\geq f(d_2)\geq \cdots \geq f(d_k)$; how large can the gap between the most popular and second most popular distance be? Formally, estimate $\max (f(d_1)-f(d_2))$, where the maximum is over all $A$ of size $n$.
status: One can ask more generally about $\max (f(d_r)-f(d_{r+1}))$. Clemen, Dumitrescu, and Liu [CDL25] have shown that $\max (f(d_1)-f(d_2))\gg n\log n$, and more generally that for any $1\leq k\leq \log n$ there exists a set $A$ of $n$ points with $f(d_r)-f(d_{r+1})\gg \frac{n\log n}{r}$. They conjecture that $n\log n$ can be improved to $n^{1+c/\log\log n}$ for some constant $c>0$.
solved_when: The quantity $\max (f(d_1)-f(d_2))$ is determined up to constants (in particular, whether it grows faster than $n\log n$, e.g. like the conjectured $n^{1+c/\log\log n}$ for some constant $c>0$).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle how unevenly distance multiplicities can be distributed among the points of a planar set.

title: Erdős problem #961
open: Let $f(k)$ be the minimal $n$ such that every set of $n$ consecutive integers all greater than $k$ contains an integer divisible by some prime exceeding $k$ — equivalently, how long can a run of consecutive $k$-smooth integers be? The problem is to estimate $f(k)$.
status: Sylvester and Schur (see [Er34]) proved $f(k)\leq k$, and Erdős [Er55d] proved $f(k)<3\frac{k}{\log k}$. Jutila [Ju74] and Ramachandra and Shorey [RaSh73] proved $f(k) \ll \frac{\log\log\log k}{\log \log k}\frac{k}{\log k}$. It is likely that $f(k) \ll (\log k)^{O(1)}$.
solved_when: An asymptotic upper bound for $f(k)$ is established; conjecturally this means proving $f(k) \ll (\log k)^{O(1)}$, improving the current $\ll \frac{\log\log\log k}{\log \log k}\frac{k}{\log k}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and is essentially equivalent to problem [683]; a resolution advances a classical thread on runs of smooth integers.

title: Erdős problem #962
open: How long can a run of consecutive integers be if every member of the run has a prime divisor larger than the length of the run? Formally, if $k(n)$ is the maximal $k$ for which there exists $m\leq n$ such that each of $m+1,\ldots,m+k$ is divisible by some prime $>k$, estimate $k(n)$ — in particular, is it true that $\log k(n) \leq (\log n)^{1/2+o(1)}$?
status: Erdős [Er65] wrote it is 'not hard to prove' that $\log k(n)\geq (\log n)^{1/2-o(1)}$ and it 'seems likely' that $k(n)=o(n^\epsilon)$, but had no non-trivial upper bound for $k(n)$. In [Er76e] he gives an argument proving $\log k(n) \gg \sqrt{\log n\log\log n}$ and thought this bound was 'fairly sharp'. Tao in the comments has given a simple argument proving $k(n) \leq (1+o(1))n^{1/2}$. In [Er76e] Erdős reports he could prove $k(n) \leq \exp(-(\log n)^c)n^{1/2}$ for some constant $c>0$, but could not prove that $k(n) \leq n^{1/2-c}$ for a constant $c>0$, which he said 'seems a ridiculously weak result'. Tang has proved a lower bound of $\log k(n)\geq \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-o(1)\right)\sqrt{\log n\log\log n}$.
solved_when: The growth of $k(n)$ is determined up to $(1+o(1))$ factors in the exponent, or at least the conjectured bound $\log k(n) \leq (\log n)^{1/2+o(1)}$ is proved or disproved.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would resolve a half-century-old gap between the lower bounds Erdős could prove and the upper bounds available even with Tao's argument.

title: Erdős problem #963
open: How large a dissociated subset must every $n$-point set of reals contain? Formally, if $f(n)$ is the maximal $k$ such that every $A\subset\mathbb{R}$ of size $n$ contains a dissociated $B\subseteq A$ with $|B|\geq k$ (all subset sums $\sum_{b\in S}b$ distinct for $S\subseteq B$), is it true that $f(n)\geq \lfloor \log_2 n\rfloor$?
status: Erdős noted that the greedy algorithm gives $f(n)\geq \lfloor \log_3 n\rfloor$. The problem is tracked at erdosproblems.com/963, with Erdős references [Er65] and [Va99,1.22].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $f(n)\geq \lfloor \log_2 n\rfloor$ for all $n$; more generally, sharp asymptotic estimates for $f(n)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolves a basic quantitative question about the structure of subset sums in arbitrary real sets.

title: Erdős problem #968
open: Let $u_n = p_n/n$, where $p_n$ is the $n$th prime. Does the set of indices $n$ with $u_n < u_{n+1}$ have positive density?
status: Erdős and Prachar [ErPr61] proved that $\sum_{p_n < x} |u_{n+1} - u_n| \asymp (\log x)^2$, and that the set of $n$ with $u_n > u_{n+1}$ has positive density. As with many of Erdős's questions, by 'positive density' he most likely meant positive lower density — i.e., there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that for all large $x$ the number of such $n \le x$ is at least $cx$. Erdős also asks whether $u_n < u_{n+1} < u_{n+2}$ or $u_n > u_{n+1} > u_{n+2}$ have infinitely many solutions.
solved_when: There exists a constant $c > 0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $x$, the number of $n \le x$ with $u_n < u_{n+1}$ is at least $cx$ (positive lower density).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it probes how evenly the prime-counting ratio $p_n/n$ oscillates, complementing the known positive density of decreasing steps.

title: Erdős problem #969
open: How large is the error term in the count of squarefree integers? Determine the order of magnitude of $E(x)$ in the asymptotic $Q(x)=\frac{6}{\pi^2}x+E(x)$, where $Q(x)$ counts the squarefree integers in $[1,x]$.
status: It is elementary to prove $E(x)\ll x^{1/2}$, and the prime number theorem implies $o(x^{1/2})$. The best known unconditional upper bound is of the shape $x^{1/2-o(1)}$, due to Walfisz [Wa63]. Evelyn and Linfoot [EvLi31] proved $E(x)\gg x^{1/4}$, and this is likely the true order of magnitude. The Riemann Hypothesis would follow from $E(x)\ll x^{1/4}$. The true order of magnitude is unknown even assuming the Riemann Hypothesis; conditional on this assumption, the best known upper bound is $E(x)\ll x^{\frac{11}{35}+o(1)}$, due to Liu [Li16].
solved_when: The order of magnitude of $E(x)$ is determined; this is expected to be $x^{1/4}$, and a proof that $E(x)\ll x^{1/4}$ would already imply the Riemann Hypothesis.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and the error term is intimately tied to the Riemann Hypothesis.

title: Erdős problem #970
open: How large must a block of consecutive integers be to guarantee it contains a number coprime to any integer having at most $k$ prime factors? Formally, if $h(k)$ denotes Jacobsthal's function — the minimal $m$ such that every set of $m$ consecutive integers contains an integer coprime to $n$ whenever $n$ has at most $k$ prime factors — determine the order of magnitude of $h(k)$; in particular, is $h(k) \ll k^2$?
status: The bound $h(k) \ll k^2$ is a conjecture of Jacobsthal. Iwaniec [Iw78] proved $h(k) \ll (k\log k)^2$. The best known lower bound is $h(k) \gg \frac{(\log k)(\log\log\log k)}{(\log\log k)^2}k$, due to Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard, and Tao [FGKMT18]. This is a more general form of the function considered in [687].
solved_when: The order of magnitude of $h(k)$ is determined; a definitive answer to whether $h(k) \ll k^2$ (Jacobsthal's conjecture) suffices for that specific question.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; it measures how regularly coprimality appears in short intervals.

title: Erdős problem #971
open: For a modulus $d$ and residue $a$, let $p(a,d)$ be the least prime congruent to $a \pmod{d}$. Is there a constant $c>0$ such that, for all large $d$, the inequality $p(a,d) > (1+c)\phi(d)\log d$ holds for $\gg \phi(d)$ many values of $a$?
status: Erdős [Er49c] could prove the statement is true for an infinite sequence of $d$. He also proved that, for any $\epsilon>0$, one has $p(a,d) < \epsilon\,\phi(d)\log d$ for $\gg_\epsilon \phi(d)$ many values of $a$. Key references: erdosproblems.com/971; [Er65b] [Er49c].
solved_when: A constant $c>0$ is exhibited such that, for all sufficiently large $d$, the bound $p(a,d) > (1+c)\phi(d)\log d$ holds for $\gg \phi(d)$ residues $a$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems; its full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution settles a long-standing entry in that catalogue.

title: Erdős problem #972
open: Let $\alpha>1$ be irrational. Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $\lfloor p\alpha\rfloor$ is also prime?
status: Vinogradov [Vi48] proved that the sequence $\{p\alpha\}$ is uniformly distributed for every irrational $\alpha$, and hence there are infinitely many primes $p$ of the shape $p=\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ for every irrational $\alpha>1$. Indeed, this occurs if and only if $\frac{p}{\alpha}\leq n<\frac{p+1}{\alpha}$, which is true if and only if $\{p\alpha^{-1}\}>1-\alpha^{-1}$, which happens infinitely often by the uniform distribution of $\{p\alpha^{-1}\}$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every irrational $\alpha>1$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ for which $\lfloor p\alpha\rfloor$ is prime.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full solution history tracked at erdosproblems.com/972.

title: Erdős problem #973
open: Does there exist a constant $C>1$ such that, for every $n\geq 2$, there exists a sequence $z_i\in \mathbb{C}$ with $z_1=1$ and $\lvert z_i\rvert \geq 1$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$ with $\max_{2\leq k\leq n+1}\left\lvert \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}z_i^k\right\rvert < C^{-n}$?
status: This is Problem 7.3 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős. Erdős proved (as described on p.35 of [Tu84b]) that such a sequence does exist with $\lvert z_i\rvert\leq 1$; indeed, his construction gives $C\approx 1.32$. In [Er92f], Erdős refines this analysis, proving that if $M_2=\min_{z_j} \max_{2\leq k\leq n+1} \left\lvert \sum_{1\leq j\leq n}z_j^k \right\rvert$, where the minimum is taken over all $z_j\in \mathbb{C}$ with $\max \lvert z_j\rvert=1$, then $(1.746)^{-n} < M_2 < (1.745)^{-n}$. Tang notes in the comments that Theorem 6.1 of [Tu84b] implies that, if $\lvert z_i\rvert \geq 1$ for all $i$, then $\max_{2\leq k\leq n+1}\left\lvert \sum_{1\leq i\leq n}z_i^k \right\rvert \geq (2e)^{-(1+o(1))n}$. See also [519].
solved_when: A constant $C>1$ and, for every $n\geq 2$, a sequence $z_i\in \mathbb{C}$ with $z_1=1$ and $\lvert z_i\rvert\geq 1$ are exhibited such that the maximum over $2\leq k\leq n+1$ of $\left\lvert \sum_{1\leq i\leq n} z_i^k \right\rvert$ is less than $C^{-n}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles whether power sums of complex numbers outside the unit circle can be made exponentially small.

title: Erdős problem #975
open: Let $f\in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be an irreducible non-constant polynomial with $f(n)\geq 1$ for all large $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Does the divisor function summed along the values of $f$ obey an asymptotic law $\sum_{n\leq X} \tau(f(n))\sim cX\log X$ for some constant $c=c(f)>0$?
status: Van der Corput [Va39] proved the lower bound $\sum_{n\leq X} \tau(f(n))\gg_f X\log X$, and Erdős [Er52b] proved the matching upper bound $\sum_{n\leq X} \tau(f(n))\ll_f X\log X$ by elementary methods. The asymptotic formula is known when $f$ is an irreducible quadratic, as proved by Hooley [Ho63]; the constant $c$ depends on $f$ in a complicated fashion (see McKee [Mc95], [Mc97], [Mc99] for expressions for various types of quadratic $f$). For example, $\sum_{n\leq x}\tau(n^2+1)=\frac{3}{\pi}x\log x+O(x)$. Tao has a blog post on this topic.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every irreducible non-constant $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ with $f(n)\geq 1$ for all large $n$, there exists $c=c(f)>0$ with $\sum_{n\leq X}\tau(f(n))\sim cX\log X$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles the general divisor-sum asymptotic for polynomial sequences beyond the quadratic case.

title: Erdős problem #976
open: Given an irreducible integer polynomial $f$ of degree $d\geq 2$, how large is the greatest prime divisor of the product $\prod_{1\leq m\leq n} f(m)$? Formally, writing $F_f(n)$ for this greatest prime divisor, is it true that $F_f(n)\gg n^{1+c}$ for some constant $c>0$, or even $\gg n^d$?
status: Nagell [Na22] and Ricci [Ri34] proved $F_f(n)\gg n\log n$, which Erdős [Er52c] improved to $F_f(n)\gg n(\log n)^{\log\log\log n}$. In [Er65b] he claimed a proof of $F_f(n)\gg n\exp((\log n)^c)$ for some constant $c>0$, but said he had never published the proof, which was 'fairly complicated'; this seems to have been flawed, since Erdős and Schinzel [ErSc90] later published a weaker bound. A proof of the stronger bound was finally provided by Tenenbaum [Te90].
solved_when: An estimate of $F_f(n)$ is obtained; in particular, a proof (or disproof) that $F_f(n)\gg n^{1+c}$ for some constant $c>0$, and ideally of the stronger bound $F_f(n)\gg n^d$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/976; a sharp estimate would resolve how quickly prime factors grow in polynomial sequences.

title: Erdős problem #978
open: Does an irreducible integer polynomial of degree $k>2$ with positive leading coefficient (where $k\neq 2^l$ for any $l\geq 1$) take $(k-1)$-power-free values on a set of positive density? More sharply, if $k>3$ and for every prime $p$ there exists $n$ with $p^{k-2}\nmid f(n)$, are there infinitely many $n$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-2)$-power-free — in particular, does $n^4+2$ represent infinitely many squarefree numbers?
status: Erdős [Er53] proved there are infinitely many $n$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-1)$-power-free, except when $k=2^l$ and $2^{k-1}\mid f(n)$ for all $n$; the latter exception is possible, for example for $f(x)=k!\left(\binom{x}{k}+1\right)$. Hooley [Ho67] settled the first question, in fact providing a precise asymptotic for the number of such $n\leq x$. Heath-Brown [He06] proved the second question has a positive answer when $k\geq 10$, and Browning [Br11] extended this to $k\geq 9$, in fact establishing an asymptotic formula for the number of such $n$; these results assume there does not exist a prime $p$ such that $p^{k-2}\mid f(n)$ for all $n$, a condition Erdős did not state explicitly but which is an obvious necessary condition, discussed explicitly in [He06] and [Br11]. In [Er65b] Erdős mentions the related questions of whether $2^n\pm 1$ or $n!\pm 1$ represent infinitely many $k$th power-free integers, but calls them 'intractable at present' (see also [936]).
solved_when: A proof that, for every irreducible $f\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree $k>2$ with positive leading coefficient and $k\neq 2^l$, the set of $n\geq 1$ with $f(n)$ $(k-1)$-power-free has positive density; and, for $k>3$ under the local condition that for all primes $p$ there exists $n$ with $p^{k-2}\nmid f(n)$, a proof that infinitely many $n$ give $f(n)$ $(k-2)$-power-free — including the special case $f(n)=n^4+2$ squarefree infinitely often.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolves the natural boundary case between what sieve methods achieve ($(k-1)$-power-free values) and the harder power-free-value regime.

title: Erdős problem #979
open: For $k\geq 2$, let $f_k(n)$ count the number of ways to write $n$ as a sum of $k$ prime powers, $n=p_1^k+\cdots+p_k^k$ with all $p_i$ prime. Is $\limsup f_k(n)=\infty$ — that is, do values of $n$ exist with arbitrarily many such representations?
status: Erdős [Er37b] proved the result for $k=2$, and also for $k=3$, though the latter proof appears to be unpublished.
solved_when: It is proved that for each $k\geq 2$, the values of $f_k(n)$ are unbounded above, i.e. $\limsup_{n\to\infty} f_k(n)=\infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and resolving it would settle a question he tracked himself; it is maintained with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #982
open: If $n$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ form a convex polygon, must some vertex determine at least $\lfloor \frac{n}{2}\rfloor$ different distances to the other vertices?
status: The regular polygon shows that $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ is best possible. The conjecture would be implied if there were a vertex such that no three vertices of the polygon are equally distant from it, which Erdős also originally conjectured [Er46b], but this is false (see [97]). Let $f(n)$ be the maximal number of such distances that are guaranteed. Moser [Mo52] proved $f(n) \geq \lceil\frac{n}{3}\rceil$; Erdős and Fishburn [ErFi94] improved this to $f(n) \geq \lfloor \frac{n}{3}+1\rfloor$, then Dumitrescu [Du06b] to $f(n) \geq \lceil \frac{13n-6}{36}\rceil$, and most recently Nivasch, Pach, Pinchasi, and Zerbib [NPPZ13] to $f(n) \geq \left(\frac{13}{36}+\frac{1}{22701}\right)n-O(1)$. In [Er46b] Erdős made the even stronger conjecture that on every convex curve there exists a point $p$ such that every circle with centre $p$ intersects the curve in at most $2$ points. Bárány and Roldán-Pensado [BaRo13] noted that the boundary of any acute triangle is a counterexample. Bárány and Roldán-Pensado prove that, for any planar convex body, there is a point $p$ on the boundary such that every circle with centre $p$ intersects the boundary in at most $2$ points.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the bound $\lfloor \frac{n}{2}\rfloor$ on the number of distinct distances from some vertex of every convex $n$-gon.

title: Erdős problem #983
open: Let $n\geq 2$ and $\pi(n)<k\leq n$, and let $f(k,n)$ be the smallest integer $r$ such that any $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ of size $|A|=k$ contains more than $r$ elements divisible only by primes from some set $\{p_1,\ldots,p_r\}$. Is it true that $2\pi(n^{1/2})-f(\pi(n)+1,n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, and more generally, what is the estimate for $f(k,n)$, particularly when $\pi(n)+1<k=o(n)$?
status: It is trivial that $f(k,n)\leq \pi(n)$. Erdős and Straus [Er70b] proved that $f(\pi(n)+1,n)=2\pi(n^{1/2})+o_A\left(\frac{n^{1/2}}{(\log n)^A}\right)$ for any $A>0$, and, for any constant $1>c>0$, $f(cn,n)=\log\log n+(c_1+o(1))\sqrt{2\log\log n}$, where $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{c_1}e^{-x^2/2}\mathrm{d}x$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $2\pi(n^{1/2})-f(\pi(n)+1,n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, together with estimates for $f(k,n)$ in the range $\pi(n)+1<k=o(n)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it resolves the behavior of $f(k,n)$ exactly at and above the threshold $\pi(n)+1$, where the known asymptotic leaves the question open.

title: Erdős problem #985
open: Is it true that, for every prime $p$, there is a prime $q<p$ which is a primitive root modulo $p$?
status: This problem sits in the orbit of the Artin conjecture, which asserts that $2$ is a primitive root for infinitely many primes $p$; Hooley [Ho67b] proved this assuming the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis, and Heath-Brown [He86b] proved unconditionally that at least one of $2$, $3$, or $5$ is a primitive root for infinitely many primes $p$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every prime $p$ admits some prime $q<p$ that is a primitive root modulo $p$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, so a resolution would close a longstanding item in that catalog and advance our understanding of how small primes distribute as primitive roots.

title: Erdős problem #993
open: Is the independent set sequence of every tree or forest unimodal? That is, writing $i_k(G)$ for the number of independent sets of vertices of size $k$ in a graph $G$, must every tree or forest $T$ admit some $m\geq 0$ with $i_{0}(T)\leq i_{1}(T)\leq\cdots\leq i_{m}(T)\geq i_{m+1}(T)\geq i_{m+2}(T)\geq\cdots$?
status: The question was posed by Alavi, Malde, Schwenk, and Erdős [AMSE87], who showed the analogous statement is false for general graphs $G$ — in fact every possible pattern of inequalities is achieved by some graph. The sequence counting independent sets of edges of a given size, by contrast, was proved unimodal for any graph by Schwenk [Sc81]. In [AMSE87] the authors also ask whether every possible unimodal pattern of inequalities is achieved by some graph.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every tree or forest $T$ the vertex-independent-set numbers $i_k(T)$ form a unimodal sequence, i.e. there exists $m\geq 0$ such that the inequalities above hold.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; unimodality of such counting sequences is a basic structural question about trees beyond the general graphs where it fails.

title: Erdős problem #995
open: For a lacunary sequence of integers $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ and $f\in L^2([0,1])$, how fast can the Birkhoff sums $\sum_{1\leq k\leq N}f(\{\alpha n_k\})$ grow for almost all $\alpha$? In particular, is it true that, for almost all $\alpha$, $\sum_{1\leq k\leq N}f(\{\alpha n_k\})=o(N\sqrt{\log\log N})$?
status: Erdős [Er49d] constructed a lacunary sequence and $f\in L^2([0,1])$ such that, for every $\epsilon>0$, for almost all $\alpha$, $\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N(\log\log N)^{1/2-\epsilon}}\sum_{1\leq k\leq N}f(\{\alpha n_k\})=\infty$. He also proved that, for every lacunary sequence and $f\in L^2$, for every $\epsilon>0$, for almost all $\alpha$, the sum is $o(N(\log N)^{1/2+\epsilon})$. Erdős [Er64b] believed his lower bound was closer to the truth.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, for every lacunary sequence $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ and every $f\in L^2([0,1])$, the estimate $\sum_{1\leq k\leq N}f(\{\alpha n_k\})=o(N\sqrt{\log\log N})$ holds for almost all $\alpha$; equivalently, a sharp bound on the almost-everywhere growth rate, resolving whether the exponent $\tfrac12$ on $\log\log N$ is the truth.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/995, and it probes the boundary of almost-everywhere convergence phenomena for lacunary dilates — a natural test case for metric discrepancy theory.

title: Erdős problem #996
open: Let $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ be a lacunary sequence of integers, and let $f\in L^2([0,1])$. Let $f_n$ be the $n$th partial sum of the Fourier series of $f(x)$. Is there an absolute constant $C>0$ such that, if\[\| f-f_n\|_2 \ll \frac{1}{(\log\log\log n)^{C}}\]then\[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\leq N}f(\{\alpha n_k\})=\int_0^1 f(x)\mathrm{d}x\]for almost every $\alpha$?
status: Raikov proved the conclusion always holds (for every $f\in L^2([0,1])$, with no assumption on $\| f-f_n\|_2$) if $n_k=a^k$ for some integer $a\geq 2$. Erdős [Er64b] also asked whether this is true for $n_k=\lfloor a^k\rfloor$ for some $a>1$. Kac, Salem, and Zygmund [KSZ48] proved the conclusion holds if $\| f-f_n\|_2 \ll \frac{1}{(\log n)^{c}}$ for some constant $c>1$. Erdős [Er49d] proved the conclusion holds if $\| f-f_n\|_2 \ll \frac{1}{(\log\log n)^{c}}$ for some constant $c>1$, and Matsuyama [Ma66] improved this to $c>1/2$. In [Er64b] Erdős asked whether the conclusion holds for all bounded functions $f$ and lacunary sequences $n_k$.
solved_when: An absolute constant $C>0$ is exhibited such that whenever $\| f-f_n\|_2 \ll 1/(\log\log\log n)^{C}$, the averages $\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\leq N} f(\{\alpha n_k\})$ converge to $\int_0^1 f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ for almost every $\alpha$ (or a counterexample shows no such $C$ exists).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would complete the known hierarchy of Fourier-decay thresholds guaranteeing equidistribution of lacunary sequences for a.e. $\alpha$.

title: Erdős problem #1002
open: Does the normalized sum $f(\alpha,n)=\frac{1}{\log n}\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}(\tfrac{1}{2}-\{ \alpha k\})$ have an asymptotic distribution function as $n\to\infty$, uniformly over $\alpha\in(0,1)$? Formally, is there a non-decreasing function $g$ with $g(-\infty)=0$, $g(\infty)=1$, such that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\lvert \{ \alpha\in (0,1): f(\alpha,n)\leq c\}\rvert=g(c)$?
status: Kesten [Ke60] proved that the shifted variant $f(\alpha,\beta,n)=\frac{1}{\log n}\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}(\tfrac{1}{2}-\{\beta+\alpha k\})$ has an asymptotic distribution function $g(c)=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\rho c}\frac{1}{1+t^2}\mathrm{d}t$, where $\rho>0$ is an explicit constant.
solved_when: Such a function $g$ is constructed and proven to satisfy the above limit (with $g(-\infty)=0$, $g(\infty)=1$), or the existence of the limit is refuted.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/1002; a solution would settle the limiting distributional behavior of these discrepancy sums in diophantine approximation.

title: Erdős problem #1003
open: Are there infinitely many positive integers $n$ for which $\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)$, where $\phi$ is the Euler totient function?
status: Erdős [Er85e] says that, presumably, for every $k\geq 1$ the equation $\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)=\cdots=\phi(n+k)$ has infinitely many solutions. Erdős, Pomerance, and Sárközy [EPS87] proved that the number of $n\leq x$ with $\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)$ is at most $\frac{x}{\exp((\log x)^{1/3})}$. See [946] for the analogous question with the divisor function, and [415] for a question about more general inequality patterns among consecutive values of $\phi$.
solved_when: A proof that $\phi(n)=\phi(n+1)$ for infinitely many $n$, or a proof that only finitely many such $n$ exist.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it sits in the broader question of how multiplicatively defined arithmetic functions behave on consecutive integers.

title: Erdős problem #1004
open: Let $c>0$. If $x$ is sufficiently large then does there exist $n\leq x$ such that the values of $\phi(n+k)$ are all distinct for $1\leq k\leq (\log x)^c$, where $\phi$ is the Euler totient function?
status: Erdős, Pomerance, and Sárközy [EPS87] proved that if the values $\phi(n+k)$ are all distinct for $1\leq k\leq K$, then $K \leq \frac{n}{\exp(c(\log n)^{1/3})}$ for some constant $c>0$. See [945] for the analogous problem with the divisor function.
solved_when: There is a proof that for every $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $x$, some $n\leq x$ has the values $\phi(n+k)$ pairwise distinct for $1\leq k\leq (\log x)^c$ (or a counterexample exhibiting a $c$ for which no such $n$ exists for arbitrarily large $x$).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and a resolution would clarify how far the Euler totient function can avoid repetitions on short intervals; the problem is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #1011
open: How many edges force a triangle once a graph is required to have chromatic number at least $r$? Formally, let $f_r(n)$ be the minimal value such that every graph on $n$ vertices with at least $f_r(n)$ edges and chromatic number at least $r$ contains a triangle; determine $f_r(n)$.
status: Turán's theorem implies $f_2(n)=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1$. Erdős and Gallai [Er62d] proved $f_3(n)=\lfloor \frac{1}{4}(n-1)^2\rfloor+2$. Simonovits showed in his PhD thesis (see the discussion on p. 358 of [Si74]) that $f_r(n)=\frac{n^2}{4}-\frac{g(r)}{2}n+O(1)$, where $g(r)$ is the largest $m$ such that, for any triangle-free graph with chromatic number $\geq r$, at least $m$ vertices need to be removed to obtain a bipartite graph. Simonovits [Si74] notes $\frac{\log r}{\log\log r}r^2 \ll g(r) \ll (\log r)^2r^2$. Hunter in the comments has noted that other results imply $g(r)\asymp r^2\log r$ — in fact $(1/2-o(1))r^2\log r\leq g(r)\leq (2+o(1))r^2\log r$, with the lower bound following from work of Davies and Illingworth [DaIl22] (see [1104]) and the upper bound from work of Hefty, Horn, King, and Pfender [HHKP25] on $R(3,k)$. Ren, Wang, Wang, and Yang [RWWY24] showed that, for $n\geq 150$, $f_4(n)=\left\lfloor\frac{(n-3)^2}{4}\right\rfloor+6$.
solved_when: An exact formula (or sharp asymptotic with matching leading constants) for $f_r(n)$ is determined, including pinning down the function $g(r)$ governing the linear term in $f_r(n) = \frac{n^2}{4} - \frac{g(r)}{2}n + O(1)$ up to its exact order of growth.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and its resolution rests on the parameter $g(r)$, which itself quantifies how far triangle-free graphs of chromatic number $r$ are from bipartiteness — a question tied to Ramsey numbers $R(3,k)$.

title: Erdős problem #1013
open: Let $h_3(k)$ be the minimal number of vertices in a triangle-free graph of chromatic number $k$. Can one determine the asymptotic behavior of $h_3(k)$, and in particular show that the ratio of consecutive values tends to one, i.e. $\lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{h_3(k+1)}{h_3(k)} = 1$?
status: The function $h_3(k)$ is dual to the function $f(n)$ considered in [1104], in that $h_3(k) = n$ if and only if $n$ is minimal such that $f(n) = k$. Graver and Yackel [GrYa68] proved $h_3(k) \gg \frac{\log k}{\log\log k} k^2$. The bounds for $f(n)$ from [1104] imply $\left(\frac{1}{2}-o(1)\right) k^2 \log k \leq h_3(k) \leq (1+o(1)) k^2 \log k$. See also [920] for a generalisation to $K_r$-free graphs.
solved_when: An asymptotic formula for $h_3(k)$ as $k \to \infty$ is established, together with a proof that $\lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{h_3(k+1)}{h_3(k)} = 1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle the fundamental quantitative relationship between forbidden triangles and high chromatic number.

title: Erdős problem #1017
open: How many edge-disjoint complete graphs are needed to partition the edges of any graph with $n$ vertices and $k$ edges, when $k>n^2/4$? Formally, estimate the clique partition number $f(n,k)$ in this dense regime, sharpening the general bound of Erdős, Goodman, and Pósa.
status: The function $f(n,k)$ is sometimes called the clique partition number. Erdős, Goodman, and Pósa [EGP66] proved that $f(n,k)\leq n^2/4$ for all $k$ (and in fact the complete graphs can be taken to be edges and triangles), which is best possible in general, as witnessed for example by a complete bipartite graph. In [Er71] Erdős asks vaguely whether this result can be 'sharpened' for $k>n^2/4$. Lovász [Lo68] proved that every graph on $n$ vertices and $k$ edges is the union of $\binom{n}{2}-k+t$ complete graphs, where $t$ is maximal such that $t^2-t\leq \binom{n}{2}-k$, but without the assumption that the complete graphs are edge disjoint; this result is sharp in many cases. If $k>n^2/4$ and the graph contains no $K_4$, the problem is equivalent to finding the minimum number of edge-disjoint triangles — a special case also asked about by Erdős. A complete answer was provided by Györi and Keszegh [GyKe17], who proved that every $K_4$-free graph with $n$ vertices and $\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+m$ edges contains $m$ pairwise edge-disjoint triangles. See also [184] for an analogous problem decomposing into edges and cycles, and [583] for decomposing into paths.
solved_when: A sharp estimate of $f(n,k)$ is obtained for all $k>n^2/4$, giving the correct order (and ideally exact values) of the minimum number of edge-disjoint complete graphs needed to partition any $n$-vertex, $k$-edge graph in this range.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and resolving it completes the picture of clique partitioning beyond the extremal threshold $n^2/4$, where the general bound is no longer tight.

title: Erdős problem #1020
open: How many edges can an $r$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices have before it must contain $k$ pairwise disjoint edges? The conjectured answer, for all $r\geq 3$, is $f(n;r,k)=\max\left(\binom{rk-1}{r}, \binom{n}{r}-\binom{n-k+1}{r}\right)$, where $f(n;r,k)$ is the maximal number of edges in an $r$-uniform hypergraph with no $k$ independent edges.
status: Erdős and Gallai [ErGa59] proved this when $r=2$ (when $r=2$ it also follows from the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem). The conjectured form is best possible, witnessed by all $r$-edges on a set of $rk-1$ vertices, and all edges on a set of $n$ vertices containing at least one element of a fixed set of $k-1$ vertices. Frankl [Fr87] proved $f(n;r,k) \leq (k-1)\binom{n-1}{r-1}$. The second term in the maximum dominates when $n\geq (r+1)k$. There are many partial results in two regimes. For small $n$: trivially true if $n<kr$; Kleitman [Kl68] when $n=kr$; Frankl [Fr17] when $kr \leq n\leq k\left(r+\frac{1}{2r^{2r+1}}\right)$; Kolupaev and Kupavskii [KoKu23] when $r\geq 5$, $k>101r^3$, and $kr \leq n < k\left(r+\frac{1}{100r}\right)$. For large $n$: Erdős [Er65d] when $n>kc_r$ (where $c_r$ depends on $r$ in some unspecified fashion); Frankl and Füredi [Fr87] when $n>100k^2r$; Bollobás, Daykin, and Erdős [BDE76] when $n\geq 2kr^3$; Frankl, Rödl, and Ruciński [FRR12] whe
solved_when: The displayed formula for $f(n;r,k)$ is proved for all $r\geq 3$, all $n$, and all $k$.
why: This is the Erdős matching conjecture, one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a proof would settle the extremal behavior of matchings in uniform hypergraphs across the entire range of parameters.

title: Erdős problem #1029
open: Does the diagonal Ramsey number $R(k)$ eventually dominate $k2^{k/2}$ by an unbounded factor? Formally, is it true that $R(k)/k2^{k/2}\to\infty$?
status: In [Er93] Erdős offers \$100 for a proof of this and \$1000 for a disproof, but says 'this last offer is to some extent phoney: I am sure that [this] is true (but I have been wrong before).' Erdős and Szekeres [ErSz35] proved $k2^{k/2} \ll R(k) \leq \binom{2k-1}{k-1}$. One of the first applications of the probabilistic method pioneered by Erdős gives $R(k) \geq (1+o(1))\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}e}k2^{k/2}$, which Spencer [Sp75] improved by a factor of $2$ to $R(k) \geq (1+o(1))\frac{\sqrt{2}}{e}k2^{k/2}$. See also [77] for a more general problem concerning $\lim R(k)^{1/k}$, and discussion of upper bounds for $R(k)$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\frac{R(k)}{k2^{k/2}}\to \infty$. Erdős offered \$100 for a proof and \$1000 for a disproof.

title: Erdős problem #1030
open: Does the diagonal Ramsey sequence $R(k,k)$ grow by a fixed multiplicative margin as $k$ increases? Formally, prove the existence of some $c>0$ such that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{R(k+1,k)}{R(k,k)}>1+c$.
status: A problem of Erdős and Sós, who could not even prove whether $R(k+1,k)-R(k,k)>k^c$ for any $c>1$. It is trivial that $R(k+1,k)-R(k,k)\geq k-2$. Burr, Erdős, Faudree, and Schelp [BEFS89] proved $R(k+1,k)-R(k,k)\geq 2k-5$. See also [544] for a similar question concerning $R(3,k)$, and [1014] for the general off-diagonal case. Reference: [Er93, p. 339].
solved_when: A constant $c>0$ is exhibited for which the limit $\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{R(k+1,k)}{R(k,k)}$ exceeds $1+c$.

title: Erdős problem #1032
open: Does there exist, for arbitrarily large $n$, a $4$-chromatic critical graph on $n$ vertices whose minimum degree grows as $\gg n$? (Here $4$-chromatic critical means chromatic number $4$ with every edge's removal dropping the chromatic number to $3$.)
status: In [Er93] Erdős said he asked this 'more than 20 years ago'. Dirac gave an example of a $6$-chromatic critical graph with minimum degree $>n/2$. The problem is also open for $5$-chromatic critical graphs. Simonovits [Si72] and Toft [To72] independently constructed $4$-chromatic critical graphs with minimum degree $\gg n^{1/3}$. Toft conjectured that a $4$-chromatic critical graph on $n$ vertices has at least $(\frac{5}{3}+o(1))n$ vertices, and has examples showing this would be best possible. See also [917] and [944].
solved_when: A construction is given of $4$-chromatic critical graphs on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $\gg n$ for arbitrarily large $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #1033
open: In every graph on $n$ vertices with more than $n^2/4$ edges, some triangle must have unusually high-degree vertices; how large must the sum of the degrees of that triangle's three vertices be? Formally, letting $h(n)$ be the largest value guaranteed for such a triangle, estimate $h(n)$ — in particular, is it true that $h(n)\geq (2(\sqrt{3}-1)-o(1))n$?
status: This originates as a conjecture of Bollobás and Erdős; in [Er82e] it is asked whether $h(n)\geq \frac{3}{2}n$. It is now known that $2(\sqrt{3}-1)n + O(1) \geq h(n) \geq \frac{21}{16}n$ (note $2(\sqrt{3}-1)\approx 1.464$ and $21/16 = 1.3125$). The upper bound is due to Erdős and Laskar [ErLa85], and the lower bound due to Fan [Fa88]. The upper bound is not made explicit in [ErLa85], which is concerned with chordal subgraphs (subgraphs containing no induced cycle on $>3$ vertices); the connection is that a triangle together with all incident edges forms a chordal subgraph of $G$. Fan's paper [Fa88] makes the upper-bound construction explicit: let $m=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor+1$ and take a complete bipartite graph between parts of $k$ and $l$ vertices with $k+l=n$ and $k=cn$; choosing $c$ so that $m-kl\leq k^2/4$, one adds $m-kl$ edges among the $k$ vertices creating no triangles while giving maximum degree (among those vertices) $\lceil 2\frac{m-kl}{k}\rceil$. This yields a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $m$ edges in which every triangle uses exactly one vertex from the side with $l$ vertices and two vertices from the other side.
solved_when: $h(n)$ is estimated asymptotically; in particular, the conjectured lower bound $h(n)\geq (2(\sqrt{3}-1)-o(1))n$ is proved or refuted, improving on the known bounds $2(\sqrt{3}-1)n + O(1) \geq h(n) \geq \frac{21}{16}n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a natural extremal question about how strong a degree condition on a triangle is forced just above the Turán threshold.

title: Erdős problem #1035
open: Is there a constant $c>0$ such that every graph on $2^n$ vertices with minimum degree $>(1-c)2^n$ contains the $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$? In other words, does some fixed positive fraction of the complete graph's density force a hypercube of the matching dimension?
status: Open. Erdős [Er93] remarks that "if the conjecture is false, two related problems could be asked": determine or estimate the smallest $m>2^n$ such that every graph on $m$ vertices with minimum degree $>(1-c)2^n$ contains a $Q_n$, and determine for which $u_n$ it holds that every graph on $2^n$ vertices with minimum degree $>2^n-u_n$ contains a $Q_n$. See also [576] for the extremal number of edges that guarantee a $Q_n$.
solved_when: A constant $c>0$ is exhibited (or shown not to exist), settling for all $n$ whether every graph on $2^n$ vertices with minimum degree $>(1-c)2^n$ contains a copy of $Q_n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles a basic density threshold for embedding hypercubes and directly guides the two fallback questions Erdős attached to it.

title: Erdős problem #1038
open: What are the smallest and largest possible Lebesgue measures of the set where a monic polynomial with all roots real and lying in $[-1,1]$ takes values of magnitude less than 1? Formally, determine the infimum and supremum of $|\{x \in \mathbb{R} : |f(x)| < 1\}|$ as $f \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ ranges over all non-constant monic polynomials whose roots are all real and in $[-1,1]$.
status: A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], who proved that the measure of the set in question is always at most $2\sqrt{2}$ under the assumption that all roots lie in $\{-1,1\}$, and conjectured this is the best possible upper bound. They also noted that the infimum is less than $2$, witnessed by $f(x) = (x+1)(x-1)^m$ for $m \geq 3$, and that if the roots are restricted to $[-2,2]$ the infimum is zero, witnessed by a small perturbation of the Chebyshev polynomials. They further conjectured that with roots in $[-2,2]$ the measure is at least $n^{-c}$ for an absolute constant $c > 0$; this was proved by Pommerenke [Po61], who showed the set must in fact contain an interval of width $\gg n^{-4}$. The current best known bounds (see the discussion in the comments) are $1.519 \approx 2^{4/3} - 1 \leq \inf \leq 1.835\cdots$ and $\sup = 2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.828$.
solved_when: The exact infimum and supremum of the measure $|\{x \in \mathbb{R} : |f(x)| < 1\}|$ over non-constant monic real-rooted polynomials with roots in $[-1,1]$ are determined, closing the gap between the current bounds $2^{4/3} - 1 \approx 1.519 \leq \inf \leq 1.835\cdots$ and $\sup = 2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.828$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; settling the exact extremal measures resolves a long-standing conjecture of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian on the sharp upper bound.

title: Erdős problem #1039
open: Given a polynomial $f(z)=\prod_{i=1}^n(z-z_i)$ with all roots in the closed unit disc, how large is the largest disc contained in the sublevel set $\{z: |f(z)|<1\}$? In particular, is the radius $\rho(f)$ always bounded below by a constant times $1/n$?
