status: A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian, who note that $f(z)=z^n-1$ has $\rho(f)\leq\frac{\pi/2}{n}$, so the conjectured order is best possible up to constants. Pommerenke [Po61] proved $\rho(f)\geq\frac{1}{2en^2}$. Krishnapur, Lundberg, and Ramachandran [KLR25] improved this to $\rho(f)\gg\frac{1}{n\sqrt{\log n}}$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the bound $\rho(f)\gg 1/n$ holding for all such polynomials, or a determination of the correct order of growth of $\rho(f)$ in $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would settle the sharp quantitative relationship between the degree and the guaranteed size of the sublevel set's inscribed disc.

title: Erdős problem #1040
open: Let $F\subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be a closed infinite set, and let $\mu(F)$ be the infimum of\[\lvert \{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}\rvert,\]as $f$ ranges over all polynomials of the shape $\prod (z-z_i)$ with $z_i\in F$. Is $\mu(F)$ determined by the transfinite diameter of $F$? In particular, is $\mu(F)=0$ whenever the transfinite diameter of $F$ is $\geq 1$?
status: A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], who show that the answer is yes if $F$ is a line segment or disc, and that if the transfinite diameter is $<1$ then $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}$ always contains a disc of radius $\gg_F 1$. Erdős and Netanyahu [ErNe73] proved that if $F$ is also bounded and connected, with transfinite diameter $0<c<1$, then $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert < 1\}$ always contains a disc of radius $\gg_c 1$. The transfinite diameter of $F$, also known as the logarithmic capacity, is defined by\[\rho(F)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{z_1,\ldots,z_n\in F}\left(\prod_{i<j}\lvert z_i-z_j\rvert\right)^{1/\binom{n}{2}}.\]Aletheia [Fe26] has shown that $\mu(F)$ is not determined by the transfinite diameter of $F$, by producing two distinct closed infinite sets $F_1$ and $F_2$, both of transfinite diameter $0$, with $\mu(F_1)\geq \pi/4$ while $\mu(F_2)$ can be made arbitrarily close to $0$.
solved_when: The question of whether $\mu(F)$ is determined by the transfinite diameter of $F$ is settled by a proof or disproof; since the general determination already fails (two sets of transfinite diameter $0$ with $\mu(F_1)\geq \pi/4$ and $\mu(F_2)$ arbitrarily close to $0$), the natural remaining criterion is a characterization of exactly which features of $F$ govern $\mu(F)$, and in particular an answer to whether $\mu(F)=0$ whenever the transfinite diameter of $F$ is $\geq 1$.

title: Erdős problem #1041
open: If all roots of a polynomial $f(z)=\prod_{i=1}^n(z-z_i)$ lie strictly inside the unit disk, must two of those roots always be connectable by a path of length less than $2$ inside the sublevel set $\{z : |f(z)| < 1\}$?
status: The problem originates with Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], who proved that the set $\{z : |f(z)| < 1\}$ always has a connected component containing at least two of the roots. The question of whether such a component always admits a path of length less than $2$ remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) establishing whether, for every polynomial with all roots $|z_i| < 1$, some pair of roots is joined within $\{z : |f(z)| < 1\}$ by a path of length less than $2$.
why: A solution resolves one of Erdős's personally posed problems, settled within a question at the interface of polynomial geometry and plane topology that has remained open since it was raised.

title: Erdős problem #1045
open: Among $n$ points in the complex plane with all pairwise distances at most $2$, what configuration maximizes the product $\Delta(z_1,\ldots,z_n)=\prod_{i\neq j}|z_i-z_j|$ of pairwise distances? In particular, is the regular $n$-gon optimal — at least for infinitely many $n$ — or, as recent counterexamples suggest, does some other configuration always do better?
status: A problem of Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58], who proved that for any monic polynomial $f$, if $\{z: |f(z)|<1\}$ is connected and $f$ has roots $z_1,\ldots,z_n$, then $\prod_{i\neq j}|z_i-z_j| < n^n$. For vertices of a regular polygon, $\Delta = n^n$ when $n$ is even and $\cos(\pi/2n)^{-n(n-1)}n^n \sim e^{\pi^2/8}n^n$ when $n$ is odd. Pommerenke [Po61] proved $\Delta \leq 2^{O(n)}n^n$ for all $z_i$ with $|z_i-z_j|\leq 2$. Hu and Tang (see the comments) found examples for $n=4$ and $n=6$ showing regular polygons do not maximize $\Delta$, and Cambie (also in the comments) showed regular polygons are not maximizers for all even $n\geq 4$. It is now known that for even $n$, $\liminf \frac{\max\Delta}{n^n}\geq C$ for some $C>0$; the best available value is $C\approx 1.268$ from [CDDHT26], improved to $C\approx 1.304$ when $n$ is divisible by 6. There is substantial further discussion in the comments, and in the papers of Sothanaphan [So25] and Cambie, Decadt, Dong, Hu, and Tang [CDDHT26].
solved_when: The exact maximum of $\Delta$ over all $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|z_i-z_j|\leq 2$ is determined (or the extremal configuration is identified) for each $n$, together with the asymptotic behavior of $\max \Delta$ relative to $n^n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it sits at the interface of polynomial lemniscates and discrete geometry; resolving it would settle the sharp form of the Erdős–Herzog–Piranian bound.

title: Erdős problem #1049
open: Let $t>1$ be rational. Must the Lambert series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{t^n-1}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\tau(n)}{t^n}$, where $\tau(n)$ counts the divisors of $n$, be irrational?
status: A conjecture of Chowla. Erdős [Er48] proved that this is true if $t\geq 2$ is an integer. Key works: erdosproblems.com/1049; Erdős references: [Er88c,p.102] [Er48].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the series is irrational for every rational $t>1$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve a natural irrationality question attached to a conjecture of Chowla.

title: Erdős problem #1052
open: A unitary divisor of $n$ is a divisor $d$ with $(d,n/d)=1$, and $n$ is a unitary perfect number if it equals the sum of its proper unitary divisors. Are there only finitely many unitary perfect numbers?
status: Guy [Gu04] reports that Carlitz, Erdős, and Subbarao offer \$10 for settling this question, and that Subbarao offers 10 cents for each new example; it is problem B3 in Guy's collection [Gu04]. No odd unitary perfect numbers are known to exist, and exactly five unitary perfect numbers are known (A002827 in the OEIS): 6, 60, 90, 87360, and 146361946186458562560000.
solved_when: A proof that only finitely many unitary perfect numbers exist, or a construction exhibiting infinitely many of them.

title: Erdős problem #1053
open: Call a number $k$-perfect if $\sigma(n)=kn$, where $\sigma(n)$ is the sum of the divisors of $n$. Must the abundancy index $k$ of a $k$-perfect number satisfy $k=o(\log\log n)$?
status: A question of Erdős, as reported in problem B2 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. Guy further writes "It has even been suggested that there may be only finitely many $k$-perfect numbers with $k\geq 3$." The largest $k$ for which a $k$-perfect number has been found is $k=11$; these numbers are known as multiply perfect numbers, and when $k=2$ this is the definition of a perfect number.
solved_when: It is proved (or disproved) that for every $k$-perfect number $n$, $k=o(\log\log n)$ as $n\to\infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would clarify how large the abundancy index of multiply perfect numbers can grow, a basic structural question about these numbers.

title: Erdős problem #1054
open: Given $n$, let $f(n)$ be the least integer $m$ such that $n$ equals the sum of the $k$ smallest divisors of $m$ for some $k\geq 1$. Is $f(n)=o(n)$, or does this hold only for almost all $n$ while $\limsup f(n)/n=\infty$?
status: The question appears as problem B2 in Guy's collection [Gu04]. The function $f(n)$ is undefined for $n=2$ and $n=5$, but is likely well-defined for all $n\geq 6$, which would follow from a strong form of Goldbach's conjecture. Its values form OEIS sequence A167485; see also [468]. The strong claim $f(n)=o(n)$ was disproved by Tao in the comments to [468], where he proves that the upper density of $\{n : f(n)\leq \delta n\}$ is $\ll \delta^2$.
solved_when: A proof that either $f(n)=o(n)$ as $n\to\infty$, or a determination of the true order — in particular, whether the small-$o$ bound holds only for almost all $n$ with $\limsup f(n)/n=\infty$ — is established.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it would clarify how economically integers can be represented through initial sums of divisor sequences.

title: Erdős problem #1055
open: Are there infinitely many primes in each class of the Erdős–Selfridge classification, in which a prime $p$ belongs to class $1$ if the only prime divisors of $p+1$ are $2$ or $3$, and to class $r$ if every prime factor of $p+1$ lies in some class $\leq r-1$ with equality for at least one factor? If $p_r$ denotes the least prime in class $r$, does $p_r^{1/r}$ tend to infinity or remain bounded?
status: The classification is due to Erdős and Selfridge. It is easy to prove that the number of primes $\leq n$ in class $r$ is at most $n^{o(1)}$. The sequence $p_r$ begins $2, 13, 37, 73, 1021$ (A005113 in the OEIS). Erdős thought $p_r^{1/r}\to \infty$, while Selfridge thought it quite likely to be bounded. A similar question can be asked replacing $p+1$ with $p-1$. This is problem A18 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: For each fixed $r$, it is proved (or disproved) that infinitely many primes lie in class $r$; and the asymptotic behavior of $p_r^{1/r}$ — divergence versus boundedness — is determined.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving the growth of $p_r^{1/r}$ would settle a direct disagreement between Erdős's and Selfridge's conjectures.

title: Erdős problem #1056
open: For any given $k\geq 2$, can one find a prime $p$ and $k$ consecutive intervals of integers $I_1,\ldots,I_k$ such that the product of the integers in each interval is congruent to $1$ modulo $p$?
status: This is problem A15 in Guy's collection [Gu04], where he reports that in a 1979 letter Erdős observed that $3\cdot 4\equiv 5\cdot 6\cdot 7\equiv 1\pmod{11}$, establishing the case $k=2$. Makowski [Ma83] found, for $k=3$, that $2\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot 5\equiv 6\cdot 7\cdot 8\cdot 9\cdot 10\cdot 11\equiv 12\cdot 13\cdot 14\cdot 15\equiv 1\pmod{17}$. Noll and Simmons asked, more generally, whether there are solutions to $q_1!\equiv\cdots\equiv q_k!\pmod{p}$ for arbitrarily large $k$ (with $q_1<\cdots<q_k$).
solved_when: For every $k\geq 2$, a prime $p$ and consecutive intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_k$ are exhibited with $\prod_{n\in I_i}n \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ for all $1\leq i\leq k$; the natural criterion since no quantitative target is stated in the record.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a concrete open question from his problem list.

title: Erdős problem #1057
open: Let $C(x)$ count the Carmichael numbers in $[1,x]$. Are there, asymptotically, almost as many Carmichael numbers as integers — specifically, is $C(x)=x^{1-o(1)}$?
status: Erdős [Er56c] proved $C(x) < x \exp\left(-c \frac{\log x\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}\right)$ for some constant $c>0$. Pomerance [Po89] gave a heuristic suggesting this is the true order of growth, and in fact $C(x)= x \exp\left(-(1+o(1))\frac{\log x\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}\right)$. Alford, Granville, and Pomerance [AGP94] proved that $C(x)\to \infty$, and in fact $C(x)>x^{2/7}$ for large $x$. Harman [Ha08] improved the lower bound to $C(x)> x^{0.33336704}$, and Lichtman [Li22] improved the exponent to $0.3389$. Korselt observed that $n$ being a Carmichael number is equivalent to $n$ being squarefree and $p-1\mid n-1$ for all primes $p\mid n$; this is discussed in problem A13 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $C(x)=x^{1-o(1)}$ as $x\to\infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle the true density of Carmichael numbers, with consequences for primality testing and cryptography.

title: Erdős problem #1059
open: Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p - k!$ is composite for every $k$ with $1 \leq k! < p$?
status: A question of Erdős reported in problem A2 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. Examples are $p=101$ and $p=211$. Erdős suggested it may be easier to show that there are infinitely many $n$ such that, if $l!<n\leq (l+1)!$, then all the prime factors of $n$ are $>l$, and all the numbers $n-k!$ are composite for $1\leq k\leq l$.
solved_when: An infinitude of such primes $p$ is proven (or the problem is resolved in the negative by showing only finitely many exist).
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and would settle a natural question about how factorials obstruct prime values near primes.

title: Erdős problem #1061
open: How many pairs $(a,b)$ with $a+b\leq x$ satisfy $\sigma(a)+\sigma(b)=\sigma(a+b)$, where $\sigma$ is the sum-of-divisors function? In particular, is the count asymptotic to $cx$ for some constant $c>0$?
status: The problem is a question of Erdős, reported as problem B15 in Guy's collection [Gu04]; it is tracked at erdosproblems.com/1061 and remains open.
solved_when: An asymptotic formula for the number of solutions with $a+b\leq x$ is proved, ideally confirming the conjectured form $\sim cx$ for some constant $c>0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it resolves a long-standing entry in his problem list.

title: Erdős problem #1062
open: Let $f(n)$ be the size of the largest subset $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that no three distinct elements $a,b,c\in A$ satisfy $a\mid b$ and $a\mid c$. How large can $f(n)$ be — and in particular, is $\lim f(n)/n$ irrational?
status: The example $[m+1,3m+2]$ shows $f(n)\geq\lceil \frac{2}{3}n\rceil$. Lebensold [Le76] has shown that, for large $n$, $0.6725 n \leq f(n) \leq 0.6736 n$. This is problem B24 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: The asymptotic behavior of $f(n)$ is determined, and in particular the question of whether $\lim f(n)/n$ is irrational is settled.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #1065
open: Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p=2^kq+1$ for some prime $q$ and $k\geq 0$? Or $p=2^k3^lq+1$?
status: number theory This is mentioned in problem B46 of Guy's collection [Gu04] .

title: Erdős problem #1066
open: How large an independent set must every unit-distance graph on $n$ planar points (with mutual distances at least $1$) contain? Formally, if $g(n)$ is the largest value such that any such graph has an independent set of at least $g(n)$ vertices, estimate $g(n)$, or perhaps determine $\lim \frac{g(n)}{n}$.
status: Such graphs are always planar. Erdős initially thought $g(n)=n/3$, but Chung and Graham, and independently Pach, gave a construction showing $g(n)\leq \frac{6}{19}n$; Pach and Toth [PaTo96] improved this to $g(n)\leq \frac{5}{16}n$. On the lower side, Pollack [Po85] noted the Four colour theorem implies $g(n)\geq n/4$ since the graph is planar, and reports Pach's observation that for unit distance graphs the four colour theorem can be proved by a simple induction. This was improved to $\frac{9}{35}n$ by Csizmadia [Cs98] and then to $\frac{8}{31}n$ by Swanepoel [Sw02]. The current record bounds are therefore $\frac{8}{31}n \approx 0.258n \leq g(n) \leq 0.3125n = \frac{5}{16}n$. Pollack [Po85] also reports a letter from Erdős posing a more general problem: given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with minimum distance $1$, let $g_d(n)$ be maximal such that there always exist at least $g_d(n)$ points with mutual distances $>1$; is $g_d(n) \gg n/d$ in general? The upper bound $g_d(n) \ll n/d$ is trivial, via widely spaced unit simplices. See [1070] for a general estimate of the independence number of unit distance graphs.
solved_when: Asymptotically tight constants $c_1, c_2$ are determined with $c_1 n \leq g(n) \leq c_2 n$ and $c_1 = c_2$ — equivalently, the limit $\lim \frac{g(n)}{n}$ is found. The gap to close is $\frac{8}{31}n \approx 0.258n \leq g(n) \leq \frac{5}{16}n = 0.3125n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; closing the gap between the known constants settles a long-standing question about independence in unit distance graphs.

title: Erdős problem #1068
open: Does every graph whose chromatic number is exactly $\aleph_1$ contain a countable subgraph that is infinitely vertex-connected? Here, a graph is infinitely vertex-connected if any two vertices are joined by infinitely many pairwise vertex-disjoint paths.
status: The problem is described in [BoPi24] as a "version of the Erdős-Hajnal problem" (which is [1067]), but it does not seem to appear in [ErHa66]. Soukup [So15] constructed a graph with uncountable chromatic number in which every uncountable set is finitely vertex-connected, and a simpler construction was given by Bowler and Pitz [BoPi24]. See also [1067].
solved_when: A proof that every graph of chromatic number $\aleph_1$ contains a countable infinitely vertex-connected subgraph, or a counterexample constructing such a graph with no countable infinitely vertex-connected subgraph.
aliases: Erdős #1068; graph theory / set theory / chromatic number

title: Erdős problem #1070
open: Let $f(n)$ be the maximal number such that any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ contain $f(n)$ points with no two at distance $1$. How large is $f(n)$ — in particular, is it always true that $f(n)\geq n/4$?
status: The problem is equivalent to estimating the minimal independence number of a unit distance graph with $n$ vertices. Since $\omega\chi\geq n$, one has $f(n)\geq n/\chi$, where $\chi$ is the answer to the Hadwiger–Nelson problem [508]. The Moser spindle shows $f(n)\leq \frac{2}{7}n\approx 0.285n$. Larman and Rogers [LaRo72] noted that if $m_1$ is the supremum of the upper densities of measurable subsets of $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no unit distance pairs, then $f(n)\geq m_1 n$. Croft [Cr67] gave the best-known lower bound $m_1\geq 0.22936$, yielding $0.22936n\leq f(n)\leq \frac{2}{7}n\approx 0.285n$. Ambrus, Csiszárik, Matolcsi, Varga, and Zsámboki [ACMVZ23] proved $m_1\leq 0.247$, so this approach cannot achieve $f(n)\geq n/4$; see [232] for more on $m_1$. Matolcsi, Ruzsa, Varga, and Zsámboki [MRVZ23] improved the upper bound to $f(n)\leq (1/4+o(1))n$, and they conjecture $m_1=0.22936\cdots$ (Croft's lower bound) and $f(n)=(1/4+o(1))n$. If one additionally forbids distances $<1$, the problem becomes [1066]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/1070; Erdős references: [Er87b,p.171].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of $f(n)\geq n/4$ for all $n$, or more generally a determination of $f(n)$ up to $o(n)$, e.g. confirming or refuting the conjecture $f(n)=(1/4+o(1))n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a solution pins down the independence structure of unit distance graphs and connects directly to the Hadwiger–Nelson problem.

title: Erdős problem #1072
open: For a prime $p$, let $f(p)$ be the least integer with $f(p)!+1\equiv 0\pmod{p}$. Are there infinitely many primes for which $f(p)=p-1$, and does $f(p)/p\to 0$ for almost all primes?
status: The questions were formulated by Erdős, Hardy, and Subbarao [HaSu02], who believed that the number of $p\leq x$ with $f(p)=p-1$ is $o(x/\log x)$. They appear as problem A2 of Guy's collection [Gu04], and are tracked at erdosproblems.com/1072.
solved_when: Either it is proved or disproved that infinitely many primes satisfy $f(p)=p-1$, and it is proved or disproved that $f(p)/p\to 0$ for almost all primes.
why: A resolution would settle one of Erdős's personally posed problems and illuminate the distribution of solutions to Wilson-type congruences modulo primes.

title: Erdős problem #1073
open: Let $A(x)$ count the composite integers $u < x$ such that $u$ divides $n! + 1$ for some positive integer $n$. Is $A(x)$ extremely sparse — specifically, is $A(x) \leq x^{o(1)}$?
status: A question of Erdős raised in discussions with Hardy and Subbarao [HaSu02]. The sequence of such $u$ begins $[25, 121, 169, 437, \ldots]$ and is A256519 in the OEIS. Wilson's theorem states that $u$ is prime if and only if $(u-1)! + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{u}$. This is mentioned in problem A2 of Guy's collection.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $A(x) \leq x^{o(1)}$ as $x \to \infty$, where $A(x)$ counts composite $u < x$ with $n! + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{u}$ for some $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, raised in discussions with Hardy and Subbarao, and is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would determine whether the composite divisors of numbers of the form $n!+1$ are vanishingly rare.

title: Erdős problem #1074
open: Do the integers $m\geq 1$ for which some prime $p\not\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ divides $m!+1$ have a natural density? More precisely, if $S$ denotes this set, does $\lim \lvert S\cap[1,x]\rvert/x$ exist, and what is its value? The same question is asked for the analogous set $P$ of primes: does $\lim \lvert P\cap[1,x]\rvert/\pi(x)$ exist, and what is it?
status: The questions were raised by Erdős, Hardy, and Subbarao, who called the set $S$ 'EHS numbers' and the set $P$ 'Pillai primes', and proved that both $S$ and $P$ are infinite. Pillai [Pi30] raised the question of whether there exist any primes in $P$; this was answered by Chowla, who noted that, for example, $14!+1\equiv 18!+1\equiv 0\pmod{23}$. The sequence $S$ begins $8,9,13,14,15,16,17,\ldots$ and is A064164 in the OEIS; the sequence $P$ begins $23,29,59,61,67,71,\ldots$ and is A063980 in the OEIS. Regarding the first question, Hardy and Subbarao computed all EHS numbers up to $2^{10}$ and write '...if this trend conditions we expect [the limit] to be around $0.5$, if it exists. The frequency with which the EHS numbers occur - most often in long sequences of consecutive integers - makes us believe that their asymptotic density exists and is unity. Erdős, though initially hesitant, later agreed with this view.' Regarding the second question, they write '[from the data] it would appear that if the limit exists, it is perhaps between $0.5$ and $0.6$. But then there seems to be no reason why the ratio should not tend to $1$, even though very slowly and certainly not monotonicall
solved_when: Both limits — $\frac{\lvert S\cap[1,x]\rvert}{x}$ and $\frac{\lvert P\cap[1,x]\rvert}{\pi(x)}$ — are proven to exist, and their values are determined.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve a long-standing question about the distribution of factorial-related divisibility among integers and primes.

title: Erdős problem #1075
open: For every $r\geq 3$, is there a constant $c_r>r^{-r}$ such that, given any $\epsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, every $r$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices with at least $(1+\epsilon)(n/r)^r$ edges contains a subgraph on $m$ vertices with at least $c_r m^r$ edges, where $m=m(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$?
status: Erdős [Er64f] proved the statement with $c_r=r^{-r}$ under a stronger hypothesis, namely whenever the hypergraph has at least $\epsilon n^r$ edges. The problem as posed, with the sharper constant $c_r>r^{-r}$ and the $(1+\epsilon)(n/r)^r$ edge threshold, remains open; it is referenced in [Er74c, p. 80] and tracked at erdosproblems.com/1075.
solved_when: For some $r\geq 3$ a constant $c_r>r^{-r}$ is exhibited such that, for every $\epsilon>0$, all sufficiently large $n$, and every $r$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices with at least $(1+\epsilon)(n/r)^r$ edges, the hypergraph contains an $m$-vertex subgraph with at least $c_r m^r$ edges, where $m=m(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles a quantitative improvement in a classical density question for uniform hypergraphs.

title: Erdős problem #1082
open: Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points with no three on a line. Does $A$ determine at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances? In fact, must there exist a single point from which there are at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances?
status: This is a conjecture of Szemerédi, who proved the bound with $n/2$ replaced by $n/3$. More generally, Szemerédi gave a simple proof that if there are no $k$ points on a line then some point determines $\gg n/k$ distinct distances — a weak inverse result to the distinct distance problem [89]. The first question is a stronger form of [93]; the second is a stronger form of [982]. Szemerédi's proof is unpublished but given in [Er75f], where Erdős also asks whether $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with no three on a line determine $\gg n$ distances. Altman proved yes for vertices of a convex polyhedron (see [660] for a stronger form), and Szemerédi proved yes under the assumption that no four points lie on a plane. The second, stronger question has a negative answer: there is a construction of $8$ points such that each point has exactly three distinct distances to the others, first appearing in the literature in a paper of Erdős and Fishburn [ErFi97b], who credit it to Harborth; this configuration is studied in detail by Fishburn [Fi02]. (The construction was later found by DeepMind; an earlier construction was also given.) Key works: erdosproblems.com/1082; [Er75f,p.101] [Er87b] [Er97e].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that any $n$-point set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no three collinear points determines at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances, and correspondingly for the stronger single-point version asking for one point realizing $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances from it.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a natural quantitative link between collinearity avoidance and distinct distances in the plane.

title: Erdős problem #1084
open: How many unit distances can occur among $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ that are pairwise at distance at least $1$? Formally, letting $f_d(n)$ denote the maximum possible number of unit-distance pairs in such a separated configuration, determine or estimate $f_d(n)$.
status: This is sometimes known as the contact number problem. It is easy to see that $f_1(n)=n-1$ and $f_2(n)<3n$ (since there can be at most $6$ points of distance $1$ from any point). Erdős [Er46b] showed $f_2(n)<3n-cn^{1/2}$ for some constant $c>0$, which the triangular lattice shows is the best possible up to the value of $c$. In [Er75f] he speculated that the triangular lattice is exactly the best possible, and in particular $f_2(3n^2+3n+1)=9n^2+3n$. Harborth [Ha74b] proved this, and more generally $f_2(n)=\lfloor 3n-\sqrt{12n-3}\rfloor$ for all $n\geq 2$. In [Er75f] he claims the existence of $c_1,c_2>0$ such that $6n-c_1n^{2/3}< f_3(n) < 6n-c_2n^{2/3}$. An upper bound of $f_3(n) < 6n-0.926n^{2/3}$ for all $n\geq 2$ was proved by Bezdek and Reid [BeRe13]. In general, it is known that $(d-o(1))n \leq f_d(n) \leq 2^{O(d)}n$, the lower bound coming from points arranged in an integer grid and the upper bound from the fact that $2^{O(d)}$ many non-intersecting congruent balls can touch a fixed ball (the kissing number problem). A recent survey on contact numbers for sphere packings is by Bezdek and Khan [BeKh18]. See [223] for the analogous problem with maximal distance $1$.
solved_when: Sharp asymptotics (or exact formulas) for $f_d(n)$ are established, particularly closing the gap for $d\geq 3$ — e.g. pinning down the conjectured $f_3(n)=6n-\Theta(n^{2/3})$ behavior and narrowing the general bounds $(d-o(1))n \leq f_d(n) \leq 2^{O(d)}n$.
why: This is the contact number problem, one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would resolve a classical extremal geometry question bridging unit-distance problems and sphere-packing contact counts.

title: Erdős problem #1086
open: How few triangles of equal area must every set of $n$ points in the plane determine? Formally, letting $g(n)$ be the minimal number such that any $n$-point set in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determines at most $g(n)$ triangles of the same area, the task is to estimate $g(n)$.
status: The question is equivalent to asking how many triangles of area $1$ a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ can determine; Erdős and Purdy attribute it to Oppenheim. Erdős and Purdy [ErPu71] proved $n^2\log\log n \ll g(n) \ll n^{5/2}$ and believed the lower bound closer to the truth. The upper bound has been improved several times: by Pach and Sharir [PaSh92], Dumitrescu, Sharir, and Tóth [DST09], Apfelbaum and Sharir [ApSh10], and Apfaulbaum [Ap13]; the best known is $g(n) \ll n^{20/9}$ by Raz and Sharir [RaSh17]. For higher-dimensional generalisations, Erdős and Purdy [ErPu71] proved $g_3^2(n) \ll n^{8/3}$, improved to $g_3^2(n) \ll n^{2.4286}$ by Dumitrescu, Sharir, and Tóth [DST09], and proved $g_6^2(n) \gg n^3$; Purdy [Pu74] proved $g_4^2(n) \leq g_5^2(n) \ll n^{3-c}$ for some constant $c>0$. An observation of Oppenheim (using a construction of Lenz) detailed in [ErPu71] concerns $g_{2k+2}^k(n)$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/1086; Erdős references: [Er75f,p.104].
solved_when: Matching (up to constants) upper and lower bounds for $g(n)$ are established — in particular, determining whether the Erdős–Purdy lower bound $n^2 \log\log n$ is close to the truth or whether $g(n)$ is closer to the known upper bound $g(n) \ll n^{20/9}$. The analogous higher-dimensional quantities $g_d^r(n)$ admit the same criterion, including the cases $g_3^2(n)$ (currently $\ll n^{2.4286}$), $g_6^2(n) \gg n^3$, $g_4^2(n) \leq g_5^2(n) \ll n^{3-c}$ for some constant $c>0$, and $g_{2k+2}^k(n)$.

title: Erdős problem #1087
open: How many "degenerate" quadruples must a set of $n$ points in the plane contain, where a quadruple is degenerate if some pair of its points are the same distance apart? If $f(n)$ is the minimal number forced in any $n$-point set, is it true that $f(n) \leq n^{3+o(1)}$?
status: The question is due to Erdős and Purdy [ErPu71], who proved $n^3\log n \ll f(n) \ll n^{7/2}$. Erdős references: [Er75f,p.104].
solved_when: $f(n)$ is estimated — in particular, an answer to whether $f(n)\leq n^{3+o(1)}$, ideally pinning down its order of growth between the known bounds $n^3\log n$ and $n^{7/2}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a long-standing question in the combinatorial geometry of repeated distances.

title: Erdős problem #1088
open: Let $f_d(n)$ be the minimal $m$ such that any set of $m$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ contains a set of $n$ points such that any two determined distances are distinct. How large is $f_d(n)$? In particular, is it true that, for fixed $n\geq 3$, $f_d(n)=2^{o(d)}$?
status: It is easy to prove that $f_d(n) \leq n^{O_d(1)}$. Erdős [Er75f] claimed that he and Straus proved $f_d(n)\leq c_n^d$ for some constant $c_n>0$. When $d=1$ this is the subject of [530], and $f_1(n)\asymp n^2$. When $n=3$ this is the subject of [503]. Erdős could prove $f_2(3)=7$ and Croft [Cr62] proved $f_3(3)=9$. The results described at [503] demonstrate that $f_d(3)=d^2/2+O(d)$. The behaviour of $f_d(n)$ for fixed $d$ as $n\to \infty$ is the subject of [1208].
solved_when: An estimate of $f_d(n)$ is obtained; in particular, a proof or disproof that $f_d(n)=2^{o(d)}$ for fixed $n\geq 3$ settles the highlighted question.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #1093
open: For $n\geq 2k$, define the deficiency of $\binom{n}{k}$ as follows: it is undefined if $\binom{n}{k}$ is divisible by some prime $p\leq k$, and otherwise it is the number of integers $0\leq i<k$ for which $n-i$ is $k$-smooth (divisible only by primes $\leq k$). Are there infinitely many binomial coefficients with deficiency $1$, and are there only finitely many with deficiency greater than $1$?
status: A problem of Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge [ELS88], also asked in the 1986 problem session of West Coast Number Theory (as reported here). In [ELS93] they prove that if the deficiency exists and is $\geq 1$ then $n\ll 2^k\sqrt{k}$. There are $58$ examples with $n\leq 10^5$ of deficiency $1$, including $\binom{7}{3}, \binom{13}{4}, \binom{14}{4}, \binom{23}{5}, \binom{62}{6}, \binom{94}{10}, \binom{95}{10}$. The only known examples with deficiency $>1$ are: deficiency $2$: $\binom{44}{8}, \binom{74}{10}, \binom{174}{12}, \binom{239}{14}, \binom{5179}{27}, \binom{8413}{28}, \binom{8414}{28}, \binom{96622}{42}$; deficiency $3$: $\binom{46}{10}, \binom{47}{10}, \binom{241}{16}, \binom{2105}{25}, \binom{1119}{27}, \binom{6459}{33}$; deficiency $4$: $\binom{47}{11}$; deficiency $9$: $\binom{284}{28}$. These examples are from [ELS88] or here. See also [384] and [1094]. Barreto in the comments has given a positive answer to the second question, conditional on two (strong) conjectures.
solved_when: Both questions are answered: either infinitely many binomial coefficients with deficiency $1$ are exhibited, or it is shown only finitely many exist; and either finitely many binomial coefficients with deficiency $>1$ are shown to exist, or infinitely many are exhibited.
why: A resolution would settle one of Erdős's personally posed problems on the $p$-adic and smooth-number structure of binomial coefficients, clarifying how rarely the terms $n, n-1, \dots, n-k+1$ can simultaneously be almost entirely $k$-smooth.

title: Erdős problem #1094
open: Is the least prime factor of the binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}$ always at most $\max(n/k, k)$ whenever $n \geq 2k$, apart from finitely many exceptions? More precisely, one asks whether this holds with only the 14 explicitly listed exceptions conjectured by Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge.
status: This is a stronger form of [384] appearing in a paper of Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge [ELS88]. Erdős observed that the least prime factor is always $\leq n/k$ provided $n$ is sufficiently large depending on $k$. Selfridge [Se77] further conjectured that this always happens if $n \geq k^2-1$, except $\binom{62}{6}$. The threshold $g(k)$ below which $\binom{n}{k}$ is guaranteed to be divisible by a prime $\leq k$ is the subject of [1095]. In [ELS88] they conjecture that if $n \geq 2k$ then the least prime factor of $\binom{n}{k}$ is $\leq \max(n/k,k)$ with the 14 exceptions listed above. They also suggest the stronger conjecture that, with a finite number of exceptions, the least prime factor is $\leq \max(n/k, \sqrt{k})$, or perhaps even $\leq \max(n/k, O(\log k))$. In [ELS93] they provide further computational evidence and point out that it is consistent with what they know that the bound holds with $\leq \max(n/k, 13)$, with only 12 exceptions.
solved_when: A proof that for all $n \geq 2k$ the least prime factor of $\binom{n}{k}$ is $\leq \max(n/k,k)$ with only finitely many exceptions (ideally exactly the 14 exceptions $\binom{7}{3}, \binom{13}{4}, \binom{23}{5}, \binom{14}{4}, \binom{44}{8}, \binom{46}{10}, \binom{47}{10}, \binom{47}{11}, \binom{62}{6}, \binom{74}{10}, \binom{94}{10}, \binom{95}{10}, \binom{241}{16}, \binom{284}{28}$); refinements target the stronger bounds $\leq \max(n/k, \sqrt{k})$, $\leq \max(n/k, O(\log k))$, or $\leq \max(n/k, 13)$ with only 12 exceptions.
why: It pins down how small a prime must divide a binomial coefficient, refining older results on prime factors of $\binom{n}{k}$ and settling one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #1095
open: Let $g(k)>k+1$ be the smallest $n$ such that every prime factor of $\binom{n}{k}$ exceeds $k$. How large is $g(k)$ as a function of $k$?
status: The question originates with Ecklund, Erdős, and Selfridge [EES74], who proved $k^{1+c}<g(k)\leq \exp((1+o(1))k)$ for some constant $c>0$ and conjectured $g(k)<L_k=[1,\ldots,k]$, the least common multiple of all integers $\leq k$, for all large $k$. In [EES74] they further conjecture $\limsup \frac{g(k+1)}{g(k)}=\infty$ and $\liminf \frac{g(k+1)}{g(k)}=0$. The lower bound was improved by Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge [ELS93] and Granville and Ramaré [GrRa96]; the current record is $g(k) \gg \exp(c(\log k)^2)$ for some $c>0$, due to Konyagin [Ko99b]. Erdős, Lacampagne, and Selfridge [ELS93] write 'it is clear to every right-thinking person' that $g(k)\geq\exp(c\frac{k}{\log k})$ for some constant $c>0$. Sorenson, Sorenson, and Webster [SSW20] give heuristic evidence that $\log g(k) \asymp \frac{k}{\log k}$. See also [451] and [1094].
solved_when: An estimate of $g(k)$ matching (up to constants) the conjectured order of magnitude $\log g(k) \asymp \frac{k}{\log k}$ is obtained, or failing that, a proof that $g(k)\geq\exp(c\frac{k}{\log k})$ for some constant $c>0$ and $g(k)<L_k=[1,\ldots,k]$ (the least common multiple of $1,\ldots,k$) for all large $k$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a solution would settle the long-standing Ecklund–Erdős–Selfridge conjectures on prime factors of binomial coefficients.

title: Erdős problem #1097
open: Let $A$ be a set of $n$ integers. How many distinct common differences $d$ can arise from three-term arithmetic progressions contained in $A$? Must this count always be $O(n^{3/2})$?
status: Erdős posed the problem in the 1989 problem session of Great Western Number Theory. He states that Erdős and Ruzsa gave an explicit construction achieving $n^{1+c}$ for some $c>0$, and Erdős and Spencer gave a probabilistic construction achieving $n^{3/2}$, which Erdős speculated may be best possible. In the comment section, Chan observed that the problem is exactly equivalent to a sums-differences question of Bourgain [Bo99], introduced as an arithmetic path towards the Kakeya conjecture: find the smallest $c\in[1,2]$ such that, for any finite sets of integers $A$ and $B$ and $G\subseteq A\times B$, $|A\overset{G}{-}B| \ll \max(|A|,|B|,|A\overset{G}{+}B|)^c$ (where $A\overset{G}{+}B$ denotes the set of $a+b$ with $(a,b)\in G$). The greatest exponent achievable for the main problem equals the smallest constant for the sums-differences question. The current best bounds are $1.77898\cdots \leq c \leq 11/6 \approx 1.833$: the upper bound is due to Katz and Tao [KaTa99], the lower bound to Lemm [Le15] (with a very small further improvement noted in the record). Tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/1097.
solved_when: A bound of $O(n^{3/2})$ is proved for the number of distinct common differences (or, equivalently via Bourgain's sums-differences formulation, the smallest admissible constant $c$ is shown to equal $3/2$, improving the current range $1.77898\cdots \leq c \leq 11/6 \approx 1.833$).
why: A sharp answer would settle one of Erdős's personally posed problems and, through Chan's equivalence, resolve the exact exponent in Bourgain's sums-differences inequality, an arithmetic path toward the Kakeya conjecture.

title: Erdős problem #1100
open: How large can the number of coprime consecutive divisor pairs get? If $1=d_1<\cdots<d_{\tau(n)}=n$ are the divisors of $n$ and $\tau_\perp(n)$ counts those $i$ with $(d_i,d_{i+1})=1$, does $\tau_\perp(n)/\omega(n)\to\infty$ for almost all $n$, and is $\tau_\perp(n)<\exp((\log n)^{o(1)})$ for all $n$? More precisely, letting $g(k)=\max_{\omega(n)=k}\tau_\perp(n)$ over squarefree $n$, determine the growth of $g(k)$.
status: The function $\tau_\perp(n)$ was considered by Erdős and Hall [ErHa78]. It is trivial that $\tau_\perp(n)\geq \omega(n)$, with equality for infinitely many $n$. Erdős and Hall prove that for all $\epsilon>0$ and sufficiently large $x$, $\max_{n<x}\tau_\perp(n)>\exp((\log\log x)^{2-\epsilon})$. Erdős and Simonovits (see [Er81h]) proved $(2^{1/2}+o(1))^k<g(k)<(2-c)^k$ for some constant $c>0$.
solved_when: The asymptotic growth of $g(k)$ (restricted to squarefree $n$) is determined, together with resolution of the two conditional questions: whether $\tau_\perp(n)/\omega(n)\to\infty$ for almost all $n$, and whether $\tau_\perp(n)<\exp((\log n)^{o(1)})$ for all $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would clarify the extremal behavior of the ordering of divisors of an integer.

title: Erdős problem #1101
open: Does there exist a "good" sequence of pairwise coprime integers with convergent reciprocal sum (good meaning the gaps between integers not divisible by any $u_i$ are at most $(1+\epsilon)t_x \prod_i (1-1/u_i)^{-1}$ for large $x$) whose terms grow polynomially, $u_n < n^{O(1)}$? And does there exist such a good sequence with $u_n \leq e^{o(n)}$?
status: Erdős [Er81h] believed the answer to the first question is no and the second question is yes. He proved the existence of some good sequence (in which all the $u_i$ are primes). An easy sieve argument proves that for any sequence $u$ with those properties, $\max_{a_k<x}(a_{k+1}-a_k) > (1+o(1))t_x \prod_i (1-1/u_i)^{-1}$. The strong form of [208] asks whether the sequence of prime squares $u_i = p_i^2$ is good.
solved_when: A construction of a good sequence (in the sense defined, with $(u_i,u_j)=1$ for $i\neq j$ and $\sum 1/u_i < \infty$) is given with either $u_n < n^{O(1)}$ or $u_n \leq e^{o(n)}$, or a proof that no such sequence exists in either regime.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; it probes how dense a covering-excluding sequence can be while the maximal gap between uncovered integers stays near the sieve lower bound.

title: Erdős problem #1103
open: How fast must an infinite sequence of integers grow if every element of its sumset $A+A$ is squarefree? Erdős exhibited such a sequence with exponential growth and expected no polynomial-growth example exists — the question is to pin down the true growth rate.
status: Erdős notes there exists such a sequence which grows exponentially, but does not expect such a sequence of polynomial growth. In [Er81h] he asked whether there is an infinite sequence of integers $A$ such that, for every $a\in A$ and prime $p$, if $a\equiv t\pmod{p^2}$ then $1\leq t<p^2/2$; he noted that such a sequence has the property that every $n\in A+A$ is squarefree, and wrote that he was doubtful such a sequence exists. Indeed, there are trivially at most finitely many such $a$, since there cannot be any primes $p\in (a^{1/2},(2a)^{1/2}]$, but there exist primes in $(x,\sqrt{2}x)$ for all large $x$. For a sequence $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots$} with the squarefree-sumset property, van Doorn and Tao [vDTa25] have shown that $a_j > 0.24j^{4/3}$ for all $j$, and that there exists such a sequence (furthermore with squarefree terms) such that $a_j < \exp(5j/\log j)$ for all large $j$. A superior lower bound of $a_j \gg j^{15/11-o(1)}$ had earlier been found by Konyagin [Ko04] when considering the finite case [1109].
solved_when: The growth rate of any such sequence $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ is determined, in the sense of matching upper and lower bounds on $a_j$ up to constants or exponents, including deciding whether polynomial growth is possible.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, and resolves whether the squarefree-sumset condition forces near-polynomial or genuinely faster growth.

title: Erdős problem #1106
open: Let $p(n)$ denote the partition function and let $F(n)$ count the number of distinct prime factors of $\prod_{1\leq k\leq n}p(k)$. Does $F(n)$ exceed $n$ for all sufficiently large $n$?
status: Asked by Erdős at Oberwolfach in 1986. Schinzel noted in the Oberwolfach problem book that $F(n)\to \infty$ follows from the asymptotic formula for $p(n)$ and a result of Tijdeman [Ti73]; this is not obvious, and details are given in a paper of Erdős and Ivić (page 69 of [ErIv90]). Schinzel and Wirsing [ScWi87] proved $F(n) \gg \log n$. Ono [On00] proved that every prime divides $p(n)$ for some $n\geq 1$ (indeed, for any fixed prime, this holds for a positive density set of $n$).
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $F(n)>n$ for all sufficiently large $n$; this settles the remaining question, since $F(n)\to\infty$ is already established.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and would sharpen our understanding of how prime factors distribute across values of the partition function.

title: Erdős problem #1107
open: Fix an integer $r\geq 2$ and call a number $r$-powerful if every prime divisor $p$ of it appears to at least the $r$-th power (i.e., $p^r\mid n$). Is every sufficiently large integer expressible as the sum of at most $r+1$ $r$-powerful numbers?
status: Given in the 1986 Oberwolfach problem book as a problem of Erdős and Ivić. The claim is true when $r=2$, as proved by Heath-Brown [He88] (see [941]). See [940] for the problem of which integers are the sum of at most $r$ many $r$-powerful numbers.
solved_when: For every $r\geq 2$, it is proved that all sufficiently large integers are sums of at most $r+1$ $r$-powerful numbers; equivalently, a counterexample is exhibited for some $r$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, posed jointly with Ivić, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #1108
open: Consider the set of all finite sums of distinct factorials. Does this set contain only finitely many $k$th powers for each $k \geq 2$, and only finitely many powerful numbers? Formally, if $A = \left\{ \sum_{n\in S}n! : S\subset \mathbb{N}\textrm{ finite}\right\}$, are the $k$th powers (and powerful numbers) in $A$ finite in number?
status: Asked by Erdős at Oberwolfach in 1988. It is open even whether there are infinitely many squares of the form $1+n!$ (see [398]). The problem was motivated in part by a problem of Mahler which he discussed with Erdős a few days before his death in 1988: if $k\geq 5$ and $A_k= \left\{ \sum_{n\in S}k^n : S\subset \mathbb{N}\textrm{ finite}\right\}$, then does $A_k$ contain only finitely many squares? Mahler showed that there are infinitely many squares in $A_k$ for $k\leq 4$, and found only one square for $k\geq 5$, namely $1+7+7^2+7^3=400$. Brindza and Erdős [BrEr91] proved that, for any $r$, if $n_1!+\cdots+n_r!$ is powerful then $n_1\ll_r 1$.
solved_when: It is proved that for every $k \geq 2$, $A$ contains only finitely many $k$th powers, and that $A$ contains only finitely many powerful numbers.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/1108; a resolution would settle even the basic question of whether infinitely many squares of the form $1+n!$ exist.

title: Erdős problem #1109
open: Let $f(N)$ be the size of the largest subset $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that every $n\in A+A$ is squarefree. How large can $f(N)$ be — in particular, is it true that $f(N)\leq N^{o(1)}$, or even $f(N) \leq (\log N)^{O(1)}$?
status: First studied by Erdős and Sárközy [ErSa87], who proved $\log N \ll f(N) \ll N^{3/4}\log N$ and guessed the lower bound is nearer the truth. Sárközy [Sa92c] extended this to the case of $A+B$ and to sumsets which are $k$-power-free. Gyarmati [Gy01] gave an alternative proof of $f(N)\gg \log N$, and also gave new bounds for the case of $A+B$. Konyagin [Ko04] improved this to $\log\log N(\log N)^2\ll f(N) \ll N^{11/15+o(1)}$. The infinite analogue of this problem is [1103]; in particular, upper bounds for this $f(N)$ directly imply lower bounds for the size of the $a_j$ considered there.
solved_when: A sharp asymptotic estimate of $f(N)$ is obtained, or at minimum a proof that $f(N)\leq N^{o(1)}$ or $f(N)\leq (\log N)^{O(1)}$.
why: As one of Erdős's personally posed problems, a solution would resolve a long-standing question in combinatorial number theory about how additive structure and squarefreeness constrain each other; it is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #1110
open: For which pairs of coprime integers $p>q\geq 2$ other than $\{2,3\}$ can we determine the density of integers not representable as a sum of numbers of the form $p^kq^l$ with no summand dividing another, and are there infinitely many pairwise coprime such non-representable numbers?
status: The problem originates with Erdős and Lewin [ErLe96], who proved there are finitely many non-representable numbers if and only if $\{p,q\}=\{2,3\}$. In [Er92b] Erdős wrote 'last year I made the following silly conjecture': every integer $n$ can be written as the sum of distinct integers of the form $2^k3^l$, none of which divide any other, adding 'I mistakenly thought that this was a nice and difficult conjecture but Jansen and several others found a simple proof by induction.' The proof establishes the stronger fact that if $n$ is even all summands can be taken even: if $n=2m$ apply the inductive hypothesis to $m$; if $n$ is odd, let $3^k$ be the largest power of $3$ not exceeding $n$ and apply the hypothesis to the even number $n-3^k$. Yu and Chen [YuCh22] prove that the set of representable numbers has density zero whenever $q>3$, or $q=3$ and $p>6$, or $q=2$ and $p>10$; they also prove there are infinitely many coprime non-representable numbers if $q>3$, or $q=3$ and $p\neq 5$, or $q=2$ and $p\notin\{3,5,9\}$. The problem is tracked at erdosproblems.com/1110.
solved_when: A characterization of the density of non-representable numbers for all coprime $p>q\geq 2$ with $\{p,q\}\neq\{2,3\}$, and a determination of when infinitely many coprime non-representable numbers exist.
why: A solution completes one of Erdős's personally posed problems, determining the representability structure of integers by the multiplicative semigroup generated by two primes beyond the exceptional $\{2,3\}$ case.

title: Erdős problem #1111
open: Must every graph of sufficiently large chromatic number and bounded clique number contain two anticomplete vertex sets, each itself of large chromatic number? Formally, is it true that for all $t,c\geq 1$ there exists $d\geq 1$ such that every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)\geq d$ and $\omega(G)<t$ contains anticomplete sets $A,B$ with $\chi(A)\geq \chi(B)\geq c$?
status: This is a problem of El Zahar and Erdős [ElEr85], who showed it suffices to consider the case $t\leq c$ and proved $d(3,3)\leq 8$ and $d(t,3) \leq 2\binom{t-1}{3}+7\binom{t-1}{2}+t$ for $t>3$. They noted that a result of Wagon [Wa80b] implies $d(t,2)\leq \binom{t}{2}+1$ (and in fact $d(t+1,2)\leq d(t,2)+t$); the known exact values include $t(2,2)=2$, $t(3,2)=4$, and $t(4,2)=5$. Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour [NSS24] proved a related result: for all $t,c\geq 1$ there exists $d\geq 1$ such that if $\chi(G)\geq d$ and $\omega(G)<t$, then there are anticomplete sets $A,B$ where $\chi(B)\geq c$ and the minimum degree of the induced graph on $A$ is at least $c$. Key works: erdosproblems.com/1111; Erdős references: [Er85b] [Wa80b].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the statement above for all $t,c\geq 1$, including explicit or implicit bounds on the minimal function $d(t,c)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it probes the fundamental relationship between chromatic number and unavoidable induced substructures in graphs with bounded clique number.

title: Erdős problem #1112
open: Given $1\leq d_1<d_2$ and $k\geq 3$, is there an integer $r$ such that every lacunary sequence of positive integers $B=\{b_1<\cdots\}$ with $b_{i+1}\geq rb_i$ can be avoided by the $k$-fold sumset of some sequence $A=\{a_1<\cdots\}$ whose consecutive gaps satisfy $d_1\leq a_{i+1}-a_i\leq d_2$ — that is, $(kA)\cap B=\emptyset$, where $kA$ denotes the $k$-fold sumset?
status: Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] noted that if $B=\{b_1<b_2<\cdots\}$ with $b_1\geq 5$ and $b_{i+1}\geq 2b_i$, then there is a set $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ with $2\leq a_{k+1}-a_k\leq 3$ for all $k$ such that $(A+A)\cap B=\emptyset$. Bollobás, Hegyvári, and Jin [BHJ97] showed that such an $A$ must exist if $b_{i+1}\geq 2b_i-O(1)$, and that this is best possible. Erdős and Graham go on to say 'whether such behavior can hold for $A+A+A$ (or more summands) is not known'; the stated question is the record's best interpretation of what they intended. Bollobás, Hegyvári, and Jin [BHJ97] give a negative answer in that direction: for any sequence of integers $1\leq r_1<r_2<\cdots$, there is a $B$ with $b_{i+1}\geq r_ib_i$ such that $(A+A+A)\cap B\neq\emptyset$ for any $A$ with $2\leq a_{i+1}-a_i\leq 3$. They define $r_k(d_1,d_2)$ as the smallest such $r$, if it exists; the results above give $r_2(2,3)=2$ and that $r_3(2,3)$ does not exist. Chen [Ch00] proved that $r_2(a,b)\leq 2$ for any integers $a<b$.
solved_when: For given $d_1, d_2, k$, the problem is resolved by determining whether the quantity $r_k(d_1,d_2)$ — the smallest $r$ such that $b_{i+1}\geq rb_i$ guarantees the existence of an $A$ with $d_1\leq a_{i+1}-a_i\leq d_2$ and $(kA)\cap B=\emptyset$ — exists, and if so, computing it.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it settles the general question of when sparse sets can be avoided by iterated sumsets of sequences with bounded gaps, which the two-summand case answers affirmatively but the three-summand case already refutes for gaps in $[2,3]$.

title: Erdős problem #1113
open: Are there Sierpinski numbers — positive odd integers $m$ such that $2^km+1$ is composite for every $k\geq 0$ — for which no finite set of primes covers the sequence, i.e. no finite $P$ such that each $2^km+1$ is divisible by some $p\in P$?
status: Sierpinski [Si60] proved there are infinitely many Sierpinski numbers via covering systems, in fact a positive density set of such $m$. The smallest known Sierpinski number, believed minimal, is $78557$, found by Selfridge. Erdős and Graham [ErGr80] asked whether some Sierpinski numbers have no covering system responsible; this is formulated as problem F13 in Guy's collection [Gu04]. They conjectured yes, since otherwise infinitely many Fermat primes would follow. Izotov [Iz95], with details elaborated by Filaseta, Finch, and Kozek [FFK08], suggests $m=734110615000775^4$ is a Sierpinski number without a covering set; Izotov proved it is indeed a Sierpinski number. Filaseta, Finch, and Kozek [FFK08] propose the revised conjecture that every Sierpinski number is either a perfect power or has a finite cover.
solved_when: A specific positive odd integer $m$ is exhibited (with proof) such that $2^km+1$ is never prime for $k\geq 0$, yet no finite set of primes divides one term of every residue class of the sequence; alternatively, a proof that every Sierpinski number has a finite covering set.
why: A negative answer would imply there are infinitely many Fermat primes, while a positive answer would settle Erdős and Graham's question of whether Sierpinski numbers exist that are not "responsible" to a covering system.

title: Erdős problem #1117
open: For an entire function $f$ that is not a monomial, let $\nu(r)$ count the points on the circle $\lvert z\rvert = r$ where $\lvert f(z)\rvert$ attains its maximum over that circle. Can the number of such maximum points be large on every circle, in the sense that $\liminf_{r\to\infty} \nu(r) = \infty$?
status: This is Problem 2.16 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős. The answer to the first (limsup) question is yes, as shown by Herzog and Piranian [HePi68]. The second (liminf) question is still open, although an 'approximate' affirmative answer is given by Glücksam and Pardo-Simón [GlPa24].
solved_when: An explicit entire function (not a monomial) is constructed, or its existence proved, for which $\liminf_{r\to\infty} \nu(r) = \infty$; alternatively, a proof that no such function exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and the limsup variant is already resolved — settling the liminf question completes the problem.

title: Erdős problem #1120
open: Given a monic polynomial $f\in\mathbb{C}[z]$ of degree $n$ with all roots in $\lvert z\rvert\leq 1$, consider the sublevel set $E=\{z : \lvert f(z)\rvert\leq 1\}$. How long must a path in $E$ joining $z=0$ to the unit circle $\lvert z\rvert=1$ be in the worst case, as a function of $n$?
status: This is Problem 4.22 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős. In [Ha74] it is reported that Clunie and Netanyahu (personal communication) showed that a path always exists which joins $z=0$ to $\lvert z\rvert=1$ in $A$. Erdős wrote 'presumably this tends to infinity with $n$, but not too fast'. The trivial lower bound for the length of this path is $1$, which is achieved for $f(z)=z^n$. The interesting side of this question is the worst-case behaviour as a function of $n$. See also [1041].
solved_when: A sharp bound (up to constants, or asymptotically) on the maximum over all such polynomials $f$ of degree $n$ of the shortest path length in $E$ from $0$ to $\lvert z\rvert=1$ is determined; in particular, whether this quantity tends to infinity with $n$, and at what rate.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling the growth rate would resolve a long-standing question about the geometry of polynomial sublevel sets.

title: Erdős problem #1122
open: If an additive function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ decreases in value along consecutive integers only rarely — specifically, if the set $A=\{n\geq 1: f(n+1)<f(n)\}$ has density zero — must $f$ in fact be a constant multiple of $\log n$? Formally: if $|A\cap[1,X]|=o(X)$, is $f(n)=c\log n$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}$?
status: Erdős proved that $f(n)=c\log n$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}$ if $A$ is empty, or if $f(n+1)-f(n)=o(1)$. Partial progress was made by Mangerel [Ma22], who proved the conclusion if $|A\cap[1,X]|\ll X/(\log X)^{2+c}$ for some $c>0$, and if $f(p)$ does not have very large values (in a certain technical sense). See also [491].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $|A\cap[1,X]|=o(X)$ for an additive function $f$ implies $f(n)=c\log n$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a classical question on how weak a monotonicity-like condition already pins down the logarithmic additive functions.

title: Erdős problem #1131
open: How small can the $L^2$ norm of the sum of squares of Lagrange basis polynomials on $[-1,1]$ be made by choosing the nodes? Formally, for $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in[-1,1]$ with $l_k(x)=\prod_{i\neq k}(x-x_i)/\prod_{i\neq k}(x_k-x_i)$, what is the minimal value of $I(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\int_{-1}^1\sum_k |l_k(x)|^2\,\mathrm{d}x$ — in particular, is it true that $\min I = 2-(1+o(1))\frac{1}{n}$?
status: Erdős first conjectured that the minimum is achieved when the $x_i$ are the roots of the integral of the Legendre polynomial, since Fejer [Fe32] had earlier shown these to be minimisers of $\max_{x\in[-1,1]}\sum_k |l_k(x)|^2$. This was disproved by Szabados [Sz66] for every $n>3$. Erdős, Szabados, Varma, and Vértesi [ESVV94] proved that $2-O((\log n)^2/n)\leq \min I \leq 2-\frac{2}{2n-1}$, where the upper bound is witnessed by the roots of the integral of the Legendre polynomial as above.
solved_when: The asymptotic value of $\min I$ is determined; specifically, the conjectured asymptotic $\min I = 2-(1+o(1))\frac{1}{n}$ is proved or refuted.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with its full history at erdosproblems.com, and concerns the sharp behavior of Lagrange interpolation operators in $L^2$.

title: Erdős problem #1132
open: Given any infinite sequence $x_1,x_2,\ldots\in[-1,1]$ and the associated Lebesgue-type function $L_n(x)=\sum_{1\le k\le n}\lvert l_k(x)\rvert$ built from the Lagrange basis functions of $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, must there exist $x\in(-1,1)$ with $L_n(x)>\frac{2}{\pi}\log n-O(1)$ for infinitely many $n$? In particular, is $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{L_n(x)}{\log n}\geq\frac{2}{\pi}$ for almost all $x\in(-1,1)$?
status: A result of Bernstein [Be31] implies that the set of $x\in(-1,1)$ with $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{L_n(x)}{\log n}\geq\frac{2}{\pi}$ is everywhere dense. Erdős [Er61c] proved that for any fixed $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in[-1,1]$, $\max_{x\in[-1,1]}\sum_{1\le k\le n}\lvert l_k(x)\rvert>\frac{2}{\pi}\log n-O(1)$. Tao [Ta26b] proved that for any function $\omega(n)$ tending to infinity with $n$, there exists a dense set of $x\in(-1,1)$ with $L_n(x)\geq\frac{2}{\pi}\log n-\omega(n)$ for infinitely many $n$; Tao also notes it is unclear whether the constant in the $O(1)$ term may depend on $x$. See also [1129] for more on $L_n(x)$, and also [1153].
solved_when: One proves either that, for every infinite sequence $(x_n)$ in $[-1,1]$, some $x\in(-1,1)$ satisfies $L_n(x)>\frac{2}{\pi}\log n-O(1)$ for infinitely many $n$, or that $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{L_n(x)}{\log n}\geq\frac{2}{\pi}$ for almost all $x\in(-1,1)$; or a counterexample sequence is constructed disproving these statements.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it probes how large the Lebesgue constants of interpolation nodes must be pointwise, a fundamental question in interpolation theory.

title: Erdős problem #1133
open: Given any constant $C>0$, must there exist $\epsilon>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$, one can choose values $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in[-1,1]$ with the following property: any polynomial of degree $m<(1+\epsilon)n$ that agrees with $y_i$ at $x_i$ for at least $(1-\epsilon)n$ of the indices satisfies $\max_{x\in[-1,1]}|P(x)|>C$? In other words, can the $y_i$ always be prescribed so that no slightly-overfitting polynomial of degree below $(1+\epsilon)n$ can both match those values at most points and stay uniformly bounded by $C$?
status: Erdős proved a companion result: for any $C>0$ there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that if $n$ is sufficiently large and $m=\lfloor(1+\epsilon)n\rfloor$, then for any $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in[-1,1]$ there is a polynomial $P$ of degree $n$ with $|P(x_i)|\leq 1$ for $1\leq i\leq m$ yet $\max_{x\in[-1,1]}|P(x)|>C$. The conjectured statement would also imply this, but Erdős in [Er67, p. 72] says he could not even prove it for $m=n$.
solved_when: For every $C>0$ there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$ and any $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in[-1,1]$, there are $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in[-1,1]$ such that every polynomial of degree $m<(1+\epsilon)n$ with $P(x_i)=y_i$ for at least $(1-\epsilon)n$ indices satisfies $\max_{x\in[-1,1]}|P(x)|>C$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/1133; a proof would resolve a question Erdős himself could not settle even in the boundary case $m=n$.

title: Erdős problem #1135
open: Given any starting integer $m\geq 1$, does repeated iteration of the map $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ — defined by $f(n)=n/2$ if $n$ is even and $f(n)=(3n+1)/2$ if $n$ is odd — always reach 1? In other words, does there exist $k\geq 1$ such that $f^{(k)}(m)=1$ for every $m\geq 1$?
status: This is the infamous Collatz conjecture, not a problem due to Erdős; it was first devised by Collatz before 1952. Erdős referred to it on several occasions as 'hopeless'. As Lagarias [La16] notes, the closest Erdős ever came to working on problems of this nature is the theorem described in the remarks to [1134]. It is often claimed that Erdős offered \$500 for a solution; this claim originated in a survey article by Lagarias [La85], who reported in personal communication that it came from a conversation with Erdős and Graham around 1983, in which Graham asked Erdős to estimate the problem's value on his prize scale, to which Erdős replied \$500 — so strictly speaking Erdős never offered \$500 as a prize, but the value is included for comparing problems Erdős rated as 'prize problems'. This is Problem E16 in Guy's collection [Gu04], in which Guy quotes Erdős as saying "Mathematics may not be ready for such problems". For a detailed discussion of the history and theory surrounding this problem, see the overview by Lagarias [La10].
solved_when: For every integer $m\geq 1$ there exists a $k\geq 1$ such that $f^{(k)}(m)=1$, where $f(n)=n/2$ for even $n$ and $f(n)=(3n+1)/2$ for odd $n$; or a counterexample $m$ is exhibited whose orbit never reaches 1.
why: This is the infamous Collatz conjecture, one of the most famous unsolved problems in number theory; a resolution would settle a question Erdős himself called hopeless and rated among his prize problems.

title: Erdős problem #1137
open: Let $d_n=p_{n+1}-p_n$, where $p_n$ denotes the $n$th prime. Is it true that\[\frac{\max_{n<x}d_{n}d_{n-1}}{(\max_{n<x}d_n)^2}\to 0\]as $x\to \infty$?
status: No proof expositions exist yet; the problem is listed at erdosproblems.com/1137 with Erdős references: [Va99,1.2].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the displayed limit as $x \to \infty$, i.e. a determination of whether $\frac{\max_{n<x}d_{n}d_{n-1}}{(\max_{n<x}d_n)^2}\to 0$.

title: Erdős problem #1139
open: If $1\leq u_1<u_2<\cdots$ lists the integers having at most $2$ prime factors, must the gaps between consecutive terms be arbitrarily large relative to $\log k$ — that is, is $\limsup \frac{u_{k+1}-u_k}{\log k}=\infty$?
status: No proof expositions related to this problem exist yet; contributions of expositions are welcomed via a moderator or comment. Key references: erdosproblems.com/1139; Erdős references: [Va99,1.4].
solved_when: The stated limit superior is proved to be infinite.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a basic question about how irregularly almost-primes are distributed.

title: Erdős problem #1142
open: Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $n-2^k$ is prime for every power of two $1<2^k<n$ — and in particular, is there any such $n$ beyond $105$?
status: The only known such $n$ are $[4,7,15,21,45,75,105]$ (OEIS A039669). Mientka and Weitzenkamp [MiWe69] proved there are no other such $n\leq 2^{44}$. Vaughan [Va73] proved that the number of $n\leq N$ with $n-2^k$ prime for all $1<2^k<n$ is $< \exp\left(-c\frac{\log \log \log N}{\log\log N}\log N\right)N$ for some constant $c>0$. The problem is discussed as A19 in Guy's collection [Gu04] and on the Prime Puzzles website. Erdős made the stronger conjecture (see [236]) that the number of $1<2^k<n$ for which $n-2^k$ is prime is $o(\log n)$.
solved_when: A proof that infinitely many such $n$ exist, or a proof that none exist beyond the known list $[4,7,15,21,45,75,105]$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a classical question about how thin prime-rich shifts can be.

title: Erdős problem #1143
open: Given primes $p_1<\cdots<p_u$ and $k\geq 1$, how many multiples of at least one of the $p_i$ must every interval of $k$ positive integers contain? Formally, estimate the guaranteed minimum $F_k(p_1,\ldots,p_u)$, particularly when $k=\alpha p_u$ for constant $\alpha>2$.
status: In [Va99] it is reported that Erdős and Selfridge found "the exact bound" when $2<\alpha<3$, and that "if $\alpha>3$ then very little is known." No reference is given, and the record's author could not find a relevant paper of Erdős and Selfridge. See also [970].
solved_when: A sharp estimate of $F_k(p_1,\ldots,p_u)$ is obtained, in particular for $k=\alpha p_u$ with constant $\alpha>2$, covering both the range $2<\alpha<3$ (recovering and referencing the exact bound attributed to Erdős and Selfridge) and $\alpha>3$, where currently very little is known.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle the state of knowledge for intervals whose length is a fixed multiple of the largest prime involved.

title: Erdős problem #1144
open: Let $f$ be a random completely multiplicative function, where for each prime $p$ we independently choose $f(p)\in \{-1,1\}$ uniformly at random. Is it true that $\limsup_{N\to \infty}\frac{\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)}{\sqrt{N}}=\infty$ with probability $1$?
status: This model of a random multiplicative function is sometimes called a Rademacher function, although this name is sometimes reserved for a merely multiplicative function (which is $0$ on non-squarefree integers); see [520] for the partial sums of this alternative model. It should also be compared to another popular model of random completely multiplicative functions, Steinhaus functions, which have $f(p)$ uniformly distributed over the unit circle. Atherfold [At25] has proved that, almost surely, $\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)\ll N^{1/2}(\log N)^{1+o(1)}$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, for a random completely multiplicative function with independent uniform $f(p)\in\{-1,1\}$, the partial sums satisfy $\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{\sum_{m\leq N}f(m)}{\sqrt{N}}=\infty$ almost surely.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle the almost-sure growth behavior of partial sums of the canonical Rademacher random completely multiplicative function.

title: Erdős problem #1145
open: Let $A=\{1\leq a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ and $B=\{1\leq b_1<b_2<\cdots\}$ be sets of integers with $a_n/b_n\to 1$. If $A+B$ contains all sufficiently large positive integers then is it true that $\limsup 1_A\ast 1_B(n)=\infty$?
status: A conjecture of Erdős and Sárközy. Some condition relating $A$ and $B$ is necessary since, for example, if $A$ is the set of all integers with only even binary digits and $B$ is the set of all integers with only odd binary digits then $1_A\ast 1_B(n)=1$ for all $n$. This is a stronger form of [28] . See also [331] .

title: Erdős problem #1146
open: Are the numbers of the form $2^m3^n$ (with $m,n\geq 0$) an essential component of the natural numbers — that is, does adding this set to any other set strictly increase its Schnirelmann density? Formally, is $d_s(A+B)>d_s(B)$ for every $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $0<d_s(B)<1$, where $A=\{2^m3^n:m,n\geq 0\}$?
status: The problem is open. In [Ru99] Ruzsa states: "The simplest set with a chance to be an essential component is the collection of numbers in the form $2^m3^n$ and Erdős often asked whether it is an essential component or not; I do not even have a plausible guess." See also [37]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/1146; Erdős references: [Va99,1.19] [Ru99].
solved_when: A proof that $d_s(A+B)>d_s(B)$ for every $B\subset\mathbb{N}$ with $0<d_s(B)<1$, or a counterexample $B$ with $d_s(A+B)=d_s(B)$, where $A=\{2^m3^n:m,n\geq 0\}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and even the basic additive structure of the 2-3 smooth numbers remains beyond current technique — as the record shows, experts have no plausible guess either way.

title: Erdős problem #1150
open: Does there exist a constant $c>0$ such that, for all large $n$ and all polynomials $P$ of degree $n$ with coefficients $\pm 1$, $\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert P(z)\rvert > (1+c)\sqrt{n}$? Equivalently, can no polynomial with $\pm 1$ coefficients be "ultraflat" — staying within a fixed multiplicative factor of $\sqrt{n}$ on the unit circle?
status: The question asks whether an "ultraflat" polynomial with coefficients $\pm 1$ exists. The answer is yes if the coefficients may take arbitrary values on the unit circle (see [230]). The lower bound $\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert P(z)\rvert\geq \sqrt{n}$ is trivial from Parseval's theorem. A weaker "flatness" question is the subject of [228]. Key references: erdosproblems.com/1150; Erdős references: [Ha74,4.31] [Va99,2.36].
solved_when: A constant $c>0$ is exhibited such that for all sufficiently large $n$, every degree-$n$ polynomial with coefficients $\pm 1$ satisfies $\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert P(z)\rvert > (1+c)\sqrt{n}$; alternatively, the question is resolved negatively by constructing, for infinitely many large $n$, polynomials with $\pm 1$ coefficients whose maximum modulus on the unit circle is at most $(1+c)\sqrt{n}$ for every $c>0$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a solution would settle whether "ultraflat" polynomials with $\pm 1$ coefficients can exist — a basic question about how flat a Littlewood-type polynomial can be on the unit circle.

title: Erdős problem #1151
open: For Lagrange interpolation at Chebyshev nodes, can every closed subset of $[-1,1]$ arise as the set of limit points of the interpolants of some continuous function? Formally, given $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in[-1,1]$ the Chebyshev nodes and $\mathcal{L}^nf(x)=\sum_{1\leq i\leq n}f(a_i)\ell_i(x)$ the degree $n-1$ interpolant of $f$ at those nodes, prove that for any closed $A\subseteq[-1,1]$ there exists a continuous $f$ such that $A$ is exactly the set of limit points of $\mathcal{L}^nf(x)$.
status: The problem is stated as in [Va99,2.41], but the exact intent is unclear — for instance, whether the claim is meant for a fixed, arbitrary $x\in[-1,1]$. Erdős [Er41] proved that if $x=\cos(\pi p/q)$ for odd integers $p,q\geq 1$, then there is a continuous $f$ such that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathcal{L}^nf(x)=\infty$, the limit taken over the sequence of Chebyshev nodes. In [Er43] he claims without proof that for any closed set $A$ there exists a continuous $f$ such that the limit points of $\mathcal{L}^nf(x)$ form $A$, for specific $x$ of this shape.
solved_when: For every closed set $A\subseteq[-1,1]$, a continuous function $f$ is exhibited (or shown to exist) such that the set of limit points of $\mathcal{L}^nf(x)$, taken over the sequence of Chebyshev nodes as $n\to\infty$, equals $A$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle the intended scope of the statement as recorded in [Va99].

title: Erdős problem #1152
open: Given, for each $n$, a set of $n$ distinct points $x_{1n},\ldots,x_{nn}\in [-1,1]$ and a tolerance $\epsilon=\epsilon(n)\to 0$, must there exist a single continuous function $:[-1,1]\to \mathbb{R}$ that defeats interpolation at these points? Formally: does there always exist a continuous $f$ such that any sequence of polynomials $p_n$ with $\deg p_n < (1+\epsilon(n))n$ satisfying $p_n(x_{kn}) = f(x_{kn})$ for all $1\leq k\leq n$ must fail to converge to $f$ for almost all $x\in[-1,1]$?
status: Erdős, Kroó, and Szabados [EKS89] proved the contrasting regime: if $\epsilon>0$ is fixed and does not tend to $0$, then there exist sequences $x_{ij}$ such that, for any continuous function $f$, there is a sequence of polynomials $p_n$ with $\deg p_n < (1+\epsilon)n$ satisfying $p_n(x_{kn}) = f(x_{kn})$ for all $1\leq k\leq n$ and $p_n(x)\to f(x)$ uniformly on $[-1,1]$. The case $\epsilon(n)\to 0$ remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given that for every choice of the point arrays $x_{kn}$ and every $\epsilon(n)\to 0$, there exists a continuous $f$ such that any interpolating polynomial sequence with $\deg p_n < (1+\epsilon(n))n$ fails to satisfy $p_n(x)\to f(x)$ for almost all $x\in[-1,1]$; or, conversely, a construction of point arrays with $\epsilon(n)\to 0$ for which every continuous $f$ admits such an interpolating sequence converging to $f$ almost everywhere.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it probes the sharp threshold for when near-minimal-degree polynomial interpolation of continuous functions on $[-1,1]$ can still converge.

title: Erdős problem #1154
open: Does every real number $\alpha \in [0,1]$ occur as the Hausdorff dimension of a subring or subfield of $\mathbb{R}$? Formally: for each $\alpha \in [0,1]$, is there a ring or field contained in the reals whose Hausdorff dimension is exactly $\alpha$?
status: Erdős and Volkmann [ErVo66] proved that, for any $\alpha \in [0,1]$, there exists a group of real numbers of Hausdorff dimension $\alpha$. Falconer [Fa84] proved that any subring with Hausdorff dimension $\alpha \in (1/2,1)$ cannot be a Borel or Suslin set. Edgar and Miller [EdMi01] proved that any real closed analytic subfield of $\mathbb{R}$ has Hausdorff dimension either $0$ or $1$, and later [EdMi03] that any Borel or analytic subring of $\mathbb{R}$ either has Hausdorff dimension $0$ or equals $\mathbb{R}$. Mauldin [Ma16b] constructed subfields of $\mathbb{R}$ of any Hausdorff dimension $\alpha \in [0,1]$ assuming the continuum hypothesis, so the problem remains open in ZFC.
solved_when: A construction (in ZFC) of, for every $\alpha \in [0,1]$, a subring or subfield of $\mathbb{R}$ of Hausdorff dimension exactly $\alpha$; or a proof that some $\alpha \in [0,1]$ is unattainable.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would settle a natural question about how much geometric size an algebraic substructure of the reals can have.

title: Erdős problem #1155
open: Start with the complete graph $K_n$ and repeatedly delete the edges of a uniformly random triangle until none remain — what does the resulting graph typically look like? In particular, if $f(n)$ counts the remaining edges, is it true that $\mathbb{E}f(n)\asymp n^{3/2}$ and that $f(n)\ll n^{3/2}$ almost surely?
status: A problem of Bollobás and Erdős, described in [Va99] as "motivated by the task of generating a random triangle-free graph"; according to [Bo98], they asked it at the "Quo Vadis, Graph Theory?" conference in Fairbanks, Alaska, in 1990, "while admiring the playful bears." Grable [Gr97] proved that for every $\epsilon>0$, $\mathbb{P}(f(n)>n^{7/4+\epsilon})\to 0$. Bohman, Frieze, and Lubetzky [BFL15] proved that $f(n)=n^{3/2+o(1)}$ almost surely — that is, for every $\epsilon>0$, $\mathbb{P}(n^{3/2-\epsilon}<f(n)<n^{3/2+\epsilon})\to 1$.
solved_when: The expected number of edges remaining satisfies $\mathbb{E}f(n)\asymp n^{3/2}$ and $f(n)\ll n^{3/2}$ almost surely (equivalently, sharp concentration of $f(n)$ around $n^{3/2}$), together with a description of the typical parameters and structure of the terminal triangle-free graph.
why: A solution would give a natural random process for generating typical triangle-free graphs with controlled size, one of Erdős's personally posed problems; it is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #1156
open: Let $G$ be a random graph on $n$ vertices, in which every edge is included independently with probability $1/2$. Is there some constant $C$ such that that chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is, almost surely, concentrated on at most $C$ values?
