Is it true that, if $\omega(n)\to \infty$ sufficiently slowly, then for every function $f(n)$\[\mathbb{P}(\lvert\chi(G)-f(n)\rvert<\omega(n))<1/2\]if $n$ is sufficiently large?
status: Bollobás [Bo88] proved that $\chi(G) \sim \frac{n}{2\log_2n}$ with high probability. Shamir and Spencer [ShSp87] proved that, for any function $\omega(n)$ such that $\omega(n)/\sqrt{n}\to \infty$, there is a function $f(n)$ such that\[\mathbb{P}(\lvert\chi(G)-f(n)\rvert<\omega(n))\to 1\]as $n\to \infty$. This is proved with $\omega(n)\frac{\log n}{\sqrt{n}}\to \infty$ in Exercise 3 of Section 7.9 of Alon and Spencer [AlSp16] (a proof is also given by Scott [Sc17] ). Heckel [He21] proved that if $f$ and $\omega$ are such that\[\mathbb{P}(\lvert\chi(G)-f(n)\rvert<\omega(n))\to 1\]as $n\to \infty$ then, for any $c<1/4$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\omega(n)>n^c$. This was improved to any $c<1/2$ by Heckel and Riordan [HeRi23] .
solved_when: The question of bounded concentration is settled: either a constant $C$ is exhibited such that $\chi(G)$ is almost surely concentrated on at most $C$ values, or it is shown that no such constant exists. Equivalently for the second part, it is determined whether for every $\omega(n)\to\infty$ sufficiently slowly and every $f(n)$, $\mathbb{P}(\lvert\chi(G)-f(n)\rvert<\omega(n))<1/2$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

title: Erdős problem #1157
open: For a family $\mathcal{F}$ of $r$-uniform hypergraphs on $k$ vertices with $s$ edges, how large can an $n$-vertex $r$-uniform hypergraph be while containing no member of $\mathcal{F}$? Formally, determine the Turán number $\mathrm{ex}_r(n,\mathcal{F})$ for all $t,k,r\geq 2$.
status: This is a very difficult and general question, and many partial results are known. The paper of Brown, Erdős, and Sós [BES73] contains many of them, in particular the general lower bound, for all $k > r$ and $s > 1$: $\mathrm{ex}_r(n,\mathcal{F}) \gg_{k,s} n^{\frac{rs-k}{s-1}}$. Brown, Erdős, and Sós conjectured generally that, for all $r > t \geq 2$ and $s \geq 3$, $\mathrm{ex}_t(n,\mathcal{F}) = o(n^t)$ whenever $k \geq (r-t)s + t + 1$. The case $t = 2$ is the subject of [1178]; the case $s = r = 3$ and $k = 6$ is the subject of [716]; the case $r = 3$ and $k = s + 2$ is the subject of [1076].
solved_when: $\mathrm{ex}_r(n,\mathcal{F})$ is determined, up to constants in the exponent, for all parameters $k, r, s$; in particular, a resolution of the Brown–Erdős–Sós conjecture that $\mathrm{ex}_t(n,\mathcal{F}) = o(n^t)$ whenever $k \geq (r-t)s + t + 1$, for all $r > t \geq 2$ and $s \geq 3$, would settle the main open case.
why: This is a master problem for hypergraph Turán theory: it contains as special cases several of Erdős's most famous extremal problems, so a general solution would resolve many long-standing questions at once.

title: Erdős problem #1158
open: Is the Turán number of the complete $t$-partite $t$-uniform hypergraph with $r$ vertices per class at least $n^{t-r^{1-t}-o(1)}$ for every $t$ and $r$? Formally, is $\mathrm{ex}_t(n,K_t(r)) \geq n^{t-r^{1-t}-o(1)}$ for all $t,r$?
status: Erdős [Er64f] proved $n^{t-O(r^{1-t})}\leq \mathrm{ex}_t(n,K_t(r)) \ll n^{t-r^{1-t}}$. The lower bound is only known when $t=2$ and $2\leq r\leq 3$; the case $t=2$ is [714].
solved_when: The lower bound $\mathrm{ex}_t(n,K_t(r)) \geq n^{t-r^{1-t}-o(1)}$ is proved for all $t$ and $r$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would pin down the Turán exponent of complete multipartite hypergraphs to within the optimal $o(1)$ term.

title: Erdős problem #1159
open: Does every finite projective plane admit a set of points that meets every line in at least one but at most some bounded number of points? Formally, is there a constant $C>1$ such that every finite projective plane $P$ has a point set $S$ with $1\leq |S\cap \ell|\leq C$ for every line $\ell$?
status: A set meeting every line is called a blocking set. In [Er81], Erdős asks the stronger question of whether such a bounded blocking set exists for all pairwise balanced block designs. Erdős, Silverman, and Stein [ESS83] proved the bound $|S\cap \ell|\ll \log n$ for all lines $\ell$, where $n$ is the order of the projective plane. See [664] for a stronger question. The problem is mentioned after Problem 68 on Green's open problems list.
solved_when: A constant $C>1$ is exhibited (or proven not to exist) such that every finite projective plane of any order $n$ contains a set $S$ meeting each line in between $1$ and $C$ points, improving on the known bound $|S\cap\ell|\ll \log n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a basic question about the structure of blocking sets in projective planes.

title: Erdős problem #1160
open: Is the number of groups of order $n$ maximized, among all orders up to $2^m$, by the power of two itself — that is, is $g(n) \leq g(2^m)$ whenever $n \leq 2^m$?
status: The problem is listed as open (Question 22.16) in [BNV07], which reports it as a "quite natural conjecture, whose origin we have been unable to trace satisfactorily. We have heard it attributed at various times to various people, such as Paul Erdős and Graham Higman." Question 22.18 of [BNV07] suggests the even stronger conjecture $\sum_{n<2^m} g(n) \leq g(2^m)$ for all sufficiently large $m$ (perhaps even as soon as $m \geq 7$). Pantelidakis [Pa03] proved the original conjecture when $n$ is odd and $m \geq 3619$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the inequality $g(n) \leq g(2^m)$ for all $n \leq 2^m$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a natural conjecture about where the group-count function attains its maxima near powers of two.

title: Erdős problem #1162
open: Is there an asymptotic formula for the number of subgroups of the symmetric group $S_n$, and beyond a count, is there a statistical theorem describing the orders these subgroups take?
status: This is a problem of Erdős and Turán. Let $f(n)$ count the number of subgroups of $S_n$. Pyber [Py93] proved that $\log f(n) \asymp n^2$. Roney-Dougal and Tracey [RoTr25] have proved that $\log f(n)=\left(\frac{1}{16}+o(1)\right)n^2$. Key references: erdosproblems.com/1162; Erdős references: [Va99,5.73] [Py93].
solved_when: An asymptotic formula for $f(n)$, the number of subgroups of $S_n$, sharper than the current $\log f(n)=\left(\tfrac{1}{16}+o(1)\right)n^2$ — ideally the exact leading constant and error term — is established, with a corresponding statistical description of subgroup orders.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would complete a classical enumerative picture of the subgroup structure of symmetric groups.

title: Erdős problem #1167
open: Does a partition relation at the higher dimension imply the corresponding one dimension lower — that is, if $2^\lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha+1)_{\alpha<\gamma}^{r+1}$ holds (with $r\geq 2$ finite, $\lambda$ an infinite cardinal, and cardinals $\kappa_\alpha$ for $\alpha<\gamma$), must $\lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha)_{\alpha<\gamma}^{r}$ also hold? Here $+$ means cardinal addition, so that $\kappa_\alpha+1=\kappa_\alpha$ if $\kappa_\alpha$ is infinite.
status: A problem of Erdős, Hajnal, and Rado, sometimes known as the 'negative stepping-up lemma'. In [ErHa71] they note that the most difficult case is when $r=2$, one $\kappa_\alpha$ is singular, and the others are finite; in this case they could not prove the statement even assuming GCH. In [EHMR84] they prove it when all $\kappa_\alpha$ are finite; when $\kappa_0$ and $\kappa_1$ are infinite and $\kappa_0$ is regular with $r\geq 3$; when $\kappa_0$ is infinite and regular with $r\geq 3$; and when $\kappa_0$ and $\kappa_1$ are infinite with $r\geq 4$.
solved_when: The implication between the two displayed partition relations is proved in full generality (for all finite $r\geq 2$, infinite $\lambda$, and all sequences of cardinals $\kappa_\alpha$, $\alpha<\gamma$), or a counterexample is exhibited.
why: This is the "negative" direction of the stepping-up mechanism in partition calculus: it would tell us when passing to $2^\lambda$ and $(r+1)$-tuples genuinely forces the lower-dimensional relation at $\lambda$, and it is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #1168
open: Is the negative partition relation $\aleph_{\omega+1}\not\to (\aleph_{\omega+1}, 3,\ldots,3)_{\aleph_0}^2$ provable in ZFC alone? That is, can one establish the failure of this polarized partition relation for $\aleph_{\omega+1}$ without assuming the generalised continuum hypothesis?
status: The problem originates with Erdős, Hajnal, and Rado, who proved [EHR65] the negative partition relation assuming GCH; removing that hypothesis remains open.
solved_when: A proof of $\aleph_{\omega+1}\not\to (\aleph_{\omega+1}, 3,\ldots,3)_{\aleph_0}^2$ is given that does not assume GCH.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; settling it would remove an unwanted set-theoretic hypothesis from a classical result in combinatorial set theory.

title: Erdős problem #1169
open: Can the square of the first uncountable ordinal fail to arrow the pair $(\omega_1^2, 3)$ in dimension two — that is, is $\omega_1^2 \not\to (\omega_1^2, 3)^2$ true for every finite $k < \omega$? Formally, must there exist a 2-coloring of the pairs of ordinals below $\omega_1^2$ in which no subset of order type $\omega_1^2$ is monochromatic in the first color and no monochromatic triangle appears in the second?
status: A problem of Erdős and Hajnal. Hajnal [Ha71] proved this is true assuming the continuum hypothesis. See also [592] for a similar problem concerning countable ordinals.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) in ZFC of the partition relation $\omega_1^2 \not\to (\omega_1^2, 3)^2$ for all finite $k < \omega$; as stated, the natural criterion is a ZFC answer, improving on the CH-dependent result.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would settle a partition question at the boundary of uncountable Ramsey theory.

title: Erdős problem #1170
open: Is it consistent with the usual axioms of set theory that $\omega_2 \to (\alpha)_2^2$ holds for every $\alpha < \omega_2$ — that is, that every 2-coloring of the pairs of $\omega_2$ yields a monochromatic subset of order type $\alpha$, for each $\alpha$ below $\omega_2$?
status: Laver [La82] proved the consistency of $\omega_2 \to (\omega_1 2+1, \alpha)^2$ for all $\alpha < \omega_2$. Foreman and Hajnal [FoHa03] proved the consistency of $\omega_2 \to (\omega_1^2+1, \alpha)^2$ for all $\alpha < \omega_2$. Key references: erdosproblems.com/1170; Erdős references: [Va99,7.86] [La82].
solved_when: A model of ZFC (or a demonstrably consistent extension) is produced in which $\omega_2 \to (\alpha)_2^2$ holds for all $\alpha < \omega_2$; or the assertion is shown inconsistent.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would clarify the extent of partition relations possible at $\omega_2$.

title: Erdős problem #1171
open: Is it true that, for all finite $k<\omega$, the partition relation $\omega_1^2\to (\omega_1\omega, 3,\ldots,3)_{k+1}^2$ holds? In other words, must every coloring of the pairs of $\omega_1 \times \omega_1$ in $k+1$ colors yield either a copy of $\omega_1\omega$ in the first color or a monochromatic triangle in one of the remaining colors?
status: Baumgartner [Ba89b] proved that, assuming a form of Martin's axiom, $\omega_1\omega\to (\omega_1\omega, 3)^2$.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the stated relation $\omega_1^2\to (\omega_1\omega, 3,\ldots,3)_{k+1}^2$ for every finite $k<\omega$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it advances the infinitary Ramsey theory of $\omega_1$ and the effect of axioms like Martin's axiom on such partition relations.

title: Erdős problem #1172
open: Do these partition relations hold under the generalised continuum hypothesis: $\omega_3 \to (\omega_2,\omega_1+2)^2$, $\omega_3\to (\omega_2+\omega_1,\omega_2+\omega)^2$, and $\omega_2\to (\omega_1^{\omega+2}+2, \omega_1+2)^2$? And is it consistent with GCH that $\omega_2\to (\omega_1+\omega)_2^2$, or even that $\omega_2 \to (\xi)_2^2$ for all $\xi<\omega_2$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Hajnal. The Erdős-Rado partition theorem [ErRa56] states that $(2^{\kappa})^+ \to (\kappa^++1)_\kappa^2$ for every infinite cardinal $\kappa$.
solved_when: Each stated relation is either proved from GCH or refuted, and the consistency (or inconsistency) of $\omega_2\to (\omega_1+\omega)_2^2$, and of $\omega_2 \to (\xi)_2^2$ for all $\xi<\omega_2$, with GCH is settled.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and its history is tracked in full at erdosproblems.com/1172; settling it would resolve a specific open entry in the Erdős–Hajnal partition-calculus program.

title: Erdős problem #1173
open: Assume the generalized continuum hypothesis, and let \(f:\omega_{\omega+1}\to[\omega_{\omega+1}]^{\leq\aleph_\omega}\) be a set mapping whose images pairwise overlap only mildly, in the sense that \(|f(\alpha)\cap f(\beta)|<\aleph_\omega\) for all \(\alpha\neq\beta\). Must there exist a free set of cardinality \(\aleph_{\omega+1}\)?
status: The problem is due to Erdős and Hajnal and remains open; it is tracked as Erdős problem #1173 at erdosproblems.com, with references [Ko25b, Problem 35] and [Va99, 7.88] in Erdős's reference numbering.
solved_when: Under GCH, a proof (or refutation, via a counterexample) of the existence of a free set of cardinality \(\aleph_{\omega+1}\) for every set mapping \(f:\omega_{\omega+1}\to[\omega_{\omega+1}]^{\leq\aleph_\omega}\) satisfying \(|f(\alpha)\cap f(\beta)|<\aleph_\omega\) for all \(\alpha\neq\beta\).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and a resolution would settle a specific question in the Erdős–Hajnal program on free sets for set mappings; its full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/1173.

title: Erdős problem #1174
open: Does there exist a graph containing no $K_4$ such that every colouring of its edges with countably many colours yields a monochromatic triangle, and, at the level of infinite cardinals, a graph containing no $K_{\aleph_1}$ such that every countable-colour edge colouring yields a monochromatic $K_{\aleph_0}$?
status: This is a problem of Erdős and Hajnal. Shelah proved that a graph with either property can consistently exist. Key references: erdosproblems.com/1174; Erdős references: [Va99,7.91].
solved_when: A graph with no $K_4$ is exhibited (in ZFC, or explicitly relative to a stated consistency) whose every countable-colour edge colouring contains a monochromatic $K_3$, and likewise a graph with no $K_{\aleph_1}$ whose every countable-colour edge colouring contains a monochromatic $K_{\aleph_0}$; alternatively, a proof that no such graph exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, posed jointly with Hajnal, and is tracked with its full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would settle a natural infinite-Ramsey question about how sparsely clique-free graphs can still force monochromatic subcliques.

title: Erdős problem #1175
open: Let $\kappa$ be an uncountable cardinal. Must there exist a cardinal $\lambda$ such that every graph with chromatic number $\lambda$ contains a triangle-free subgraph with chromatic number $\kappa$? In other words, is large chromatic number alone enough to force a triangle-free subgraph of any prescribed uncountable chromatic number?
status: Shelah proved that a negative answer is consistent if $\kappa=\lambda=\aleph_1$. The problem is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/1175 (Erdős references: [Va99,7.92]).
solved_when: The question is answered affirmatively or negatively for arbitrary uncountable $\kappa$ — that is, either a proof that such a $\lambda$ exists for every uncountable $\kappa$, or a proof that for some uncountable $\kappa$ no such $\lambda$ exists.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full solution history tracked at erdosproblems.com; settling it resolves a basic question about how chromatic number and triangle-free substructures interact at uncountable cardinals.

title: Erdős problem #1176
open: If a graph has chromatic number $\aleph_1$, must its edges be colorable with $\aleph_1$ colors so that every countable coloring of the vertices leaves some vertex-color class realizing all edge colors?
status: A problem of Erdős, Galvin, and Hajnal. The consistency of the statement was proved by Hajnal and Komjáth. Tracked at erdosproblems.com/1176; Erdős references: [Va99,7.93].
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) in ZFC, or a consistency result separating the statement from known models, resolving the question for graphs of chromatic number $\aleph_1$ with $\aleph_1$ edge colors and countable vertex colorings as stated.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would clarify the infinite Ramsey-type structure of uncountable chromatic graphs.

title: Erdős problem #1177
open: If a finite 3-uniform hypergraph $G$ is avoidable at some uncountable chromatic number, how regular is the resulting family of witnesses? Formally, writing $F_G(\kappa)$ for the class of $G$-free $3$-uniform hypergraphs with chromatic number $\kappa$: if $F_G(\aleph_1)$ is non-empty, must it contain a member of cardinality at most $2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$; if $F_G(\aleph_1)$ and $F_H(\aleph_1)$ are both non-empty, must $F_G(\aleph_1)\cap F_H(\aleph_1)$ be non-empty; and, for uncountable $\kappa,\lambda$, if $F_G(\kappa)$ is non-empty must $F_G(\lambda)$ be non-empty?
status: A problem of Erdős, Galvin, and Hajnal; it remains open with no recorded progress. Tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com (erdosproblems.com/1177; Erdős references: [Va99,7.94]).
solved_when: Each of the three statements is proved or disproved: the bounded-size claim (a member of $F_G(\aleph_1)$ of cardinality at most $2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$), the intersection claim for any pair $G,H$ with non-empty $F_{(\cdot)}(\aleph_1)$, and the transfer claim across any two uncountable cardinals $\kappa,\lambda$.
why: It clarifies how finite forbidden subhypergraphs constrain chromatic behavior in the uncountable, determining whether avoiding one finite $G$ is a genuine structural restriction or a generic feature of set-sized hypergraphs.
aliases: Erdős #1177; set theory / chromatic number / hypergraphs

title: Erdős problem #1178
open: For $r\geq 3$, let $d_r(e)$ be the smallest $d$ such that $\mathrm{ex}_r(n,\mathcal{F})=o(n^2)$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the family of $r$-uniform hypergraphs on $d$ vertices with $e$ edges. Is it true that $d_r(e)=(r-2)e+3$ for all $r,e\geq 3$?
status: The conjecture is due to Brown, Erdős, and Sós [BES73], who proved the lower bound $d_r(e)\geq (r-2)e+3$ (see also [1076]). Ruzsa and Szemerédi [RuSz78] proved $d_3(3)=6$ (see [716]). Erdős, Frankl, and Rödl [EFR86] proved $d_r(3)=(r-2)3+3$ for all $r\geq 3$. Sárközy and Selkow [SaSe05] proved $d_r(e)\leq (r-2)e+2+\lfloor \log_2 e\rfloor$ for all $r,e\geq 3$. Solymosi and Solymosi [SoSo17] proved $d_3(10)\leq 14$. Conlon, Gishboliner, Levanzov, and Shapira [CGLS23] proved $d_3(e)\leq e+O\left(\frac{\log e}{\log\log e}\right)$ for all $e\geq 3$. In [Er75b] Erdős even asks whether, if $\mathcal{F}$ is the family of $3$-uniform hypergraphs on $k$ vertices with $k-3$ edges, $\mathrm{ex}_3(n,\mathcal{F})\asymp n r_{k-3}(n)$, where $r_{k-3}(n)$ is the maximal size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with no non-trivial arithmetic progression of length $k-3$; he states that Ruzsa proved the lower bound for $k=6,7,8$. See [1157] for the general case.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $d_r(e)=(r-2)e+3$ for all $r\geq 3$ and $e\geq 3$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would determine the exact vertex-edge threshold for $r$-uniform hypergraph Turán-type extremal behavior.

title: Erdős problem #1181
open: For each $n$ and $k$, let $q(n,k)$ be the least prime not dividing $\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)$. Is there a constant $c>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$, $q(n,\log n)<(1-c)(\log n)^2$?
status: The upper bound $q(n,\log n)\leq (1+o(1))(\log n)^2$ follows from observing that the primorial of $q(n,k)$ is at most $\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)$. Probabilistic heuristics described by Tao in the comments of [457] suggest $q(n,\log n)\ll \frac{\log\log n}{\log\log\log n}{\log n}$ for all $n$. The work [457] concerns lower bounds for $q(n,\log n)$, and in particular the constructions described there prove that the above upper bound would be best possible. Key works: erdosproblems.com/1181; Erdős references: [Er79d,p.78].
solved_when: A constant $c>0$ is exhibited with $q(n,\log n)<(1-c)(\log n)^2$ for all sufficiently large $n$, or the statement is disproved.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; a resolution would sharpen our understanding of how prime factors distribute across short intervals of consecutive integers.

title: Erdős problem #1182
open: How dense can an $n$-vertex connected graph be while its triangle Ramsey number stays at the minimum value $2n-1$? Formally, estimate $f(n)$, the maximum number of edges of a connected $n$-vertex graph $G$ with $R(K_3,G)=2n-1$, and $F(n)$, the maximum number such that every connected $n$-vertex graph with at most $F(n)$ edges satisfies $R(K_3,G)=2n-1$ — in particular, does $F(n)/n\to\infty$?
status: A problem of Burr, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp. It is trivial that $f(n)\geq F(n)$ and that $R(K_3,G)\geq 2n-1$ for any connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices. By a result of Chvátal, $R(K_3,T)=2n-1$ whenever $T$ is a tree on $n$ vertices, whence $F(n)\geq n-1$. Burr, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp [BEFRS80] proved $\frac{17n+1}{15}\leq F(n)\leq \left(\frac{27}{4}+o(1)\right)n(\log n)^2$, the lower bound for all $n\geq 4$; the upper bound was improved to $F(n)\leq 84n$ by Brandt [Br96], who expects that for all large $n$ we have $2n<F(n)<6n$ — which would resolve the $F(n)/n\to\infty$ question in the negative. In [BEFRS80] they also prove $n^{3/2}(\log n)^{1/2}\ll f(n)\ll n^{5/3}(\log n)^{2/3}$. The first few values of $F(n)$ and $f(n)$ (beginning with $n=2$) are $1,2,5,7,8$ and $1,2,5,8,12$ respectively, as reported in [BEFRS80]. Similar questions with $K_3$ replaced by $K_m$ (where $2n-1$ is replaced with $(m-1)(n-1)+1$) were also studied: Burr, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau, and Schelp [BEFRS80] proved $n^{\frac{2}{m-1}}\ll F_m(n)-n\ll n^{\frac{4}{m+1}+o(1)}$ and $n^{1+\frac{1}{m-1}}\ll f_m(n)\ll n^{1+\frac{2}{m}+o(1)}$.
solved_when: Asymptotically tight estimates (up to constants) for $f(n)$ and $F(n)$ are obtained. Known quantitative landmarks: the lower bound $F(n)\geq (17n+1)/15$ versus the upper bound $F(n)\leq 84n$, with Brandt's conjecture that $2n<F(n)<6n$ for all large $n$; for $f(n)$, closing the gap between $n^{3/2}(\log n)^{1/2}$ and $n^{5/3}(\log n)^{2/3}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and it pins down the sharp density threshold at which connected graphs lose the minimal triangle Ramsey behavior established for trees by Chvátal.

title: Erdős problem #1183
open: In every $2$-colouring of the subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, how large a monochromatic family closed under both unions and intersections must there be? Formally, estimating $f(n)$, the maximal value guaranteed by any such colouring — and, for the union-only variant, $F(n)$: in particular, is $F(n)\geq n^{\omega(n)}$ for some $\omega(n)\to\infty$, while $F(n)<(1+o(1))^n$?
status: This is a problem of Erdős and Ulam. It is trivial that $f(n)\geq \frac{n+1}{2}$, since there is a sequence of $n+1$ nested subsets, and this seems to be all they knew: Erdős [Er78] wrote 'we have no plausible conjecture for the true order of magnitude of $f(n)$'. They similarly had no good guess about $F(n)$. In [Er78] Erdős wrote that if the colouring assigns all subsets of the same size the same colour, then Howorka had proved $F(n)>n^{\omega(n)}$ for some $\omega(n)\to\infty$, but gave no reference.
solved_when: The order of magnitude of $f(n)$ is determined (up to which of the competing bounds above is tight), and correspondingly for $F(n)$ the conjectured bounds $F(n)\geq n^{\omega(n)}$ for some $\omega(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ and $F(n)<(1+o(1))^n$ are settled (proved or refuted).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with Ulam), tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a basic Ramsey-theoretic question about unavoidable monochromatic substructure in the Boolean lattice.

title: Erdős problem #1184
open: Let $f(n,k)$ count the number of $1\leq i\leq k$ such that $P(n+i)>k$, where $P(m)$ is the largest prime divisor of $m$. Is it true that, if $\alpha>1$ is such that $n=k^{\alpha+o(1)}$, then $f(n,k)=(1-\rho(\alpha)+o(1))k$, where $\rho$ is the Dickman function?
status: Erdős [Er76e] proved that, for every $\alpha>1$, if $k$ is sufficiently large and $n>k^\alpha-k$ then $f(n,k) > (1-\frac{1}{\alpha}+c_\alpha)k$ for some constant $c_\alpha>0$, and if $1<\alpha<2$ and $n\leq k^\alpha-k$ then $f(n,k) < (\alpha-1+o(1))k$. He knew of no non-trivial bounds when $\alpha \geq 2$. Ramachandra, Shorey, and Tijdeman [RST75b] proved that if $n>\exp(c(\log k)^2)$ for a constant $c>0$ then $f(n,k)\geq k-\pi(k)$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that for every $\alpha>1$ with $n=k^{\alpha+o(1)}$, the asymptotic $f(n,k)=(1-\rho(\alpha)+o(1))k$ holds, where $\rho$ is the Dickman function.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would determine the exact asymptotic density of integers in a short interval whose largest prime factor exceeds the interval length.

title: Erdős problem #1186
open: How few monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progressions must any $2$-colouring of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ contain? Formally, letting $\delta_k$ be such that every $2$-colouring has at least $(\delta_k+o(1))n^2$ monochromatic $k$-term arithmetic progressions, give reasonable bounds for $\delta_k$, or even an asymptotic formula.
status: In [Er80] Erdős said 'perhaps one can get an asymptotic formula' for $\delta_k$, but this seems unlikely. Van der Waerden's theorem implies $\delta_k\gg_k 1$, while the probabilistic method gives $\delta_k \leq \frac{1}{(k-1)2^{k}}$. Parrilo, Robertson, and Saraceno [PRS08] proved $\frac{1675}{32768}\approx 0.0511\leq \delta_3 \leq \frac{117}{2192}\approx 0.0533$ and conjectured the upper bound is correct; Graham offered \$100 for determining $\delta_3$ at a conference in 1999. The finite-field analogue, replacing $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ by $\mathbb{F}_p$ and denoted $\tilde{\delta}_k$, is more tractable: a random colouring gives $\tilde{\delta}_k\leq 1/2^{k}$, and $\tilde{\delta}_3=1/8$ is straightforward (see, for example, [Wo10]). Improving on Cameron, Cilleruelo, and Serra [CCS07], Wolf [Wo10] proved $\frac{1}{32}\leq \tilde{\delta}_4\leq \left(1-\frac{1}{259200}\right)\frac{1}{16}$; Lu and Peng [LuPe12] improved these to $\frac{7}{192}\leq \tilde{\delta}_4\leq \frac{17}{300}$.
solved_when: Nontrivial explicit upper and lower bounds on $\delta_k$ are established (ideally an asymptotic formula); in particular, the exact value of $\delta_3$ is determined, settling Graham's offered \$100 prize.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and determining the forced density of monochromatic arithmetic progressions is a fundamental quantitative refinement of Ramsey-type results in additive combinatorics.

title: Erdős problem #1188
open: Let $F(x)$ count the minimal distinct covering systems — covering systems of distinct moduli $1<n_1<\cdots<n_k$ with congruence classes $a_i\pmod{n_i}$, no proper subset of which is again a covering system — having all moduli in $[1,x]$. How fast does $F(x)$ grow as $x\to\infty$?
status: Erdős [Er80] asked this without the minimality assumption, in which case the problem is trivial (any system containing a fixed covering system works, giving $\gg 2^x$ such systems). He expected $F(x)\to\infty$ 'very slowly'. In [Er80] Erdős also asked to estimate the number $G(x)$ of irreducible covering sets in $[1,x]$ (sets of moduli containing no proper subset of moduli forming a covering system, perhaps with a different choice of congruence classes); trivially $G(x)\leq F(x)$. See [1189] for more on irreducible covering sets. Hough's solution [Ho15] of [2] implies $F(x)\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$, and a lower bound $F(x)\gg \log x$ follows by elementary means, as observed by van Doorn in the comments. The lower bound construction of Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba [BBMST24] implies at least $\exp(k^{3+o(1)})$ minimal distinct covering systems with all moduli at most $\prod_{p<k}p=e^{(1+o(1))k}$, hence $F(x)\geq \exp((\log x)^{3-o(1)})$ — so $F(x)$ grows faster than any polynomial.
solved_when: An asymptotic (or tight upper and lower bounds) for $F(x)$ is obtained, resolving Erdős's expectation that $F(x)\to\infty$ 'very slowly'; current lower bounds give $F(x)\geq \exp((\log x)^{3-o(1)})$.

title: Erdős problem #1189
open: How many irreducible covering sets of size $k$ exist, and how large can their members and reciprocal sums be? More precisely — for irreducible covering sets $1<n_1<\cdots<n_k$ — determine or estimate the number of such sets, the minimum and maximum of $n_k$, the maximum of $\sum\frac{1}{n_i}$, and whether infinitely many $n$ have their divisors $>1$ forming an irreducible covering set.
status: This differs subtly from the more usually studied notion of minimal covering system: an irreducible covering set corresponds to the set of moduli of a minimal covering system, but not necessarily vice versa. The divisors of $12$ (which are $>1$) form an example of an irreducible covering set. Sun [Su07] proved that, for any odd prime $p$, the divisors (which are $>1$) of $2^{p-1}p$ form an irreducible covering set, settling the final question. Simpson [Si85] proved $n_k\leq 2^{k-1}$. Letting $I(k)$ count irreducible covering sets of size $k$, Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba [BBMST24] proved $I(k)\leq\exp((c+o(1))k^{3/2}/(\log k)^{1/2})$ by showing the right-hand side is an asymptotic for the number of minimal covering systems on $k$ moduli. It is trivial that $\sum\frac{1}{n_i}>1$ for any irreducible covering set. See also [1188].
solved_when: Determinations or estimates are obtained for: the count $I(k)$ of irreducible covering sets of size $k$ (with the upper bound $I(k)\leq\exp((c+o(1))k^{3/2}/(\log k)^{1/2})$ as the current benchmark), the minimum and maximum of $n_k$ (with the known bound $n_k\leq 2^{k-1}$), the value or estimate of $\max\sum\frac{1}{n_i}$ (noting the trivial lower bound $\sum\frac{1}{n_i}>1$), and the question of infinitely many $n$ whose divisors $>1$ form an irreducible covering set — though this last question is already settled affirmatively by Sun's result for divisors of $2^{p-1}p$.

title: Erdős problem #1191
open: How sparse can an infinite Sidon set be? Formally, must every infinite Sidon set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ satisfy $\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x^{1/2}}(\log x)^{1/2}=0$, and conversely does there exist one with $\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x^{1/2}}(\log x)^{c}>0$ for some $c>0$?
status: Erdős proved (see for example [HaRo66]) that if $A$ is an infinite Sidon set then $\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x^{1/2}}(\log x)^{1/2}\leq c$ for some constant $c>0$. In [Er80] he offered $1000 'for clearing up the problems' raised by this; he may have meant for finding the optimal function $f$ such that $\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x^{1/2}}f(x)=0$ for all infinite Sidon sets $A$. The second question is a stronger form of [39]. See also [729] for the behaviour of the $\limsup$.
solved_when: The liminf behavior of infinite Sidon sets at the $\sqrt{x}$ scale is determined: either it is shown that every infinite Sidon set $A$ has $\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x^{1/2}}(\log x)^{1/2}=0$, or an infinite Sidon set $A$ is constructed with $\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x^{1/2}}(\log x)^{c}>0$ for some $c>0$ (resolving Erdős's $1000 question, [Er80,p.98]).
why: This asks for the optimal function $f$ with $\liminf_{x\to\infty}\frac{|A\cap[1,x]|}{x^{1/2}}f(x)=0$ for all infinite Sidon sets $A$, pinning down the fundamental sparsity threshold for Sidon sequences.

title: Erdős problem #1192
open: Does every order $r\geq 2$ admit an additive basis $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ that represents every large integer as $n=a_1+\cdots+a_r$ with $a_i\in A$ essentially as rarely as possible? Formally, does there exist, for all $r\geq 2$, a basis $A$ of order $r$ (so that $f_r(n)>0$ for all large $n$) such that $\sum_{n\leq x}f_r(n)^2\ll x$ for all $x$?
status: Erdős and Rényi proved by the probabilistic method that there exists a set $A$ such that $\sum_{n\leq x}f_r(n)^2\ll x$ and $\lvert A\cap[1,x]\rvert\gg x^{1/r}$ for all $x$. Ruzsa [Ru90] proved that the answer is yes for $r=2$.
solved_when: For every $r\geq 2$, a set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ is exhibited (or proven to exist) that is a basis of order $r$, i.e. $f_r(n)>0$ for all large $n$, and satisfies $\sum_{n\leq x}f_r(n)^2\ll x$ for all $x$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and asks whether the probabilistic intuition behind thin bases holds in an extremal, square-sum-bounded sense for every representation order.

title: Erdős problem #1194
open: If every positive integer $n$ has a unique representation as $a_n-b_n$ with $a_n,b_n$ in a set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$, how fast must the sequence $a_n/n$ grow? In particular, what is the true order of growth of $a_n$ as a function of $n$?
status: Such a set is called a perfect difference set; they can be constructed, for example, by a greedy approach (as detailed by Lev [Le04]). The greedy construction achieves $a_n\ll n^3$. Erdős [Er80] wrote it is 'easy to see' that $\limsup_{n\to\infty} a_n/n=\infty$: since $A$ must be a Sidon set, if $a_n\leq f(n)n$ for all $n$, then all differences in $[1,x/f(x)]$ can be realised by differences from $A\cap[1,x]$, giving $|A\cap[1,x]|^2\gg x/f(x)$, while Erdős (see for example [HaRo66]) proved that for infinitely many $x$, $|A\cap[1,x]|\ll (x/\log x)^{1/2}$ — a contradiction for suitable $f$. This proves $a_n\gg n\log n$ for infinitely many $n$. Cilleruelo and Nathanson [CiNa08] describe a method for constructing dense perfect difference sets from dense Sidon sets, allowing many results for the latter to transfer to the former. GPT-5.4 Pro (see the comments) has given an argument proving $a_n\gg n^{2-o(1)}$ infinitely often; in fact $a_n\gg n^2/f(n)$ infinitely often for any function $f$ with $\sum \frac{1}{nf(n)}$ divergent.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are established for $a_n$ up to constant (or logarithmic) factors; the gap currently runs from $a_n\gg n\log n$ (infinitely often) to $a_n\ll n^3$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolves the extremal behavior of perfect difference sets — sets where every integer is uniquely a difference.
aliases: Erdős #1194; additive combinatorics / additive basis / sidon sets

title: Erdős problem #1199
open: Is it true that in any $2$-colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ there exists an infinite set $A$ such that all elements of $A+A$ are the same colour? Equivalently, does every red/blue colouring of the natural numbers admit an infinite monochromatic sumset $A+A$?
status: The statement is a conjecture of Owings [Ow74]. Hindman [Hi79] has shown that it is false for $3$-colourings. If one does not require the elements $2a$ for $a\in A$ to also be the same colour, the answer is yes by Hindman's theorem (see [532]).
solved_when: A proof that every $2$-colouring of $\mathbb{N}$ contains an infinite set $A$ with all elements of $A+A$ the same colour, or a counterexample: a $2$-colouring admitting no such infinite monochromatic sumset.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and its resolution would settle a natural Ramsey-theoretic question at the boundary between Hindman's theorem and its known failure for three colours.

title: Erdős problem #1200
open: Can every large integer up to $x$ be covered by a system of prime congruences whose total reciprocal cost is bounded independently of $x$? Formally: does there exist a constant $C$ such that for all large $x$ there are primes $p_1<\ldots<p_k<x$ with $\sum 1/p_i < C$ and residue classes $a_i \pmod{p_i}$ such that every integer $n<x$ satisfies at least one of the congruences?
status: This is a conjecture of Erdős and Ruzsa which Erdős described in [Er80] as 'surprising'; he noted that if it is correct then 'very likely' the $\epsilon_n$ in [688] is $\gg 1$, while certainly proving $\epsilon_n \geq c$ would prove the conjecture (taking $P$ to be all primes in $[x^c,x]$). In [ErRu80] it is asked as a question: if $p_1<\cdots<p_k<x$ are primes with $\sum 1/p_i \leq C$ and $a_i \pmod{p_i}$ are any residue classes, must there always be $\gg_K x$ integers $n<x$ avoiding all of them? (a positive answer would disprove the main conjecture). Erdős and Ruzsa [ErRu80] proved that for any $C>0$ there exists a set of primes $P$ with $\sum_{p\in P} 1/p \leq C$ such that the number of integers $n\leq x$ divisible by at least one $p\in P$ is $\gg_C x$. See also [783] and [784].
solved_when: A constant $C$ and, for all sufficiently large $x$, primes $p_1<\cdots<p_k<x$ with $\sum 1/p_i < C$ and residue classes $a_i \pmod{p_i}$ covering every integer $n<x$ are exhibited; or a proof that for any such system with $\sum 1/p_i \leq C$ there are $\gg_K x$ integers $n<x$ avoiding all the classes, which would disprove the conjecture.
why: A positive answer would, per Erdős, make it 'very likely' that the $\epsilon_n$ in [688] satisfies $\epsilon_n \gg 1$, and this is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #1201
open: Is it true that for every $\epsilon,\eta>0$ there exists a $k$ such that the density of $n$ for which $P(n(n+1)\cdots(n+k))>n^{1-\epsilon}$ is at least $1-\eta$, where $P(m)$ denotes the greatest prime divisor of $m$? In other words, can a long enough block of consecutive integers starting at $n$ almost always be guaranteed to contain a prime factor larger than $n^{1-\epsilon}$?
status: Erdős wrote he could prove the statement for $\epsilon=1/2$; the general case remains open. Tracked at erdosproblems.com/1201; Erdős references: [Er80,p.107].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) is given of the statement above for arbitrary $\epsilon,\eta>0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked publicly, so a resolution settles a long-standing entry in his problem collection concerning prime divisors of products of consecutive integers.

title: Erdős problem #1203
open: Does the maximum over shifts $k$ of $\omega(n+k)\frac{\log\log k}{\log k}$ tend to infinity with $n$? Formally, if $\omega(n)$ counts the distinct prime divisors of $n$, prove that $F(n)=\max_k \omega(n+k)\frac{\log\log k}{\log k}$ satisfies $F(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$.
status: In the number-theoretic setting it is easy to prove that $F(n)\geq 1-o(1)$. See also [248], [679], and [890].
solved_when: A proof that $F(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #1204
open: How small can the largest element of an admissible $k$-tuple be? Formally, for an admissible sequence $0\leq a_1<\cdots<a_k$ (one that misses at least one residue class modulo every prime $p$), writing $A(k)=\min a_k$, is it true that $A(k)\sim k\log k$? Similarly, estimate $B(k)=\min (a_1+\cdots+a_k)/k$.
status: Erdős [Er80] attributes the problem to Elliott. The bounds in [Er80] are misstated, but it is known that $(1/2+o(1))k\log k \leq A(k)\leq (1+o(1))k\log k$. The upper bound, which Erdős attributes to Davenport, follows simply by taking the $k$ smallest primes $>k$; its lower-order terms were improved by Hensley and Richard [HeRi73] (see Section 10 of [Po14c]). The lower bound is originally due to Elliott [El65], but was rediscovered by the Polymath project on bounded gaps between primes (see [Po14c]). An upper bound of $\pi(x+y)\leq \pi(x)+(1+o(1))\pi(y)$ (see [855]) together with the prime tuples conjecture would imply $A(k)\geq (1+o(1))k\log k$. Trivially $B(k)<A(k)$; taking the first $k$ primes $>k$ gives $B(k)\leq (1/2+o(1))k\log k$, and since $a_j\geq A(j)$ we have $B(k)\geq \frac{1}{k}\sum_{1\leq j\leq k}A(j)$, whence if $A(k)\geq (c-o(1))k\log k$ then $B(k)\geq (c/2-o(1))k\log k$, so it is likely that $B(k)\sim (1/2+o(1))k\log k$. In [Er80] Erdős also asks about the behaviour of $a_k$ where $a_1<a_2<\cdots$ is the greedy admissible sequence (i.e. $a_1=0$ and $a_{i+1}$ is the smallest integer $>a_{i-1}$ such that...).
solved_when: Asymptotic formulae are established for $A(k)$ (conjecturally $A(k)\sim k\log k$) and for $B(k)$, for which $(1/2+o(1))k\log k$ is the expected order.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, attributed to Elliott, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; it controls how tightly prime-tuple candidates can be packed, a basic question underlying bounded-gap methods.

title: Erdős problem #1206
open: Do the cubes up to $N^3$ contain a Sidon subset of size comparable to $N$? Equivalently, is there an infinite set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ of positive density such that $\{a^3 : a\in A\}$ is a Sidon set?
status: The question may also be asked for higher powers, and [324] suggests that for fifth powers $\{n^5 : n\geq 1\}$ may itself be a Sidon set. Gabdullin and Konyagin [GaKo24] proved there is a constant $c>0$ such that $\{n^3 : N-cN^{1/2}\leq n\leq N\}$ is a Sidon set. Garaev, Garayev, and Konyagin [GGK26] improved the exponent $1/2$ to $4/7-o(1)$ for infinitely many $N$, and to $3/5$ for all $N$ when $n^3$ is replaced by $n^4$. In [Er80] Erdős defines $g_k(A)$ as the maximal size of a Sidon set of $\{a^k : a\in A\}$ and asks whether $g_k(A)\geq g_k(\{1,\ldots,N\})$ where $N=\lvert A\rvert$ (see [530] for the linear analogue); see also [773] for an analogous question about squares.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $\{1,2^3,\ldots,N^3\}$ contains a Sidon set of size $\gg N$, equivalently the existence (or nonexistence) of an infinite positive-density set $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ whose cubes form a Sidon set.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it probes how sparse powers must be forced into Sidon structure — a basic test of additive structure in polynomial sequences.

title: Erdős problem #1207
open: In any set of $n$ points in the plane, how large a subset can we always find containing no isosceles triangle? Formally, letting $P_d(n)$ denote the largest such guaranteed size in $\mathbb{R}^d$, estimate $P_d(n)$ — in particular, is it true that $P_2(n) < n^{1-c}$ for some constant $c>0$?
status: Erdős [Er80] attributes this problem to Riddell and states it is not hard to prove that $P_d(n) > n^{\epsilon_d}$ where $\epsilon_d \to 0$ as $d \to \infty$; indeed, one can take any subset of points with all distinct distances, whence $P_d(n) \geq f_d(n) \geq n^{\frac{1}{3d-3}-o(1)}$ with $f_d(n)$ defined as in [1208]. Erdős suggested that perhaps the worst set of points is the set of lattice points in a sphere of suitable radius. The case $d=1$ is equivalent to finding sets with no three-term arithmetic progressions, and is the $k=3$ case of [201]. The bound of Pach and Tardos [PaTa02] on the maximum number of isosceles triangles in a point set, together with a random deletion argument, shows that $P_2(n) \gg n^{0.432}$. In Section 5.3 of [BMP05] they claim that the regular polygon shows that $P_2(n) \ll n^{1/2}$ but give no details; this seems to be incorrect, since an isosceles triangle from the vertices of a regular polygon corresponds to three points whose angles form an arithmetic progression, which shows $P_2(n) \ll r_3(n)$, where $r_3(n)$ is the maximum size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ without a non-trivial three-term arithmetic progression (see [140]).
solved_when: An estimate of $P_d(n)$ is obtained, with the concrete target being a proof (or disproof) that $P_2(n) < n^{1-c}$ for some constant $c>0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; it connects planar distance geometry to the theory of three-term-arithmetical-progression-free sets.

title: Erdős problem #1209
open: If a fast-growing sequence of integers $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ admits a single shift $n$ for which every $n+a_k$ is prime, must infinitely many such $n$ exist? The same question may be asked with "squarefree" in place of "prime", and in particular for the sequence $a_k = 2^{2^k}$ — asking whether some $n$ makes $n+2^{2^k}$ always prime, or always squarefree, or prime or squarefree infinitely often.
status: For the first two questions Erdős [Er80] wrote 'unless I overlook a trivial way of getting a counterexample these questions are quite hopeless'. There is indeed a trivial counterexample (a variant of the construction in [429]): define $a_1=2$ and for $k\geq 2$ let $a_k>a_{k-1}$ be a prime such that $a_k+k\equiv 0\pmod{q_k}$, where $q_k$ is some prime not dividing $k$. This sequence can be made to grow arbitrarily fast, and a similar construction with $\pmod{q_k^2}$ provides a counterexample to the squarefree question. ebarschkis and GPT have proved that there are no $n$ such that $n+2^{2^k}$ is always prime: let $n\geq 3$ be any odd integer. If $k$ is chosen sufficiently large, and $p=n+2^{2^{k}}$ is prime, then the multiplicative order of $2^{2^k}\pmod{p}$, say $m$, is odd, and hence if $l$ is chosen such that $2^l\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ then $p\mid n+2^{2^{k+rl}}$ for all $r\geq 1$. See also [429] and [1102].
solved_when: Either a proof that one such $n$ forces infinitely many such $n$ (for prime or squarefree shifts), or a counterexample construction is exhibited; likewise, a determination for the specific sequence $2^{2^k}$ of whether any $n$ yields all-prime or all-squarefree values, or values that are prime or squarefree infinitely often.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling the remaining cases would resolve a long-standing entry in his problem catalogue.

title: Erdős problem #1210
open: If $A\subseteq [1,n)$ is a set of integers with every pair of distinct elements coprime, must the sum $\sum_{a\in A}\frac{1}{n-a}$ be bounded by $\sum_{p<n}\frac{1}{p}+O(1)$?
status: In [Er80] Erdős claims he 'did not state [this] quite correctly' in [Er77c]. The problem in [Er77c] to which Erdős is presumably referring states that if $n<q_1<\cdots<q_k\leq m$ is the set of primes in $(n,m]$, then $\sum \frac{1}{q_i-n}< \sum_{p<m-n}\frac{1}{p}+O(1)$. See also [460] and [950].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the displayed bound for all finite pairwise-coprime sets $A\subseteq [1,n)$, with an absolute implied constant in the $O(1)$ term.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve a concrete question about how large reciprocal sums of pairwise-coprime sets can be.

title: Erdős problem #1212
open: In the graph on coprime pairs $(x,y)\in\mathbb{N}^2$, where adjacent vertices differ by $1$ in exactly one coordinate, does there exist an infinite path along which every vertex $(x,y)$ satisfies $\min(x,y)>1$ and has at least one of $x,y$ composite?
status: Herzog and Stewart studied this graph, which they called visible lattice points, proved it has only one infinite component, and conjectured that if $p$ is prime and $p\nmid a$ then $(a,p)$ always belongs to the infinite component — according to [Er80], though no such results of Herzog and Stewart could be found; their paper [HeSt71] concerns which finite patterns appear in the set of visible lattice points and does not address this question. Erdős originally posed the question with only the condition $\min(x,y)>1$, and, as he recounts in [Er80], "foolishly offered 25 dollars for a proof. In the evening Stewart gave the simple proof: $(p_k,p_{k+1})$ can be joined to $(p_{k+1},p_{k+2})$." Indeed, if $p_k$ is the $k$th prime, the path $(p_k,p_{k+1})\to(p_k,p_{k+1}+1)\to\cdots\to(p_k,p_{k+2})\to(p_k+1,p_{k+2})\to(p_{k+1},p_{k+2})$ is permissible provided the interval $[p_{k+1},p_{k+2}]$ contains no multiple of $p_k$, which holds whenever $p_{k+2}<2p_k$, true for all $k\geq 4$. The current question adds the requirement that at least one coordinate be composite; one could further demand the path be monotone.
solved_when: An explicit infinite path in the coprime-pair graph is produced (or its existence proved) such that every vertex $(x,y)$ on it has $\min(x,y)>1$ and at least one composite coordinate; a stronger variant asks the same for a monotone path, where every step increases the distance from the origin.
why: A solution resolves one of Erdős's personally posed problems, fully tracked at erdosproblems.com, sharpening his original question by ruling out the prime–prime vertices that Stewart's easy construction exploited.

title: Erdős problem #1218
open: Assuming the Generalised Continuum Hypothesis, and taking $\beta=\omega_{\omega+1}$, is it true that $\aleph_{\beta+1} \not\to (\aleph_\beta,4,\ldots,4)^3$, where there are countably infinitely many copies of $4$? Equivalently, under GCH, can every colouring of the triples of $\aleph_{\beta+1}$ avoid both a monochromatic $\aleph_\beta$-sized set and a monochromatic $4$-set in one of the other colours?
status: This is a problem of Erdős, Hajnal, and Rado. In [ErHa71] Erdős and Hajnal describe this as the only problem of its type (concerning generalisations of Ramsey's theorem for cardinal numbers), not involving strongly inaccessible cardinals, that remains unsolved assuming GCH — though they likely meant this question as representative of an edge case uncovered by existing results rather than the sole literal instance. In general, Erdős, Hajnal, and Rado [EHR65] conjectured that if $\beta>\mathrm{cf}(\beta)>\mathrm{cf}(\beta)-1>\mathrm{cr}(\beta)$, then $\aleph_{\beta+1}\not\to (\aleph_\beta, (4)_{\aleph_{\mathrm{cr}(\beta)}})^3$; $\beta=\omega_{\omega+1}$ is the smallest ordinal satisfying this condition. This case represented the main unknown for their methods. They proved (assuming GCH), among many other results, that if $r\geq 2$ then $\aleph_{\beta+r-2}\to (\aleph_\beta, (b)_{n-1})^r$ if and only if $b\leq\aleph_{\mathrm{cr}(\beta)}$, except possibly when either $r\geq 3$, $\beta>\mathrm{cf}(\beta)>\mathrm{cf}(\beta)-1>\mathrm{cr}(\beta)$, and $b$ is finite, or possibly when $\aleph_{\mathrm{cf}(\beta)}$ is inaccessible and $>\aleph_0$.
solved_when: A proof or disproof, under GCH with $\beta=\omega_{\omega+1}$, of the partition relation $\aleph_{\beta+1} \not\to (\aleph_\beta,4,\ldots,4)^3$ with countably many copies of $4$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would close the main edge case left open by the classical Erdős–Hajnal–Rado programme on generalised Ramsey theorems for cardinal numbers.

title: Erdős problem #1220
open: Let $\lambda$ be a singular cardinal such that both $\lambda$ and $\mathrm{cf}(\lambda)$ are $\aleph_0$-inaccessible. Does \[\lambda \to (\lambda,\aleph_1)^2\] hold?
status:
This is a problem of Erdős, Hajnal, and Rado, who note that the answer is positive under GCH or "some other additional assumptions" on $\lambda$. The $\aleph_0$-inaccessibility conditions are necessary: $	au^{\aleph_0}
ot	o (	au^+,\aleph_1)^2$, and if $\mathrm{cf}(\kappa)
ot	o (\mathrm{cf}(\kappa),\aleph_1)^2$ then $\kappa
ot	o (\kappa,\aleph_1)^2$. The simplest case is $\lambda=\aleph_{\mathfrak{c}^+}$, where the second condition implies the first by a theorem of Shelah [Sh82].
solved_when: A proof or refutation of the partition relation $\lambda \to (\lambda,\aleph_1)^2$ is given for every singular cardinal $\lambda$ with both $\lambda$ and $\mathrm{cf}(\lambda)$ $\aleph_0$-inaccessible — that is, for all $\mu<\kappa$, $\mu^{\aleph_0}<\kappa$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and a resolution would complete our understanding of when the negative partition relation for uncountable cardinals can be avoided; it is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/1220.

title: Erdős problem #1221
open: Is it true that the extremal gaps between $r$-consecutive points on the circle must grow (after the natural normalization) as the number of skipped points $r$ tends to infinity? Formally, with $\Lambda_r$, $\lambda_r$, and $\mu_r$ defined as above, do $r(\Lambda_r-1)$, $r(1-\lambda_r)$, and $r(\mu_r-1)$ all tend to infinity as $r\to\infty$?
status: A question of de Bruijn and Erdős, who [dBEr49] proved that $\Lambda_1=\frac{1}{\log 2}$, $\lambda_1=\frac{1}{\log 4}$, and $\mu_1=2$; a witnessing sequence is $a_k=\log_2(2k-1)$. They also proved that for any $r\geq 1$, $\Lambda_r \geq \frac{1}{\log(1+1/r)}$, $\lambda_r \leq \frac{r}{r+1}\frac{1}{\log(1+1/r)}$, and $\mu_r \geq 1+\frac{1}{r}$.
solved_when: It is proved that $r(\Lambda_r-1)$, $r(1-\lambda_r)$, and $r(\mu_r-1)$ each tend to infinity as $r\to\infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it would resolve the asymptotic behavior of the de Bruijn–Erdős extremal quantities for $r$-consecutive spacings on the circle.

title: Erdős problem #9
open: Let $A$ be the set of odd integers $\geq 1$ that cannot be written as $p + 2^k + 2^l$ with $p$ prime and $k, l \geq 0$. Is the upper density of $A$ positive?
status: Crocker [Cr71] proved there are infinitely many odd integers not of the form $p+2^k+2^l$, in fact $\gg \log\log N$ such integers in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Pan [Pa11] improved this to $\gg_\epsilon N^{1-\epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon>0$. Erdős believed the result cannot be proved by covering systems, i.e. integers of the form $p+2^k+2^l$ exist in every infinite arithmetic progression. In [Er80] Erdős conjectured 'with some trepidation' that for any finite set of primes $P$ all large integers $n$ can be written as $n = m+2^k+2^l$ where $m$ is a multiple of one of the primes in $P$. The sequence of such numbers is A006286 in the OEIS. See also [10], [11], and [16]; the problem is discussed as A19 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that the upper density of $A$ within the odd integers is positive; alternatively, a proof that the count of such integers up to $N$ grows faster than the current lower bound $\gg_\epsilon N^{1-\epsilon}$ toward a positive proportion.
why: It tests whether the set of primes shifted by sums of two powers of two forms an additive basis for the odd integers, a benchmark question Erdős posed personally and whose history is fully tracked at erdosproblems.com.
aliases: Erdős #9; number theory / additive basis / primes

title: Erdős problem #19
open: If a graph is an edge-disjoint union of $n$ copies of $K_n$, must it have chromatic number exactly $n$? Formally: does every such graph $G$ satisfy $\chi(G)=n$?
status: Conjectured by Erdős, Faber, and Lovász (apparently 'at a party in Boulder, Colarado in September 1972' [Er81]). Kahn [Ka92] proved $\chi(G)\leq (1+o(1))n$ (for which Erdős gave him a 'consolation prize' of \$100). Hindman [Hi81] proved the conjecture for $n<10$. Special cases were established by Romero and Sáches-Arroyo [RoSa07], Araujo-Pardo and Vázquez-Ávila [ArVa16], and Alesandroi [Al21]. Kang, Kelly, Kühn, Methuku, and Osthus [KKKMO21] proved the answer is yes for all sufficiently large $n$. In [Er97d] Erdős asks how large $\chi(G)$ can be if the copies of $K_n$ are only required to intersect in triangle-free subgraphs, or in at most one edge. In [Er93] Erdős and Füredi conjecture the generalisation that if $G$ is the union of $n$ copies of $K_n$ pairwise intersecting in at most $k$ vertices, then $\chi(G)\leq kn$; this was proved for all sufficiently large $n$ (not depending on $k$) by Kang, Kelly, Kühn, Methuku, and Osthus [KKKMO24]. Horák and Tuza [HoTu90] proved $\chi(G)\leq n^{3/2}$ if $G$ is the union of $n$ copies of $K_n$, and hence this conjecture also holds in that range.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample) that every graph which is an edge-disjoint union of $n$ copies of $K_n$ has $\chi(G)=n$, for all $n$; the conjecture carries a \$500 prize from Erdős.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, the Faber–Lovász conjecture, and a resolution settles a classic question in graph coloring with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #20
open: Is there a constant $c_k > 0$, depending only on $k$, such that every family of at least $c_k^n$ $n$-uniform sets contains a $k$-sunflower? Formally, letting $f(n,k)$ be the minimal size guaranteeing a $k$-sunflower, is $f(n,k) < c_k^n$ for some constant $c_k > 0$?
status: Erdős and Rado [ErRa60] originally proved $f(n,k) \leq (k-1)^n n!$. Kostochka [Ko97] improved this slightly (in particular establishing an upper bound of $o(n!)$, for which Erdős awarded him the consolation prize of \$100), but the bound stood at $n^{(1+o(1))n}$ for a long time until Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang [ALWZ20] proved $f(n,k) < (Ck\log n \log\log n)^n$ for some constant $C > 1$. This was refined slightly, independently by Rao [Ra20], Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan, and Park [FKNP19], and Bell, Chueluecha, and Warnke [BCW21], leading to the current record $f(n,k) < (Ck\log n)^n$ for some constant $C > 1$. This proof was streamlined by Hu. A constant of $C = 64$ was achieved in the presentation by Stoeckl. In [Er81] Erdős offered \$1000 for a proof or disproof even just in the special case $k = 3$, which he expected "contains the whole difficulty"; he also wrote "I really do not see why this question is so difficult". The usual focus is the regime where $k = O(1)$ is fixed (say $k = 3$) and $n$ is large, although for the opposite regime Kostochka, Rödl, and Talysheva [KRT99] have shown $f(n,k) = (1 + O_n(k^{-1/2^n}))k^n$.
solved_when: A proof or disproof is given that $f(n,k) < c_k^n$ for some constant $c_k > 0$, even just in the special case $k = 3$. (Erdős offered \$1000 for this.)
why: Resolving the $k = 3$ case — which Erdős expected "contains the whole difficulty" — would settle one of his personally posed problems and close the long-standing gap between the current $(Ck\log n)^n$ bound and the conjectured exponential one.

title: Erdős problem #36
open: What is the optimal constant $c>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $N$, every balanced partition $A\sqcup B=\{1,\ldots,2N\}$ with $|A|=|B|=N$ admits some $x$ with at least $cN$ representations $a-b=x$, $a\in A$, $b\in B$?
status: This is the minimum overlap problem. The example (with $N$ even) $A=\{N/2+1,\ldots,3N/2\}$ shows that $c\leq 1/2$; indeed, Erdős initially conjectured that $c=1/2$. The lower bound $c\geq 1/4$ is trivial, and Scherk improved this to $1-1/\sqrt{2}=0.29\cdots$. The current records are $0.379005 < c < 0.380876$: the lower bound is due to White [Wh22] and the upper bound to the TTT-Discover LLM [YKLBMWKCZGS26], improving slightly on earlier bounds due to AlphaEvolve [GGTW25] and Haugland [Ha16]. The problem is discussed as problem C17 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: The exact value of the optimal constant $c$ is determined (equivalently, the gap between the current bounds $0.379005 < c < 0.380876$ is closed).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #82
open: Must every graph on $n$ vertices contain a regular induced subgraph whose order grows faster than $\log n$? Formally, if $F(n)$ is the largest integer such that every graph on $n$ vertices contains a regular induced subgraph on at least $F(n)$ vertices, prove that $F(n)/\log n\to\infty$.
status: Conjectured by Erdős, Fajtlowicz, and Stanton. It is known that $F(5)=3$ and $F(7)=4$. Ramsey's theorem implies $F(n)\gg \log n$. Bollobás observed $F(n)\ll n^{1/2+o(1)}$; Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov [AKS07] improved this to $n^{1/2}(\log n)^{O(1)}$; Dyson and McKay [DyMc26] further improved it to $F(n)\ll n^{1/2}$. In [Er93] Erdős asks whether, if $t(n)$ is the largest trivial (either empty or complete) subgraph which a graph on $n$ vertices must contain (so that $t(n)\gg \log n$ by Ramsey's theorem), then $F(n)-t(n)\to\infty$. Equivalently, defining $G(n)$ as the minimal $m$ such that every graph on $m$ vertices contains a regular induced subgraph on at least $n$ vertices, the problem asks whether $G(n)\leq 2^{o(n)}$. Fajtlowicz, McColgan, Reid, and Staton [FMRS95] showed $G(1)=1$, $G(2)=2$, $G(3)=5$, $G(4)=7$, and $G(5)\geq 12$. Boris Alexeev and Brendan McKay (see the comments and this site) have computed $G(5)=17$, $G(6)\geq 21$, and $G(7)\geq 29$. Dyson and McKay [DyMc26] have proved $G(7)\geq 30$, and $G(k)\geq \frac{9}{163}k^
solved_when: A proof that $F(n)/\log n\to\infty$ is exhibited; equivalently, in the Ramsey-style formulation where $G(n)$ is the least $m$ such that every graph on $m$ vertices contains a regular induced subgraph on at least $n$ vertices, a proof that $G(n)\leq 2^{o(n)}$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and asks whether regular induced subgraphs are quantitatively more unavoidable than the trivial (empty or complete) subgraphs forced by Ramsey's theorem.

title: Erdős problem #98
open: Let $h(n)$ be such that any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, with no three on a line and no four on a circle, determine at least $h(n)$ distinct distances. Does $h(n)/n\to \infty$?
status: Erdős could not even prove $h(n)\geq n$. Pach has shown $h(n)<n^{\log_2 3}$. Erdős, Füredi, and Pach [EFPR93] have improved this to $h(n) < n\exp(c\sqrt{\log n})$ for some constant $c>0$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $h(n)/n\to\infty$ for point sets in general position in this sense — no three collinear, no four cocircular — is given; in particular, settling whether $h(n)$ grows superlinearly in $n$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and it probes how far general-position assumptions alone can force many distinct distances.

title: Erdős problem #124
open: If $3\leq d_1<\cdots<d_r$ are integers with $\sum_{1\leq i\leq r}\frac{1}{d_r-1}\geq 1$, must all sufficiently large integers be expressible as $\sum_i c_ia_i$ with $c_i\in\{0,1\}$ and $a_i\in P(d_i,0)$, where $P(d,k)$ denotes the set of integers that are sums of distinct powers $d^i$ with $i\geq k$? More generally, if additionally $\mathrm{gcd}(d_1,\ldots,d_r)=1$, must all sufficiently large integers be expressible this way with $a_i\in P(d_i,k)$ for any $k\geq 1$?
status: The second question was conjectured by Burr, Erdős, Graham, and Li [BEGL96], who proved it for $\{3,4,7\}$. The first question was asked separately by Erdős in [Er97] and [Er97e] (with some ambiguity over whether he intended $P(d,0)$ or $P(d,1)$; he certainly mentions no gcd condition). A simple positive proof of the first question was provided (and formalised in Lean) by Aristotle thanks to Alexeev; see the comments for details. In [BEGL96] they record that Pomerance observed the condition $\sum 1/(d_i-1)\geq 1$ is necessary (for both questions), but give no details; Tao has sketched an explanation in the comments. That $\mathrm{gcd}(d_1,\ldots,d_r)=1$ is a necessary condition in the second question is trivial. Melfi [Me04] gives a construction, for any $\epsilon>0$, of an infinite set of $d_i$ with $\sum_i \frac{1}{d_i-1}<\epsilon$ for which every sufficiently large integer is a finite sum $\sum_i c_ia_i$ with $c_i\in\{0,1\}$ and $a_i\in P(d_i,0)$. See also [125].
solved_when: For every $d\geq 1$, $k\geq 0$, and every tuple $3\leq d_1<\cdots<d_r$ satisfying the stated conditions, it is proved that all sufficiently large integers admit a representation $\sum_i c_ia_i$ with $c_i\in\{0,1\}$ and $a_i\in P(d_i,k)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; settling it determines exactly when collections of base-$d$ digit sequences combine to form complete additive sequences.
aliases: Erdős #124; number theory / base representations / complete sequences

title: Erdős problem #129
open: In an $r$-colouring of the edges of a large complete graph, must there always be a set of $n$ vertices that avoids a monochromatic triangle in at least one colour sooner than exponentially in $\sqrt{n}$? Formally, with $R(n;k,r)$ the smallest $N$ such that every $r$-colouring of $K_N$ contains an $n$-vertex set with no $K_k$ in at least one colour, is there a constant $C = C(r) > 1$ with $R(n;3,r) < C^{\sqrt{n}}$?
status: Conjectured by Erdős and Gyárfás, who proved the existence of some $C>1$ such that $R(n;3,r)>C^{\sqrt{n}}$. When $r=k=2$ this recovers the classic Ramsey numbers. Erdős thought it likely that for all $r,k\geq 2$ there exist $C_1,C_2>1$ (depending only on $r$) such that $C_1^{n^{1/k-1}}< R(n;k,r) < C_2^{n^{1/k-1}}$. Antonio Girao has pointed out that the problem as written is easily disproved: $R(n;3,2) \geq C^{n}$, since a random red/blue colouring of $K_N$ yields, for $N \leq C^n$ with $C>1$ absolute, that every set of $n$ vertices contains a red triangle and a blue triangle (using that every $n$-vertex set contains $\gg n^2$ edge-disjoint triangles). Perhaps Erdős had a different problem in mind, but it is not clear what; presumably one where the natural probabilistic argument delivers a bound like $C^{\sqrt{n}}$, as Erdős and Gyárfás claim to have achieved via the probabilistic method.
solved_when: A proof that $R(n;3,r) < C^{\sqrt{n}}$ for some constant $C = C(r) > 1$; alternatively, a determination of what problem Erdős actually intended, if this statement is not it.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with its full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, and resolving the discrepancy between the stated conjecture and the easy counterexample would clarify what question Erdős meant to ask.

title: Erdős problem #142
open: Is there an asymptotic formula for $r_k(N)$, the largest size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ containing no non-trivial $k$-term arithmetic progression? That is, can one determine $r_k(N)$ up to $1+o(1)$ as $N\to\infty$?
status: Erdős remarked this is 'probably unattackable at present'. In [Er97c] Erdős offered $1000, but given that he elsewhere offered $5000 just for (essentially) showing that $r_k(N)=o_k(N/\log N)$ (see [3]), that value seems odd; in [Er81] he offers $10000, stating it is 'probably enormously difficult'. The best known upper bounds for $r_k(N)$ are due to Kelley and Meka [KeMe23] for $k=3$, Green and Tao [GrTa17] for $k=4$, and Leng, Sah, and Sawhney [LSS24] for $k\geq 5$. An asymptotic formula is still far out of reach, even for $k=3$. In [Er80] and [Va99] he asks (much more reasonably) for the order of magnitude of $r_k(N)$, and in [Er80] he remarks that we do not even know whether $r_k(n)/r_{k+1}(n)\to 0$ for any $k\geq 3$. See also [3] and [139].
solved_when: An asymptotic formula for $r_k(N)$ is proved, even for a single fixed $k\geq 3$; the natural quantitative target is $r_k(N) = (c_k + o(1))N$ or an equivalent $1+o(1)$ determination for fixed $k$ as $N\to\infty$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying a $10000 prize; it represents the ultimate goal in the study of progression-free sets, beyond which even the order of magnitude of $r_k(N)$ is currently unknown.

title: Erdős problem #167
open: If a graph contains at most $k$ pairwise edge-disjoint triangles, can it always be made triangle-free by deleting at most $2k$ edges?
status: This is a problem of Tuza (per erdosproblems.com/167; Erdős references: [Er88] [Ha99]). Trivially, $G$ can be made triangle-free after removing at most $3k$ edges, and the examples of $K_4$ and $K_5$ show that $2k$ would be best possible. Haxell [Ha99] improved the trivial $\leq 3k$ bound to $\leq (3-\frac{3}{23}+o(1))k$, and Kahn and Park [KaPa22] proved the conjecture for random graphs.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that every graph with at most $k$ edge-disjoint triangles has a triangle-free subgraph obtained by removing at most $2k$ edges.
why: It is a personally posed problem of Erdős, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolves the optimal constant in a natural covering-versus-packing question for triangles.

title: Erdős problem #177
open: How small can we force the discrepancy of the two-coloring of the natural numbers when we measure it along arithmetic progressions of a fixed common difference? Formally, find the smallest function $h(d)$ such that there exists $f:\mathbb{N}\to\{-1,1\}$ with $\max_{P_d}\left\lvert \sum_{n\in P_d}f(n)\right\rvert\leq h(d)$ for every $d\geq 1$, where $P_d$ ranges over all finite arithmetic progressions with common difference $d$.
status: Cantor, Erdős, Schreiber, and Straus [Er66] proved that $h(d)\ll d!$ is possible. Van der Waerden's theorem implies that $h(d)\to \infty$. Beck [Be17] has shown that $h(d) \leq d^{8+\epsilon}$ is possible for every $\epsilon>0$. Roth's famous discrepancy lower bound [Ro64] implies that $h(d)\gg d^{1/2}$.
solved_when: The optimal order of $h(d)$ is determined, closing the gap between the known lower bound $h(d)\gg d^{1/2}$ and upper bound $h(d)\leq d^{8+\epsilon}$ for every $\epsilon>0$.

title: Erdős problem #398
open: Are the only solutions to $n! = x^2 - 1$ the ones with $n = 4, 5, 7$?
status: Erdős and Graham describe this old conjecture as 'almost certainly true but it is intractable at present'. Overholt [Ov93] showed that it has only finitely many solutions assuming a weak form of the ABC conjecture. There are no other solutions below $10^9$ (see the OEIS page). Naciri [Na25] proved that there are only finitely many solutions if $x \pm 1$ is either $k$-free (for some $k \geq 2$) or a prime power (Cambie explains both facts in the comments), and that if $x \pm 1$ is $7$-free then $n = 4, 5, 7$ give the only solutions.
solved_when: It is proved that $n = 4, 5, 7$ are the only values of $n$ for which $n! + 1$ is a perfect square.
why: This is the Brocard–Ramanujan conjecture, one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/398.

title: Erdős problem #416
open: Does the counting function $V(x)$ for values of Euler's totient function satisfy $V(2x)/V(x)\to 2$, and does it admit a full asymptotic formula?
status: Pillai [Pi29] proved $V(x)=o(x)$. Erdős [Er35b] proved $V(x)=x(\log x)^{-1+o(1)}$. Maier and Pomerance [MaPo88] proved $V(x)=\frac{x}{\log x}e^{(C+o(1))(\log\log\log x)^2}$ for some explicit constant $C>0$. Ford [Fo98] improved this to $V(x)\asymp\frac{x}{\log x}e^{C_1(\log\log\log x-\log\log\log\log x)^2+C_2\log\log\log x-C_3\log\log\log\log x}$ for some explicit constants $C_1,C_2,C_3>0$. This falls just short of an asymptotic formula for $V(x)$ and of determining whether $V(2x)/V(x)\to 2$. In [Er79e] Erdős asks further to estimate the number of $n\leq x$ such that the smallest solution to $\phi(m)=n$ satisfies $kx<m\leq (k+1)x$. See also [417] and [821]. This is discussed in problem B36 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: An asymptotic formula for $V(x)$ is established, which in particular settles whether $V(2x)/V(x)\to 2$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and completing the known sharp estimates to a true asymptotic would settle the remaining fine structure of how totient values are distributed.

title: Erdős problem #423
open: Understand the asymptotic behaviour of the Hofstadter–Ulam-type sequence defined by $a_1=1$, $a_2=2$, and, for $k\geq 3$, letting $a_k$ be the least integer greater than $a_{k-1}$ that is a sum of at least two consecutive terms of the sequence. In particular, is it true that $a_n=n+o(n)$?
status: The problem was asked by Hofstadter (in [Er77c] Erdős says Hofstadter was inspired by a similar question of Ulam). The sequence begins $[1,2,3,5,6,8,10,11,\ldots]$ and is A005243 in the OEIS. Bolan and Tang [Ta26] have independently proved that infinitely many integers do not appear in the sequence; in fact, $a_n-n$ is nondecreasing and unbounded. Tang [Ta26] proved $a_n \ll n^{\frac{1}{c-1}+o(1)}$, where $c$ is any exponent such that $|A-A|\geq |A|^{c-o(1)}$ for all convex sets $A$. The bounds of Cushman [Cu25] yield $a_n \ll n^{\frac{688}{413}+o(1)} \leq n^{1.6659+o(1)}$, and the conjecture of Erdős and Hegyvári that one can take $c=2$ would imply $a_n \leq n^{1+o(1)}$. Tang further proved the improved lower bound $a_n = n+\Omega(\log\log n)$.
solved_when: A determination of the asymptotic behaviour of $a_n$; the conjectured truth is $a_n=n+o(n)$.
why: A solution would resolve one of Erdős's personally posed problems, revealing how sparse the representable-by-consecutive-sums sequence really is; progress is tied directly to the convex set difference problem, where $c=2$ would yield $a_n\leq n^{1+o(1)}$.

title: Erdős problem #451
open: How large must $n_k$ be — the smallest integer greater than $2k$ such that $\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n_k-i)$ has no prime factor in $(k,2k)$ — as a function of $k$?
status: Erdős and Graham write 'we can prove $n_k>k^{1+c}$ but no doubt much more is true'. In [Er79d] Erdős writes that probably $n_k<e^{o(k)}$ but $n_k>k^d$ for all constant $d$. Adenwalla observes that an easy upper bound is $n_k\leq \prod_{k<p<2k}p=e^{O(k)}$. van Doorn and Tang [vDTa26] (using an argument generated by GPT 5.5 Pro and Tang) have proved that $n_k> \exp\left(c\frac{(\log k)^2}{\log\log k}\right)$ for some constant $c>0$. See also [1095].
solved_when: Asymptotic control of $n_k$ is achieved, e.g. matching the conjectured behavior that $n_k < e^{o(k)}$ while $n_k > k^d$ for every constant $d$; any proof establishing or refuting these bounds, or closing the gap between the lower bound $\exp(c(\log k)^2/\log\log k)$ and the upper bound $e^{O(k)}$, counts.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, and its resolution would determine sharp growth for a natural primality avoidance condition.

title: Erdős problem #467
open: Can every large interval of integers be "covered from both sides" by residue classes at the primes up to $x$? Formally: prove that for all large $x$ there exist a choice of congruence classes $a_p$ for all primes $p\leq x$ and a decomposition $\{p\leq x\}=A\sqcup B$ into two non-empty sets such that, for all $n<x$, there exist $p\in A$ and $q\in B$ with $n\equiv a_p\pmod{p}$ and $n\equiv a_q\pmod{q}$.
status: The problem sits in number theory, and this formulation is a reconstruction: the presentation in [ErGr80] is missing some crucial quantifiers, so the intended statement may have been misinterpreted.
solved_when: The statement above is proved: for all sufficiently large $x$, such congruence classes $a_p$ and such a splitting $A\sqcup B$ (both non-empty) exist with every $n<x$ covered by at least one prime from each part.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and resolving it would settle a question whose full history is tracked at erdosproblems.com/467.

title: Erdős problem #483
open: Let $f(k)$ be the minimal $N$ such that any $k$-colouring of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ forces a monochromatic solution to $a+b=c$. How fast does $f(k)$ grow — in particular, is $f(k) < c^k$ for some constant $c>0$?
status: The values of $f(k)$ are the Schur numbers. The best-known bounds for large $k$ are $(380)^{k/5}-O(1)\leq f(k) \leq (e-\tfrac{1}{6}) k!$; note $380^{1/5}\approx 3.2806$. The lower bound is due to Ageron, Casteras, Pellerin, Portella, Rimmel, and Tomasik [ACPPRT21], improving previous bounds of Exoo [Ex94] and Fredricksen and Sweet [FrSw00]. The upper bound is due to Xu, Xie, and Chen [XXC02], improving previous bounds of Wan [Wa97] and Whitehead [Wh73]; see Eliahou [El20] for more on the upper bound. The known values are $f(1)=2$, $f(2)=5$, $f(3)=14$, $f(4)=45$, and $f(5)=161$ (see A030126), with $f(5)=161$ established by Heule [He17]. See also [183], where a folklore observation gives $f(k)\leq R(3;k)-1$.
solved_when: The growth rate of $f(k)$ is determined, or at least it is shown that $f(k) < c^k$ for some constant $c>0$ (or refuted).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems on Schur numbers, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle the basic asymptotic behaviour of one of the classical quantities of Ramsey-theoretic additive combinatorics.
aliases: Erdős #483; number theory / additive combinatorics / ramsey theory

title: Erdős problem #507
open: How small must the smallest triangle determined by three of $n$ points in the unit disk be? Formally, if $\alpha(n)$ is the largest value such that every $n$-point set in the unit disk contains three points forming a triangle of area at most $\alpha(n)$, estimate $\alpha(n)$ as a function of $n$.
status: This is a geometric form of Heilbronn's triangle problem. Trivially $\alpha(n) \ll 1/n$, and Erdős observed $\alpha(n)\gg 1/n^2$. The current best bounds are $\frac{\log n}{n^2}\ll \alpha(n) \ll \frac{1}{n^{7/6+o(1)}}$. The lower bound is due to Komlós, Pintz, and Szemerédi [KPS82]. The upper bound is due to Cohen, Pohoata, and Zakharov [CPZ24], improving on their earlier work [CPZ23], which itself improved an exponent of $8/7$ due to Komlós, Pintz, and Szemerédi [KPS81].
solved_when: The order of $\alpha(n)$ is determined up to constants: matching upper and lower bounds, closing the gap between the current lower bound $\log n/n^2$ and upper bound $1/n^{7/6+o(1)}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (Problem 77 on Green's open problems list), and settling it would resolve the long-standing gap in the planar Heilbronn triangle problem for the disk.

title: Erdős problem #539
open: How small can the set of "reduced ratios" from an $n$-element set of natural numbers be? Formally, let $h(n)$ be the largest integer such that $\left\{ \frac{a}{(a,b)} : a,b\in A\right\}$ has size at least $h(n)$ for every $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ of size $n$; estimate $h(n)$.
status: Erdős and Szemerédi proved $n^{1/2}\ll h(n)\ll n^{1-c}$ for some constant $c>0$, and Freiman and Lev improved the upper bound to $h(n)\ll n^{2/3}$. Granville and Roesler [GrRo99] give proofs of these bounds and reformulate the problem in combinatorial geometry: given $A\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^d$ of size $n$, bound the minimum size of $\{\delta(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}) : \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\in A\}$, where $\delta(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$ has $i$th coordinate $\max(0, a_i-b_i)$; using this formulation they obtained improved lower bounds in fixed small dimension $d$.
