Building on the same reformulation, ProofCouncil proved $h(n)\leq e^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}n^{1/2}$, and hence $h(n)=n^{1/2+o(1)}$.
solved_when: The asymptotic order of $h(n)$ is determined, with matching lower and upper bounds. The current best bounds range from $h(n)\gg n^{1/2}$ to $h(n)\ll n^{2/3}$, and the record shows $h(n)\leq e^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}n^{1/2}$ has been claimed, which would give $h(n)=n^{1/2+o(1)}$; a solution pins down the exact exponent (ideally $h(n)=n^{1/2+o(1)}$ with matching lower bound).
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; determining the answer resolves a natural multiplicative-analog question about how much structure a set loses under pairwise reduction.

title: Erdős problem #544
open: Do consecutive diagonal Ramsey numbers with a triangle eventually drift apart — specifically, does $R(3,k+1)-R(3,k)\to\infty$ as $k\to\infty$? More sharply, is $R(3,k+1)-R(3,k)=o(k)$, or can the gaps be a positive proportion of $k$?
status: A problem of Erdős and Sós. It is known (see [165]) that $R(3,k)\asymp \frac{k^2}{\log k}$. The OpenAI bound of [1014] implies $R(3,k+1)-R(3,k)\ll k^{-c}R(3,k)$ for some constant $c>0$. This problem is #8 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection. See also [165] and [1014].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $R(3,k+1)-R(3,k)\to\infty$, and a resolution of whether $R(3,k+1)-R(3,k)=o(k)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems (with Sós), tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would reveal how smoothly the Ramsey function $R(3,k)$ grows across consecutive values.

title: Erdős problem #554
open: Is a monochromatic odd cycle easier to force than a monochromatic triangle, as the number of colours grows? Formally, show that $\lim_{k\to\infty} R_k(C_{2n+1})/R_k(K_3) = 0$ for every $n\geq 2$.
status: A problem of Erdős and Graham; open even for $n=2$. Schur [Sc16] proved $C^k \ll R_k(K_3) \ll k!$ for some constant $C>0$, and Erdős conjectured (see [183]) that $R_k(K_3) \leq C^k$ for some constant $C>0$. Bondy and Erdős [BoEr73] and Erdős and Graham [ErGr75] proved $n2^k+1 \leq R_k(C_{2n+1}) \leq 2n(k+2)!$; the lower bound is sharp for fixed $k$ and large enough $n$, as shown by Jenssen and Skokan [JeSk21]. Day and Johnson [DaJo17] proved that, for fixed $n$, $R_k(C_{2n+1}) \geq 2n(2+c_n)^{k-1}$ for all large $k$, for some constant $c_n>0$. Axenovich, Cames van Batenburg, Janzer, Michel, and Rundström [ACJMR25] improved the upper bound to $R_k(C_{2n+1}) \leq (4n-2)^k k^{k/n}+1$; in particular, there exists an absolute constant $c>0$ such that $R_k(C_{2n+1}) \leq (Cn)^k k!^{1/n}$. The problem is #23 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
solved_when: For each fixed $n\geq 2$, it is proved that $\lim_{k\to\infty} R_k(C_{2n+1})/R_k(K_3) = 0$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and resolving it would clarify the asymptotic separation between odd-cycle and triangle Ramsey numbers in the multicolour setting.

title: Erdős problem #580
open: If a graph on $n$ vertices has at least $n/2$ vertices of degree at least $n/2$, must it contain every tree on at most $n/2$ vertices? This is the Loebl–Komlós–Sós-type conjecture of Erdős, Füredi, Loebl, and Sós, and the question is whether the conjecture holds exactly, for all $n$, in the original unrelaxed form.
status: A conjecture of Erdős, Füredi, Loebl, and Sós. Ajtai, Komlós, and Szemerédi [AKS95] proved an asymptotic version, where at least $(1+\epsilon)n/2$ vertices have degree at least $(1+\epsilon)n/2$ and $n$ is sufficiently large depending on $\epsilon$. Zhao [Zh11] proved the conjecture holds for all sufficiently large $n$. Komlós and Sós conjectured the generalisation that if at least $n/2$ vertices have degree at least $k$, then $G$ contains any tree with $k$ vertices. See also the entry in the graphs problem collection (erdosproblems.com/580).
solved_when: Every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with at least $n/2$ vertices of degree at least $n/2$ is shown to contain every tree on at most $n/2$ vertices (with no $\epsilon$-relaxation and no lower bound on $n$).
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and settles the exact threshold case of a degree condition forcing universal tree containment.

title: Erdős problem #670
open: Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a set of $n$ points such that all pairwise distances differ by at least $1$. Is the diameter of $A$ at least $(1+o(1))n^2$?
status: The lower bound of $\binom{n}{2}$ for the diameter is trivial. Erdős [Er97f, p.6] proved the claim when $d=1$. The quantifiers are slightly ambiguous, but likely Erdős had in mind the regime where $d$ is fixed and the $o(1)$ term $\to 0$ as $n\to \infty$ (perhaps at a rate which depends on $d$). In the regime where $n$ grows with $d$, the claim was disproved by Ho [Ho26]: there exist infinitely many $n$ and, with $d=n^2-n$, a set $A\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ such that all pairwise distances differ by at least $1$, with diameter at most $\left(1-\frac{1}{\pi^2}+o(1)\right)n^2\approx 0.898n^2$.
solved_when: The answer is affirmative (with quantifiers as stated, in the regime where $d$ is fixed and the $o(1)$ term $\to 0$ as $n\to \infty$) or a matching counterexample is constructed, improving on the known diameter bound of $\left(1-\frac{1}{\pi^2}+o(1)\right)n^2\approx 0.898n^2$ in the regime where $n$ grows with $d$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com/670; resolving it settles whether the trivial $\binom{n}{2}$ lower bound on the diameter is asymptotically tight for separated distance sets.

title: Erdős problem #687
open: How far can a fixed choice of one residue class $a_p \pmod{p}$ for every prime $p\leq x$ cover the initial interval of integers? Formally, if $Y(x)$ is the maximal $y$ such that every integer in $[1,y]$ is congruent to at least one of the $a_p \pmod{p}$, give good estimates for $Y(x)$ — in particular, can one prove $Y(x)=o(x^2)$, or even $Y(x)\ll x^{1+o(1)}$?
status: This function (associated with Jacobsthal) is closely related to the problem of gaps between primes (see [4]). The best known upper bound is due to Iwaniec [Iw78], $Y(x) \ll x^2$. The best lower bound is $Y(x) \gg \frac{\log x}{\log\log\log x}x$, improving on a previous bound of Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard, and Tao [FGKMT18]. Maier and Pomerance have conjectured that $Y(x)\ll x(\log x)^{2+o(1)}$. In [Er80] Erdős writes "It is not clear who first formulated this problem - probably many of us did it independently. I offer the maximum of \$1000 dollars and $1/2$ my total savings for clearing up of this problem." In [Er80] Erdős also asks about a weaker variant in which all except $o(y/\log y)$ of the integers in $[1,y]$ are congruent to at least one of the $a_p \pmod{p}$, and in particular asks if the answer is very different. See also [688] and [689]. A more general Jacobsthal function is the focus of [970].
solved_when: Good estimates for $Y(x)$ are obtained; specifically, an upper bound of the form $Y(x)=o(x^2)$ or, at the strongest, $Y(x)\ll x^{1+o(1)}$.
why: This Jacobsthal-type function is closely related to gaps between primes, and settling it addresses one of Erdős's personally posed problems, carrying his $1000 prize and tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #709
open: How large must an interval be to guarantee it contains, for any $n$-element set $A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\subseteq [2,\infty)\cap\mathbb{N}$, a system of distinct integers $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ with $a_i\mid x_i$? More precisely, letting $f(n)$ be the least number such that every interval of $f(n)\max(A)$ consecutive integers works, obtain good bounds for $f(n)$ — ideally an asymptotic formula.
status: The problem originates with Erdős and Surányi [ErSu59], who proved $(\log n)^c \ll f(n) \ll n^{1/2}$ for some constant $c>0$. The lower bound can be improved, using van Doorn's lower bound for [711] from [vD26], to $\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\ll f(n)$. See also [708].
solved_when: Sharp bounds (or an asymptotic formula) for $f(n)$ are established, improving on the current knowledge that $\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\ll f(n)\ll n^{1/2}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; settling it resolves a natural quantitative question in divisibility and covering behavior of integer intervals.

title: Erdős problem #711
open: Can one always find, in a short interval $(m, m+f)$, distinct integers $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ with $k \mid a_k$ for each $1 \le k \le n$, with $f$ barely larger than $n$? Formally, for $f(n,m)$ the minimal such value, prove that $\max_m f(n,m) \le n^{1+o(1)}$, and that $\max_m (f(n,m) - f(n,n)) \to \infty$.
status: A problem of Erdős and Pomerance [ErPo80], who proved that $\max_m f(n,m) \ll n^{3/2}$ and $n(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n})^{1/2} \ll f(n,n) \ll n(\log n)^{1/2}$. In [Er92c] Erdős offered 1000 rupees for a proof of either; for uniform comparison across prizes this has been converted using 1992 exchange rates. van Doorn [vD26] has provided an affirmative answer to the second question, proving that, for all large $n$, there exists $m = m(n)$ such that $f(n,m) - f(n,n) \gg \frac{\log n}{\log\log n} n$. See also [710].
solved_when: A proof is given that $\max_m f(n,m) \le n^{1+o(1)}$, or that $\max_m (f(n,m) - f(n,n)) \to \infty$; Erdős offered a prize (1000 rupees, converted to $78) for a proof of either statement.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #742
open: Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices with diameter $2$ such that deleting any edge increases the diameter. Is it true that $G$ has at most $n^2/4$ edges?
status: This is a conjecture of Murty and Plesnik (see [CaHa79]), though Füredi credits the conjecture to Murty and Simon, and further mentions that Erdős told him the conjecture goes back to Ore in the 1960s. It is true for sufficiently large $n$, proved by Füredi [Fu92]. Key works: erdosproblems.com/742; Erdős references: [Er81] [Fu92].
solved_when: A proof (for sufficiently large $n$) that every diameter-$2$ edge-critical graph on $n$ vertices has at most $n^2/4$ edges; the complete bipartite graph shows this bound would be best possible.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com.

title: Erdős problem #811
open: For which graphs $G$ does every balanced edge-colouring of $K_n$ (with $m=e(G)$ colours, every vertex seeing exactly $\lfloor n/m\rfloor$ edges of each colour, and $n\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ large) necessarily contain a rainbow copy of $G$? In particular, must any balanced 6-colouring of $K_{6n+1}$ contain a rainbow $C_6$ and a rainbow $K_4$?
status: In [Er91] Erdős credits this problem to himself, Pyber, and Tuza; it was explored by Erdős and Tuza [ErTu93]. In [Er96] Erdős seems to suggest this might be true for every graph $G$, and specifically asks (as in [Er91] and [Er96]) whether any balanced edge-colouring of $K_{6n+1}$ by $6$ colours must contain a rainbow $C_6$ and $K_4$. Quantitatively, defining $d_G(n)$ as the minimal value (if it exists) such that for large $n$, any colouring of $K_n$ with $e(G)$ colours whose every colour class has minimum degree $\geq d_G(n)$ contains a rainbow $G$, Erdős and Tuza [ErTu93] proved $\lfloor n/6\rfloor \leq d_{C_4}(n) \leq \left(\frac{1}{4}-c\right)n$ for some constant $c>0$. Axenovich and Clemen [AxCl24] proved that infinitely many graphs lack this property: for any odd $\ell \geq 3$ and $m=\lfloor \sqrt{\ell}+3.5\rfloor$ there exist arbitrarily large $n$ such that $K_n$ has a balanced edge-colouring using $\ell$ colours with no rainbow $K_m$; they conjecture that $K_m$ lacks this property (record truncated). Key references: erdosproblems.com/811; [Er91] [Er93,p.346] [Er96] [ErTu93] [AxCl24].
solved_when: A characterization is given of the graphs $G$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n\equiv 1\pmod{e(G)}$, every balanced edge-colouring of $K_n$ with $e(G)$ colours contains a rainbow copy of $G$ — including resolution of the specific challenge of rainbow $C_6$ and $K_4$ in any balanced 6-colouring of $K_{6n+1}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com, and its resolution would settle a natural local-uniformity analogue of Ramsey theory for which counterexamples are already known to exist for some graphs.

title: Erdős problem #931
open: Are there only finitely many pairs of blocks of consecutive integers — one of length $k_1$ starting after $n_1$, one of length $k_2$ starting after $n_2$, with $k_1\geq k_2\geq 3$ and $n_2\geq n_1+k_1$ — such that the products $\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(n_1+i)$ and $\prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2}(n_2+j)$ have exactly the same prime factors?
status: In number theory, Tijdeman gave the example $19,20,21,22$ and $54,55,56,57$. Erdős [Er76d] was unsure of the conjecture and thought perhaps that if the two products have the same prime factors then $n_2>2(n_1+k_1)$; he may have intended to permit finitely many counterexamples. Without that caveat the statement is false: AlphaProof found the counterexample $10! = 2^8\cdot 3^4\cdot 5^2\cdot 7$ and $14\cdot 15\cdot 16 = 2^5\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7$, with $n_1=0$, $k_1=10$, $n_2=13$, and $k_2=3$. The problem is discussed as B35 in Guy's collection [Gu04]; see also [388].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that, for all $k_1\geq k_2\geq 3$, only finitely many $n_2\geq n_1+k_1$ admit such a pair of products with identical sets of prime factors — possibly after allowing finitely many counterexamples, per the variant Erdős may have intended.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and a resolution would settle a long-standing question about the multiplicative structure of consecutive integers.

title: Erdős problem #1016
open: How many extra edges beyond $n$ are needed to force a graph on $n$ vertices to contain a cycle of every length from $3$ to $n$? Formally, letting $h(n)$ be the minimal such excess, is it true that $h(n) \geq \log_2 n + \log_* n - O(1)$, where $\log_* n$ is the iterated logarithmic function?
status: Such graphs are called pancyclic. The problem originates with Bondy [Bo71], who claimed (without details) a proof of $\log_2(n-1)-1 \leq h(n) \leq \log_2 n + \log_* n + O(1)$. Erdős [Er71] believed the upper bound is closer to the truth but could not even prove $h(n) - \log_2 n \to \infty$. A proof of the lower bound is provided by Griffin [Gr13]. The first published proof of the upper bound appears in Chapter 4.5 of George, Khodkar, and Wallis [GKW16].
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the lower bound $h(n) \geq \log_2 n + \log_* n - O(1)$; more broadly, a determination of $h(n)$ up to $O(1)$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, with full history tracked at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle the exact edge cost of pancyclicity, a quantity first estimated by Bondy.

title: Erdős problem #1060
open: Let $f(n)$ count the number of solutions to $k\sigma(k)=n$, where $\sigma(k)$ is the sum of divisors of $k$. Is it true that $f(n)\leq n^{o(\frac{1}{\log\log n})}$, or perhaps even that $f(n)\leq (\log n)^{O(1)}$?
status: This is discussed in problem B11 of Guy's collection [Gu04], and is tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com/1060. It remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the bound $f(n)\leq n^{o(\frac{1}{\log\log n})}$ is given; the stronger target is $f(n)\leq (\log n)^{O(1)}$.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, and a solution would settle how often the map $k \mapsto k\sigma(k)$ can collide.

title: Erdős problem #1063
open: Let $k\geq 2$ and define $n_k\geq 2k$ to be the least value of $n$ such that $n-i$ divides $\binom{n}{k}$ for all but one $0\leq i<k$. Estimate $n_k$.
status: A problem of Erdős and Selfridge posed in [ErSe83]. Erdős and Selfridge noted (and a proof can be found in [Mo85]) that if $n\geq 2k$ then there must exist at least one $0\leq i<k$ such that $n-i$ does not divide $\binom{n}{k}$. The known initial values are $n_2=4$, $n_3=6$, $n_4=9$, and $n_5=12$. Monier [Mo85] observed that $n_k\leq k!$ for $k\geq 3$, since $\binom{k!}{k}$ is divisible by $k!-i$ for $1\leq i<k$. Cambie observes in the comments that this can be improved to $n_k\leq k[2,3,\ldots,k-1]\leq e^{(1+o(1))k}$, where $[\cdots]$ is the least common multiple. The problem is discussed as B31 in Guy's collection [Gu04].
solved_when: An asymptotic estimate of $n_k$ is obtained — in particular, an improvement beyond the current bound $n_k\leq k[2,3,\ldots,k-1]\leq e^{(1+o(1))k}$ (and the earlier $n_k\leq k!$ for $k\geq 3$), ideally matching the true growth of $n_k$.
why: It is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com, and resolving it advances the study of divisibility properties of binomial coefficients, a core theme in combinatorial number theory.

title: Erdős problem #1083
open: How few distinct distances can a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d\geq 3$) be forced to determine? If $f_d(n)$ denotes this minimum, is it true that $f_d(n)=n^{\frac{2}{d}-o(1)}$, matching the lattice construction up to subpolynomial factors?
status: Erdős [Er46b] proved $n^{1/d}\ll_d f_d(n)\ll_d n^{2/d}$, the upper bound coming from lattice points. Clarkson, Edelsbrunner, Gubias, Sharir, and Welzl [CEGSW90] proved $f_3(n)\gg n^{1/2}$. Aronov, Pach, Sharir, and Tardos [APST04] proved $f_d(n)\gg n^{\frac{1}{d-90/77}-o(1)}$ for any $d\geq 3$ (e.g. $f_3(n)\gg n^{0.546}$). Solymosi and Vu [SoVu08] proved $f_3(n)\gg n^{3/5}$ and $f_d(n)\gg_d n^{\frac{2}{d}-\frac{c}{d^2}}$ for all $d\geq 4$ for some constant $c>0$ (their $d=3$ result is slightly weaker as stated, but combined as a black box with the later Guth–Katz bound for [89] it yields the recorded consequence). The function $f_d(n)$ is essentially the inverse of $g_d(n)$ from [1089] — with these definitions, $g_d(n)>m$ iff $f_d(m)<n$ — but the emphasis here is on fixed $d$ as $n\to\infty$.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) that $f_d(n)=n^{\frac{2}{d}-o(1)}$ for fixed $d\geq 3$; equivalently, lower bounds matching Erdős's $n^{2/d}$ upper bound up to $n^{o(1)}$ factors.
why: This is the natural higher-dimensional generalisation of the distinct distances problem, resolving the gap between the known lower bounds and the lattice upper bound and completing Erdős's personally posed question.

title: Erdős problem #1085
open: How many pairs of points at distance exactly 1 can occur among $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and how small can the maximum be? Formally, letting $f_d(n)$ denote the minimal number such that some set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ has at most $f_d(n)$ unit-distance pairs, estimate $f_d(n)$.
status: The most difficult cases are $d=2$ and $d=3$. For $d=2$ the problem is the unit distance problem [90], with best known bounds $n^{1+c} < f_2(n) \ll n^{4/3}$ for some small constant $c>0$: the lower bound is due to an internal model at OpenAI, at least for infinitely many $n$ (see [90]), and the upper bound to Spencer, Szemerédi, and Trotter [SST84]. For $d=3$ the best bounds are $n^{4/3}\log\log n \ll f_3(n) \ll n^{3/2}\beta(n)$, where $\beta(n)$ is a very slowly growing function; the lower bound is due to Erdős [Er60b] and the upper bound to Clarkson, Edelsbrunner, Guibas, Sharir, and Welzl [CEGSW90]. For $d\geq 4$, a construction of Lenz (taking points on orthogonal circles) gives $f_d(n)\geq \frac{p-1}{2p}n^2-O(1)$ with $p=\lfloor d/2\rfloor$, and Erdős [Er60b] showed the Erdős–Stone theorem implies $f_d(n) \leq (\frac{p-1}{2p}+o(1))n^2$. Erdős [Er67e] determined $f_d(n)$ up to $O(1)$ for all even $d\geq 4$; Brass [Br97] determined $f_4(n)$ exactly; Swanepoel [Sw09] determined $f_d(n)$ exactly for even $d\geq 6$. For odd $d\geq 5$, Erdős and Pach [ErPa90] proved there exist constants $c_1(d),c_2(d)>0$ such that $\frac{p-1}{2p}n^2 + c_1 n^{4/3} \leq f_d(n)$ (record as given is truncated at this point). Key references: erdosproblems.com/1085; Erdős references: [Er75f,p.103].
solved_when: Asymptotically tight bounds (up to constants, or exact where the record indicates exact determination is the goal) on $f_d(n)$ are obtained — in particular closing the gaps between $n^{1+c} \ll f_2(n) \ll n^{4/3}$ for $d=2$ and between $n^{4/3}\log\log n \ll f_3(n) \ll n^{3/2}\beta(n)$ for $d=3$, with $c>0$ a small constant.

title: Erdős problem #1104
open: How large can the chromatic number of a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices be? Formally, if $f(n)$ is the maximum chromatic number of a triangle-free graph on $n$ vertices, determine its order of growth.
status: The best bounds available are $(1-o(1))(n/\log n)^{1/2} \leq f(n) \leq (2+o(1))(n/\log n)^{1/2}$. The upper bound is due to Davies and Illingworth [DaIl22]; the lower bound follows from a construction of Hefty, Horn, King, and Pfender [HHKP25]. One can ask a similar question for the maximum possible chromatic number of a triangle-free graph on $m$ edges, denoted $g(m)$. Davies and Illingworth [DaIl22] prove $g(m) \leq (3^{5/3}+o(1))\left(\frac{m}{(\log m)^2}\right)^{1/3}$, while Kim [Ki95] gave a construction implying $g(m) \gg (m/(\log m)^2)^{1/3}$. The function $f(n)$ is the inverse to the function $h_3(k)$ considered in [1013], and a generalisation of $f(n)$ is considered in [920].
solved_when: The asymptotic behavior of $f(n)$ is determined up to the leading constant — ideally matching upper and lower bounds, and at minimum closing the gap between the current $(1-o(1))(n/\log n)^{1/2}$ lower and $(2+o(1))(n/\log n)^{1/2}$ upper bounds.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, tracked with full history at erdosproblems.com; resolving it would settle a classic extremal question about how sparse graphs can still force high chromatic number.

title: Erdős problem #1163
open: Can one give a statistical description of the arithmetic structure of the orders of subgroups of the symmetric group $S_n$?
status: The problem appears in [Va99] as a problem of Erdős and Turán, and its record at erdosproblems.com/1163 reproduces it verbatim (Erdős references: [Va99,5.74] [Va99]); the intended meaning of the question is itself not entirely settled.
solved_when: A characterization (by statistical means) of which positive integers, or which distributional patterns, arise as orders of subgroups of $S_n$, of the sort the problem envisions, is provided.
why: This is one of Erdős's personally posed problems, stated as a problem of Erdős and Turán, with its full history tracked publicly; resolving it would clarify the multiplicative structure hidden in the subgroup lattice of the symmetric groups.

title: Erdős problem #1208
open: How large a subset with all pairwise distances distinct must every set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ contain? Formally, for $d\geq 2$, estimate $F_d(n)$ — the minimal size of such a "distinct distances" subset guaranteed in every $n$-point set — for fixed $d$ as $n\to\infty$.
status: It is known that $\frac{n^{1/3}}{(\log n)^{1/3}}\ll F_2(n)\ll n^{1/2-c}$ for some constant $c>0$; the lower bound is due to Charalambides [Ch13], the upper bound to Lee, Pohoata, and Zhu [LPZ26]. Thiele [Th95] proved $F_d(n)\gg n^{1/(3d-2)}$ for all $d\geq 3$, improved to $F_d(n)\gg_d n^{1/(3d-3)}(\log n)^{1/3-2/(3d-3)}$ by Conlon, Fox, Gasarch, Harris, Ulrich, and Zbarsky [CFGHUZ15]. The integer lattice shows $F_d(n)\ll n^{1/d}$ for $d\geq 2$; Erdős and Guy [ErGu70] showed the grid problem's answer is at least $n^{2/(3d)-o(1)}$ (and at most $n^{1/d}$), and Lefmann and Thiele [LeTh95] improved this lower bound to $n^{2/(3d)}$. The case $d=1$ is the subject of [530], where Komlós, Sulyok, and Szemerédi [KSS75] proved $F_1(n)\asymp n^{1/2}$. See also [1207]. The behaviour of $F_d(n)$ for fixed $n\geq 3$ as $d\to\infty$ is the subject of [1088].
solved_when: The order of $F_d(n)$ is determined (up to constants) for each fixed $d\geq 2$ as $n\to\infty$; currently the gap is between lower bounds near $n^{1/(3d-3)}$ and the upper bound $n^{1/d}$ from lattice examples.
why: Closing the gap between the known lower and upper bounds determines the true guaranteed size of a distinct-distance subset, resolving one of Erdős's personally posed problems on distinct distances in Euclidean space.
